1A

Kotlin Basics & Null Safety

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: Core Kotlin syntax and the type-system mechanism that eliminates NullPointerExceptions at compile time.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

VAL vs VAR

val  = assign once — PREFER
var  = mutable — use sparingly

NULLABLE TYPES

String   → NEVER null (compiler)
String?  → can be null (handle it)

SAFE OPERATORS

?.      safe call, short-circuits
?:      Elvis: default/throw/return
!!      force-unwrap — AVOID
?.let{} block only if non-null

SMART CAST

if (x != null) {
  x.doSomething()  // non-null
}
// Fails on var fields!

PREFER OVER !!

requireNotNull(x) { "msg" }
checkNotNull(x)   { "msg" }
x ?: return
x ?: throw IllegalStateException()

LATEINIT vs BY LAZY

lateinit var  → var, ref types only
               UninitializedPropertyAccessException
               NOT thread-safe

by lazy       → val only
               computed once, cached
               SYNCHRONIZED by default

Key Gotchas at a Glance

GotchaRule
Smart cast fails on varCapture to local val first
lateinit not thread-safeSynchronize access if concurrent
lazy with NONE not thread-safeOnly use in single-threaded context
Platform types (T!) from JavaAnnotate Java with @Nullable/@NotNull
!! in testsAcceptable. In production: code smell
lazy for mutable valuesUse function or StateFlow instead
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

!! in Production

// ❌ BAD — crashes if userData is null
val name = userData!!.name
// ✅ GOOD — explicit contract with early exit
val name = userData?.name ?: return
// or: assert with a meaningful message
val name = requireNotNull(userData) { "userData must not be null here" }.name

lateinit for Primitives

// ❌ BAD — won't compile: lateinit not allowed on Int
lateinit var count: Int
// ✅ GOOD
var count: Int = 0

Ignoring isInitialized

// ❌ BAD — throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException
fun track() = analytics.track("event")  // may not be initialized yet
// ✅ GOOD
fun track() {
    if (::analytics.isInitialized) analytics.track("event")
}

Mutable State in Compose / Flow

// ❌ BAD — var breaks unidirectional data flow
var userName: String = ""
// ✅ GOOD — val + StateFlow
val userName: StateFlow<String> = _userName.asStateFlow()

lazy on a Value That Changes

// ❌ BAD — lazy caches the first value; token updates not reflected
val token: String by lazy { prefs.getToken() }
// ✅ GOOD — use a function or StateFlow for mutable values
fun getToken(): String = prefs.getToken()

Threading / Lifecycle Traps

  • lateinit is not thread-safe — avoid concurrent access without synchronization.
  • by lazy default (SYNCHRONIZED) uses a lock — correct. Choose NONE only in verified single-threaded contexts.
  • Smart casts fail inside lambdas on var fields — capture to a local val first.

Production Best Practices

  1. Prefer val over var everywhere possible.
  2. Prefer T? with ?. / ?: over !!.
  3. Use requireNotNull() / checkNotNull() to document invariants with a message.
  4. Model optional API fields as T? in domain model — never use sentinel values.
  5. Use by lazy for expensive one-time inits (parsers, formatters, heavy config).
  6. Use lateinit only for DI / lifecycle-bound non-null properties; check isInitialized if any doubt.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the difference between val and var in Kotlin?
val is an immutable reference — assigned once, cannot be reassigned (like Java final). var is mutable — can be reassigned at any time. Neither controls whether the object itself is mutable — a val list can still have items added if it's a MutableList.
B2 — What is the difference between String and String?? How does the compiler enforce it?
Easy▼
String is a non-null type; the compiler guarantees it will never hold null. String? is nullable; the compiler forces you to handle the null case (via ?., ?:, or a null check) before calling any method on it. Assigning null to a String is a compile error.
B3 — What does the Elvis operator ?: do? Give an example.
Easy▼
Returns the left-hand expression if non-null, otherwise evaluates and returns the right-hand expression. Example: val name = user?.name ?: "Guest" — if user is null or user.name is null, name becomes "Guest". The right side can also be a return or throw.

Intermediate

I1 — When would you use lateinit var vs by lazy? What happens if you access lateinit before init?
Medium▼
lateinit var: for non-null var properties that can't be initialized at declaration time (DI injection, lifecycle callbacks). Reference types only. Throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException if accessed before init — check with ::prop.isInitialized.

by lazy: for non-null val properties with an expensive computation that should run once and be cached. Thread-safe by default. Cannot be re-initialized.

They're complementary: lazy requires val, lateinit requires var.
I2 — Why avoid !! in production? What are the better alternatives?
Medium▼
!! bypasses compile-time null safety — if the value is null at runtime, it throws KotlinNullPointerException, defeating the purpose of the type system. Better alternatives:
• requireNotNull(x) { "descriptive message" }
• x ?: return (early exit)
• x ?: throw IllegalStateException("...")
• Restructure so null is impossible at the call site
I3 — Explain smart casts. When does a smart cast fail?
Medium▼
Smart cast is when the compiler automatically promotes a nullable type to non-null after a null check (or is type check), so you don't need explicit casting.

Smart cast fails when the compiler can't guarantee the value hasn't changed between the check and the use:
1. var properties — another thread could reassign them
2. Mutable class members — a custom getter could return a different value each time

Fix: capture to a local val before using.
I4 — Rewrite without any !!: fun getDisplayName(user: User?): String { return user!!.profile!!.displayName!! }
MediumCoding▼
// Option 1: concise safe-call chain
fun getDisplayName(user: User?): String =
    user?.profile?.displayName ?: "Unknown"

// Option 2: early-return pattern (more explicit)
fun getDisplayName(user: User?): String {
    val profile = user?.profile ?: return "Unknown"
    return profile.displayName ?: "Unknown"
}

Senior / Scenario

S1 — What's wrong with this ViewModel code? How do you fix it?
var userSession: UserSession? = null; viewModelScope.launch { userSession = repo.getSession(); dashboard.load(userSession!!.token) }
HardScenario▼
Problems:
1. userSession is a var — the compiler cannot smart-cast it because another coroutine could reassign it between assignment and userSession!!.token
2. !! crashes if getSession() returns null

Fix: capture to a local val — the compiler can smart-cast a local val: 
fun loadDashboard() {
    viewModelScope.launch {
        val session = repository.getSession() ?: run {
            _uiState.value = UiState.Error("No session")
            return@launch
        }
        dashboard.load(session.token)  // session is non-null here
    }
}
S2 — A junior dev maps email: String? in the DTO to domain with userProfile.email = dto.email!!. What's wrong? How do you enforce the right pattern?
Hard▼
Problem: The !! asserts the email is never null from the DTO — a contract violation. The DTO declares it nullable for a reason: the backend may omit it. This will crash in production when the backend returns a user without an email.

Fix: The mapper must be honest about nullability: 
fun UserDto.toDomain() = UserProfile(
    email = email  // String? maps to String? — honest contract
)
If the domain requires a non-null email, that validation belongs in the UseCase as business logic, not in the mapper.
S3 — by lazy is used to init an OkHttpClient in a Repository. App crashes in prod with ConcurrentModificationException inside the initializer. Why? How do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
Why: by lazy default mode is SYNCHRONIZED — it uses a lock to ensure single initialization. The ConcurrentModificationException is not caused by two threads entering the initializer simultaneously (the lock prevents that). More likely: the initializer lambda itself modifies a collection (e.g., adding interceptors) that is concurrently iterated, or OkHttpClient builder internal state is being mutated by another thread.

If the developer changed the mode to LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE for performance, then yes — two threads could enter the initializer simultaneously, causing the exception.

Fix: Revert to SYNCHRONIZED (default) and ensure the initializer lambda is free of concurrent collection mutation. Use Hilt to scope OkHttpClient as a @Singleton instead of using lazy manually.
1B

Kotlin Functions

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: Default & named arguments, vararg, extension functions, infix, higher-order functions, lambdas, function references, and SAM conversions — the full Kotlin function toolkit.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

DEFAULT + NAMED ARGS

fun f(a: Int, b: Int = 0) {}
f(1)            // b = 0
f(a = 1, b = 2) // named, order-free
@JvmOverloads   // needed for Java

VARARG

fun log(vararg msgs: String)
log("a", "b", "c")
val arr = arrayOf("x","y")
log(*arr)  // spread operator

EXTENSION FUNCTIONS

fun Type.name() = ...
// static dispatch
// member ALWAYS beats extension
// can't access private members
// can have nullable receiver: T?.

INFIX

infix fun Int.times(f: ()->Unit)
3 times { doSomething() }
// rules: 1 param, member/extension

HIGHER-ORDER FUNCTIONS

fun exec(block: () -> Unit)
fun map(f: (T) -> R): R
fun make(): () -> Unit  // returns fn
// trailing lambda: exec { ... }
// function type: (A, B) -> C

LAMBDAS + REFS

val f: (Int) -> Int = { it * 2 }
// implicit 'it' for 1 param
// lambda with receiver: T.() -> R
// ref: ::fn, Class::fn, ::Class
list.map(::toDomain)  // concise

SAM CONVERSION

// Java SAM: automatic
executor.execute { doWork() }
// Kotlin SAM: fun interface
fun interface Validator {
  fun validate(v: T): Boolean
}
val v = Validator { it.isNotBlank() }

KEY GOTCHAS

Extension ≠ override
Lambdas allocate (use inline for perf)
Default args ≠ Java overloads
return in lambda = return from HOF
return@label = return from lambda
Capture Activity? → memory leak
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Extension Function Shadowed by Member

class Foo { fun bar() = "member" }
fun Foo.bar() = "extension"  // ❌ never called — member always wins
Foo().bar()  // "member"

Context Leak in Lambda

// ❌ BAD — Activity captured in a long-lived lambda
class MyActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val handler = Handler(Looper.getMainLooper())
    override fun onCreate(...) {
        handler.postDelayed({ updateUI() }, 5000)  // captures Activity
    }
}
// ✅ GOOD — use WeakReference or cancel in onDestroy
private val weakActivity = WeakReference(this)
handler.postDelayed({ weakActivity.get()?.updateUI() }, 5000)

Default Args and Java Interop

// ❌ BAD — Java can't use default args without @JvmOverloads
fun connect(host: String, port: Int = 443) { }
// Java: connect("host", 443) only — no default available
// ✅ GOOD — generates overloaded methods for Java
@JvmOverloads
fun connect(host: String, port: Int = 443) { }

Lambda Allocation in Hot Paths

// ❌ BAD — new lambda object created on every RecyclerView bind
override fun onBindViewHolder(holder: VH, position: Int) {
    holder.itemView.setOnClickListener { onItemClick(position) }  // allocation
}
// ✅ GOOD — pass listener reference; set once in onCreateViewHolder
override fun onCreateViewHolder(parent: ViewGroup, viewType: Int): VH {
    val holder = VH(inflate(parent))
    holder.itemView.setOnClickListener { onItemClick(holder.bindingAdapterPosition) }
    return holder
}

Overusing Extension Functions

// ❌ BAD — business logic in an extension on a primitive
fun String.isValidBankAccountNumber(): Boolean = matches(Regex("^[0-9]{9,18}$"))
// Business rule leaks into a generic utility layer
// ✅ GOOD — keep in domain validator / use case
class AccountNumberValidator {
    fun isValid(accountNumber: String): Boolean = accountNumber.matches(Regex("^[0-9]{9,18}$"))
}

Production Best Practices

  1. Use default + named args instead of Builder pattern for data config objects.
  2. Put extension functions in a dedicated file matching the extended type (ViewExtensions.kt, StringExtensions.kt).
  3. Prefer function references over lambdas in mapper chains — they're compiler-verified.
  4. Use inline for higher-order functions called in performance-sensitive code (see 1I).
  5. Never capture long-lived references (Activity, Fragment) in lambdas stored beyond their lifecycle.
  6. Add @JvmOverloads on functions with defaults when the module is consumed by Java code.
  7. Keep extension functions stateless and pure — no side effects, no dependencies on external state.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What are named arguments? Why are they useful?
Named arguments let you specify parameters by name at the call site, making the order irrelevant. They're useful when a function has many parameters (especially booleans), making the call self-documenting. Example: createRequest(url = "...", timeout = 60) — the reader immediately knows what each value is without checking the function signature.
B2 — What is an extension function? What can it NOT do?
Easy▼
An extension function lets you add a new function to an existing class without modifying or inheriting from it. It's called with dot notation as if it's a member. What it CANNOT do: (1) access private/protected members — it only sees the public API; (2) override existing member functions — member always takes precedence on same signature; (3) modify the class's state in any privileged way.
B3 — What is a SAM conversion?
Easy▼
SAM (Single Abstract Method) conversion allows a Kotlin lambda to be used wherever a Java interface with a single abstract method is expected. Kotlin automatically wraps the lambda in an anonymous class implementing the interface. Example: setOnClickListener { handleClick() } — the lambda is converted to View.OnClickListener automatically. For Kotlin interfaces, use fun interface to enable the same behavior.

Intermediate

I1 — What is the difference between a higher-order function and a regular function? Give a real Android example.
Medium▼
A higher-order function either takes a function as a parameter, returns a function, or both. A regular function only works with data. Real Android example: safeApiCall { api.getUser(id) } — the lambda is the network call. The wrapper function owns error handling, dispatcher, and Result wrapping. This is the Strategy pattern without an interface — the behaviour is injected as a value.
I2 — What is the difference between a function reference and a lambda? When would you use each?
Medium▼
They're equivalent at runtime. A function reference (::fn or Class::fn) refers to an existing named function. A lambda is an inline anonymous function. Use function reference when: (1) a named function already exists that does exactly what you need — .map(::toDomain); (2) it's more readable. Use a lambda when: you need to write the logic inline, or there are transformations the existing function doesn't cover.
I3 — What is a "lambda with receiver" and where is it used in Android?
Medium▼
A lambda with receiver is a lambda where this inside the block refers to the receiver object rather than the outer class. Type: T.() -> R. Used in: (1) Kotlin scope functions — apply { }, run { }, with { }; (2) DSL builders — e.g., buildString { append("...") }; (3) Jetpack Compose implicit receiver lambdas. This is what makes apply { visibility = VISIBLE } work — inside the lambda, this is the View.
I4 — (Coding) Rewrite using an extension function and function reference: list.map { it.name.trim().lowercase() }
MediumCoding▼
// Extension on User
fun User.normalizedName(): String = name.trim().lowercase()

// Usage with function reference
list.map(User::normalizedName)

// Or top-level extension + reference
fun normalizedName(user: User) = user.name.trim().lowercase()
list.map(::normalizedName)

Senior / Scenario

S1 — (Scenario) A junior dev wrote 6 overloaded fetchProducts() methods to support optional filters. You're reviewing the PR. How do you refactor?
HardScenario▼
Consolidate into one function with default arguments. Identify all the varying parameters across the 6 overloads and make each one a named parameter with a sensible default: 
// Before: 6 overloaded methods

// After: 1 function, default args
suspend fun fetchProducts(
    category: String? = null,
    minPrice: Double? = null,
    maxPrice: Double? = null,
    inStockOnly: Boolean = false,
    sortBy: SortOrder = SortOrder.DEFAULT,
    page: Int = 1
): Result<List<Product>>
If the module is also consumed by Java code, add @JvmOverloads. If the filter combinations grow to a large data class, consider a ProductFilter data class as a single parameter — but that's only warranted at high complexity.
S2 — Extension functions vs utility class: which do you prefer and why? What's the trade-off?
Hard▼
Prefer extension functions in Kotlin — they're idiomatic, discoverable via IDE autocomplete on the type, and don't require an instance of a utility class. Trade-offs: Extensions: statically dispatched (no polymorphism), can't access private members, may scatter logic across files if not organized. Utility class: testable as a unit (can be mocked/injected), centralizes logic, needed when logic requires injected dependencies. Rule: pure transformations (formatting, parsing, mapping) → extension. Logic with dependencies (business validation, formatting with locale from DI) → use case or injected service.
S3 — (Debug) A ViewModel function captures this (the ViewModel) in a lambda passed to a repository. The repository stores the lambda. What's the risk? How do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
Risk: The repository is typically a singleton (Hilt @Singleton). It now holds a reference to the ViewModel through the stored lambda. When the user navigates away and the ViewModel is supposed to be destroyed, the repository's reference keeps it alive → memory leak. The ViewModel holds a reference to Compose state or Fragment context → entire screen kept in memory.

Fix: (1) Don't store lambdas that capture ViewModel state in longer-lived components. (2) Use a callback interface that can be set to null in onCleared(). (3) Better: use Flow — the repository emits data via Flow; the ViewModel collects it. No lambda stored, lifecycle handled by viewModelScope.
1C

Kotlin Scope Functions

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: let, run, with, apply, also — when to use each, how they differ, and why picking the wrong one is a common interview trap.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet
FunctionRefReturnsMnemonicTypical use
letitLambda result"Let me transform it"Null-safe block, transform, temp scope
runthisLambda result"Run a computation on this"Compute result using object's members
withthisLambda result"Work with this object"Group operations — non-extension
applythisObject"Apply config to this, return it"Object initialization / builder
alsoitObject"Also do this side effect"Logging, debugging in chains

NULL-SAFE PATTERN

token?.let { t ->
  "Bearer $t"   // returns String?
}

// vs run (also null-safe):
token?.run { "Bearer $this" }

BUILDER PATTERN

Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java)
  .apply {
    putExtra("id", id)
    addFlags(FLAG_SINGLE_TOP)
  }  // returns the Intent

SIDE EFFECT IN CHAIN

api.getUser()
  .also { Timber.d("$it") }  // logs
  .also { cache.save(it) }   // caches
  .toDomain()                // transforms

VIEWBINDING GROUP

with(binding) {
  tvName.text = user.name
  tvEmail.text = user.email
  btnSave.isEnabled = true
}

KEY GOTCHAS

apply returns object → don't use for result
also returns object → don't use for transform
with(null) → NPE → use ?.let or ?.run
return in lambda = non-local return!
use return@let to exit lambda only
max 2 nesting levels → else extract fn

DECISION SHORTCUT

Need the object back?
  → apply (this) or also (it)

Need a result?
  → let (it) or run (this) or with(obj)

Null-safe block?
  → ?.let { } or ?.run { }
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Wrong scope function — apply vs let confusion

// ❌ BAD — apply returns the object, not the block result
val isValid = user.apply {
    name = name.trim()
    name.isNotBlank()   // this result is DISCARDED — apply returns 'user'
}  // isValid is a User, not Boolean!
// ✅ GOOD — run returns the lambda result
val isValid = user.run {
    name = name.trim()
    name.isNotBlank()   // returned as Boolean
}

also vs let confusion

// ❌ BAD — also returns original object, not transform result
val header: String = token.also { "Bearer $it" }
// header == token (original String), NOT "Bearer token"
// ✅ GOOD — let returns the lambda result
val header: String = token.let { "Bearer $it" }
// header == "Bearer token"

Deep nesting — unreadable

// ❌ BAD — nested scope functions kill readability
val result = user?.let { u ->
    u.session?.run {
        token.let { t ->
            buildHeader(t)
        }
    }
}
// ✅ GOOD — extract to a named function
fun buildAuthHeader(user: User?): String? {
    val token = user?.session?.token ?: return null
    return buildHeader(token)
}

using with on nullable

// ❌ BAD — with() doesn't handle null
with(user) { tvName.text = name }  // NPE if user is null
// ✅ GOOD — use let for nullable
user?.let { with(it) { tvName.text = name } }
// or simpler:
user?.run { tvName.text = name }

return inside scope function

// ❌ BAD — non-local return inside non-inline lambda surprises
fun process(user: User?) {
    user?.let {
        if (it.isBlocked) return  // returns from 'process', not just let!
        doSomething(it)
    }
}
// ✅ GOOD — use labeled return to exit the lambda only
user?.let {
    if (it.isBlocked) return@let
    doSomething(it)
}

Production Best Practices

  1. apply for object initialization/configuration — returns the object.
  2. let for null-safety blocks and transforms — use a named param instead of it when nesting.
  3. also strictly for side effects (logging, analytics) — never for transforms.
  4. run when you need the object's members as this and want a computed result back.
  5. with when you have a non-null object and need to group member accesses without a return value.
  6. Never nest scope functions more than 2 levels — extract a named function.
  7. Name the it parameter explicitly when there are nested lambdas or when the type isn't obvious from context.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — Name the five scope functions and the two axes that distinguish them.
The five are: let, run, with, apply, also.

Axis 1 — Object reference inside the block: this (apply, run, with) vs it (let, also).
Axis 2 — Return value: returns the object itself (apply, also) vs returns the lambda result (let, run, with).
B2 — What does apply return? Give a real Android example.
Easy▼
apply returns the original object (the receiver). Classic use: configuring an Intent or Bundle at creation: 
val intent = Intent(this, DetailActivity::class.java).apply {
    putExtra("id", productId)
    addFlags(Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP)
}
B3 — What is the primary difference between also and let?
Easy▼
Both use it as the object reference. The difference is the return value. also returns the original object — used for side effects (logging, analytics) that shouldn't change what's being chained. let returns the result of the last expression — used for transformations and null-safe execution blocks.

Intermediate

I1 — What is the difference between run and with? When would you pick one over the other?
Medium▼
Both use this as the object reference and return the lambda result. The difference is syntax: run is an extension function called on the object (obj.run { }), while with is a regular function that takes the object as an argument (with(obj) { }).

Pick run when: you want to chain it onto an expression, or combine with a safe call (obj?.run { }).
Pick with when: the object is already assigned to a variable and you want to group a series of operations without needing a return value — e.g., setting multiple ViewBinding properties.
I2 — (Coding) What does this code print? val x = "hello".also { it.uppercase() }; println(x)
MediumCoding▼
Prints "hello". also returns the original receiver, not the result of the lambda. The it.uppercase() expression inside the block is evaluated but its result is discarded. To get "HELLO", you'd use let: val x = "hello".let { it.uppercase() } → prints "HELLO".
I3 — What happens when you use a bare return inside a let block? How do you fix it?
Medium▼
A bare return inside a lambda performs a non-local return — it exits the enclosing named function entirely, not just the let block. This can cause hard-to-find bugs where a function returns early unexpectedly.

Fix: use a labeled return to exit only the lambda: 
user?.let {
    if (it.isBlocked) return@let  // exits let block only
    processUser(it)
}
Note: non-local returns are only possible in lambdas passed to inline functions. Since scope functions are inline, this behavior applies to all five.
I4 — (Coding) Refactor: val b = Bundle(); b.putString("k","v"); b.putInt("n",1); startActivity(Intent(this, X::class.java).also { it.putExtras(b) })
MediumCoding▼
startActivity(
    Intent(this, X::class.java).apply {
        putExtra("k", "v")   // apply: this = Intent, configure it
        putExtra("n", 1)
    }
)
apply is the right choice — we're configuring the Intent at creation and returning it. The separate Bundle is unnecessary here since Intent has putExtra directly.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Code review: a colleague used apply to validate a form and assigned the result to a Boolean. What's the bug? Rewrite it.
HardScenario▼
// ❌ Bug: apply returns the object (FormState), not Boolean
val isValid: Boolean = formState.apply {
    amount > 0 && account.isNotBlank()  // result discarded!
}  // compile error: FormState cannot be assigned to Boolean
// ✅ Fix: use run — returns lambda result
val isValid: Boolean = formState.run {
    amount > 0 && account.isNotBlank()
}
This would actually be a compile error (type mismatch) rather than a silent bug — but it's still a sign the developer confused the two functions.
S2 — When would you NOT use a scope function and write an explicit local variable instead?
Hard▼
Use an explicit local variable when:
  1. The block logic exceeds 5–6 lines — at that point, extract a named function; scope functions should be concise.
  2. Nesting would exceed 2 levels — nested scope functions are harder to read and debug.
  3. The variable needs to be reused in multiple places in the same scope — a named variable is more readable and debuggable (you can set a breakpoint on it).
  4. Code review feedback: if the team isn't familiar with scope functions, an explicit variable is clearer in a shared codebase.
  5. Debugging complex state bugs — the explicit variable shows up in the debugger with its name; a scope function's intermediate value may be harder to inspect.
S3 — (Scenario) A junior dev complains: "I used ?.let but the block sometimes still gets a NullPointerException on it.address.city." What's happening?
HardScenario▼
?.let only guarantees that the direct receiver (user) is non-null inside the block. It does not guarantee that nested properties (user.address, user.address.city) are non-null. it is non-null, but it.address might be null if address: Address? in the model.

Fix: chain the safe calls inside the block, or use nested ?.let: 
user?.let { u ->
    val city = u.address?.city ?: "Unknown"
    showCity(city)
}
The broader lesson: ?.let handles one level of nullability — the receiver. Model your domain properly with T? at every level and chain safe calls as needed.
1D

Kotlin OOP

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: Classes, constructors, init, inheritance, interfaces, abstract classes, visibility modifiers, and open/final/abstract — how Kotlin's OOP differs from Java and why it matters for Android architecture.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

CLASS DEFAULTS

class Foo      // final, public
open class Foo // extensible
abstract class Foo // no instantiate
// Members also final by default
open fun bar() // can override
final fun baz() // cannot override

CONSTRUCTORS

class Foo(val x: Int) // primary
// init runs after primary
init { require(x > 0) }
// secondary must delegate
constructor(s: String) : this(s.toInt())
// prefer default args over secondary

INTERFACE vs ABSTRACT

Interface:
  - no constructor, no backing fields
  - multiple implementations
  - mockable / fake-able
  - default methods OK

Abstract class:
  - has constructor + state
  - single inheritance
  - template method pattern

VISIBILITY

public    → everywhere (default)
internal  → same Gradle module
protected → class + subclasses
private   → class only (or file)
// No package-private in Kotlin
// Use internal for module encap

ANDROID PATTERNS

interface UserRepository   // contract
internal class UserRepositoryImpl // hidden
open class BaseViewModel          // extensible
abstract class BaseUseCase  // template
@HiltViewModel class PayVM       // final+DI

KEY GOTCHAS

final-by-default → add open to allow mock
internal → same module, not same package
init order = declaration order
interface property = no backing field
2 interfaces same default → must override
composition > deep inheritance
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Forgetting open on a class that needs to be subclassed

// ❌ BAD — Hilt proxy / Mockito subclassing will fail at runtime
class BaseViewModel : ViewModel()  // final — cannot mock or proxy
// ✅ GOOD
open class BaseViewModel : ViewModel()

Leaking implementation through public visibility

// ❌ BAD — implementation class is public; other modules can depend on it directly
class UserRepositoryImpl : UserRepository { ... }  // public by default
// ✅ GOOD — internal hides it from other modules; only Hilt module sees it
internal class UserRepositoryImpl : UserRepository { ... }

init block ordering trap

class Foo(val x: Int) {
    val doubled = x * 2   // ✅ property initializers run top-to-bottom

    init {
        // ❌ BAD: if 'tripled' is declared AFTER this init block,
        // accessing it here throws UninitializedPropertyAccessException
        println(tripled)
    }

    val tripled = x * 3   // declared AFTER init — not yet initialized when init runs
}

Property initializers and init blocks run in declaration order. Never access a property in an init block that is declared after it.

Abstract class vs interface — wrong choice

// ❌ BAD — abstract class used as a pure contract (no state, no constructors)
abstract class UserRepository {
    abstract suspend fun getUser(id: String): User
}
// ✅ GOOD — interface is the right tool for a pure contract
interface UserRepository {
    suspend fun getUser(id: String): User
}
// Benefit: implementation can implement multiple interfaces; can be mocked

Production Best Practices

  1. Classes are final by default — only add open when inheritance is deliberately designed and documented.
  2. Keep implementation classes internal in multi-module apps — expose only interfaces across module boundaries.
  3. Prefer interfaces for cross-layer contracts (Repository, Service); abstract classes for shared state (BaseViewModel).
  4. Use protected for base class helpers intended only for subclasses — don't make them public.
  5. Prefer constructor injection — Hilt's @Inject constructor documents all dependencies explicitly.
  6. Declare properties before the init block that needs them — or initialize them in the init block itself.
  7. Prefer composition over inheritance beyond 1–2 levels deep.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the default visibility of a Kotlin class and its members? How does it differ from Java?
In Kotlin, the default visibility is public (unlike Java where it's package-private). However, classes in Kotlin are final by default (unlike Java where they're open/extensible). To allow subclassing in Kotlin you must mark the class open. Java requires final to prohibit subclassing — the opposite approach.
B2 — What is the init block? When does it run?
Easy▼
The init block is a body of code that runs as part of the primary constructor, immediately after property initializers. Multiple init blocks are allowed — they run in top-to-bottom declaration order, interleaved with property initializers. Use it for validation (require()), complex initialization that can't be expressed in a single expression, or initialization that depends on constructor parameters.
B3 — What is the difference between interface and abstract class in Kotlin?
Easy▼
Interface: no constructors, no backing fields (only abstract getters), can have default method implementations, a class can implement multiple interfaces.

Abstract class: can have constructors, backing fields (actual state), both abstract and concrete methods. A class can only extend one abstract class.

Use interface for pure contracts (testability, DI); use abstract class when shared state or constructor parameters are needed.

Intermediate

I1 — What does internal mean? How is it different from private? Give an Android multi-module example.
Medium▼
internal means visible within the same Gradle module. private on a class member means visible only within that class; on a top-level declaration it means visible only within that file.

Multi-module example: In :data module, UserRepositoryImpl is marked internal. The :feature-profile module cannot reference it directly even though it depends on :data. It can only use the public interface UserRepository. Hilt's module in :data (which is in the same module as the impl) binds the interface to the implementation.
I2 — (Coding) What is wrong with this code and how do you fix it?
MediumCoding▼
class Config(val env: String) {
    init {
        println(label)   // ❌ — 'label' declared AFTER this init block
    }
    val label = "$env config"
}
Problem: Property initializers and init blocks run in declaration order. label is declared after the init block, so when init runs, label has not been initialized yet → UninitializedPropertyAccessException at runtime.

Fix: Move label before the init block, or access it in a later init block: 
class Config(val env: String) {
    val label = "$env config"  // declared first
    init { println(label) }    // ✅ now initialized
}
I3 — Can a Kotlin class implement two interfaces that both define a default implementation for the same method? What happens?
Medium▼
Yes, a class can implement two such interfaces, but if both provide a default implementation for the same method, the implementing class must override that method — otherwise it's a compile error. Inside the override, you can delegate to either interface's default with super<InterfaceName>.method(): 
interface A { fun greet() = println("Hello from A") }
interface B { fun greet() = println("Hello from B") }
class C : A, B {
    override fun greet() { super<A>.greet() }  // must disambiguate
}
I4 — When would you use a secondary constructor vs default arguments in Kotlin?
Medium▼
Almost always prefer default arguments — they're more concise, idiomatic, and work with named arguments. Secondary constructors should be used when: (1) the class needs completely different initialization paths that can't be captured by defaults (e.g., constructing from a JSON string vs individual fields); (2) interoperability with Java requires overloaded constructors (@JvmOverloads is the cleaner alternative); (3) you're subclassing a Java class with multiple constructors and need to delegate to different parent constructors.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — (Scenario) A teammate made UserRepositoryImpl public. What are the risks? How do you enforce the right pattern?
HardScenario▼
Risks: (1) Feature modules can depend directly on the implementation — violating DIP. If the implementation changes (e.g., adding a constructor parameter), every direct user breaks. (2) Tests may use the concrete class instead of the interface, making them harder to fake. (3) The implementation's internal details (caching, retries) are now part of the "public API" — any refactor becomes a breaking change.

Fix: Mark UserRepositoryImpl as internal. The Hilt module that binds it is in the same module so it still works. Add a lint rule or ArchUnit test to prevent cross-module direct usage of impl classes. In code review, flag any import of an Impl class in a feature module.
S2 — Design a BaseUseCase abstract class that wraps all use cases in a Result with correct CancellationException handling.
HardCoding▼
abstract class BaseUseCase<in P, out R> {
    // Subclasses implement this — business logic only
    protected abstract suspend fun execute(params: P): R

    // Callers use invoke() — gets error handling for free
    suspend operator fun invoke(params: P): Result<R> = try {
        Result.success(execute(params))
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e  // CRITICAL: never swallow coroutine cancellation
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        Result.failure(e)
    }
}

// Usage:
class GetUserUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository
) : BaseUseCase<String, User>() {
    override suspend fun execute(params: String) = repo.getUser(params)
}
Key point: CancellationException must be rethrown — swallowing it breaks coroutine cancellation throughout the scope.
S3 — When would you choose composition over inheritance for a ViewModel scenario? Give a concrete example.
HardScenario▼
Scenario: You have BaseViewModel with error handling, and now you need two orthogonal concerns: pagination logic and analytics tracking. You could add both to the base class or create a deep hierarchy — but that couples all ViewModels to pagination and analytics whether they need it or not.

Composition approach: 
// Each concern is a separate class injected via constructor
class PaginationController(private val pageSize: Int = 20) {
    fun nextPage() = ...
}

class AnalyticsDelegate @Inject constructor(private val tracker: Tracker) {
    fun trackScreen(name: String) = tracker.track(name)
}

@HiltViewModel
class ProductListViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val pagination: PaginationController,  // composed
    private val analytics: AnalyticsDelegate        // composed
) : ViewModel() { ... }
This is testable (mock each dependency independently), avoids a bloated base class, and each concern is independently reusable. Kotlin's by delegation can make this even cleaner by auto-delegating interface calls.
1E

Kotlin Special Classes

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: data classes, enum classes, sealed classes & interfaces, object declarations, companion objects, anonymous objects — the Kotlin class variants that power Android architecture daily.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

DATA CLASS

Auto: equals/hashCode/toString
      copy() / componentN()
Only primary constructor params
All params → val (avoid var!)
Body props excluded from equals
Can't be open/abstract/sealed

ENUM CLASS

Fixed set of named instances
Properties: name, ordinal (0-based)
entries (1.9+) replaces values()
Can have constructor params + fns
Store code field, NOT ordinal in DB
Use when: fixed constants

SEALED CLASS / INTERFACE

Closed hierarchy → exhaustive when
sealed class  → shared state OK
sealed interface → multi-interface OK
data object  → no-data subtypes (1.9+)
NEVER use else on sealed when
Prefer sealed interface in new code

OBJECT / COMPANION

object Foo { }  // singleton
companion object { }  // tied to class
// Both: not truly static JVM
// Add @JvmStatic for Java interop
// object = hard to test → use Hilt
// companion = factory + constants

ANONYMOUS OBJECT

val x = object : SomeInterface {
  override fun method() { }
}
// One-off, local scope
// Captures outer this → leak risk
// For SAM → use lambda instead

KEY GOTCHAS

data class var → breaks hashSet
body props excluded from copy/equals
enum ordinal → fragile for DB/API
object singleton → untestable
else on sealed when → misses new types
data object toString = "Loading"
plain object toString = "Foo@abc123"
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

data class with var — breaks equals/hashCode contract

// ❌ BAD — mutable data class breaks structural equality guarantees
data class CartItem(var quantity: Int, val productId: String)
val item = CartItem(1, "p1")
val set = hashSetOf(item)
item.quantity = 2    // mutates! hashCode changes → item "lost" in the set
println(item in set)  // false! bucket changed
// ✅ GOOD — all val; use copy() for updates
data class CartItem(val quantity: Int, val productId: String)
val updated = item.copy(quantity = 2)   // new object

Body property included in equals — invisible bug

// ❌ BAD — 'displayName' is in the body; NOT compared in equals()
data class Product(val id: String) {
    var displayName: String = ""   // body property — ignored by equals/hashCode
}
val a = Product("1").apply { displayName = "Phone" }
val b = Product("1").apply { displayName = "Laptop" }
println(a == b)  // true! displayName not in equals
// ✅ GOOD — all meaningful fields in primary constructor
data class Product(val id: String, val displayName: String)

sealed class when without else — missing new subtype

// ❌ BAD — using else loses the compile-time exhaustiveness guarantee
when (state) {
    is UiState.Loading -> showLoading()
    is UiState.Success -> showData()
    else -> showError()  // silently swallows new subtypes added later
}
// ✅ GOOD — no else; adding a new sealed subtype causes compile error here
when (state) {
    is UiState.Loading -> showLoading()
    is UiState.Success -> showData()
    is UiState.Error   -> showError()
}

object singleton vs Hilt — testability trap

// ❌ BAD — singleton object impossible to replace in tests
object AnalyticsManager {
    fun track(event: String) { /* sends to Firebase */ }
}
// In tests: can't inject a no-op; real events fire
// ✅ GOOD — interface + Hilt @Singleton
interface Analytics { fun track(event: String) }
class FirebaseAnalytics @Inject constructor() : Analytics { ... }
// Test: inject FakeAnalytics that does nothing

enum ordinal as persisted value — fragile

// ❌ BAD — storing ordinal in DB; reordering enum breaks all stored data
dao.insert(order.copy(statusCode = status.ordinal))

// ✅ GOOD — store name or a stable Int field
enum class OrderStatus(val code: Int) {
    PLACED(1), SHIPPED(2), DELIVERED(3), CANCELLED(4)
}
dao.insert(order.copy(statusCode = status.code))  // stable

Production Best Practices

  1. All data class primary constructor properties should be val — use copy() for updates.
  2. Use sealed interface over sealed class when subtypes need no shared state — more flexible.
  3. Never use else in a when on a sealed type — defeats the exhaustiveness guarantee.
  4. Use data object (Kotlin 1.9+) for no-data sealed subtypes — correct toString() and equality.
  5. Use enum class for fixed constants; use a stable explicit code: Int field if persisting to DB.
  6. Keep companion object lean — factory methods and constants only, not utility functions.
  7. Prefer Hilt @Singleton over raw object for anything that needs to be replaced in tests.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What does a data class auto-generate? What is NOT included in equals/hashCode?
Auto-generated: equals(), hashCode(), toString(), copy(), and componentN() functions for destructuring — all based on properties declared in the primary constructor only.

NOT included: properties declared in the class body (outside the primary constructor). This is a common source of bugs — if you add a var property in the body, two instances with different body-property values will still be considered equal if their constructor properties match.
B2 — What is a sealed class? How does it enable exhaustive when?
Easy▼
A sealed class defines a closed type hierarchy — all direct subclasses must be in the same compilation unit (package in Kotlin 1.5+). Because the compiler knows every possible subtype at compile time, a when expression on a sealed type can be exhaustive without an else branch. If you add a new subtype later, every when expression that doesn't handle it becomes a compile error — preventing silent bugs.
B3 — What is the difference between object and companion object?
Easy▼
object is a standalone singleton class declaration — it exists independently. companion object lives inside another class and its members are accessed via the enclosing class name (like Java static members, but not truly static in JVM bytecode). Only one companion object per class is allowed. Add @JvmStatic to companion members for actual Java static interop. Common use: companion object { fun newInstance() } for Fragment factories.

Intermediate

I1 — When would you use a sealed class vs an enum class?
Medium▼
Enum: fixed set of named constants where all instances share the same data shape. Good for: PaymentStatus, Theme, NetworkType. Each enum value is a singleton.

Sealed class: fixed set of subtypes where each subtype can carry different data. Good for: UiState (Loading has no data, Success has a list, Error has a message), Result, navigation events. Each subtype can have its own constructor and multiple instances.

Rule: if the variants have the same fields → enum. If each variant needs different data → sealed.
I2 — (Coding) What is wrong? data class User(val id: String) { var name = "" }; val a = User("1").apply { name = "Alice" }; val b = User("1").apply { name = "Bob" }; println(a == b)
MediumCoding▼
Prints true — which is likely NOT what the developer intended.

name is declared in the class body, not the primary constructor. Data class equals() and hashCode() are generated only from primary constructor properties (id here). So two User objects with the same id but different name values are considered equal.

Fix: move name to the primary constructor: data class User(val id: String, val name: String)
I3 — What is data object? Why is it better than plain object for sealed subtypes?
Medium▼
data object (Kotlin 1.9+) is a singleton with auto-generated equals(), hashCode(), and toString() — like a data class with no properties.

Why better for sealed subtypes: a plain object's toString() returns the JVM identity string like "UiState$Loading@1a2b3c" — useless for logging and debugging. A data object's toString() returns "Loading" — much cleaner. Also, equals() works correctly (two references to the same singleton are equal), though for objects this is true anyway since there's only one instance.
I4 — Why should you never use else in a when expression on a sealed type?
Medium▼
Using else defeats the compile-time exhaustiveness guarantee. If you add a new subtype to the sealed hierarchy later, the when with else will silently handle it with the else branch — the compiler won't warn you. You could be rendering the wrong UI for a new state for weeks without realizing.

Without else, adding a new sealed subtype causes a compile error at every when expression that doesn't handle it. This is intentional — it forces you to explicitly handle every state, making the system fail fast at compile time rather than silently at runtime.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Design a complete UiState and ViewEvent sealed hierarchy for a payment screen. Justify your choices.
HardCoding▼
// State — flows in StateFlow, represents current screen state
sealed interface PaymentUiState {
    data object Idle       : PaymentUiState
    data object Loading    : PaymentUiState
    data class  Success(val transactionId: String) : PaymentUiState
    data class  Error(val message: String, val retryable: Boolean) : PaymentUiState
}

// Events — one-time side effects in SharedFlow(replay=0)
sealed interface PaymentEvent {
    data class  NavigateToReceipt(val txId: String) : PaymentEvent
    data class  ShowSnackbar(val msg: String) : PaymentEvent
    data object NavigateBack : PaymentEvent
}
Justifications: sealed interface (not class) — no shared state; subtypes can implement other interfaces. data object for Idle/Loading — no data, but clean toString(). data class for Success/Error — each has different fields. Events separate from state — state is persistent (StateFlow), events fire once (SharedFlow replay=0) to prevent re-delivery on recomposition.
S2 — (Scenario) A junior dev stored PaymentStatus.ordinal in the Room database. Three months later, the team added a new status between PROCESSING and SUCCESS. What broke and how do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
What broke: ordinal is the zero-based position in the enum declaration. Adding a new status shifted all ordinals after it by 1. Every row in the DB that had ordinal 2 (SUCCESS) is now interpreted as the new status. Orders that were previously marked SUCCESS are now read back as the wrong status — silent data corruption.

Fix: Add a stable code: Int field to the enum that never changes regardless of declaration order: 
enum class PaymentStatus(val code: Int) {
    PENDING(1), PROCESSING(2), UNDER_REVIEW(5), SUCCESS(3), FAILED(4)
}
Write a Room migration to convert stored ordinal values to the new stable codes. Going forward, always persist status.code, not status.ordinal. Add a Room TypeConverter that converts by code.
S3 — (Scenario) copy() on a data class gives you a "deep copy" — true or false? What are the implications in an Android app?
HardScenario▼
False. copy() performs a shallow copy — only the top-level object is a new instance. Any nested objects (lists, other data classes) are shared references.

Implications: 
data class Cart(val items: MutableList<Item>)
val cart1 = Cart(mutableListOf(Item("A")))
val cart2 = cart1.copy()
cart2.items.add(Item("B"))   // MUTATES cart1.items too!
Fix: use immutable collections (List not MutableList) in data classes. If you need a deep copy, manually create new instances. In StateFlow with Compose, sharing mutable lists between states causes incorrect recomposition — Compose compares by reference for stability. Always use immutable List<T> in your UI state data classes.
1F

Generics & Variance

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: Generics, in / out variance annotations, covariance, contravariance — the type-system mechanics behind Flow, StateFlow, Result, and Clean Architecture generics.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

VARIANCE AT A GLANCE

Invariant (default):
  MutableList<Dog> ≠ MutableList<Animal>

out T (covariant = producer):
  List<Dog> IS-A List<Animal>
  Flow<Dog> IS-A Flow<Animal>
  T only in OUT positions (return/val)

in T (contravariant = consumer):
  Comparator<Animal> IS-A Comparator<Dog>
  T only in IN positions (params)

ANDROID EXAMPLES

Flow<out T>       → covariant
StateFlow<out T>  → covariant (subtype of Flow)
List<out T>       → covariant (read-only)
MutableList<T>    → invariant
Comparator<in T>  → contravariant
UiState<out T>    → covariant (design pattern)
BaseUseCase<in P, out R>

NOTHING + COVARIANCE

Nothing = bottom type = subtype of all
// With sealed class UiState<out T>:
data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>()
// Assignable to UiState<List<User>> ✅
// Because Nothing IS-A List<User>
// and UiState is covariant

TYPE BOUNDS

fun <T : Comparable<T>> max(a: T, b: T): T
// multiple bounds:
fun <T> f(x: T) where T : A, T : B

// Star projection:
fun print(list: List<*>)
// = List<out Any?> — read-only unknown

GOTCHAS

out T: var property ❌ (in-position)
out T: val property ✅
in T: return type ❌ (out-position)
in T: fun param ✅
Type erasure: List<Dog> == List<Cat> at runtime
Use reified inline for runtime type checks

JAVA COMPARISON

Java use-site:
  List<? extends Animal> = out Animal
  List<? super Dog>       = in Dog

Kotlin declaration-site (cleaner):
  class Box<out T>  // annotated once
  // no per-call-site repetition
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

out T with mutable state — type safety violation attempt

// ❌ Won't compile — correctly rejected by the compiler
class BadBox<out T>(var value: T) // ❌ var exposes T in in-position (setter)

// ✅ GOOD — val only for covariant types
class Box<out T>(val value: T)   // ✅ read-only property

Forgetting Nothing for no-data sealed subtypes

// ❌ BAD — UiState.Loading has type param UiState<Unit> — awkward
sealed class UiState<out T> {
    object Loading : UiState<Unit>()   // Unit — leaks into type signature
}
val s: UiState<List<User>> = UiState.Loading  // ❌ won't compile
// ✅ GOOD — Nothing is subtype of every type; works with covariant out T
data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>()
val s: UiState<List<User>> = UiState.Loading  // ✅

Type erasure at runtime

// ❌ BAD — generic type erased at runtime
fun <T> isListOf(list: List<*>): Boolean = list is List<T>  // ❌ unchecked cast warning

// ✅ GOOD — use reified with inline (covered in 1I)
inline fun <reified T> isListOf(list: List<*>): Boolean =
    list.all { it is T }

Production Best Practices

  1. Use out T for read-only wrappers: UiState<out T>, ApiResult<out T>, Resource<out T>.
  2. Use Nothing as type arg for no-data sealed subtypes — allows assignment to any covariant generic.
  3. Expose StateFlow as StateFlow (not Flow) in ViewModels — provides .value access; covariance means it's still assignable to Flow when needed.
  4. Don't over-annotate — most application-level classes are invariant and that's fine.
  5. Use where T : SomeInterface for multiple type bounds instead of complex inheritance.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What does it mean for a generic type to be invariant? Give an Android example.
Invariant means no subtype relationship exists between generic types even if their type arguments have a subtype relationship. MutableList<Dog> is NOT a subtype of MutableList<Animal>, even though Dog extends Animal. This prevents type-unsafe mutations: if it were allowed, you could add a Cat to a list that was expected to contain only Dogs. Android example: MutableStateFlow<UiState> — invariant because it supports both reads and writes.
B2 — What does out T mean? Give a real Kotlin/Android example.
Easy▼
out T declares covariance — T appears only in output positions (return types, val properties). This means if Dog is a subtype of Animal, then Producer<Dog> is a subtype of Producer<Animal>.

Real example: Flow<out T> in Kotlin coroutines. Because Flow is covariant, StateFlow<Dog> (which extends Flow<Dog>) can be assigned to a Flow<Animal> variable. Also: List<out T> is covariant because it's read-only — no add() method takes T as a parameter.
B3 — What is Nothing and why is it used with covariant sealed classes?
Easy▼
Nothing is Kotlin's bottom type — a subtype of every type. No instance of Nothing can be created. Because of covariance: if Nothing is a subtype of T, and UiState is covariant (out T), then UiState<Nothing> is a subtype of UiState<T> for ANY T. This means data object Loading : UiState<Nothing> is assignable to UiState<List<Transaction>>, UiState<UserProfile>, etc. — one Loading object works for all generic types.

Intermediate

I1 — Why is List covariant but MutableList invariant in Kotlin?
Medium▼
List<out T> is read-only — it has no add(T) or set(T) methods. T only appears in output positions (get, iterator, etc.). Because it can never be used to write a T, it's safe to treat a List<Dog> as a List<Animal> — you can only read animals from it, and dogs are animals.

MutableList<T> has add(T) where T is in an input position. If it were covariant, you could assign a MutableList<Dog> to MutableList<Animal> and call add(Cat()) — corrupting the dog list. Invariance prevents this.
I2 — (Coding) Why won't this compile? How do you fix it?
MediumCoding▼
class Box<out T>(var value: T)  // ❌
Problem: var value: T generates a setter that takes T as a parameter — an input position. out T restricts T to output positions only. The setter violates this, so the compiler rejects it.

Fix: Use val instead of var: 
class Box<out T>(val value: T)  // ✅ val = getter only = out position
I3 — What is declaration-site variance vs use-site variance? Which does Kotlin prefer?
Medium▼
Declaration-site variance: annotate the class/interface once — class Flow<out T>. Every usage site automatically gets the covariance. Kotlin-idiomatic.

Use-site variance (type projection): annotate at each call site — fun copy(src: Array<out T>). Used when the class itself can't be annotated (e.g., invariant Java classes like Array).

Kotlin prefers declaration-site — less repetition, clearer intent. Java only has use-site wildcards (? extends T, ? super T). Kotlin supports both but declaration-site is idiomatic for your own code.
I4 — What is contravariance? Give a real Android/Kotlin use case.
Medium▼
Contravariance (in T): T appears only in input positions. The subtype relationship is reversed — Consumer<Animal> is a subtype of Consumer<Dog> because a consumer that can handle animals can certainly handle dogs.

Real Kotlin example: Comparator<in T>. A Comparator<Animal> that compares by name can be used to sort a list of dogs — dogs are animals, so the comparator works. You can pass an animalComparator wherever a dogComparator is needed.

Android example: BaseUseCase<in P, out R> — the params type P is consumed (input), so contravariant; the result R is produced (output), so covariant.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Design a generic Resource<T> sealed class for the data layer. Justify the variance annotation.
HardCoding▼
sealed class Resource<out T> {           // out T: only produced, never consumed
    data class  Success<T>(val data: T) : Resource<T>()
    data class  Error(val exception: Throwable) : Resource<Nothing>()
    data object Loading : Resource<Nothing>()
}

// Extension to transform the data
fun <T, R> Resource<T>.map(f: (T) -> R): Resource<R> = when (this) {
    is Resource.Success -> Resource.Success(f(data))
    is Resource.Error   -> this
    Resource.Loading    -> Resource.Loading
}
Justification: out T because Resource only wraps and exposes data — it never accepts T as input anywhere. This allows: (1) Resource.Loading and Resource.Error with Nothing to satisfy any Resource<T>; (2) a Resource<Dog> to be assigned to Resource<Animal> when the consuming code only reads.
S2 — (Scenario) A teammate asks: "Why can I assign a StateFlow<UiState> to a Flow<UiState> variable but not a MutableStateFlow to a MutableSharedFlow?" Explain.
HardScenario▼
StateFlow → Flow is valid because both are declared as interface Flow<out T> and interface StateFlow<out T> : Flow<T>. StateFlow IS-A Flow — it extends it. The covariance (out T) isn't even needed here; it's a direct subtype relationship via interface inheritance.

MutableStateFlow → MutableSharedFlow is invalid because MutableStateFlow and MutableSharedFlow are separate interfaces in different parts of the hierarchy. MutableStateFlow<T> extends both StateFlow<T> and MutableSharedFlow<T>, so a MutableStateFlow IS-A MutableSharedFlow — actually this assignment IS valid. If it fails in practice it may be a generics invariance issue with a specific type argument.

The key insight: variance enables subtype relationships based on type params. Direct interface inheritance enables them based on the class hierarchy. Both matter.
S3 — When would you use star projection * vs a bounded type parameter vs a concrete type?
Hard▼
Concrete type (List<String>): use when you know and care about the exact type at compile time. Most common case.

Bounded type parameter (<T : Serializable>): use when you don't know the exact type but need it to satisfy a constraint. The type is known within the function scope. Use this for generic utility functions.

Star projection (List<*>): use when you truly don't care about the type and only need to work with the container, not the elements — e.g., logging a list's size, checking if it's empty, or passing to a reflection API. Elements read as Any?. Cannot write. Use sparingly — it loses type information.
1G

Delegation & Operators

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: Class delegation ( by ), property delegation, by lazy , observable , vetoable , custom delegates, operator overloading, and destructuring — Kotlin features used throughout Android architecture.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

CLASS DELEGATION

class Repo(logger: Logger) : Logger by logger
// Forwards ALL Logger methods to 'logger'
// Composition over inheritance
// Delegate fixed at construction time
// Can delegate multiple interfaces

PROPERTY DELEGATION

val x by lazy { compute() }   // val, once
var y by observable("") { p,o,n -> }
var z by vetoable(0) { p,o,n -> n>=0 }
// Custom: operator fun getValue/setValue
// Jetpack: by viewModels(), by navArgs()

OPERATOR OVERLOADING

operator fun plus(o: T): T    // a + b
operator fun minus(o: T): T   // a - b
operator fun invoke(): R      // a()
operator fun get(i: Int): T   // a[i]
operator fun compareTo(o: T): Int  // >/<
operator fun contains(e: T): Boolean  // in

DESTRUCTURING

val (a, b, c) = dataClassObj
val (key, value) = mapEntry
val (_, amount, _) = tx  // skip with _
// data class: auto component1()..N()
// custom: operator fun componentN()

KEY GOTCHAS

operator keyword required
predefined function name required
operators should be PURE (no side effects)
by lazy: val only, thread-safe default
delegation fixed at construction
destructuring positional → fragile

ANDROID DELEGATES

by lazy          → ViewBinding, clients
by viewModels()  → ViewModel in Fragment
by activityViewModels() → shared ViewModel
by navArgs()     → Safe Args
by mutableStateOf() → Compose state
custom delegate  → EncryptedPrefs, logging
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Delegate object created every time

// ❌ BAD — new delegate object created per property access (if not cached)
class Foo {
    val x by ExpensiveDelegate()  // new instance each time Foo is instantiated
}
// ✅ GOOD — cache the delegate or use a factory function
fun <T> prefs(key: String, default: T) = PrefsDelegate(sharedPrefs, key, default)
var token by prefs("token", "")  // cleaner factory usage

Operator overloading with side effects — confusing

// ❌ BAD — + operator triggers a network call? Never expected
operator fun Cart.plus(item: Item): Cart {
    repository.addItemToCart(item)  // side effect in +!
    return copy(items = items + item)
}
// ✅ GOOD — operator returns new value, side effects in ViewModel/UseCase
operator fun Cart.plus(item: Item): Cart = copy(items = items + item)
// Let the ViewModel call repository.addItem() separately

Class delegation with val — delegate fixed at construction

// The delegate is the object passed at construction — cannot change later
class Repo(logger: Logger) : Logger by logger

// If you need to swap the delegate at runtime → use manual forwarding instead

Destructuring with position — fragile if data class changes

// ❌ BAD — positional destructuring breaks if fields are reordered
val (id, name, email, phone) = user  // breaks if User adds a field at position 2
// ✅ GOOD — use named properties unless destructuring is clearly for iteration
val id = user.id
val name = user.name
// Destructure only in for loops or when all fields are needed in order

Production Best Practices

  1. Use class delegation to compose multiple interfaces without inheritance hierarchies.
  2. Custom property delegates are excellent for cross-cutting concerns: encryption, preferences, logging on set.
  3. Operator overloading: only for value types with natural arithmetic semantics — never with side effects.
  4. Keep destructuring to data classes with stable field order, or map iteration — avoid for complex classes.
  5. Prefer by lazy over lateinit for immutable computed properties.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the difference between class delegation and property delegation in Kotlin?
Class delegation: forwards interface method calls to a delegate object. class A(b: SomeInterface) : SomeInterface by b — all methods of SomeInterface are auto-forwarded to b. This is composition over inheritance.

Property delegation: delegates the get/set logic of a property to an object that implements operator fun getValue/setValue. val x by lazy { ... } — the Lazy object handles when and how x's value is computed. They solve different problems at different levels.
B2 — What does Delegates.observable do? Give a use case.
Easy▼
Delegates.observable(initialValue) { property, oldValue, newValue -> } — a property delegate that calls the lambda every time the property is assigned a new value. The lambda receives the property metadata, the old value, and the new value. It does NOT prevent the change (use vetoable for that).

Android use case: trigger analytics when a user's status changes, or call notifyDataSetChanged() on a RecyclerView adapter when the data property is updated.
B3 — What requirements must a class meet to be a property delegate?
Easy▼
The class must implement (or provide as extension functions):
• operator fun getValue(thisRef: T?, property: KProperty<*>): R — for val properties
• operator fun setValue(thisRef: T?, property: KProperty<*>, value: R) — additionally for var properties

Alternatively, the class can implement the ReadOnlyProperty<T, R> or ReadWriteProperty<T, R> stdlib interfaces, which declare the same methods. The operator keyword is required.

Intermediate

I1 — How does by lazy achieve thread safety? What modes are available?
Medium▼
by lazy { } creates a SynchronizedLazyImpl by default. On first getValue call it checks if the value has been initialized (double-checked locking with @Volatile field). If not, it acquires a lock, checks again, runs the initializer, and caches the result. Subsequent calls return the cached value without locking.

Three modes:
• SYNCHRONIZED (default) — thread-safe, uses a lock
• PUBLICATION — multiple threads may initialize, but only first written is used; safe for concurrent access without a lock
• NONE — no synchronization; fastest, but only safe in single-threaded contexts
I2 — (Coding) Implement a custom property delegate that logs every get and set with Timber.
MediumCoding▼
class LoggingDelegate<T>(private var value: T) {
    operator fun getValue(ref: Any?, prop: KProperty<*>): T {
        Timber.d("GET ${prop.name} = $value")
        return value
    }
    operator fun setValue(ref: Any?, prop: KProperty<*>, newValue: T) {
        Timber.d("SET ${prop.name}: $value → $newValue")
        value = newValue
    }
}

// Usage:
var isLoading: Boolean by LoggingDelegate(false)
I3 — What does operator fun invoke() enable? Why is it used for use cases?
Medium▼
operator fun invoke() makes an object instance callable like a function — obj() calls obj.invoke(). For use cases in Clean Architecture: instead of useCase.execute(params), you write useCase(params) or even just val result = getUser(userId). This makes the call site read like a function call — the use case name IS the operation. Combined with suspend it integrates naturally with coroutines. This is the standard pattern in clean architecture Kotlin code.
I4 — Why is positional destructuring fragile? When is it safe to use?
Medium▼
Destructuring is positional — val (a, b, c) = obj calls component1(), component2(), component3(). If the data class changes — a field is inserted, removed, or reordered — the destructuring silently assigns the wrong values. No compile error.

Safe to use: (1) Map entry iteration: for ((key, value) in map) — Map.Entry has stable component1()/component2(); (2) Pair/Triple; (3) partition result: val (positives, negatives) = list.partition { it > 0 }; (4) When all fields are immediately needed and the class is stable/simple. Avoid for complex domain models with more than 3 fields.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Design a property delegate that caches a value and invalidates the cache after a timeout (TTL).
HardCoding▼
class TtlDelegate<T>(
    private val ttlMs: Long,
    private val loader: () -> T
) {
    private var cachedValue: T? = null
    private var lastLoaded: Long = 0L

    operator fun getValue(ref: Any?, prop: KProperty<*>): T {
        val now = System.currentTimeMillis()
        if (cachedValue == null || now - lastLoaded > ttlMs) {
            cachedValue = loader()
            lastLoaded = now
        }
        return cachedValue!!
    }
}

// Usage: refresh config every 5 minutes
val remoteConfig: AppConfig by TtlDelegate(5 * 60 * 1000L) { api.fetchConfig() }
Note: for production use, this needs thread-safety (synchronize around cache check/set or use @Volatile + double-checked). Also a suspend version would be needed for async loaders in coroutines.
S2 — (Scenario) A junior dev wants to override equals() and hashCode() on a class to support a == b and if (a in list). They ask if they should use operator overloading instead. What's your answer?
HardScenario▼
No — use equals() + hashCode(), not operator overloading, for equality and membership.

a == b in Kotlin calls equals() — not an operator. The operator fun equals override is just the regular equals() with the operator keyword, which is required for structural equality. a in list calls list.contains(a) which also uses equals().

The right approach: use a data class — it auto-generates correct equals() and hashCode() from primary constructor properties. Only if you need non-default equality (e.g., case-insensitive comparison) should you manually override both. Operator overloading (plus, minus, etc.) is for arithmetic-style operations, not equality.
1H

Kotlin Collections

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: List, Set, Map (mutable vs immutable), map/filter/flatMap/fold/reduce, and Sequences vs collections — the complete functional collection toolkit for Android production code.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

COLLECTION TYPES

listOf()        → List (read-only)
mutableListOf() → MutableList
setOf()         → Set (no dups, insertion order)
mapOf()         → Map (key unique)
emptyList()     → singleton, no alloc
ArrayList(cap)  → pre-sized

CORE OPERATORS

map { }          → transform 1:1
filter { }       → keep matching
flatMap { }      → map + flatten
fold(init) { }   → aggregate (safe empty)
reduce { }       → aggregate (throws empty)
groupBy { }      → Map<K, List<T>>
associateBy { }  → Map<K, T> (1:1)
partition { }    → Pair<List,List>

QUERIES

any { }           → true if 1+ match
all { }           → true if all match
none { }          → true if 0 match
count { }         → matching count
first/last { }    → throws if empty
firstOrNull { }   → null if empty
find { }          → firstOrNull alias
sumOf / maxOf / minOf / averageOf

SEQUENCES

list.asSequence()  → lazy chain
generateSequence(seed) { next }
// lazy: no intermediate lists
// take(n) short-circuits
// terminal: toList/first/count/etc
// re-evaluates on each terminal call
// Only use for large data + many ops

MAP UTILITIES

getOrDefault(k, def)
getOrElse(k) { compute() }
getOrPut(k) { compute() }  // cache
mapValues { (k,v) -> }
filterValues { }
filterKeys { }
toSortedMap()
entries / keys / values

GOTCHAS

reduce → throws on empty → use fold
MutableList in Compose state → broken
Sequence re-evaluated per terminal op
Sequence not faster for small lists
List is read-only, NOT truly immutable
associateBy: duplicate keys → last wins
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

reduce on empty collection — crashes

// ❌ BAD — throws UnsupportedOperationException if list is empty
val total = transactions.reduce { acc, t -> acc + t.amount }  // CRASH if empty
// ✅ GOOD — fold is always safe
val total = transactions.fold(0.0) { acc, t -> acc + t.amount }

mutable collection in StateFlow — Compose stability issue

// ❌ BAD — MutableList in state breaks Compose structural equality
data class UiState(val items: MutableList<Item>)
// Compose can't detect changes; recomposition may be missed
// ✅ GOOD — immutable List; create new state on update
data class UiState(val items: List<Item> = emptyList())
// Update: _uiState.value = _uiState.value.copy(items = newItems)

Sequence misuse — worse performance for small lists

// ❌ BAD — sequence overhead worse than eager for tiny list
val result = listOf("a", "b", "c")
    .asSequence()
    .map { it.uppercase() }
    .toList()  // more overhead than just .map { }
// ✅ GOOD — sequence only for large data + multiple operations
val result2 = listOf("a", "b", "c").map { it.uppercase() }  // just use map directly

Sequence evaluated multiple times

// ❌ BAD — sequence re-evaluated on each terminal operation
val seq = list.asSequence().filter { it.isActive }
val count = seq.count()    // evaluates full pipeline
val first = seq.first()    // evaluates full pipeline AGAIN
// ✅ GOOD — materialize once if needed multiple times
val filtered = list.asSequence().filter { it.isActive }.toList()
val count = filtered.size
val first = filtered.first()

Production Best Practices

  1. Use immutable List<T> in domain models and UI state — mutable collections in state cause Compose stability issues.
  2. Prefer fold over reduce unless you're certain the collection is non-empty.
  3. Use asSequence() for processing >1000 elements with multiple chained operators.
  4. Use emptyList() for empty defaults — returns a singleton, no allocation.
  5. Pre-size ArrayList(capacity) when the final size is known in advance.
  6. Use associateBy to convert a list to a Map for O(1) lookups by ID.
  7. Use getOrPut for simple caching patterns in MutableMaps.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the difference between List and MutableList in Kotlin?
List<T> is a read-only interface — it has no add(), remove(), or set operations. MutableList<T> extends List<T> and adds mutation methods. Note: List is read-only, not truly immutable — the underlying object could be a MutableList that someone else holds a mutable reference to. In practice, use List everywhere in domain models and UI state for safety. Only use MutableList when you explicitly need to build or modify a list locally.
B2 — What is the difference between fold and reduce?
Easy▼
fold(initial) { acc, element -> } starts with an explicit initial value. Safe on empty collections (returns the initial value). Can produce a different type from the list's element type.

reduce { acc, element -> } uses the first element as the initial accumulator. Throws UnsupportedOperationException on an empty collection. Result must be the same type as the elements.

Rule: use fold by default; use reduce only when you can guarantee non-empty and want the same type.
B3 — What is the difference between map and flatMap?
Easy▼
map transforms each element 1:1 — the result list has the same number of elements. flatMap maps each element to a collection, then flattens all those collections into one — the result list can have a different (usually larger) number of elements.

Example: orders.map { it.items } → List<List<Item>> (nested). orders.flatMap { it.items } → List<Item> (flat). Use flatMap to aggregate nested lists.

Intermediate

I1 — When should you use Sequence instead of a regular collection? What are the trade-offs?
Medium▼
Use Sequence when: the dataset is large (>1000 elements) AND you have multiple chained operators AND there's a limiting terminal operation (take, first, find) that can short-circuit.

Trade-offs:
Pros: No intermediate list allocations between operators; lazy evaluation stops at the first N results.
Cons: Per-element overhead (Sequence wrapping); sequences re-evaluate the entire pipeline on each terminal call (don't call multiple terminals on the same sequence); no benefit and possible degradation for small lists.

Rule of thumb: benchmark before switching. If the profiler shows collection operator allocations as a bottleneck, switch to Sequence. Otherwise, eager collections with their JIT optimization are often faster for typical list sizes in Android.
I2 — (Coding) Given a list of transactions, group them by type, sum the amounts per type, and return the top-3 types by amount.
MediumCoding▼
data class Transaction(val type: String, val amount: Double)

fun top3TypesByAmount(txs: List<Transaction>): List<Pair<String, Double>> =
    txs
        .groupBy { it.type }
        .mapValues { (_, list) -> list.sumOf { it.amount } }
        .entries
        .sortedByDescending { it.value }
        .take(3)
        .map { it.key to it.value }
I3 — What is the difference between groupBy and associateBy?
Medium▼
groupBy { keySelector } → Map<K, List<T>> — each key maps to a list of elements. Multiple elements can share the same key. Use when multiple elements have the same key value (e.g., group transactions by type).

associateBy { keySelector } → Map<K, T> — each key maps to exactly one element. If multiple elements share the same key, the last one wins (earlier ones are overwritten). Use when keys are unique (e.g., build a lookup map from users by userId).
I4 — (Coding) Why does this cause a bug in Compose and how do you fix it?
data class UiState(val items: MutableList<Product> = mutableListOf())
MediumCoding▼
Bug: Compose uses structural equality (equals/hashCode) to detect state changes. data class includes items in equals(). But MutableList.equals() compares content — so if you mutate the list in-place (add/remove items), the data class object itself doesn't change (same reference), and StateFlow won't emit a new value (it checks if the new value equals the old). Recomposition is skipped; UI shows stale data.

Fix: Use immutable List<T> and create a new state object on every update: 
data class UiState(val items: List<Product> = emptyList())

// In ViewModel — creates new state with new list reference:
_uiState.update { it.copy(items = newItems) }

Senior / Scenario

S1 — You have a list of 100,000 user events. You need: filter active users, take their first 3 events, sort by timestamp, and take the top 10 users by event count. Should you use Sequence? How would you structure it?
HardScenario▼
Yes — Sequence is appropriate here for the early filtering stage, but structure matters: 
val result = allEvents   // 100,000 events
    .asSequence()
    .filter { it.userId in activeUserIds }   // lazy, no intermediate list
    .groupBy { it.userId }                    // terminal op — materializes filtered set
    .mapValues { (_, events) ->
        events.sortedBy { it.timestamp }.take(3)   // per-user, small
    }
    .entries
    .sortedByDescending { it.value.size }
    .take(10)
    .toList()
Key point: groupBy is a terminal operation on the sequence — it materializes the filtered results. After that, you're back to eager collection operations which are fine since the intermediate set is much smaller. The sequence benefit is the initial filter on 100K elements without creating a full intermediate list.
S2 — (Scenario) A colleague says "List in Kotlin is immutable, so it's thread-safe." Is this correct?
HardScenario▼
Partially correct, but the reasoning is wrong.

List<T> is read-only, not immutable. The underlying JVM object could be a MutableList. Another thread holding a MutableList reference to the same object could add/remove elements while another thread is iterating — causing ConcurrentModificationException.

However, in practice in Android: if you follow the rule "domain layer produces immutable List, ViewModel holds it in StateFlow, UI only reads it," then the list is effectively safe because you never hold a MutableList reference in a shared scope — you create a new List on each state update. This is a convention-based safety, not a type-system guarantee.

For true thread-safety with concurrent mutation, use CopyOnWriteArrayList, or manage access with a Mutex in coroutines, or use kotlinx.collections.immutable persistent collections.
1I

Inline & Recursion

Tier 1 Mod 1
