Key Concept: inline , noinline , crossinline , reified type parameters, and tail recursion — performance and type-safety features that power Kotlin's standard library and Flow operators.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

INLINE

inline fun f(block: () -> T): T
// Copies body + lambdas to call site
// Benefits: no lambda alloc, non-local return, reified
// Cost: larger bytecode per call site
// Only for small HOF called frequently

NOINLINE / CROSSINLINE

noinline block: () -> T
// Lambda stays as object
// Use: pass to another fn, store, return

crossinline block: () -> T
// Lambda inlined but NO non-local return
// Use: lambda called in Thread/Handler/async

REIFIED

inline fun <reified T> f(): T
// Type T available at runtime
// Requires inline (substituted per call site)
// Use: T::class.java, is T, as T
// Examples: fromJson<User>(), startActivity<PayAct>()

TAILREC

tailrec fun f(n: Int, acc: Int = 0): Int =
    if (n == 0) acc else f(n-1, acc+n)
// Recursive call must be LAST operation
// Compiled to a loop — no stack growth
// Use accumulator pattern for tail position

INLINE STDLIB EXAMPLES

let, run, with, apply, also → inline
repeat, forEach → inline
use → inline
Flow.map, filter, transform → inline
// That's why non-local return works in
// scope functions!

KEY GOTCHAS

reified requires inline
non-local return requires inline
tailrec ignored if call not in tail pos
noinline needed if lambda is stored/passed
inline large fn → APK size bloat
crossinline prevents non-local return
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Inlining large functions — APK bloat

// ❌ BAD — large function inlined; body copied at every call site
inline fun complexSetup(block: () -> Unit) {
    // 50 lines of setup code...
    block()
    // 30 lines of teardown...
}
// Called 10 times → 800 lines of bytecode vs 80
// ✅ GOOD — keep inline functions small (under ~10 lines)
inline fun <T> timed(block: () -> T): T {
    val t = System.nanoTime(); return block().also { Timber.d("${System.nanoTime()-t}ns") }
}

tailrec warning ignored — no optimization applied

// ❌ BAD — NOT tail position! Compiler silently skips optimization
tailrec fun factorial(n: Int): Int =
    if (n <= 1) 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)  // multiplication happens AFTER call
// tailrec keyword is silently ignored — no loop generated
// ✅ GOOD — accumulator pattern puts call in tail position
tailrec fun factorial(n: Int, acc: Long = 1): Long =
    if (n <= 1) acc else factorial(n - 1, acc * n)  // call IS the last op

noinline forgotten — compile error

// ❌ BAD — passing inlined lambda to a function that needs a function object
inline fun withDelay(action: () -> Unit) {
    handler.postDelayed(action, 1000)  // ❌ Handler.postDelayed needs a Runnable object
}
// ✅ GOOD — noinline keeps it as a lambda object
inline fun withDelay(noinline action: () -> Unit) {
    handler.postDelayed(action, 1000)
}

Production Best Practices

  1. Use inline only for higher-order functions that are small and called frequently.
  2. Use reified to eliminate boilerplate Class<T> parameters from generic functions.
  3. Always use an accumulator with tailrec to place the recursive call in tail position.
  4. Use noinline when a lambda needs to be passed to another function, stored, or returned.
  5. Use crossinline when the lambda is called in a different context (Thread, Handler, async callback).
  6. Verify tailrec optimization works — Kotlin compiler warns if it can't apply it (but sometimes silently skips).
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What does the inline keyword do? What problem does it solve?
The inline keyword instructs the compiler to copy the function body — and the bodies of any lambda parameters — directly into the call site. This eliminates the overhead of creating lambda objects on the heap and the virtual method dispatch for every call. It solves the performance cost of higher-order functions: without inlining, every filter { } or let { } call creates a new anonymous class instance.
B2 — What is a reified type parameter and why does it require inline?
Easy▼
A reified type parameter is one that's available at runtime — you can call T::class.java, use is T, and as T inside the function. Normally, JVM erases generic types at runtime, making this impossible.

It requires inline because inlining is the mechanism: when the function is inlined, the compiler substitutes the actual type at each call site. So T::class.java is replaced with UserProfile::class.java at one call site and Order::class.java at another. Without inlining there'd be one copy of the bytecode and the type would be erased.
B3 — What is tail recursion? Why is it useful and what does tailrec require?
Easy▼
Tail recursion is when the recursive call is the last operation in the function — nothing else happens after it returns. This allows the compiler to reuse the current stack frame instead of allocating a new one, converting the recursion to an iterative loop. This prevents StackOverflowError for deep recursion (thousands/millions of steps).

tailrec requirement: the recursive call must be in tail position — the very last thing the function does. n * factorial(n-1) is NOT tail position (multiplication happens after the call). factorial(n-1, acc * n) IS tail position. Use an accumulator parameter to restructure if needed.

Intermediate

I1 — What is the difference between noinline and crossinline?
Medium▼
noinline: the lambda is NOT inlined — it's kept as a regular lambda object. Use when the lambda needs to be stored in a variable, passed to another function expecting a function type, or returned from the inline function.

crossinline: the lambda IS inlined (no object allocation) but non-local returns are forbidden. Use when the lambda is called inside another lambda or a different execution context (like a Thread or Handler callback). The reason: the lambda body is inlined at the call site, but when it's inside a Thread block, a return couldn't reliably exit the outer function because execution has moved to a different thread.
I2 — (Coding) Write a reified extension function that safely gets an extra from an Intent.
MediumCoding▼
inline fun <reified T> Intent.getExtraOrNull(key: String): T? =
    extras?.get(key) as? T

// Usage:
val orderId: String? = intent.getExtraOrNull("order_id")
val amount: Double? = intent.getExtraOrNull("amount")

// Or with a required version:
inline fun <reified T> Intent.requireExtra(key: String): T =
    getExtraOrNull(key) ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("Missing required extra: $key")
I3 — Why does a return inside a let { } block sometimes exit the outer function? How do you prevent it?
Medium▼
let is an inline function. When a function is inline, its lambda body is copied into the call site. A bare return inside an inline lambda is a non-local return — it exits the enclosing named function, not just the lambda.

Example: if you're inside a function and write user?.let { return }, that return exits the outer function entirely.

To exit only the lambda, use a labeled return: return@let. This limits the return to the lambda scope only: 
user?.let {
    if (it.isBlocked) return@let   // exits let only
    processUser(it)
}
I4 — (Coding) Why doesn't tailrec optimize this? Fix it.
MediumCoding▼
// ❌ Not tail-recursive — multiplication happens AFTER the recursive call
tailrec fun factorial(n: Int): Long =
    if (n <= 1) 1 else n * factorial(n - 1)
// The last operation is multiplication, not the recursive call
// ✅ Fix — accumulator puts recursive call in tail position
tailrec fun factorial(n: Int, acc: Long = 1L): Long =
    if (n <= 1) acc
    else factorial(n - 1, acc * n)   // call is the LAST thing — tail position
// Now: tailrec compiles this to a while loop — no stack growth

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Why are Kotlin's scope functions (let, run, apply, etc.) inline? What benefits does this give them?
Hard▼
All five scope functions are inline. Benefits:

1. Zero lambda allocation: calling user?.let { } millions of times (e.g., in a hot loop or for every item in a large list) doesn't create a new anonymous class instance each time.

2. Non-local return: you can write return inside a run { } or let { } block to exit the enclosing function — useful for early return patterns without breaking the fluent style.

3. Performance transparency: the compiler inlines them, so there's no extra call stack frame or virtual dispatch overhead. They behave as if you wrote the code inline manually.

This is intentional design — scope functions are meant to be used pervasively throughout Kotlin code. Making them inline ensures they have zero performance cost at any call frequency.
S2 — (Scenario) You write an inline function that takes two lambdas. One needs to be stored in a list for later execution. What happens and how do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
Problem: When a function is marked inline, ALL lambda parameters are inlined by default. An inlined lambda doesn't exist as an object — it's just code pasted at the call site. If you try to store it in a list (which requires an object reference), the compiler rejects it with an error: "Illegal usage of inline-parameter."

Fix: Mark the lambda that needs to be stored as noinline: 
inline fun setupWithCallback(
    action: () -> Unit,              // inlined — no object
    noinline onComplete: () -> Unit  // noinline — kept as object
) {
    action()                          // inlined at call site
    callbacks.add(onComplete)         // stored as object — works
}
You get the inlining benefit for action (no allocation) while onComplete remains a proper function object that can be stored, called later, and referenced by multiple consumers.
1J

Equality, Interop & Errors

Tier 1 Mod 1
Key Concept: == vs === , Kotlin–JVM interoperability, Kotlin compilation basics, exceptions, and the Result type — the final Kotlin unit before moving into Android fundamentals.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

== vs ===

==   → equals() → structural
===  → reference → same object
// StateFlow uses == to detect changes
// data class: == uses constructor props
// regular class: == = === (no override)
// String ==: value comparison ✅

RESULT<T>

runCatching { block() } → Result<T>
.getOrNull()   // T? on failure
.getOrThrow()  // T, rethrows exception
.getOrDefault(v)
.map { }       // transform on success
.onSuccess { } // side effect
.onFailure { } // side effect
.fold(onSuccess = { }, onFailure = { })

EXCEPTIONS

All Kotlin exceptions: UNCHECKED
try { } catch (e: T) { } finally { }
try is an expression (returns value)
throw is an expression (type: Nothing)
@Throws(IOException::class) for Java
runCatching: always rethrow CancellationException!

JAVA INTEROP

@JvmStatic    → companion → true static
@JvmOverloads → default args → overloads
@JvmField     → property → field (no getter)
@Throws(E::class) → checked for Java
Platform type T! → unknown nullability
KSP > KAPT (faster annotation processing)

COMPILATION

.kt → IR → .class → D8/R8 → .dex
data class   → equals/hashCode/copy/componentN
companion    → inner static class + INSTANCE
extension fn → static method (receiver=param)
default args → $default + bitmask
inline fn    → body copied at call site

KEY GOTCHAS

runCatching swallows CancellationException
StateFlow needs data class for correct ==
Platform types from Java → defensive ?: use
@JvmStatic needed for Java companion access
Result vs sealed: domain vs UI layer
try {} catch {} is an expression in Kotlin
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

runCatching swallows CancellationException

// ❌ BAD — CancellationException caught and wrapped, coroutine not cancelled
val result = runCatching { api.call() }
// If coroutine is cancelled during api.call(), CancellationException is swallowed!
// ✅ GOOD — always rethrow CancellationException
val result = runCatching { api.call() }
    .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }

// Or use a safeRunCatching wrapper:
suspend inline fun <T> safeRunCatching(block: suspend () -> T): Result<T> = try {
    Result.success(block())
} catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }
  catch (e: Exception) { Result.failure(e) }

StateFlow with regular class — no emission

// ❌ BAD — regular class; StateFlow.value = x checks x == current
// Regular class inherits equals() from Any → reference comparison
class ProfileState(val name: String)
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")  // emits again! different object references
// ✅ GOOD — data class; structural equality prevents duplicate emissions
data class ProfileState(val name: String)
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")
_state.value = ProfileState("Alice")  // NOT emitted — == returns true

Platform types — silent NPE from Java

// ❌ BAD — Java returns String! (platform type); assigned as non-null
val name: String = javaApi.getName()  // crashes if getName() returns null
// ✅ GOOD — treat Java returns defensively
val name: String = javaApi.getName() ?: "Unknown"
// Or: annotate the Java side with @NotNull / @Nullable

Production Best Practices

  1. Use data class for all StateFlow state types — structural equality ensures correct emission/de-dup.
  2. Always rethrow CancellationException — wrap all runCatching with a re-throw check.
  3. Use Result<T> in data/domain layer, sealed UiState in presentation layer — they serve different purposes.
  4. Add @Throws to Kotlin functions called from Java that may throw checked exceptions.
  5. Add @JvmStatic to companion object methods used from Java — avoids MyClass.Companion.method() verbosity.
  6. Prefer KSP over KAPT for annotation processors in new code — significantly faster build times.
  7. Use try as an expression for simple parse operations: val n = try { s.toInt() } catch { 0 }.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the difference between == and === in Kotlin?
== is structural equality — it calls equals(). === is referential equality — it checks whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory. For a data class, == compares field values (auto-generated equals()). For a regular class with no equals() override, == behaves the same as === (reference comparison, inherited from Any).
B2 — Does Kotlin have checked exceptions? How do you expose checked exceptions to Java callers?
Easy▼
No — all Kotlin exceptions are unchecked. You are never forced to declare which exceptions a function throws, nor are callers forced to catch them. This is a deliberate design decision that avoids Java's checked exception verbosity.

To expose a checked exception contract to Java callers, annotate the Kotlin function with @Throws(IOException::class). This tells the Java compiler to treat it as a checked exception, enabling Java's try/catch requirement.
B3 — What is runCatching and what does it return?
Easy▼
runCatching { block } executes a block and wraps the result in a Result<T>. If the block succeeds, it returns Result.success(value). If it throws any exception, it returns Result.failure(exception). You can then chain map, onSuccess, onFailure, fold, and getOrNull on the result.

Intermediate

I1 — Why is StateFlow UI state broken if you use a regular class instead of a data class?
Medium▼
MutableStateFlow.value = newValue checks if newValue == currentValue before emitting. If they're equal, no emission occurs — this is the de-duplication mechanism.

A regular class inherits equals() from Any, which compares by reference. So every new instance is "different" even if the content is identical — the state always emits. This can cause unnecessary recompositions.

Conversely, if the same instance is mutated in-place (mutable properties), the reference stays the same — == returns true — and no emission occurs even though the content changed. Either way breaks the reactive contract. Fix: use data class with all val properties.
I2 — What is a platform type in Kotlin? How do you handle it safely?
Medium▼
A platform type (expressed as T! in error messages) is a type from Java code that has no nullability annotation. Kotlin cannot determine if it's nullable or non-null, so it defers to the developer. You can assign it to either T or T? — but if you assign to T and Java returns null, you get a NPE.

Safe handling: (1) Annotate the Java side with @Nullable/@NotNull — Kotlin then knows the contract. (2) Defensively treat all Java returns as nullable: javaApi.getName() ?: "default". (3) In modern code, use Kotlin APIs that are already annotated.
I3 — (Coding) What's the critical bug in this code? Fix it.
MediumCoding▼
// ❌ BUG
suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): Result<User> =
    runCatching { api.getUser(id) }
Bug: runCatching catches ALL exceptions, including CancellationException. When the coroutine is cancelled (e.g., user navigates away), the cancellation exception is caught and wrapped in a Result.failure. The coroutine thinks it completed normally — it doesn't propagate the cancellation. The scope doesn't cancel properly, causing leaked coroutines.

// ✅ Fixed
suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): Result<User> =
    runCatching { api.getUser(id) }
        .onFailure { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }
I4 — What is the difference between KAPT and KSP? Which should you use in new projects?
Medium▼
KAPT (Kotlin Annotation Processing Tool): converts Kotlin source to Java stubs, then runs Java annotation processors. Works with all Java annotation processors but adds a full compilation step — significantly slower, especially on incremental builds.

KSP (Kotlin Symbol Processing): processes Kotlin symbols directly without Java stub generation — typically 2x faster than KAPT. Has a Kotlin-first API. Supported by major Android libraries: Hilt (1.0.0+), Room (2.4.0+), Moshi, Glide.

Use KSP in new projects wherever the library supports it. Only fall back to KAPT for processors that haven't migrated to KSP yet.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — (Scenario) A developer reports "my UI sometimes doesn't update when the state changes." You look at the ViewModel and see _state.value = ProfileState(name = newName) where ProfileState is a regular class. Diagnose and fix.
HardScenario▼
Diagnosis: MutableStateFlow.value = x uses == (structural equality) to decide whether to emit. ProfileState is a regular class — it inherits equals() from Any, which compares by reference. So every ProfileState(name = newName) creates a new object, and ===-based comparison makes it always emit (new reference ≠ old reference) — that would actually cause over-emission.

But the "UI doesn't update" scenario happens if the developer is mutating the existing object: profileState.name = newName (if name is a var). The reference hasn't changed, so == (reference for non-data class) returns true — no emission.

Fix: 1. Make ProfileState a data class with val properties — now == compares field values. 2. Never mutate state in-place; always create a new object: _state.value = _state.value.copy(name = newName) 
data class ProfileState(val name: String)
_state.value = _state.value.copy(name = newName)  // emits if name changed
S2 — When would you choose Result<T> over a sealed class for error handling? Give a specific architecture example.
HardScenario▼
Use Result<T> at the repository and use-case layer — it's the boundary between exception-throwing code (network, database) and your clean domain logic. The repository wraps a Retrofit call with runCatching; the use case propagates or maps the result. No custom state is needed here — it's just success/failure.

Use sealed class at the presentation layer — because UI has states beyond just success/failure: Loading, Empty, Refreshing, etc. Each state may carry different data, and the when expression must be exhaustive.

The pattern in production: 
// Data layer → Result
suspend fun getUser(): Result<User> = runCatching { api.getUser() }

// Presentation layer → sealed UiState
getUser().fold(
    onSuccess = { UiState.Success(it) },
    onFailure = { UiState.Error(it.message) }
)
They complement each other — Result handles the exception boundary; sealed UiState handles the display contract.
S3 — You have a Kotlin library consumed by a Java project. List all the annotations you'd apply and why.
HardScenario▼
@JvmStatic — on companion object members: generates a true Java static method so Java can call MyClass.method() instead of MyClass.Companion.method().

@JvmOverloads — on functions with default parameters: generates Java-visible overloaded methods so Java callers can omit optional parameters.

@JvmField — on val/var properties you want exposed as Java fields: removes the getter/setter and exposes the field directly. Useful for constants.

@Throws(ExceptionType::class) — on suspend functions or functions that throw: tells Java's compiler to treat them as checked exceptions.

@JvmName — when Kotlin generates a method name that clashes with another JVM method name (e.g., extension functions on the same receiver type).

@Nullable / @NotNull — on all public function parameters and return types: prevents Java from treating them as platform types, giving Java callers proper nullability warnings.

Also: avoid using Kotlin-specific features in the public API surface (default arguments without @JvmOverloads, companion objects without @JvmStatic, extension functions in interfaces).

Android Components Overview

Tier 2 Mod 2
Key Concept: Tier 2 Activity · Fragment · Service · BroadcastReceiver · ContentProvider · Application · Context
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Quick Revision Sheet

ComponentEntry PointLifecycle LengthHas UI?Modern Alternative
ActivityIntent / LauncherScreen lifetime✅Compose screen (in single-activity)
FragmentFragmentManager.add/replaceActivity or back-stack✅Composable function
Service (Started)startService / startForegroundServiceUntil stopSelf❌WorkManager / Coroutine
Service (Bound)bindServiceWhile bound❌Bound service still valid for IPC
Service (Foreground)startForegroundServiceUntil stopSelf❌ (notification)Still required for ongoing user-aware tasks
BroadcastReceiverIntent broadcastonReceive() only❌Dynamic receiver + WorkManager for work
ContentProviderContentResolverProcess lifetime❌Room / DataStore (internal); CP for cross-app
ApplicationProcess startProcess lifetime❌n/a (required for DI init)

Context Golden Rules

  • Singleton / long-lived object → applicationContext (never Activity context)
  • Inflate view / show dialog → Activity/Fragment context
  • Hilt DI → use @ApplicationContext qualifier for non-UI injection
  • Never store Activity in static / companion object field

Background Restrictions (API 26+)

  • Cannot call startService() from background → use startForegroundService() + startForeground() within 5 s
  • Most implicit broadcasts cannot have static receivers → register dynamically
  • Deferrable work → WorkManager

Component Security

  • Set android:exported="false" unless cross-app access is needed
  • Add android:permission for exported components that should be restricted
  • Required: android:exported must be explicit on API 31+ for components with intent-filters
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Context Leaks

❌ Bad

// Stores Activity context in a long-lived object
class ImageLoader(val ctx: Context)

// Passed from Fragment — leaks Fragment/Activity
ImageLoader(requireContext())

✅ Good

// Use applicationContext for singletons
class ImageLoader(val ctx: Context)

ImageLoader(requireContext().applicationContext)

BroadcastReceiver — Long Work

❌ Bad

override fun onReceive(ctx: Context, intent: Intent) {
    // Blocking network call — ANR risk
    apiClient.syncNow()
}

✅ Good

override fun onReceive(ctx: Context, intent: Intent) {
    // Enqueue WorkManager — fast, non-blocking
    WorkManager.getInstance(ctx).enqueue(syncRequest)
}

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Static Activity reference: companion object { var activity: Activity? } — will leak. Never do this.
  • Starting Activity from Application context: requires FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK — avoid unless necessary (notifications, deep links from services).
  • Fragment over-creation: Not using findFragmentByTag before add leads to duplicate fragments after rotation.
  • Service not stopped: Started services that never call stopSelf() or stopService() drain battery.
  • Exported components without permission: android:exported="true" without android:permission exposes your components to any app (security hole).
  • Application class bloat: Heavy sync init in Application.onCreate() slows cold start. Use App Startup library or lazy init.
  • ContentProvider in multi-process: Accessing your own ContentProvider from multiple processes leads to unexpected instantiation. Prefer single-process with explicit initialization order.
API 26+ Background Restrictions: Apps in background cannot start Services. Use startForegroundService() + call startForeground() within 5 seconds, or use WorkManager for deferrable tasks.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What are the four main Android app components?
Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, ContentProvider. All must be declared in AndroidManifest.xml. Each has a distinct lifecycle and purpose managed by the Android system (ActivityManagerService).
Q2: Basic What is the difference between Application context and Activity context?
Application context lives for the process lifetime; Activity context lives until the Activity is destroyed. Use Application context for long-lived singletons (databases, Retrofit, DI). Use Activity context only for UI operations (inflate views, show dialogs, start activities). Storing Activity context in a singleton causes memory leaks because the Activity cannot be GC'd.
Q3: Basic What restrictions apply to BroadcastReceivers?
onReceive() must complete quickly (ideally <10 s). No long-running or async work. Post-API 26, most implicit broadcasts cannot use statically declared receivers in the manifest — use dynamic registration. If work is needed, enqueue a WorkManager task inside onReceive().
2B

Activity Lifecycle & State

Tier 2 Mod 2
Key Concept: Tier 2 onCreate · onStart · onResume · onPause · onStop · onDestroy · config changes · process death · onSaveInstanceState
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Quick Revision Sheet

Lifecycle at a Glance

CallbackActivity Visible?Interactive?Key Work
onCreateNoNosetContentView, ViewModel init, observe
onStartYes (partial)NoStart lightweight observers
onResumeYesYes ✅Acquire camera/sensors, resume media
onPausePartialNoRelease camera/sensors, pause media, save critical data
onStopNoNoUnregister receivers, stop polling
onDestroyNoNoLast cleanup; NOT guaranteed on process death

State Survival Matrix

MechanismRotationProcess DeathBack pressed
ViewModel✅❌❌
SavedStateHandle✅✅❌
onSaveInstanceState Bundle✅✅❌
Room / DataStore✅✅✅

Golden Rules

  • Use ViewModel for all UI state
  • Use SavedStateHandle for small survival-critical state
  • Collect Flows with repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) or collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
  • Release exclusive resources in onPause()
  • Never rely on onDestroy() for critical saves
  • onSaveInstanceState → small primitives / IDs only (Bundle size ~1 MB limit)
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Collecting Flow in onCreate Without repeatOnLifecycle

❌ Bad — collects in background, wastes resources

override fun onCreate(...) {
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        // Keeps collecting even when Activity is stopped
        viewModel.uiState.collect { render(it) }
    }
}

✅ Good — pauses when not STARTED

override fun onCreate(...) {
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
            viewModel.uiState.collect { render(it) }
        }
    }
}

Doing Work in onDestroy

onDestroy() is NOT guaranteed to be called (process death). Never save critical data here. Use onPause() for must-save data or a ViewModel + Room for persistence.

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Heavy work in onCreate/onResume: Causes jank and slow start. Move I/O to ViewModel/coroutine.
  • Leak via anonymous inner class: An inner class in Activity captures Activity reference. If passed to a background thread, leaks the Activity.
  • Not restoring state from Bundle: After process death + relaunch, the user sees a blank screen instead of their previous position.
  • Forgetting isFinishing() check in onStop: Some cleanup (like analytics flush) should only happen if actually finishing, not just hiding.
  • Starting Activity from onResume in a loop: If you start another Activity in onResume and that Activity finishes back to you, you get an infinite loop.
  • Network calls in lifecycle callbacks: Put them in ViewModel with viewModelScope. Callbacks may be called multiple times on rotation.
Best Practice checklist:
  • Use ViewModel for all UI state — it survives rotation automatically
  • Use SavedStateHandle for small state that must survive process death
  • Use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) to collect Flows
  • In Compose, use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() from lifecycle-runtime-compose
  • Never call blocking operations in lifecycle callbacks
  • Release exclusive resources (camera, GPS) in onPause(), not onStop()
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic List the six Activity lifecycle callbacks in order and describe what each one means.
onCreate → Activity created; onStart → visible but not interactive; onResume → foreground, interactive; onPause → partially hidden (another Activity/dialog in front), release exclusive resources; onStop → fully hidden; onDestroy → being destroyed (finish or config change). onRestart is called between onStop and onStart when coming back to a stopped Activity.
Q2: Basic What is the difference between a configuration change and process death?
Configuration change (rotation, locale): Activity is torn down and recreated. ViewModel survives via ViewModelStore. onSaveInstanceState is called.
Process death: OS kills entire process silently. No callbacks after onStop. ViewModel is gone. Only saved instance state Bundle + Room/DataStore data survives. On relaunch, the system reconstructs the back stack and passes the Bundle to onCreate.
Q3: Basic When is onSaveInstanceState called?
Before onStop, when the Activity may be destroyed and recreated. This includes rotation, going to home screen, receiving a phone call, going to another app. It is NOT called when the user presses Back (intentional finish) because there's no expectation of restoration.

⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Forgetting setIntent() in onNewIntent()

❌ Bad — stale intent after restart

override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    // Does NOT call setIntent(intent)
    // If Activity is recreated, getIntent() returns OLD intent
    val id = getIntent().getStringExtra("id")
}

✅ Good

override fun onNewIntent(intent: Intent) {
    super.onNewIntent(intent)
    setIntent(intent)    // Update so getIntent() returns new one
    val id = intent.getStringExtra("id")
}

singleTask Unexpectedly Destroys Back Stack

Gotcha: Declaring your HomeActivity as singleTask means that whenever it is launched (e.g. from a notification), ALL Activities above it in the task are destroyed. Users lose navigation state. Only use singleTask when popping the back stack is intentional.

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Using singleInstance for regular screens: Activities in separate tasks cannot share ViewModels and have broken Back navigation. Only use for truly isolated system-level screens.
  • Not handling FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK correctly: When starting an Activity from a Service, Application, or BroadcastReceiver (non-Activity context), FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK is required. Omitting it causes RuntimeException.
  • Deep links with wrong launch mode: A deep link to a singleTask Activity destroys the back stack the user had. Prefer Navigation Component's deep link handling with addToBackStack.
  • Duplicate Activities from double-tap: Users tapping a button twice quickly can start two Activities. Use singleTop or disable the button after first tap + re-enable in onResume.
  • Ignoring task affinity: android:taskAffinity combined with singleTask can route Activities to unexpected tasks. Default affinity is the package name.
Modern best practice: In single-activity apps with Navigation Component, you rarely need launch modes. Use launchSingleTop = true and popUpTo in NavOptions for the equivalent behaviour. Reserve manifest launch modes for the MainActivity and cross-app deep-link scenarios.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What are the four Activity launch modes?
standard, singleTop, singleTask, singleInstance.
• standard: new instance every launch
• singleTop: reuse if at stack top (onNewIntent called), else new instance
• singleTask: one instance per task; pops all above it on re-launch (onNewIntent called)
• singleInstance: one instance, own exclusive task
Q2: Basic What is onNewIntent() and when is it called?
onNewIntent() is called when a new Intent arrives for an existing Activity instance (instead of creating a new one). Called for singleTop if the Activity is at the top of the stack, and for singleTask/singleInstance when the instance already exists. Always call setIntent(intent) inside onNewIntent() to keep getIntent() up-to-date after potential future recreations.
Q3: Basic What Intent flags would you use to implement a logout flow where the user cannot go Back to the account screens?
FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK combined with FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK:
intent.flags = Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK or Intent.FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TASK
This clears all Activities in the task before starting LoginActivity, so Back press exits the app rather than returning to any account screen.
2D

Fragments

Tier 2 Mod 2
Key Concept: Tier 2 Fragment lifecycle · View lifecycle · FragmentManager · transactions · back stack · communication · Navigation Component
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Quick Revision Sheet

Fragment Lifecycle Order

CallbackView available?Key work
onAttachNoAccess Activity context
onCreateNoInit non-UI, get arguments
onCreateViewCreatingInflate layout, return view
onViewCreatedYes ✅Setup UI, observers, listeners
onDestroyViewDestroyedNull binding (_binding = null)
onDestroyNoFragment object cleanup

Critical Rules

  • observe(viewLifecycleOwner) — NEVER observe(this) in Fragment
  • _binding = null in onDestroyView — ALWAYS for ViewBinding Fragments
  • Arguments via Bundle/Safe Args — NEVER constructor parameters
  • childFragmentManager for nested Fragments — NEVER supportFragmentManager
  • Shared state → activityViewModels()
  • One-shot results → Fragment Result API

ViewModel Scope

DelegateScopeUse
viewModels()This FragmentFragment-private state
activityViewModels()Host ActivityShared between sibling Fragments
viewModels({ requireParentFragment() })Parent FragmentNested Fragment → parent sharing
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Pitfall 1: Observing with 'this' Instead of viewLifecycleOwner

❌ Bad — potential duplicate observers

// 'this' is the Fragment object lifecycle
// When Fragment goes to back stack: View destroyed but Fragment lives
// When returning: onCreateView() called again — new observer added
// Now TWO observers active — duplicate updates
viewModel.products.observe(this) { ... }

✅ Good — tied to View lifecycle

// viewLifecycleOwner starts fresh each onCreateView
// Auto-removed in onDestroyView — no duplicates
viewModel.products.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { ... }

Pitfall 2: ViewBinding Memory Leak

❌ Bad — binding holds View reference

private lateinit var binding: FragmentBinding

override fun onCreateView(...): View {
    binding = FragmentBinding.inflate(inflater)
    return binding.root
    // binding never nulled — leaks View after back stack
}

✅ Good — null in onDestroyView

private var _binding: FragmentBinding? = null
private val binding get() = _binding!!

override fun onDestroyView() {
    super.onDestroyView()
    _binding = null   // releases View reference
}

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Accessing view in onCreate(): View is not created yet — always use onViewCreated().
  • Fragment constructor arguments: Never pass arguments to Fragment constructors. Use Fragment.newInstance() with a Bundle or Safe Args. On recreation, the framework uses the no-arg constructor — custom constructors cause crashes.
  • commitAllowingStateLoss(): Called after onSaveInstanceState — state loss means the Fragment transaction may be lost. Use commit() and ensure transactions happen at the right lifecycle moment.
  • Nested fragments with wrong FragmentManager: Always use childFragmentManager for nested Fragments (inside another Fragment), not parentFragmentManager or supportFragmentManager.
  • Duplicate Fragments after rotation: Not using tags + findFragmentByTag before add creates duplicates after system-restored Fragments.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What is the Fragment lifecycle and how does it differ from Activity lifecycle?
Fragment lifecycle has extra steps: onAttach (before onCreate), onCreateView (inflate layout), onViewCreated (view ready — most setup goes here), onDestroyView (view destroyed, Fragment may stay alive on back stack), and onDetach (after onDestroy). The key difference from Activity: a Fragment has two separate lifecycles — the Fragment object and its View. The Activity has only one lifecycle. Fragment's View is destroyed when it goes on the back stack, while the Fragment object persists.
Q2: Basic What is viewLifecycleOwner and why is it important?
viewLifecycleOwner is the LifecycleOwner tied to the Fragment's View lifecycle (created in onCreateView, destroyed in onDestroyView). It is different from the Fragment itself as a LifecycleOwner (which lives longer). Using viewLifecycleOwner for LiveData/Flow observers ensures the observer is removed in onDestroyView. Using 'this' (the Fragment) keeps observers active between onDestroyView and onCreateView — leading to duplicate observers when the Fragment returns from the back stack.
Q3: Basic How do you pass data to a Fragment correctly?
Use arguments Bundle with companion object newInstance(), or Safe Args via Navigation Component. Never use constructor arguments — the Fragment framework instantiates Fragments using the no-arg constructor on recreation (rotation, process death), so custom constructors cause InstantiationException.
companion object {
    fun newInstance(productId: String) = ProductDetailFragment().apply {
        arguments = Bundle().apply { putString("productId", productId) }
    }
}
// In Fragment: val id = requireArguments().getString("productId")

Intents

Tier 2 Mod 2
Key Concept: Tier 2 Explicit · Implicit · Intent Filters · PendingIntent · Deep Links · App Links
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Quick Revision Sheet

Intent TypeTargetUse CaseRisk
ExplicitExact classIn-app navigation, own ServicesCouples to class name; breaks across modules
ImplicitAction/category/dataShare, dial, open URLNo handler crash; security if not validated
PendingIntentWraps IntentNotifications, AlarmManager, widgetsrequestCode collision; FLAG_MUTABLE misuse

PendingIntent Flags (API 31+ required)

FlagMeaning
FLAG_IMMUTABLEReceiving app cannot modify extras — use by default
FLAG_MUTABLEReceiving app can modify (e.g. inline reply action) — use only when needed
FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENTUpdate existing PendingIntent's extras with new Intent's extras
FLAG_CANCEL_CURRENTCancel existing PendingIntent and create new one
FLAG_ONE_SHOTCan only be used once; after firing, becomes invalid

Deep Link vs App Link

Deep LinkApp Link
SchemeAny (myapp://, https://)HTTPS only
VerificationNoneassetlinks.json on domain
ChooserMay appearNever (direct)
autoVerifyNot setandroid:autoVerify="true"

Golden Rules

  • Always check resolveActivity() before firing implicit Intents
  • PendingIntent API 31+: always add FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE
  • Use TaskStackBuilder for notification PendingIntents to ensure correct back stack
  • Never pass large objects (Bitmap, List) as Intent extras — pass IDs
  • Validate all data in exported components with intent-filters
  • Use FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION when sharing files via FileProvider
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

Implicit Intent with No Handler — Crash

❌ Bad — ActivityNotFoundException

// On devices without an email app — crashes
val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SENDTO)
intent.data = Uri.parse("mailto:support@bank.com")
startActivity(intent)  // CRASH if no handler

✅ Good — check first

val intent = Intent(Intent.ACTION_SENDTO)
intent.data = Uri.parse("mailto:support@bank.com")
if (intent.resolveActivity(packageManager) != null) {
    startActivity(intent)
} else {
    showToast("No email app found")
}

PendingIntent — Missing FLAG_IMMUTABLE (API 31+)

API 31+ requires PendingIntent to explicitly specify FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE. Omitting this throws IllegalArgumentException. Almost always use FLAG_IMMUTABLE unless the PendingIntent needs to be modified by the receiving app (e.g. Android Auto inline replies).

Other Critical Pitfalls

  • Passing large objects via Intent extras: Intents go through the Binder IPC buffer (1 MB limit). Passing large Bitmaps or lists causes TransactionTooLargeException. Pass IDs and load data in the target component.
  • Receiving implicit Intents in unexported components: On API 31+, any component with an intent-filter must declare android:exported="true|false" explicitly or the app won't install.
  • Not using FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION: When sharing files via FileProvider, the receiving app needs temporary permission to read the URI. Missing this causes permission denied on the target app.
  • Deep link not handled after process death: If the Activity is killed and relaunched via a deep link, intent.data must be parsed in onCreate — not just in onNewIntent. Both paths must be handled.
  • PendingIntent requestCode collision: Using the same requestCode for different PendingIntents causes FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT to overwrite the previous one's extras. Use unique requestCodes (e.g., notification ID or entity ID hashCode).
Security best practice for implicit Intents received: Validate all data received via Intent. An implicit Intent can be sent by any app. Never trust extras without validation — especially in components marked android:exported="true".
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What is the difference between an explicit and an implicit Intent?
Explicit Intent specifies the exact component (Activity/Service class name) to start. Used for in-app navigation. Implicit Intent specifies an action (e.g. ACTION_SEND) and optional data type/category. The OS resolves which app/component can handle it based on manifest intent-filters. The system shows a chooser if multiple apps match.
Q2: Basic What is a PendingIntent and when is it used?
A PendingIntent is a token wrapping an Intent that grants another process the ability to execute it with your app's permissions, even when your app is not running. Used for: notification taps (NotificationCompat), scheduled alarms (AlarmManager), widget interactions, and deferred system actions. API 31+ requires FLAG_IMMUTABLE or FLAG_MUTABLE explicitly.
Q3: Basic What happens if you try to start an implicit Intent with no handler?
ActivityNotFoundException is thrown at runtime, crashing the app. Fix: always call intent.resolveActivity(packageManager) first and handle the null case gracefully. Note: On Android 11+ (API 30), resolveActivity() requires a <queries> element in the manifest for non-system apps to be visible.
3A

App Startup

Tier 1 Mod 3
Key Concept: Tier 1 · Senior Differentiator Zygote · SystemServer · AMS/ATMS · PMS · WMS · ActivityThread · Application Creation
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Revision Sheet (Quick Memory Anchors)

  • Zygote: Pre-loaded ART template process; creates app processes via fork() using Copy-on-Write (COW).
  • ActivityThread: Main entry point of the app process containing public static void main().
  • Execution Order: Zygote.fork() → ActivityThread.main() → Looper.prepareMainLooper() → ContentProvider.onCreate() → Application.onCreate() → Activity.onCreate() → Activity.onResume() → ViewRootImpl.performTraversals().
  • SurfaceFlinger: System-wide compositor process that accepts rendered graphic buffers from apps and outputs them to the display hardware.
  • Startup Types: Cold (> process creation), Warm (process alive, recreate Activity), Hot (Activity brought to top).
  • Optimization: Baseline Profiles, Jetpack App Startup, Deferring SDKs to Dispatchers.Default/IO, reportFullyDrawn().
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls & Memory/Performance Traps

1. ContentProvider Auto-Initialization Abuse: Many third-party libraries (e.g., Firebase, WorkManager, LeakCanary) use hidden ContentProviders to initialize themselves automatically. Their onCreate() runs on the Main thread before Application.onCreate(), causing hidden 200–500ms lag. Use tools:node="remove" in manifest and initialize manually if needed.
2. Synchronous Disk I/O & SharedPreferences: Reading large SharedPreferences or calling Room/SQLite on the main thread during Application.onCreate() blocks ART while loading DEX code, causing micro-jank and ANR risk.
3. Complex Custom Splash Activities: Using an explicit SplashActivity that calls startActivity() to transition to MainActivity creates an extra process overhead and adds 100–300ms delay. Use the official androidx.core:core-splashscreen library.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: BASIC 1. What is the entry point method of an Android application process?
The entry point is ActivityThread.main(String[] args). It initializes the Main Looper, creates the ActivityThread instance, attaches to ATMS, and begins the main Looper.loop() message processing pump.
Q2: BASIC 2. What is the role of Zygote in Android startup?
Zygote is a daemon process pre-loaded with core Android framework classes and native libraries. Instead of booting an ART VM from scratch for every app, Android forks the Zygote process using Copy-On-Write memory, saving RAM and slashing process boot time.
Q3: BASIC 3. What are the three types of app starts, and which is slowest?
Cold start (slowest — creates new process and VM from scratch), Warm start (process exists, recreates Activity), and Hot start (fastest — brings existing in-memory Activity to the foreground).
3B

Main Thread Internals

Tier 1 Mod 3
Key Concept: Tier 1 · Core Framework Internals Main Thread · UI Thread · Looper · MessageQueue · Handler · Epoll · Choreographer
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Revision Sheet (Quick Memory Anchors)

  • Looper: One per thread (stored in ThreadLocal); loops forever calling MessageQueue.next().
  • MessageQueue: Priority queue linked list sorted by execution timestamp (when).
  • Handler: Produces messages (sendMessage) and consumes messages (handleMessage / Runnable.run).
  • Linux Epoll: nativePollOnce() sleeps the thread; nativeWake() wakes it up via eventfd.
  • Message Pooling: Message.obtain() reuses instances from a linked list pool (max 50) to avoid GC churn.
  • Choreographer: Coordinates animation, input, and traversal callbacks synced to display VSYNC pulses.
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls & Memory Leak Traps

1. Non-Static Inner Handler Memory Leaks: Defining an anonymous inner Handler inside an Activity retains an implicit reference to the Activity.this. If a message is posted with a 10-minute delay (postDelayed), the message in the global MessageQueue holds a reference to the Handler, which in turn holds the Activity, leaking the entire Activity hierarchy.
2. ANR (Application Not Responding): The Main thread looper must process every message in < 5 seconds (for input events, < 5000ms). If a single message blocks the thread on disk/DB/network, subsequent touch event messages pile up unhandled, triggering an ANR dialog.
3. Forgetting to Quit Background HandlerThreads: HandlerThread.start() creates an infinite loop. Failing to call handlerThread.quitSafely() when the owning component is destroyed permanently leaks the underlying OS thread and memory.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: BASIC 1. What are the four core components of Android's message handling mechanism?
The four components are Message (the data packet/task), MessageQueue (the chronological queue), Looper (the infinite pump iterating through the queue), and Handler (the interface to enqueue and process messages).
Q2: BASIC 2. Can a standard background thread have a Looper?
Yes. By default, standard Java/Kotlin threads do not have a Looper. You can attach one by calling Looper.prepare() followed by Looper.loop(), or by using the built-in HandlerThread class.
Q3: BASIC 3. Why is Message.obtain() preferred over new Message()?
Message.obtain() retrieves a recycled Message instance from a global object pool (holding up to 50 items). This prevents continuous object allocation and garbage collection churn during high-frequency events like touches or animations.
3C

Binder & IPC

Tier 1 Mod 3
Key Concept: Tier 1 · Architecture Core Binder Driver · IPC · AIDL · Parcelable · ServiceManager · Memory Mapping (mmap)
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Revision Sheet (Quick Memory Anchors)

  • Binder: Single-copy Linux kernel IPC driver using mmap().
  • Buffer Limit: ~1MB (1016 KB) shared across all in-flight transactions per process.
  • AIDL: Generates Proxy (marshals to Parcel, calls transact) and Stub (unmarshals in onTransact).
  • Security: Binder.getCallingUid() / Binder.getCallingPid() validated at the kernel level.
  • Death Recipient: IBinder.linkToDeath() notifies client when remote process terminates.
  • Oneway: Keyword for non-blocking asynchronous calls (no return value, cannot throw remote exceptions).
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls & TransactionTooLargeException

1. TransactionTooLargeException (The 1MB Binder Limit): The total in-flight Binder buffer across ALL transactions in a process is capped at ~1MB (1016 KB). Passing large Bitmaps, large JSON strings, or large lists through Intent.putExtra() or AIDL will instantly crash with TransactionTooLargeException. Always pass small IDs, URIs, or use SharedMemory/CursorWindow.
2. Blocking the UI Thread with Synchronous IPC: AIDL calls are synchronous and blocking by default. If the remote service is busy or deadlocked, the client's calling thread will freeze. Never call AIDL methods on the Main thread.
3. Forgetting oneway for Fire-and-Forget Calls: If you don't need a return value, use the oneway AIDL keyword. Oneway transactions are asynchronous and non-blocking.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: BASIC 1. What is Binder in Android?
Binder is Android's core Inter-Process Communication (IPC) and Remote Procedure Call (RPC) mechanism. It allows sandboxed processes to call methods on remote objects located in other processes as if they were local.
Q2: BASIC 2. What is AIDL and why is it used?
AIDL (Android Interface Definition Language) is an IDL used to define the programming interface that both the client and service agree upon to communicate across processes via IPC. It automatically generates the boilerplate Proxy and Stub code.
Q3: BASIC 3. What causes a TransactionTooLargeException?
It occurs when data passed via Binder (in an Intent or AIDL call) exceeds the 1MB buffer limit shared across all active Binder transactions in that process.
3D

Process Model

Tier 1 Mod 3
Key Concept: Tier 1 · Senior Architecture Process Priority · oom_adj / oom_score_adj · LMK · Application Sandbox · UID · ANR Internals
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Revision Sheet (Quick Memory Anchors)

  • Sandbox: Linux UID per app; files in /data/data/<package> restricted by OS permissions.
  • oom_score_adj: -1000 (System) to 1000 (Cached background). High score killed first.
  • LMKD: User-space daemon sending SIGKILL when RAM is low. No lifecycle callbacks execute.
  • State Survives Death: SavedStateHandle, onSaveInstanceState, Room/DataStore.
  • ANR Timeouts: 5s (Input), 10s (Foreground Broadcast), 60s (Background Broadcast), 200s (Foreground Service).
  • Multi-Process (android:process): Re-runs Application.onCreate(); no shared memory; isolated heaps.
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls & Common Mistakes

1. Relying on Static Singletons for Transient State: A common architectural mistake is storing authentication tokens or user drafts in global Kotlin object Singletons. When the app is in the background and the OS kills the process, the user returns and the Activity restarts with null Singleton fields, resulting in NullPointerException or silent logout.
2. Expecting onDestroy() to Run Before Process Death: Never write cleanup or database commits inside onDestroy() expecting them to execute during low memory termination. onDestroy() is skipped entirely during LMK SIGKILL. Commit important state in onPause() / onStop() or write to disk.
3. Multi-Process Application.onCreate() Duplication: Adding android:process=":remote" to a Service causes the entire Application.onCreate() to run twice (once per process). If you initialize Firebase, Room, or DI graphs globally in Application.onCreate() without checking the current process name, you waste memory and cause database lock conflicts.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: BASIC 1. What determines which process Android terminates when RAM is low?
The Low Memory Killer daemon (lmkd) uses the process's oom_score_adj value. Processes with higher scores (such as cached background apps with no visible components, score 900–1000) are killed first.
Q2: BASIC 2. Does Activity.onDestroy() run when an app is killed due to low memory?
No. When LMK kills a background process, the kernel sends an immediate SIGKILL. The process terminates instantly without executing any cleanup or lifecycle callbacks like onDestroy() or Application.onTerminate().
Q3: BASIC 3. What is the ANR timeout for user touch input?
5 seconds. If the Main thread fails to process an input event (such as a tap or keypress) within 5 seconds, an ANR dialog is triggered.
4A

ViewModel

Tier 1 Mod 4
Key Concept: Tier 1 · Architecture Core ViewModel · ViewModelStore · ViewModelProvider · viewModelScope · SavedStateHandle · NonConfigurationInstances
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Revision Sheet (Quick Memory Anchors)

  • ViewModel: Survives rotation; dies on finish() or process death.
  • ViewModelStore: Internal map (Map<String, ViewModel>) retained across rotations.
  • viewModelScope: Built-in CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate) cancelled in onCleared().
  • SavedStateHandle: Key-value store surviving both rotation AND process death.
  • Leak Rule: Never store View, Fragment, or Activity references in a ViewModel.
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls & Memory Leak Traps

1. Holding References to Context / Activity / Views: Never pass an Activity, Fragment, View, or Context (except ApplicationContext via AndroidViewModel) into a ViewModel. When the Activity rotates, the old Activity is destroyed; if the ViewModel retains it, the entire Activity hierarchy leaks in RAM.
2. Creating ViewModel Instances with new / constructor directly: Calling val vm = MyViewModel() directly bypasses the ViewModelProvider and ViewModelStore. The instance will NOT survive rotation and viewModelScope will not be lifecycle-managed.
3. Storing Massive Lists in SavedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle writes to the OS onSaveInstanceState bundle. Saving 5MB of cached product JSON into it will trigger a fatal TransactionTooLargeException.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: BASIC 1. Why does ViewModel survive screen rotation while Activity does not?
Because during configuration change, ComponentActivity retains its ViewModelStore via the platform's retainNonConfigurationInstances() mechanism. The newly created Activity retrieves this retained store and re-attaches the existing ViewModel instances.
Q2: BASIC 2. When is ViewModel.onCleared() called?
It is called when the owning ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity/Fragment) is permanently destroyed (e.g. user presses Back, finish() is called, or Fragment is popped off the back stack) — NOT during configuration changes.
Q3: BASIC 3. What dispatcher does viewModelScope use by default?
It uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate backed by a SupervisorJob().
4B

LiveData

Tier 1 Mod 4
Key Concept: Tier 1 · Architecture Core Lifecycle Awareness · Observer Pattern · setValue vs postValue · MediatorLiveData · LiveData vs StateFlow
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Revision Sheet (Quick Memory Anchors)

  • Active States: STARTED and RESUMED.
  • Auto Cleanup: Removed on DESTROYED.
  • setValue: Main thread only, synchronous, immediate dispatch.
  • postValue: Any thread, asynchronous, posts to Main Looper, conflates rapid calls.
  • Fragment Rule: Always use viewLifecycleOwner.
  • MediatorLiveData: Combines multiple LiveData sources into one.
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls & Memory Leak Traps

1. Using this instead of viewLifecycleOwner in Fragments: In Fragments, observing LiveData using this (Fragment instance) instead of viewLifecycleOwner creates duplicate observers on every navigation return because the Fragment view is destroyed on onDestroyView() but the Fragment instance lives on in the back stack!
2. Missing Emissions with Rapid postValue(): postValue() only holds the latest value in mPendingData. If you emit progress updates (1%, 2%, 3%) in a tight loop via postValue(), intermediate values will be skipped.
3. Using LiveData in Repositories or Domain Layer: LiveData is tied to the Android framework UI thread. Putting LiveData inside pure domain models or data layers breaks clean architecture and unit testability.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: BASIC 1. What does it mean that LiveData is lifecycle-aware?
It means LiveData respects the lifecycle state of components like Activities and Fragments, only emitting updates to active observers (STARTED or RESUMED) and automatically cleaning up observers when the component is DESTROYED.
Q2: BASIC 2. What is the difference between setValue() and postValue()?
setValue() must be called from the Main thread and executes immediately. postValue() can be called from background threads and posts a task to the Main thread's message queue to execute setValue().
Q3: BASIC 3. What lifecycle owner should be used when observing LiveData inside a Fragment?
Always use viewLifecycleOwner. Using the Fragment instance (this) leads to duplicate observers and memory leaks when the Fragment's view is destroyed and recreated on the back stack.
4C

Lifecycle

Tier 1 Mod 4
Key Concept: Tier 1 · Architecture Core LifecycleOwner · DefaultLifecycleObserver · lifecycleScope · repeatOnLifecycle · flowWithLifecycle
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Revision Sheet (Quick Memory Anchors)

  • LifecycleOwner: Produces Lifecycle events and tracks current state.
  • DefaultLifecycleObserver: Preferred interface for lifecycle callbacks (replaces annotations).
  • repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED): Cancels on ON_STOP, restarts on ON_START.
  • launchWhenStarted: Deprecated (pauses consumer, keeps upstream flow alive).
  • collectAsStateWithLifecycle(): Compose-native lifecycle-safe flow collector.
  • ProcessLifecycleOwner: Tracks app-wide foreground / background transitions.
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls & Memory Leak Traps

1. Using launchWhenStarted with Cold Flows: launchWhenStarted does not cancel the coroutine when the app goes into the background; it merely suspends the receiver. If collecting a cold flow emitting location updates or database queries, the producer continues running in the background, causing severe battery drain.
2. Collecting Multiple Flows in a Single repeatOnLifecycle without child launches: Putting two sequential flowA.collect() and flowB.collect() inside a single repeatOnLifecycle block will cause flowB to never start because flowA.collect() suspends indefinitely! Each flow collection must be wrapped in its own launch { ... } inside the block.
3. Using Deprecated @OnLifecycleEvent Annotation: The annotation-based lifecycle observer requires reflection or KAPT code generation at runtime. Always implement DefaultLifecycleObserver.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: BASIC 1. What is a LifecycleOwner in Android?
A LifecycleOwner is an interface implemented by components that have an Android lifecycle (such as ComponentActivity and Fragment). It exposes a getLifecycle() method returning a Lifecycle object.
Q2: BASIC 2. Why is DefaultLifecycleObserver preferred over @OnLifecycleEvent?
DefaultLifecycleObserver uses direct interface method overrides, avoiding the runtime reflection overhead and annotation-processing compilation penalties of the deprecated @OnLifecycleEvent annotation.
Q3: BASIC 3. When does lifecycleScope get cancelled?
lifecycleScope is tied directly to the LifecycleOwner and is cancelled automatically when the lifecycle reaches the Lifecycle.State.DESTROYED state.
5A

Coroutines Fundamentals

Tier 1 Mod 5
Key Concept: What a coroutine is, how it differs from a thread, CoroutineScope, CoroutineContext, Job, and Dispatchers — the core concepts every Android engineer must own.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Thread vs Coroutine

Thread: ~1-2 MB stack, OS-managed
Coroutine: ~few hundred bytes, heap

Thread.sleep() → blocks thread
delay()        → suspends coroutine

Threads: thousands max
Coroutines: 100,000+ ok

CoroutineContext operators

val ctx = Dispatchers.IO + Job()
// + creates new context
// [key] retrieves element
ctx[Job]          // the Job
ctx[Dispatcher]   // IO

Job states

New → Active → Completing
             ↓
         Cancelling → Cancelled
             ↓
          Completed

Dispatcher selection

Main      → UI updates
IO        → Network, DB, Files
Default   → CPU work (sort, parse)
Unconfined→ Tests / special cases
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common mistakes

Pitfall 1 — Blocking the main thread
Calling Thread.sleep() or blocking network code on Dispatchers.Main freezes the UI. Always use delay() inside coroutines and withContext(Dispatchers.IO) for I/O.
Pitfall 2 — Leaking coroutines with GlobalScope
GlobalScope.launch creates coroutines that live forever — they outlive Activities, ViewModels, even the app screen. Use viewModelScope or lifecycleScope.
Pitfall 3 — Creating a new Job in scope
viewModelScope.launch(Job()) { ... } breaks structured concurrency — the new Job has no parent, so cancellation from the scope won't propagate to this child. Never add a raw Job to a launch/async call; use SupervisorJob at scope level.
Best Practice — Inject Dispatchers
Never hardcode Dispatchers.IO directly in production classes. Inject a CoroutineDispatcher interface so tests can inject TestCoroutineDispatcher. 
// ✅ Testable — inject dispatcher
class UserRepository(
    private val api: UserApi,
    private val ioDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO
) {
    suspend fun getUser(id: String) = withContext(ioDispatcher) {
        api.fetchUser(id)
    }
}
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is a coroutine and how does it differ from a thread?
Basic⌄
A coroutine is a suspendable computation — it can pause at suspension points (marked with suspend) without blocking its thread. State is saved on the heap via a Continuation object. Threads are OS-managed with 1–2 MB stacks; coroutines cost ~hundreds of bytes and are library-managed, making 100,000 concurrent coroutines feasible.
What is CoroutineContext and what elements does it contain?
Basic⌄
CoroutineContext is an immutable indexed set of elements. Key elements: Job (lifecycle, parent-child links), ContinuationInterceptor / Dispatcher (which thread to run on), CoroutineName (debugging), CoroutineExceptionHandler (uncaught error handling). Combine them with + operator.
Which Dispatcher would you use for a database query and why?
Basic⌄
Dispatchers.IO. It uses a thread pool optimised for blocking I/O with up to 64 threads (+ CPU count), so blocking JDBC/file calls don't starve CPU threads. For Room with suspend DAO functions, Room handles the dispatcher internally. For custom blocking calls, wrap with withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
How does the Kotlin compiler implement suspend functions? Walk through the transformation.
Intermediate⌄
The compiler performs Continuation-Passing Style (CPS) transformation. Each suspend function gets an extra Continuation<T> parameter and becomes a state machine. Each suspension point is a label. On suspension, local variables are stored in the Continuation (heap), the function returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, freeing the thread. On resume, the dispatcher calls continuation.resume(value) and execution picks up at the saved label.
Why should you never use GlobalScope in Android?
Intermediate⌄
GlobalScope has no parent Job and lives for the entire app process. Coroutines launched in it are never automatically cancelled — they survive screen rotations, ViewModel clears, and even back navigation. This causes memory leaks, duplicate API calls, and crashes when coroutines try to update destroyed UI components. Use viewModelScope or lifecycleScope instead.
What is the difference between Dispatchers.IO and Dispatchers.Default? When does it matter?
Intermediate⌄
Since Kotlin 1.7, both share the same thread pool internally. The difference is the concurrency limit: Default limits to CPU count (e.g., 8 on an 8-core device) — suitable for CPU-bound work where more parallelism adds contention. IO allows up to 64 + CPU threads — suitable for blocking I/O where threads spend most time waiting. Using IO for CPU work wastes threads; using Default for I/O creates bottlenecks.
Why should dispatchers be injected rather than referenced directly?
Intermediate⌄
Hardcoded Dispatchers.IO makes unit tests non-deterministic and slow because tests run on real thread pools. By injecting a CoroutineDispatcher interface, tests can provide StandardTestDispatcher or UnconfinedTestDispatcher which give full control over execution. This also makes classes more composable — a caller can provide a dispatcher matching their concurrency model.
A coroutine in a banking app is processing a payment when the user rotates the device. The ViewModel is recreated. What happens and why?
Senior⌄
The ViewModel survives rotation (it's not destroyed), so viewModelScope coroutines continue running undisturbed. The new Activity attaches to the same ViewModel and its StateFlow/LiveData re-emits the current state. If the ViewModel were cleared (e.g., user navigates away), viewModelScope is cancelled, which cancels all children cooperatively. For critical financial operations that must complete regardless, they should be delegated to a WorkManager task or a Service scope — not tied to the ViewModel's lifecycle.
Explain how parent-child Job relationships work in structured concurrency.
Senior⌄
When a coroutine is launched inside a scope, the new coroutine's Job becomes a child of the scope's Job. This creates a hierarchy: cancelling a parent cancels all children; a parent won't complete until all children complete; a child failure propagates up and cancels siblings (unless using SupervisorJob). This tree structure is the core of structured concurrency — no coroutine can outlive its scope, preventing leaks. The child coroutine inherits the parent's CoroutineContext but replaces the Job element with its own new Job.
Design a coroutine scope for a Repository that should survive configuration changes but not the app process exit. Justify your choices.
Senior⌄
Use a custom scope tied to the ViewModel or application component: val scope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.IO + exceptionHandler). SupervisorJob ensures one failed child (e.g., one fetch failing) doesn't cancel the others. Dispatchers.IO is the default for repository work. Inject this scope via Hilt using @ApplicationScoped for app-level repositories, or let ViewModel provide it via viewModelScope for UI-bound repos. For true process-level durability (crash recovery), delegate to WorkManager.
5B

Builders &amp; Dispatchers

Tier 1 Mod 5
Key Concept: launch , async/await , withContext , runBlocking — when each builder fits, plus dispatcher internals and thread pool selection.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Builder summary

launch { }     → Job (fire&forget)
async { }      → Deferred<T>
withContext(D) → T (inline switch)
runBlocking { }→ T (blocks thread)

Parallel pattern

coroutineScope {
  val a = async { fetchA() }
  val b = async { fetchB() }
  Result(a.await(), b.await())
}

Dispatcher quick ref

Main    → UI (1 thread)
IO      → I/O (64+nCPU max)
Default → CPU (nCPU max)
IO.limitedParallelism(4)
        → custom pool view

Common mistake

// ❌ Sequential — NOT parallel
val a = async { .. }.await()
val b = async { .. }.await()

// ✅ Parallel
val da = async { .. }
val db = async { .. }
da.await(); db.await()
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — async without await loses exceptions
If you create a Deferred and never call .await(), any exception thrown inside the async block is silently ignored until await() is called. Always await() inside a try/catch or use coroutineScope.
Pitfall 2 — withContext inside async adds unnecessary nesting
async { withContext(IO) { ... } } — just use async(Dispatchers.IO) { ... }. The dispatcher can be passed directly to the builder.
Pitfall 3 — runBlocking in tests with real delay()
runBlocking { delay(5000) } actually waits 5 seconds in tests. Use runTest from kotlinx-coroutines-test which uses a virtual clock and skips delays.
Best Practice — coroutineScope for structured parallel work
Always wrap parallel async calls in coroutineScope { } or supervisorScope { } rather than launching them in the outer scope. This ensures all parallel work completes (or fails) before the enclosing function returns.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What does launch return and when would you use it?
Basic⌄
launch returns a Job. Use it for fire-and-forget operations where you don't need a result — updating UI state from a ViewModel, sending analytics events, triggering a background sync. You can call job.cancel() to stop it early.
What is the difference between async and withContext?
Basic⌄
async creates a new child coroutine that runs concurrently — it starts immediately and returns a Deferred<T> you later await(). withContext suspends the current coroutine, switches to the given context, does the work sequentially, then returns the result directly — no new coroutine, no Deferred. Use async for parallel work, withContext for dispatcher switching.
Why is runBlocking forbidden in Android production code?
Basic⌄
runBlocking blocks the calling thread until all coroutines inside complete. If called on the main thread, it freezes the UI — causing ANR if it takes more than ~5 seconds. If called on a Dispatcher.IO thread, it wastes a thread from the pool. It is only appropriate in tests (runTest is better) and in non-Android main() entry points.
How would you run two API calls in parallel and wait for both results?
Intermediate⌄
Use coroutineScope { } with two async blocks: val a = async { api.fetchA() }; val b = async { api.fetchB() } — both start immediately and run in parallel. Then val result = Result(a.await(), b.await()). The coroutineScope wrapper ensures both complete before returning, and if either fails, both are cancelled.
What is Dispatchers.Unconfined and when should you use it?
Intermediate⌄
Dispatchers.Unconfined runs the coroutine on the current thread until the first suspension point, then resumes on whatever thread the suspending function uses. It has no thread confinement. In production, this is unpredictable — avoid it. In tests, it can be useful as it executes eagerly, similar to UnconfinedTestDispatcher.
What happens if an async block throws and you never call await()?
Intermediate⌄
The exception is stored in the Deferred and only re-thrown when .await() is called. If you never call await(), the exception is silently swallowed in most cases — except when using coroutineScope or when the Deferred is part of a structured scope that completes. This is a dangerous pattern; always ensure every async result is either awaited or explicitly cancelled.
What is limitedParallelism() and when would you use it in production?
Intermediate⌄
Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(n) creates a view of the IO dispatcher that caps concurrent coroutines at n. Use it to match a resource pool size — e.g., if your JDBC connection pool has 4 connections, use limitedParallelism(4) for database coroutines. Without it, 64 IO threads compete for 4 connections, causing timeout cascades under load.
Design the concurrency strategy for a checkout flow that must: (1) validate stock, (2) charge payment, (3) update inventory, (4) send confirmation email — where steps 1+2 can be parallel but 3+4 depend on both completing successfully.
Senior⌄
Use structured concurrency: coroutineScope { val stockOk = async { validateStock() }; val charged = async { chargePayment() }; val (s, c) = stockOk.await() to charged.await() }. If either fails, the other is cancelled. Then sequentially: updateInventory(s, c); sendConfirmation(c). Steps 3 and 4 are sequential because inventory must be updated before confirmation is accurate. Wrap the whole thing in try/catch for rollback logic. Use coroutineScope not supervisorScope here — partial success in checkout is a business error.
Explain how the Kotlin compiler optimises withContext when called back-to-back on the same dispatcher.
Senior⌄
The Kotlin coroutine runtime performs fast-path optimisation: if the current dispatcher is already the target dispatcher, withContext does not create a new coroutine or do any thread switching — it executes inline. This means withContext(Dispatchers.Main) called from a Main dispatcher coroutine has near-zero overhead. The check happens in ContinuationInterceptor.isDispatchNeeded() — if it returns false, the block runs directly.
A junior developer wrote: async(Dispatchers.IO) { fetchData() }.await() at the top level of a ViewModel function. What are the issues and how would you fix it?
Senior⌄
Issues: (1) async { }.await() immediately is functionally identical to withContext but creates unnecessary overhead (new coroutine, Deferred allocation). (2) If this is directly in a suspend fun or launch block without coroutineScope, exceptions from the async may not propagate correctly to the parent. Fix: replace with withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { fetchData() } — semantically identical but correct and efficient. If real parallelism is needed, wrap in coroutineScope and keep multiple async blocks un-awaited until all are launched.
5C

Structured Concurrency &amp; Key Differences

Tier 1 Mod 5
Key Concept: The hierarchy: CoroutineScope → CoroutineContext → Job → children. Plus the most-asked comparison questions: launch vs async, coroutineScope vs supervisorScope, Job vs SupervisorJob, delay vs Thread.sleep.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Scope comparison

coroutineScope  → Job (fail = cancel all)
supervisorScope → SupervisorJob (fail = isolated)
viewModelScope  → SupervisorJob + Main
lifecycleScope  → SupervisorJob + Main

delay vs Thread.sleep

delay(1000)       // suspend, frees thread
Thread.sleep(1000)// blocks thread
                  // use delay() always

Cancellation flow

cancel() → CancellationException
         → flows DOWN to children
         → does NOT flow up to parent

Exception → flows UP to parent
          → cancels ALL siblings

withContext vs async

withContext(IO) { }    // sequential
                       // no Deferred
async(IO) { }.await()  // concurrent
                       // use for parallel
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Breaking hierarchy with a new Job
launch(Job()) { } — adding a new Job as the coroutine context disconnects the child from the parent's job. Cancelling the parent won't cancel this child. Never pass a raw Job() to launch or async.
Pitfall 2 — SupervisorJob in the wrong place
launch(SupervisorJob()) { child1; child2 } — the SupervisorJob here is the parent of the launched coroutine, not of child1/child2. Use supervisorScope { } inside to get the supervisor semantics for children.
Best Practice — coroutineScope for suspend functions
Any suspend fun that launches multiple coroutines should use coroutineScope { } or supervisorScope { } to define a proper boundary. This makes the function's concurrency observable and its lifecycle tied to the call site.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is structured concurrency and why does it matter?
Basic⌄
Structured concurrency is the guarantee that every coroutine belongs to a scope and cannot outlive it. When a scope is cancelled, all coroutines inside are cancelled too. This prevents coroutine leaks — the most common async bug before structured concurrency, where coroutines would hold references to destroyed UI components.
What is the difference between delay() and Thread.sleep()?
Basic⌄
delay() is a suspend function: it suspends the coroutine, freeing the thread to run other coroutines, and resumes after the specified time. It also respects cancellation — if the coroutine is cancelled during a delay, a CancellationException is thrown. Thread.sleep() blocks the OS thread entirely for the duration — other coroutines on that thread can't run, and it cannot be cancelled cooperatively.
What is the difference between coroutineScope and supervisorScope?
Basic⌄
coroutineScope uses a regular Job: if any child fails, all siblings are cancelled and the exception propagates to the caller. supervisorScope uses a SupervisorJob: each child is independent; a failure in one does not affect others. Use coroutineScope for all-or-nothing (transactions), supervisorScope for partial-results-ok (dashboard loading).
What is the difference between launch and async in terms of exception handling?
Intermediate⌄
With launch, exceptions propagate immediately to the parent Job. With async, the exception is stored in the Deferred and only re-thrown when .await() is called. This means you can use try/catch around await(). However, in a coroutineScope, even async exceptions cancel siblings when the scope is cancelled — the storage is temporary until you await.
Why does adding a new Job() to a launch call break structured concurrency?
Intermediate⌄
When you do scope.launch(Job()) { }, the new Job replaces the parent Job in the context — disconnecting the child from the parent's lifecycle. Cancelling the scope no longer cancels this child. It becomes an orphaned coroutine. The fix is to never pass a raw Job to builders. If you need isolation, use supervisorScope at the scope level instead.
How does cancellation propagation differ from exception propagation?
Intermediate⌄
Cancellation (via cancel()) sends a CancellationException downward — it cancels children but not the parent. The parent continues after cancelling a child. Non-cancellation exceptions propagate upward — they cancel the parent and all siblings. This asymmetry is deliberate: cancellation is a normal lifecycle event (user navigated away), while exceptions indicate unexpected failures that should abort the whole operation.
When would you choose supervisorScope over coroutineScope in a ViewModel?
Intermediate⌄
Use supervisorScope when loading multiple independent data sources for the same screen (e.g., user profile + recommendations + ads). If recommendations fail, you still want to show the profile. Use coroutineScope when the data is interdependent (e.g., first get an auth token, then use it to fetch data — token failure should abort the whole flow).
