A coroutine throws an unhandled exception inside supervisorScope but there's no CoroutineExceptionHandler. What happens?
Senior⌄
In a supervisorScope, the failed child's exception is not propagated to siblings or the parent scope. However, it still needs to be handled. If the child was created with launch and has no handler, the exception reaches the global uncaught exception handler — on Android this means a crash. With async, the exception is stored in the Deferred until await(). The correct pattern inside supervisorScope: wrap each child's logic in try/catch, or add a CoroutineExceptionHandler to the child's context.
Explain the 3 guarantees of structured concurrency and how each prevents a common production bug.
Senior⌄
(1) No leaks: coroutines auto-cancel with their scope — prevents callbacks firing after Activity destroy, preventing NPEs and outdated UI updates. (2) Error propagation: failures are never silently dropped — in coroutineScope, a silent failure in one operation doesn't leave the app in an inconsistent partial state. (3) Completion guarantee: parent waits for all children — a function that returns only after all its spawned work is done, preventing data races where callers assume work is complete when it isn't.
Design the concurrency model for a banking dashboard that must show balance (critical), recent transactions (important), and promotional offers (optional). Handle failures gracefully.
Senior⌄
Use supervisorScope for isolation, async with runCatching for each source: val balance = async { runCatching { balanceRepo.get() } } (critical — show error state if fails), val txns = async { runCatching { txnRepo.get() } } (show empty state if fails), val offers = async { runCatching { offerRepo.get() } } (silently omit if fails). All run in parallel. Compose the UI state from the three Results, using fallbacks for non-critical failures. Total latency = max(each call's latency) instead of sum.
5D

Cancellation &amp; Exceptions

Tier 1 Mod 5
Key Concept: Cooperative cancellation, CancellationException, isActive/ensureActive/yield, NonCancellable, exception propagation, CoroutineExceptionHandler, SupervisorJob — everything about keeping coroutines safe.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Cancellation checks

isActive       // check, no throw
ensureActive() // throw if cancelled
yield()        // throw + yield CPU
delay(0)       // also checks

CancellationException rules

// ALWAYS re-throw it!
catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e  // never swallow
}
catch (e: Exception) { handle() }

NonCancellable cleanup

finally {
  withContext(NonCancellable) {
    db.close()    // suspend ok
    audit.log()   // suspend ok
  }
}

ExceptionHandler scope

// ✅ Root coroutine — fires
scope.launch(handler) { throw E() }

// ❌ Child coroutine — no effect
scope.launch {
  launch(handler) { throw E() }
}
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Tight loop without cancellation check
A CPU-intensive loop with no suspension points is not cancellable. Even if you call job.cancel(), the coroutine keeps running until the loop finishes. Fix: add ensureActive() or yield() inside the loop.
Pitfall 2 — Catching CancellationException
Catching Exception or Throwable and not re-throwing will swallow CancellationException, breaking cooperative cancellation — the coroutine continues running after cancel() is called.
Pitfall 3 — Using CoroutineExceptionHandler on child coroutines
CoroutineExceptionHandler only fires on root coroutines (those whose parent is a Job without a coroutine parent, e.g. scope.launch). Adding it to a child launch { } has no effect — exceptions still propagate to the parent.
Best Practice — Always use NonCancellable for critical cleanup
Any suspend call in a finally block needs withContext(NonCancellable) { }. This includes: closing network connections, committing database transactions, writing audit logs, sending analytics events.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What does "cooperative cancellation" mean in coroutines?
Basic⌄
Cancellation is cooperative — the coroutine is not forcefully stopped; instead, calling cancel() marks the Job as cancelling and throws CancellationException at the next suspension point. Code between suspension points runs to completion. If a coroutine has no suspension points (e.g., a tight CPU loop), it cannot be cancelled unless you add explicit checks like ensureActive().
What is CancellationException and how should you handle it?
Basic⌄
CancellationException is a subclass of IllegalStateException used to signal cooperative cancellation. It should always be re-thrown when caught. Catching it with a broad catch (e: Exception) and not rethrowing breaks cancellation — the coroutine continues running after being cancelled. Rule: catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e } always comes first.
When would you use withContext(NonCancellable)?
Basic⌄
When you need to run suspend calls inside a finally block after a coroutine has been cancelled. Normally, any suspension inside a cancelled coroutine throws CancellationException immediately, preventing cleanup. withContext(NonCancellable) overrides this, letting cleanup code (close connections, audit logs, commit transactions) complete even in a cancelled coroutine.
A tight data processing loop is not responding to cancel(). Why and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
The loop has no suspension points — cancellation can only happen at suspension points. Fix: add ensureActive() at the top of each iteration (checks and throws CancellationException if cancelled) or yield() (also yields the thread to other coroutines). For example: for (item in items) { ensureActive(); process(item) }. Both options make the loop respect cancellation.
Where should you place CoroutineExceptionHandler — on the scope, root coroutine, or child coroutine?
Intermediate⌄
On the scope or root coroutine — never on a child coroutine. The handler only fires when an exception has propagated all the way up to the root of the coroutine hierarchy (a coroutine whose parent context is a bare Job, not another coroutine). Adding it to a child launch has no effect — the exception still propagates to the parent.
Does CoroutineExceptionHandler catch exceptions from async { }.await()?
Intermediate⌄
No. The handler only catches exceptions from launch-based coroutines. Exceptions from async { }.await() are re-thrown at the await() call site and must be caught with try/catch there. This is a common misconception — developers add a handler expecting it to catch all errors, but async failures still require local handling.
What is the danger of using runCatching with suspend functions?
Intermediate⌄
runCatching catches ALL exceptions, including CancellationException. If used inside a coroutine, it may silently trap a cancellation signal, breaking cooperative cancellation. The coroutine would continue executing as if nothing happened. Workaround: after calling runCatching, check if the result contains a CancellationException and re-throw it: result.exceptionOrNull()?.let { if (it is CancellationException) throw it }.
Design cancellation-safe order processing for a banking app that must always write an audit log, even when cancelled.
Senior⌄
Structure the processing as: try { processPayment(order) } catch (e: CancellationException) { markOrderCancelled(order); throw e } catch (e: Exception) { markOrderFailed(order, e) } finally { withContext(NonCancellable) { auditLog.write(order) } }. The finally with NonCancellable guarantees the audit log is written regardless of outcome. Re-throwing CancellationException after marking the order cancelled ensures structured concurrency still works. The catch for Exception handles business failures gracefully without breaking cancellation.
Explain why a coroutine can appear "stuck" even after calling scope.cancel().
Senior⌄
Three root causes: (1) The coroutine is in a tight loop with no suspension points — cancellation can't be delivered. Fix: add ensureActive(). (2) The code caught CancellationException and didn't rethrow — the coroutine thinks it's still running normally. Fix: always rethrow CancellationException. (3) The coroutine holds a NonCancellable context from a misused withContext(NonCancellable) not just in finally — if wrapped around a long operation, cancellation is indefinitely blocked. Fix: use NonCancellable only in finally blocks.
What is the difference between ensureActive() and yield() and when would you choose each?
Senior⌄
ensureActive() only checks the cancellation flag and throws CancellationException if cancelled — no suspension, no thread yield. It has minimal overhead and is ideal for high-speed loops that must remain cancellable but should not voluntarily give up the CPU. yield() also throws on cancellation but additionally suspends the coroutine, allowing other coroutines on the same dispatcher to run. Use yield() in CPU-heavy loops that run on a limited pool (Default) where fairness matters — without it, a single heavy coroutine can starve others on the same thread.
5E

Scopes, Concurrency &amp; Testing

Tier 1 Mod 5
Key Concept: lifecycleScope, viewModelScope, custom scopes. Race conditions with Mutex/Semaphore/AtomicInteger. runTest, StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher, virtual time control.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Scope summary

viewModelScope: SupervisorJob+Main
              cancelled in onCleared()
lifecycleScope: cancelled in DESTROYED
  → always use viewLifecycleOwner
repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) for flows

Sync primitives

Mutex()          // exclusive lock (not reentrant)
Semaphore(n)     // limit to N concurrent
AtomicInteger()  // lock-free counter
limitedParallelism(1) // confinement

Test dispatchers

StandardTest  → manual, queued
UnconfinedTest→ eager, runs inline
advanceUntilIdle() // drain all
advanceTimeBy(ms)  // virtual clock

Test template

@Test fun test() = runTest {
  val vm = ViewModel(
    StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler))
  vm.load()
  assertEquals(Loading, vm.state.value)
  advanceUntilIdle()
  assertEquals(Success, vm.state.value)
}
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Mutex deadlock
Never call mutex.withLock from inside another mutex.withLock on the same Mutex. Unlike Java's reentrant locks, Kotlin's Mutex is NOT reentrant — it will deadlock.
Pitfall 2 — repeatOnLifecycle vs launchWhenStarted
launchWhenStarted (deprecated) pauses collection but does NOT cancel the upstream flow — the producer keeps emitting. repeatOnLifecycle cancels and re-starts the entire collector, stopping the upstream producer. Always use repeatOnLifecycle.
Pitfall 3 — runTest vs runBlocking in tests
Using runBlocking in tests runs coroutines with real time — delay(5000) waits 5 real seconds. Use runTest which uses virtual time — all delays are skipped unless you explicitly advance.
Best Practice — Prefer single-thread confinement over Mutex for state
Instead of Mutex, confine mutable state to a single-threaded dispatcher: val stateDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1). All reads/writes happen on one thread — no locks needed, no deadlock risk.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is viewModelScope and when is it cancelled?
Basic⌄
viewModelScope is a CoroutineScope provided by the ViewModel Kotlin extension. It uses SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Main.immediate. It's automatically cancelled when ViewModel.onCleared() is called — which happens when the ViewModel is no longer needed (e.g., the associated Fragment/Activity is permanently destroyed). This means all coroutines are cancelled automatically, preventing leaks.
Why should you use repeatOnLifecycle instead of launchWhenStarted?
Basic⌄
launchWhenStarted only pauses collection when the lifecycle goes below STARTED — the upstream flow still runs and produces values (wasting resources, potential memory buildup). repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) cancels the entire collection block when STOPPED and re-launches it when STARTED — fully stopping the producer. This is the correct pattern for lifecycle-aware collection.
What is a Mutex and how does it differ from Java's synchronized?
Basic⌄
Kotlin's Mutex is coroutine-aware — it suspends the waiting coroutine instead of blocking the thread. Java's synchronized blocks the OS thread. This means with Mutex, a waiting coroutine frees the thread for other coroutines to run. Important: Mutex is NOT reentrant — a coroutine that already holds the lock and tries to acquire it again will deadlock. Java's synchronized is reentrant by default.
What is the difference between StandardTestDispatcher and UnconfinedTestDispatcher?
Intermediate⌄
StandardTestDispatcher: coroutines are queued but don't execute until you explicitly advance time (advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy(), runCurrent()). This lets you assert intermediate states (e.g., Loading before data arrives). UnconfinedTestDispatcher: coroutines run eagerly on the current thread as soon as launched. Better for flow collection tests where you want emissions to be immediately available.
How would you limit concurrent API calls to a maximum of 5 at a time?
Intermediate⌄
Use Semaphore(5): val semaphore = Semaphore(5). Wrap each API call: semaphore.withPermit { api.call() }. When 5 calls are active, additional coroutines suspend at withPermit until a permit is released. This is cleaner than managing a custom counter and doesn't block threads — suspended coroutines free the thread while waiting.
How do you test a ViewModel that has a 3-second loading delay?
Intermediate⌄
Inject a test dispatcher: class MyViewModel(private val dispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO). In the test: runTest { val vm = MyViewModel(StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)); vm.load(); assertEquals(Loading, vm.state.value); advanceUntilIdle(); assertEquals(Success(...), vm.state.value) }. The 3-second delay is skipped by the virtual clock — test runs instantly.
Two coroutines are simultaneously trying to update a list. What is the safest approach?
Intermediate⌄
Three options, ordered by preference: (1) State confinement: use Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(1) — all mutations go through a single-threaded dispatcher, no locks needed. (2) Mutex: mutex.withLock { list.add(item) } — suspends waiting coroutines without blocking threads. (3) Use StateFlow/Channel: emit updates through a single-writer flow, never mutate shared state directly. Option 1 is usually preferred for simplicity.
Design a test that verifies a ViewModel shows Loading → Error states when an API throws after 2 seconds.
Senior⌄
runTest { val dispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler); val fakeRepo = FakeRepo { delay(2000); throw IOException() }; val vm = MyViewModel(fakeRepo, dispatcher); vm.load(); assertEquals(Loading, vm.state.value); advanceTimeBy(2000); runCurrent(); // process exception; assertEquals(Error("network"), vm.state.value) }. Key: advanceTimeBy(2000) moves the virtual clock forward, then runCurrent() processes the resulting exception handling. StandardTestDispatcher gives precise control over state transitions.
What is the difference between collectAsStateWithLifecycle() and collectAsState() in Compose?
Senior⌄
collectAsState() collects the flow as long as the Composition is active — it doesn't respect Android lifecycle. If the app goes to background, collection continues (wasting resources, potentially processing stale data). collectAsStateWithLifecycle() (from lifecycle-compose library) uses repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) semantics — collection pauses when the app goes to background and resumes when it returns. Always prefer collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in production Android apps.
You notice that your Mutex-protected code sometimes deadlocks in production. What are the root causes and how do you diagnose?
Senior⌄
Root causes: (1) Non-reentrant deadlock — a coroutine holding the mutex calls a function that also tries to acquire the same mutex. (2) Nested Mutex acquisition in wrong order across two mutexes (classic ABBA deadlock). (3) withLock block suspends (via suspend call) and another coroutine holding a different lock tries to acquire this one. Diagnosis: enable coroutine debug mode (-Dkotlinx.coroutines.debug), check thread dumps, look for coroutines in Waiting state at Mutex.lock(). Prevention: never call unknown suspend functions inside a locked block; prefer state confinement over Mutex.
6A

Flow Core

Tier 1 Mod 6
Key Concept: Cold Flow vs hot StateFlow vs hot SharedFlow. collect vs collectLatest. The definitive StateFlow vs SharedFlow vs LiveData comparison. Most-asked Flow questions.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Flow types

Flow<T>      cold  each collector fresh
StateFlow<T> hot   always has value
SharedFlow<T>hot   configurable replay

StateFlow pattern

private val _state = MutableStateFlow(Loading)
val state: StateFlow<T> = _state.asStateFlow()
// Update:
_state.value = Success(data)
_state.update { it.copy(loading=false) }

SharedFlow for events

MutableSharedFlow<Event>(
  replay = 0,           // no replay
  extraBufferCapacity=1 // buffer 1
)

collect vs collectLatest

collect        // process all, sequential
collectLatest  // cancel previous on new emit
               // use for: search, debounce
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — StateFlow for events
Using StateFlow for one-time UI events (navigation, snackbar) causes the event to replay on configuration change — the user sees the navigation happen again or the snackbar re-appears. Use SharedFlow(replay=0) for events.
Pitfall 2 — Missing StateFlow deduplication
StateFlow uses equals() to check if a new value differs from the current. If your state class doesn't implement equals() correctly (e.g., a regular class, not a data class), StateFlow may silently drop updates. Always use data classes for state.
Pitfall 3 — Collecting Flow in ViewModel
Calling flow.collect { } inside a ViewModel is usually wrong — it creates an infinite suspension that never returns. Use stateIn() or shareIn() to convert a Flow to a StateFlow/SharedFlow that the ViewModel exposes. (See 6D for stateIn/shareIn.)
Best Practice — Expose StateFlow, not MutableStateFlow
Always expose the read-only StateFlow<T> interface: val state: StateFlow<T> = _state.asStateFlow(). The UI should never mutate state directly. Only the ViewModel mutates via _state.value = ... or _state.update { ... }.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is the difference between a cold and hot Flow?
Basic⌄
Cold Flow: the block runs fresh for each collector — nothing executes until collect() is called. Each collector gets its own independent execution. Hot Flow (StateFlow/SharedFlow): runs independently of collectors, always producing values. New collectors get the current/recent values without triggering a new execution.
What is StateFlow and what makes it different from a regular Flow?
Basic⌄
StateFlow is a hot flow that always holds a current value (requires an initial value). It replays the current value to every new subscriber. It uses equals() to deduplicate — if you set the same value again, no emission occurs. Unlike regular Flow, it's multicast — multiple collectors share one execution. It's the recommended ViewModel UI state holder in Android.
When would you use SharedFlow instead of StateFlow?
Basic⌄
Use SharedFlow for one-time events that should not be replayed on configuration changes: navigation commands, showing snackbars, triggering dialogs, playing sounds. With replay=0, rotating the device won't re-trigger the event. StateFlow would replay the current value to every new collector — wrong for events.
What is the difference between collect and collectLatest?
Intermediate⌄
collect processes every emission sequentially — if the lambda takes time, the next emission waits. collectLatest cancels the current lambda when a new emission arrives and starts fresh with the new value. Use collectLatest for search queries (only process the latest keystroke), live updates where only the freshest value matters.
Why should you always use data classes for StateFlow state objects?
Intermediate⌄
StateFlow uses equals() for deduplication. Data classes auto-generate structural equals() — two instances with the same fields are equal, so updating state to the same values won't trigger unnecessary recompositions. Regular classes don't override equals(), so every assignment emits even if nothing changed, causing unnecessary UI updates. Also, data classes support copy() for immutable updates.
A cold Flow is collected from two places in the UI simultaneously. What happens?
Intermediate⌄
Each collector starts an independent execution of the flow's block — two network/database calls happen. This is correct for some use cases (e.g., two independent widgets both need the latest price) but often undesirable (duplicate network calls, inconsistent data). The fix is to convert the cold Flow to a hot StateFlow using stateIn() in the ViewModel — then both collectors share one upstream execution.
Why should you expose StateFlow<T> instead of MutableStateFlow<T> from a ViewModel?
Intermediate⌄
Encapsulation. MutableStateFlow exposes .value as settable — any code that gets the reference can modify state. This breaks the UDF (Unidirectional Data Flow) principle where state should only flow down from the ViewModel. Expose val state: StateFlow<T> = _state.asStateFlow() — read-only, the UI can only observe, never write.
Your ViewModel navigation event fires twice after a screen rotation. What is the root cause and fix?
Senior⌄
Root cause: the event is stored in a StateFlow or a SharedFlow with replay > 0. After rotation, the new collector immediately receives the last emitted event and triggers navigation again. Fix: use MutableSharedFlow(replay=0) for events. replay=0 means new collectors don't receive past events. Also ensure collection is inside repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) so the collector is recreated, not just a stale collector receiving past buffered events.
Compare StateFlow with LiveData — when would you still use LiveData in 2024?
Senior⌄
StateFlow advantages over LiveData: fully coroutine-native, no Android framework dependency (testable without AndroidX), richer operator chain (map, filter, combine), works with Flow operators. LiveData advantages: built-in lifecycle awareness (no repeatOnLifecycle boilerplate), automatic dispatch to main thread. In 2024, prefer StateFlow + collectAsStateWithLifecycle() for all new code. LiveData is acceptable in legacy XML-view code where the automatic lifecycle handling reduces boilerplate, or in Room queries that you don't want to migrate.
Design the state and event architecture for a checkout screen that has: loading state, form validation errors, a payment processing state, and a navigation-to-confirmation event.
Senior⌄
Use a sealed state class in StateFlow: sealed class CheckoutState { object Loading; data class Form(val errors: List<Error>, val isSubmitting: Boolean); object Success }. For navigation event: SharedFlow<CheckoutEvent>(replay=0, extraBufferCapacity=1) where CheckoutEvent.NavigateToConfirmation(orderId). The distinction: state represents what the screen should currently show (StateFlow replaying current state on rotation is correct). Navigation event should NOT replay — use SharedFlow replay=0 to prevent duplicate navigation after rotation.
6B

Flow Operators

Tier 1 Mod 6
Key Concept: Transforming, combining, flatMapping, timing, error handling, and lifecycle operators. Production examples for each. flatMapConcat vs flatMapMerge vs flatMapLatest comparison.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

FlatMap comparison

flatMapConcat  sequential, ordered
flatMapMerge   concurrent, unordered
flatMapLatest  cancel prev on new emit

Combining

combine(a,b) { x,y -> }  either emits
zip(a) { x, y -> }       1:1 pair
merge(a, b, c)           interleave all

Error handling

.catch { e -> emit(fallback) }
.retry(3) { e -> e is IOException }
.retryWhen { cause, attempt ->
  delay(2.pow(attempt) * 1000L)
  attempt < 3
}

Timing

debounce(300)          wait 300ms silence
distinctUntilChanged() skip duplicates
sample(1000)           emit every 1s
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Lifecycle Operators

onStart, onEach, onCompletion

// onStart: called before flow starts collecting
repo.getProducts()
    .onStart { _loading.value = true }
    .onEach { product -> cacheProduct(product) }  // side effect per item
    .onCompletion { cause ->
        _loading.value = false
        if (cause != null) logError(cause)
    }
    .collect { displayProduct(it) }

// Production: full pipeline with loading, error, completion
fun getTransactionFlow(accountId: String) =
    repo.transactions(accountId)
        .onStart { emit(Resource.Loading) }
        .map { Resource.Success(it) }
        .catch { emit(Resource.Error(it)) }
        .onCompletion { /* cleanup */ }
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is the difference between map and transform in Flow?
Basic⌄
map transforms each emission 1:1 — one input always produces exactly one output. transform is more flexible — you can call emit() zero or multiple times. Use transform to skip some emissions (like filter) or to expand one value into multiple (like a 1:n mapping).
What does debounce do and when would you use it?
Basic⌄
debounce(n) only emits a value after n milliseconds of silence from the upstream. If a new value arrives before n ms, the timer resets. Classic use case: search-as-you-type — don't fire an API call for every keystroke; wait until the user pauses typing for 300ms.
Explain the difference between combine and zip.
Basic⌄
combine: emits a new combined value whenever either source emits, using the latest value from the other. If flow A emits 3 times and flow B emits 2 times, you can get up to 5 combined emissions. zip: pairs emissions 1:1. Waits for both sources to emit before combining. If A emits 3 times and B emits 2 times, you get 2 paired emissions (stops when the shorter one completes).
What is the difference between flatMapConcat, flatMapMerge, and flatMapLatest?
Intermediate⌄
flatMapConcat: sequential — waits for each inner flow to complete before starting the next. Order guaranteed. Use for ordered operations like paginated loading. flatMapMerge: concurrent — starts all inner flows simultaneously. Results arrive in any order. Use for parallel fetches. flatMapLatest: when a new outer emission arrives, the previous inner flow is cancelled and a new one starts. Only the latest matters. Use for search queries.
Does the catch operator handle exceptions thrown inside the collect lambda?
Intermediate⌄
No. catch is a transparent operator that only catches exceptions thrown by the upstream (the flow chain above it in the pipeline). Exceptions thrown inside the collect { } collector lambda are downstream and are NOT intercepted by catch. To handle collector exceptions, wrap the collect call in a try/catch.
How would you implement exponential backoff retry in a Flow?
Intermediate⌄
Use retryWhen: .retryWhen { cause, attempt -> if (cause is IOException && attempt < 3) { delay(1000L * (1 shl attempt.toInt())); true } else false }. The attempt starts at 0. Delays: 1000ms, 2000ms, 4000ms (powers of 2). Only retry IOExceptions, not business logic errors. After 3 attempts, return false to stop retrying and let the exception propagate.
Build a search pipeline that: debounces 300ms, ignores blank input, cancels stale requests, and handles network errors gracefully.
Intermediate⌄
searchQuery.debounce(300).filter { it.isNotBlank() }.distinctUntilChanged().flatMapLatest { query -> repo.search(query).catch { emit(SearchResult.Error(it)) } }.collect { result -> renderResult(result) }. Explanation: debounce waits for typing pause; filter ignores empty; distinctUntilChanged avoids re-searching same query; flatMapLatest cancels previous request on new keystroke; catch inside the flatMapLatest handles errors per query without breaking the outer flow.
What is onEach and how does it differ from map?
Senior⌄
onEach is for side effects — it performs an action on each emission but passes the original value through unchanged. map transforms the value into a different value. Use onEach for logging, caching, analytics tracking, or setting loading states without changing the stream's data type. Example: flow.onEach { cache.save(it) }.map { toUiModel(it) } — cache the raw data, then transform to UI model.
How would you merge live price updates for 100 products into a single UI-updating stream without overwhelming the main thread?
Senior⌄
Use flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) to limit concurrent inner flows: productIds.flatMapMerge(concurrency = 20) { id -> priceSocket.streamPrice(id) }.conflate(). The concurrency parameter prevents 100 simultaneous socket connections. conflate() at the end drops intermediate updates if the UI can't keep up — only the latest price per product matters. Then collect on Main dispatcher for UI updates. The concurrency limit matches realistic socket pool size.
Explain how you would use the Resource pattern (Loading/Success/Error) with Flow operators.
Senior⌄
Wrap the repository flow: fun getDataFlow(id: String): Flow<Resource<Data>> = repo.getStream(id).map<Data, Resource<Data>> { Resource.Success(it) }.onStart { emit(Resource.Loading) }.catch { emit(Resource.Error(it)) }. The onStart emits Loading before any data arrives. map wraps success data. catch catches upstream errors and emits Error. The UI collects a single flow that handles all three states. Important: onStart must come before catch so the Loading emission isn't caught by catch.
6C

Builders &amp; Channels

Tier 1 Mod 6
Key Concept: flow{} , flowOn , callbackFlow , channelFlow . Channel types: Rendezvous, Buffered, Conflated, Unlimited. Backpressure strategies.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

callbackFlow template

callbackFlow {
  val cb = register { trySend(it) }
  awaitClose { unregister(cb) }
}

flowOn scope

flow { emit(item) }
  .map { transform(it) } // ← IO
  .flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
  .collect { render(it) } // ← Main

Channel types

Rendezvous  capacity=0  handshake
Buffered    capacity=64 queue
Conflated   capacity=1  latest only
Unlimited   capacity=∞  never suspends

Backpressure

buffer(n)     // concurrent + queue
conflate()    // drop old, keep latest
collectLatest // cancel old on new
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Missing awaitClose in callbackFlow
If you don't call awaitClose { } in a callbackFlow, the flow completes immediately after the block ends — before any callbacks fire. You also miss the chance to unregister the callback, causing memory leaks.
Pitfall 2 — emit() from different coroutine inside flow{}
flow { } is single-coroutine only. Calling emit() from a coroutine launched inside flow { } throws "Flow invariant violated". Use channelFlow { } instead for concurrent emissions.
Pitfall 3 — flowOn affects upstream, not downstream
A common mistake: putting flowOn(IO) after collect { }. flowOn only applies to operators above it. The collector always runs on the coroutine that called collect (e.g., viewModelScope's Main dispatcher).
Best Practice — trySend vs send in callbackFlow
Use trySend(value) in callbacks — it's non-suspending and returns a ChannelResult. send(value) suspends until there's space in the buffer, which is not valid in a regular (non-suspending) callback. If you need to know if the send was dropped, check the result.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is callbackFlow and when would you use it?
Basic⌄
callbackFlow is a Flow builder that creates a Channel internally, allowing you to bridge callback-based APIs (GPS, Bluetooth, WebSocket, Firebase) to the Kotlin Flow world. Callbacks call trySend(value) (non-suspending) to put values in the channel, and awaitClose { } handles cleanup when the flow is cancelled.
What is the purpose of awaitClose in callbackFlow?
Basic⌄
awaitClose { } does two things: (1) it keeps the callbackFlow alive — without it, the flow would complete immediately after the block, before any callbacks fire; (2) its lambda runs when the flow collector cancels, providing the cleanup hook to unregister the callback. Missing awaitClose causes both premature completion and listener leaks.
What does flowOn do and where does it apply?
Basic⌄
flowOn(dispatcher) changes the dispatcher for all operators upstream (above it in the chain). It does NOT affect the collector — the collector always runs on the coroutine that called collect(). It creates a coroutine boundary between the upstream and downstream sections, allowing them to run on different threads concurrently.
What are the 4 channel capacity types and when would you use each?
Intermediate⌄
Rendezvous (0): strict handshake — sender and receiver must be ready simultaneously. Good for controlled producer-consumer pairs. Buffered: N items queued; sender suspends when full. Good for bursty producers that outpace consumers temporarily. Conflated: 1-element buffer, overwrites; sender never suspends. Good for state updates where only the latest matters (sensor data, UI state). Unlimited: unbounded queue; sender never suspends. Use carefully — can OOM with fast producers.
Why can't you call emit() from a different coroutine inside flow { }?
Intermediate⌄
flow { } is a sequential cold flow builder — it enforces that emissions come from a single coroutine, preserving sequential guarantees. Calling emit() from a launched coroutine inside flow{} would violate this contract, potentially causing concurrent emission which is not safe for all collectors. The runtime throws "Flow invariant violated" to catch this. Use channelFlow { } for concurrent emissions.
What is the difference between buffer() and conflate() for backpressure?
Intermediate⌄
buffer(n) allows the producer to run ahead of the consumer by up to n items — both run concurrently with a queue between them. No items are lost; sender suspends when buffer is full. conflate() is a special case: the producer and consumer run concurrently, but intermediate values are dropped — the consumer only ever processes the most recent value. Use buffer() when you need all items (events, orders); use conflate() when only the latest matters (GPS updates, price ticks).
How do you bridge a Bluetooth LE scan callback to a Flow in Android?
Intermediate⌄
fun bleScanFlow(scanner: BluetoothLeScanner): Flow<ScanResult> = callbackFlow { val callback = object : ScanCallback() { override fun onScanResult(callbackType: Int, result: ScanResult) { trySend(result) } override fun onScanFailed(errorCode: Int) { close(BleScanException(errorCode)) } }; scanner.startScan(callback); awaitClose { scanner.stopScan(callback) } }. Key points: use trySend() (not send()), call close() on error, and always stopScan in awaitClose.
A GPS flow emitting 10 updates/second is connected to a route calculation that takes 500ms. What happens and how do you handle it?
Senior⌄
Without backpressure handling: the callbackFlow's internal channel buffers updates (default 64); once full, trySend() starts dropping updates silently. The route calculation falls further and further behind, processing stale GPS data. Fix: callbackFlow { ... }.conflate() — the producer runs at full speed but only the latest GPS update is processed by the route calculator. Since route calculation needs the current position, dropping intermediate positions is correct. Add .flowOn(Dispatchers.Default) to move the heavy calculation off Main.
Explain how flowOn creates a coroutine boundary and what happens to backpressure at that boundary.
Senior⌄
flowOn creates a Channel between the upstream (new coroutine on the specified dispatcher) and the downstream (existing collector coroutine). This channel acts as a buffer between the two. By default, the channel is buffered (64 items). If the upstream produces faster than the downstream consumes, the buffer fills and the upstream suspends. This is similar to calling .buffer(64).flowOn(dispatcher) explicitly. You can control the buffer size using buffer(n) placed before flowOn.
When would you use a raw Channel instead of Flow?
Senior⌄
Raw Channel is appropriate when: (1) you need bidirectional communication between exactly two coroutines (producer-consumer pair, not broadcast); (2) you need to close the channel explicitly from the producer side with a result or error; (3) you're implementing a work queue where multiple producers send to one consumer (fan-in pattern). In most Android code, Flow provides a better abstraction with operators, lifecycle support, and backpressure. Use Channels for internal coroutine-to-coroutine communication; expose Flow for the outside world.
6D

Sharing: stateIn &amp; shareIn

Tier 1 Mod 6
Key Concept: stateIn() converts cold Flow to StateFlow. shareIn() to SharedFlow. SharingStarted strategies: Eagerly, Lazily, WhileSubscribed(5000). When to use each.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

stateIn pattern

flow.map { toUiState(it) }
  .catch { emit(Error(it)) }
  .stateIn(
    scope = viewModelScope,
    started = WhileSubscribed(5_000),
    initialValue = Loading
  )

shareIn pattern

coldFlow.shareIn(
  scope = repositoryScope,
  started = WhileSubscribed(5_000),
  replay = 1  // 0 for events, 1+ for state
)

SharingStarted guide

Eagerly          → app-global (auth)
Lazily           → keep-alive after start
WhileSubscribed  → ViewModel (default)
  (5000)         → safe for rotation

stateIn vs MutableStateFlow

// Manual (verbose)
init {
  launch { repo.flow().collect { _s.value=it }}
}

// stateIn (clean)
val s = repo.flow().stateIn(
  scope, WhileSubscribed(5000), Loading)
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Using Eagerly in ViewModel
SharingStarted.Eagerly in a ViewModel starts the upstream immediately and keeps it running forever in viewModelScope. If the ViewModel is created but the screen is never shown, the network/DB query still runs. Use WhileSubscribed(5000) instead — starts when the UI collects and stops when it leaves.
Pitfall 2 — stateIn without initial value in cold start
The initialValue in stateIn is what collectors get before the first upstream emission. If you pass a blank/empty value and the UI renders it, the user sees an empty flash before real data loads. Design your state to include a Loading sentinel: stateIn(scope, WhileSubscribed(5000), UiState.Loading).
Best Practice — stateIn in ViewModel, shareIn in Repository
Use stateIn in ViewModels (to expose UI state as StateFlow). Use shareIn in Repositories (to share one upstream data source — WebSocket, GPS — among multiple subscribers without creating duplicate connections).
Best Practice — WhileSubscribed timeout for config changes
The 5000ms timeout in WhileSubscribed(5000) is the standard for ViewModels. It bridges Android configuration changes (rotation, language change) which typically complete in under 1 second. For app-global state (auth, user session), use Eagerly on the application scope.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What does stateIn() do?
Basic⌄
stateIn() converts a cold Flow into a hot StateFlow. It starts a shared coroutine in the given scope that collects the upstream Flow and broadcasts the latest value to all subscribers. The initialValue is returned to new subscribers before the first upstream emission. Multiple collectors share one upstream execution.
What is WhileSubscribed(5000) and why is 5000ms the standard value?
Basic⌄
WhileSubscribed(5000) starts the upstream when the first subscriber joins and stops it 5 seconds after the last subscriber leaves. The 5-second value is chosen to survive Android configuration changes (screen rotation destroys and recreates Activity in ~100–500ms). The upstream doesn't stop during rotation. When the user navigates away permanently, it stops after 5 seconds, freeing resources.
What is the difference between stateIn and shareIn?
Basic⌄
stateIn produces a StateFlow: requires an initial value, always has a current value, uses equals() deduplication, suitable for UI state. shareIn produces a SharedFlow: no initial value required, configurable replay (0 for events, 1+ for state), no deduplication. Use stateIn in ViewModels for UI state; use shareIn in Repositories for shared connections (WebSocket, GPS).
Why is SharingStarted.Eagerly dangerous in a ViewModel?
Intermediate⌄
Eagerly starts the upstream immediately when the scope starts (ViewModel init) and never stops until the scope is cancelled. This means network/DB calls start even if no collector ever subscribes — wasteful. It also means the upstream runs even when the app is in the background. Use WhileSubscribed to only run while the UI is active.
A ViewModel has a cold Room Flow. Three Compose composables all collect it. How many DB queries happen and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
Three DB queries — each collector starts an independent Room subscription (cold Flow). Fix: convert to a hot flow with stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(5000), initialValue) in the ViewModel. Now there's one shared Room subscription, and all three Compose composables observe the same StateFlow. Result: one DB query regardless of subscriber count.
How is stateIn different from manually collecting a Flow into a MutableStateFlow?
Intermediate⌄
Functionally equivalent, but stateIn is a one-liner that handles: (1) the coroutine launching; (2) the SharingStarted lifecycle policy (WhileSubscribed stops the upstream when no subscribers — impossible to express concisely with manual approach); (3) cancellation and restart logic. Manual approach requires boilerplate in init {} and careful handling of stopping/restarting.
When would you use shareIn in a Repository instead of stateIn?
Intermediate⌄
Use shareIn in a Repository when you want to share an expensive upstream (WebSocket connection, Bluetooth GATT, GPS listener) among multiple ViewModels. shareIn with replay=1 means any new subscriber immediately gets the latest value without opening a new connection. Use stateIn in ViewModel for the UI-facing StateFlow (requires initial value, deduplication).
What happens to a stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)) flow when the user rotates the device?
Senior⌄
The Activity is destroyed (Compose unsubscribes) and recreated (Compose resubscribes), typically within 200–500ms. The 5000ms timeout means the upstream does NOT stop — it keeps running throughout. When the new Activity subscribes, it immediately gets the latest StateFlow value and the ongoing upstream. No data is lost, no network call is restarted. Without the 5000ms timeout (WhileSubscribed(0)), the upstream would stop on destroy and restart on the new Activity, causing a brief loading flash.
Design a Repository that shares a WebSocket price feed among multiple ViewModels with appropriate lifecycle management.
Senior⌄
class PriceRepository(socket: PriceSocket, scope: CoroutineScope) { val prices: SharedFlow<Map<String,Price>> = socket.priceFlow().scan(emptyMap()) { acc, update -> acc + (update.symbol to update) }.shareIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), replay=1) }. The scan accumulates the latest price per symbol. shareIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)) means the WebSocket connects when the first ViewModel subscribes and disconnects 5s after all ViewModels unsubscribe (navigation away). replay=1 ensures new ViewModels instantly get the latest price map without waiting for the next WebSocket message.
What is the difference between SharingStarted.Lazily and WhileSubscribed(Long.MAX_VALUE)?
Senior⌄
Functionally nearly identical in practice — both start on first subscriber and stop only when the scope is cancelled. The subtle difference: Lazily is a first-class API with clear semantics. WhileSubscribed(Long.MAX_VALUE) technically stops after MAX_VALUE milliseconds (after ~292 million years, so effectively never). In practice, use Lazily when you want "start on first subscriber, keep forever" semantics. Use Eagerly when you want to pre-warm before any subscriber. Use WhileSubscribed(5000) for the standard ViewModel use case.
7A

Compose Fundamentals

Tier 1 Mod 7
Key Concept: @Composable, declarative vs imperative UI, the Composition, recomposition mechanics, slot table, State<T>, remember, and the composable lifecycle.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Declarative UI

Imperative: find view → mutate it
Declarative: describe what to show
            → Compose handles update

Text(state.value)  // re-runs when value changes

State declaration

var x by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
// by = delegate: read/write directly
// without by: state.value required

Composition lifecycle

1. Enter: first call, remember init
2. Recompose: state changed, re-run
3. Leave: removed, cleanup effects

remember rules

remember { }        // survives recompose
remember(key) { }   // re-init if key changes
rememberSaveable{}  // survives process death
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Side effects in composable body
Composables can run multiple times. Writing to a database, logging analytics, or network calls in the composable body (not in a LaunchedEffect) will happen on every recomposition — potentially thousands of times. Side effects must always be in LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, or SideEffect.
Pitfall 2 — Creating objects without remember
Creating a new list, Painter, Animator, or any object directly in a composable body allocates a new object on every recomposition. Wrap with remember { } to create once and store in the slot table.
Pitfall 3 — Reading State outside of composable context
If you read a State<T> inside a lambda (like an onClick handler) without reading it in the composable body, the composable doesn't subscribe — it won't recompose when the state changes. Ensure state reads happen directly in the composable body.
Best Practice — Keep composables stateless
Composables should ideally be pure functions: same inputs → same output. Push state up to the ViewModel or calling composable. Stateless composables are easier to test, preview, and reuse.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is the difference between declarative and imperative UI?
Basic⌄
Imperative UI: you manage view objects explicitly — find a TextView, call setText(), handle null checks, manage lifecycle. You describe HOW to change the UI. Declarative UI (Compose): you describe WHAT the UI should look like for a given state. When state changes, the framework re-runs your description and applies the diff. You don't touch existing views — you re-describe the desired output.
What triggers recomposition in Compose?
Basic⌄
Recomposition is triggered when a State<T> value that was read during the last composition changes. Compose tracks every State read inside a composable function — when any of those states change, the composable is scheduled for recomposition. Only composables that read the changed state are recomposed — not the entire UI tree.
What is remember and why do you need it?
Basic⌄
remember { } stores a value in the slot table so it persists across recompositions. Without it, the code inside runs on every recomposition — creating new objects, resetting state. Use remember for: mutableStateOf holders, expensive objects (formatters, painters), list instances. remember does NOT survive Activity recreation — use rememberSaveable for that.
What is the Composition and what is the slot table?
Intermediate⌄
The Composition is the in-memory representation of the UI — a tree built from composable function calls. The slot table is the data structure that backs it: a flat array where each composable call occupies slots storing its runtime state and remember values. The composable's identity in the slot table is its position in the call hierarchy (call site), not a runtime object reference.
How does Compose "skip" composables during recomposition?
Intermediate⌄
If all parameters of a composable are equal to their previous values (using equals()), Compose skips executing that composable entirely — its output is assumed unchanged. This is "smart recomposition." For a composable to be skippable, all its parameters must be stable types (primitives, String, data classes, @Stable annotated classes). Unstable types (like plain List<>) prevent skipping.
A composable creates a new List inside its body on every recomposition. Is this a problem and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
Yes. Without remember, a new list is allocated on every recomposition — causing unnecessary GC pressure and potentially triggering further recompositions if the list is passed as a parameter (since new list instance != old list instance in equals()). Fix: val items = remember(key) { buildList { ... } }. If the list is derived from state, use remember(sourceData) { processData(sourceData) } — only recomputes when sourceData changes.
Why might a composable lose its state when a condition around it flips?
Intermediate⌄
Compose identifies composables by their position in the call tree (slot table). if (condition) ComponentA() else ComponentB() — both A and B occupy the same position. When condition flips, Compose sees the previous composable leaving and a new one entering at that position. The new composable's remember values start fresh — state is lost. Fix: use key(condition) { ComponentA() } or restructure so both branches are independent positions.
A developer calls an analytics tracking function directly in the composable body. What is wrong?
Senior⌄
Composables can recompose many times — every state change triggers re-execution. Calling analytics directly in the body would log the event on every recomposition, potentially hundreds of times. Additionally, composables may be run during previews, tests, or Compose internal optimizations (recomposition can be speculative). Side effects must be in LaunchedEffect or SideEffect: LaunchedEffect(Unit) { analytics.track("ScreenView") } — runs once when the composable enters composition.
Explain how the snapshot system works in Compose and how it enables fine-grained recomposition.
Senior⌄
Compose's snapshot system is a transactional state system. Every State value has a list of observers (composable scopes). During composition, reading a State registers the current composition scope as an observer. When you write to a State, it creates a new snapshot. The write is committed atomically — all observers are notified and scheduled for recomposition. This is how two different composables can read the same State and only both recompose when that specific state changes, while other composables that don't read it are untouched. The snapshot system also enables multi-thread safety for State mutations.
How does key() affect composable identity and recomposition in a LazyColumn?
Senior⌄
Without key: each item's identity is its index. Insert an item at position 0 → all items shift → Compose thinks every item changed → full recomposition of all items, all remember values reset. With key = { item.id }: each item's identity is its unique ID. Insert at 0 → only the new item is created, existing items keep their position (by key) → Compose skips recomposing unchanged items. This is critical for lists with animations — without keys, items appear to "jump" because all are treated as new.
7B

State Management

Tier 1 Mod 7
Key Concept: remember vs rememberSaveable, mutableStateOf, derivedStateOf. State hoisting, UDF (Unidirectional Data Flow). ViewModel as state holder. collectAsStateWithLifecycle. When to use local vs hoisted state.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

State survival

remember         → recomposition only
rememberSaveable → + rotation + death
ViewModel        → + rotation, complex data

State hoisting

// Stateless (preferred):
fun SearchBar(
  query: String,           // ← down
  onQueryChange: (String)->Unit // ↑ up
)

collectAsState

collectAsState()               // ❌ background
collectAsStateWithLifecycle()  // ✅ STARTED only

derivedStateOf

val showFab by remember {
  derivedStateOf { 
    scrollState.value > 100
  }
}
// recomposes only on threshold cross
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Using remember for state that must survive rotation
Search query, scroll position, form input — these must survive rotation. remember loses them. Use rememberSaveable for small values or ViewModel + SavedStateHandle for complex data. A classic bug: user fills a form, rotates device, all fields reset.
Pitfall 2 — collectAsState instead of collectAsStateWithLifecycle
collectAsState() continues collecting when the app goes to background — processing updates the user can't see, potentially doing network calls or DB queries. Always use collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in production.
Pitfall 3 — Hoisting too high
Moving state to a parent/ancestor that doesn't need it creates unnecessary recompositions in the ancestor. Hoist state to the LOWEST common ancestor that needs it — not all the way to the ViewModel unless the state is business-critical.
Best Practice — derivedStateOf for expensive filtered lists
For any list filtering or sorting that runs during recomposition, wrap in derivedStateOf. Source state can change frequently (scroll, typing); the derived list should only recompute when actual filter parameters change.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is the difference between remember and rememberSaveable?
Basic⌄
remember stores values in the composition's slot table — survives recomposition but is lost on configuration changes (rotation, language change) and process death. rememberSaveable additionally saves the value to the Bundle/SavedState system, surviving both configuration changes and process death. For primitive types it works automatically; for complex types you need a custom Saver.
What is state hoisting and why is it important?
Basic⌄
State hoisting is moving state from a composable to its caller, making the composable stateless. Instead of the composable owning state internally, it receives the current value as a parameter and reports changes via a lambda callback. Benefits: the composable becomes testable (control state in tests), reusable (caller decides initial state), previewable (pass any state in preview), and follows UDF (single source of truth).
What is Unidirectional Data Flow in Compose?
Basic⌄
State flows down the composable tree as parameters, events flow up as lambda callbacks. The ViewModel holds and owns the state (single source of truth). It exposes state as StateFlow. The UI consumes state via collectAsStateWithLifecycle() and sends events (user clicks) back to the ViewModel via callbacks. The ViewModel mutates state in response to events, triggering a new UI render.
What is derivedStateOf and when should you use it?
Intermediate⌄
derivedStateOf { } creates a State that is computed from other State values. It only recomputes when its dependencies change, and only triggers recomposition when the computed result is different. Use it when source state changes frequently but derived result changes rarely: scroll position (60fps) → show FAB (boolean, changes rarely); item list → filtered list (filtered count changes occasionally).
Why use collectAsStateWithLifecycle instead of collectAsState?
Intermediate⌄
collectAsState() keeps collecting the Flow even when the app is in the background (Activity paused/stopped). collectAsStateWithLifecycle() uses repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) semantics — collection pauses when the app goes to background and resumes when it comes to foreground. This prevents unnecessary processing when the UI is invisible, saving battery and avoiding potential issues with background-only updates.
A form composable has 5 fields. Which state should use remember, rememberSaveable, and ViewModel?
Intermediate⌄
The field values (text, selections) that the user typed: rememberSaveable or ViewModel + SavedStateHandle — user would be frustrated if their input reset on rotation. UI-only state like "is this field focused" or "show password": remember — acceptable to reset on rotation. If the form involves business logic (validation, submission state, server errors): ViewModel StateFlow with collectAsStateWithLifecycle(). Rule: data the user entered → survives rotation; pure UI decoration → doesn't need to.
What is the difference between derivedStateOf and remember(key)?
Intermediate⌄
remember(key) { compute() }: re-runs compute() when key changes, always triggers recomposition. derivedStateOf { compute() }: re-runs when State dependencies read inside the lambda change. Crucially, it only triggers recomposition if the result changes — an additional optimization. Use derivedStateOf when the computation's input (State) changes more often than the output (e.g., filtering a 1000-item list when only 1 item changes but the filtered result doesn't change).
Design the state management for a banking transfer screen with: amount input, recipient selection, real-time validation, and submit-in-progress state.
Senior⌄
ViewModel owns all: data class TransferState(val amount: String = "", val amountError: String? = null, val recipient: Contact? = null, val isSubmitting: Boolean = false) as MutableStateFlow. ViewModel handles events: onAmountChange (validates), onRecipientSelect, onSubmit (sets isSubmitting). Submit button enabled via derivedStateOf { state.amountError == null && state.recipient != null && !state.isSubmitting }. Amount + recipient persist across rotation via SavedStateHandle in ViewModel. No rememberSaveable needed — ViewModel handles it. UI is fully stateless composable.
When should you hoist state to the ViewModel vs keep it in rememberSaveable?
Senior⌄
Use ViewModel when: (1) state is shared across multiple composables; (2) state requires business logic (validation, computation); (3) state needs to survive process death with unlimited size (SavedStateHandle for complex objects); (4) state comes from or must be synced to a data layer. Use rememberSaveable when: (1) state is purely local UI state in one composable; (2) it's a primitive or Bundle-serializable value; (3) no business logic needed; (4) examples: expanded/collapsed, scroll offset for a sub-list. rememberSaveable keeps components self-contained; ViewModel provides testability and data layer access.
A ScrollState-based parallax header is causing 60fps recompositions. How do you fix it using derivedStateOf?
Senior⌄
Instead of reading scrollState.value directly in composables that don't need continuous updates: val isHeaderCollapsed by remember { derivedStateOf { scrollState.value > COLLAPSE_THRESHOLD } } and val headerAlpha by remember { derivedStateOf { (1f - scrollState.value / FADE_RANGE).coerceIn(0f, 1f) } }. The scrollState changes 60fps but isHeaderCollapsed changes once (boolean threshold). The alpha changes continuously — for this, accept the 60fps recomposition on the alpha composable specifically, or use the Modifier.graphicsLayer approach which doesn't trigger recomposition at all.
7C

Side Effects

Tier 1 Mod 7
Key Concept: LaunchedEffect, DisposableEffect, SideEffect, rememberCoroutineScope, produceState, derivedStateOf, snapshotFlow — every side-effect API with its precise use case.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Which API when?

One-time init      → LaunchedEffect(Unit)
Key-sensitive       → LaunchedEffect(key)
Listener reg/unreg → DisposableEffect(key)
Every recompose    → SideEffect
Button click       → rememberCoroutineScope

LaunchedEffect

LaunchedEffect(Unit)   // once
LaunchedEffect(key)    // on key change
// cancelled when composable leaves
// key: anything with equals()

DisposableEffect

DisposableEffect(key) {
  val cb = register(listener)
  onDispose {
    unregister(cb)  // always called
  }
}

snapshotFlow

// Compose State → Flow
LaunchedEffect(Unit) {
  snapshotFlow { scrollState.value }
    .debounce(300)
    .collect { onScroll(it) }
}
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — LaunchedEffect(Unit) for key-sensitive operations
Using LaunchedEffect(Unit) means the effect never re-runs when parameters change. If you load data by ID and the ID can change (navigation backstack, deep links), use LaunchedEffect(id). Forgetting to pass the correct key is a common source of stale data bugs.
Pitfall 2 — SideEffect for one-time operations
SideEffect runs on EVERY successful recomposition. Using it to log a screen view would fire the analytics event on every UI update, not just once. Use LaunchedEffect(Unit) for one-time effects.
Pitfall 3 — rememberCoroutineScope for one-time initialization
rememberCoroutineScope is for user-triggered events (button clicks). For automatic initialization on screen enter, use LaunchedEffect. Using rememberCoroutineScope + launching in the body (not a callback) will launch on every recomposition — same as calling the code directly.
Best Practice — DisposableEffect for any listener registration
Any time you register a listener, callback, or observer in a composable, always use DisposableEffect with onDispose cleanup. This prevents listener leaks when the composable leaves the composition.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is LaunchedEffect and how does the key work?
Basic⌄
LaunchedEffect(key) launches a coroutine that is tied to the composition. When the composable enters composition, the coroutine starts. If the key changes on recomposition, the current coroutine is cancelled and a new one starts. When the composable leaves composition, the coroutine is cancelled. The key can be any value — Compose uses equals() to detect changes.
What is DisposableEffect and when must you use onDispose?
Basic⌄
DisposableEffect(key) runs a non-suspending setup block when the composable enters composition or when the key changes. The block must end with onDispose { } which runs when: the composable leaves composition, or the key changes (before re-running the setup block). onDispose is mandatory — it provides the cleanup for listeners, observers, resources registered in the setup block.
When should you use SideEffect vs LaunchedEffect?
Basic⌄
SideEffect runs after EVERY successful recomposition — use for continuously syncing Compose state to external non-Compose systems (e.g., updating an analytics SDK's current screen, updating a legacy View's property). LaunchedEffect(Unit) runs once when the composable enters composition — use for one-time initialization, loading data, starting observation. Never use SideEffect for one-time operations.
When would you use rememberCoroutineScope instead of LaunchedEffect?
Intermediate⌄
rememberCoroutineScope when you need to launch a coroutine in response to a user event (button click, gesture) — from a non-composable callback context where you can't call suspend functions directly. LaunchedEffect when the coroutine should start automatically based on composition entry or a state change. Rule: event-triggered → rememberCoroutineScope; automatic/reactive → LaunchedEffect.
A composable uses LaunchedEffect(Unit) to load data for a product. The user navigates to a different product. What happens and how do you fix it?
Intermediate⌄
With LaunchedEffect(Unit), the effect runs only once when the composable enters composition. If the same composable recomposes with a different productId, the effect does NOT re-run — the old data stays. Fix: LaunchedEffect(productId). Now when productId changes (e.g., navigation to a different product), the old coroutine is cancelled and a new one starts loading the new product.
How do you register and unregister a lifecycle observer safely in Compose?
Intermediate⌄
Use DisposableEffect(lifecycleOwner): in the block, create and add the observer; in onDispose, remove it. Use LocalLifecycleOwner.current to get the current lifecycle owner and pass it as the key — if the owner changes (e.g., nested Navigation), the effect re-runs. Without DisposableEffect (e.g., registering directly in the body), the observer would be added on every recomposition and never removed — a leak.
What is snapshotFlow and what can you do with it that you can't do with just collecting a StateFlow?
Intermediate⌄
snapshotFlow { } converts any Compose State read inside its lambda into a Flow. Unlike a StateFlow (which has a value), snapshotFlow can read any combination of State values: snapshotFlow { state1 + state2 } — emits when either state1 or state2 changes. You can then apply all Flow operators: debounce, distinctUntilChanged, flatMapLatest. This enables complex reactive patterns on local Compose state that wouldn't be possible with just StateFlow.
Design an auto-save feature for a notes app that saves to the database after the user stops typing for 2 seconds.
Senior⌄
@Composable fun NoteEditor(noteId: String, viewModel: NoteViewModel) { val content by viewModel.content.collectAsStateWithLifecycle(); LaunchedEffect(Unit) { snapshotFlow { content }.debounce(2000).distinctUntilChanged().drop(1) // skip initial load .collect { text -> viewModel.saveNote(noteId, text) } }; TextField(value = content, onValueChange = viewModel::onContentChange) }. snapshotFlow converts the content state to Flow. debounce(2000) waits 2s after last keystroke. distinctUntilChanged prevents saving if content didn't change. drop(1) skips the initial emission when the composable enters (don't save before user types).
What is produceState and how is it different from LaunchedEffect + mutableStateOf?
Senior⌄
produceState(initialValue, key) { value = compute() } is syntactic sugar for LaunchedEffect + mutableStateOf — internally it does exactly that. The difference is idiomatic: produceState returns a State<T> directly, making it ideal for composable functions that compute and return a State (not just a void composable). It also provides awaitDispose { } for cleanup. Use produceState when building a composable abstraction over an async data source; use LaunchedEffect when the coroutine is a side effect of an existing composable, not its primary purpose.
A developer registers a BroadcastReceiver in a composable body (not in DisposableEffect). What bugs will occur?
Senior⌄
Three bugs: (1) The receiver is registered on EVERY recomposition — if the screen recomposes 10 times, 10 receivers are registered. Each will respond to broadcasts, causing the handler to fire 10x. (2) No unregistration ever happens — when the composable leaves composition, no cleanup runs. The receiver continues receiving broadcasts forever, holding a reference to the composable's context. (3) Memory leak — the receiver holds a context reference; if the context is Activity-scoped, the Activity leaks. Fix: DisposableEffect with onDispose { context.unregisterReceiver(receiver) }.
7D

Compose Performance

Tier 1 Mod 7
Key Concept: Smart recomposition, stability system, @Stable/@Immutable, unstable List<>, LazyColumn keys, remember for expensive computations, derivedStateOf, lambda stability, Compose compiler metrics.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Stability rules

Stable:   primitives, String,
          data class (all val+stable),
          @Stable, @Immutable
Unstable: List<T>, MutableList,
          HashMap, regular class

Fix unstable List

// Option 1: wrapper
@Immutable data class Items(val list: List<T>)

// Option 2: ImmutableList
ImmutableList<T> // kotlinx.collections.immutable

LazyColumn key

items(
  items = list,
  key = { it.id }  // ← always provide
) { item -> ItemCard(item) }

Performance toolbox

derivedStateOf { } // for high-freq state
remember(key) { }  // memoize expensive ops
graphicsLayer { }  // draw-phase changes
@Immutable class   // trust equals()
compiler metrics   // diagnose issues
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Passing List<T> to composables
List<T> is unstable — any composable that takes it as a parameter cannot be skipped. In a list screen, this means every item recomposes whenever the parent updates. Use ImmutableList<T> (kotlinx.collections.immutable) or wrap in an @Immutable data class.
Pitfall 2 — Lambdas capturing non-stable values
A lambda that captures a List<T> or any unstable value is itself unstable. This prevents the composable receiving it from skipping. Fix: ensure captured values are stable, or use remember { { ... } } to stabilize the lambda reference.
Pitfall 3 — LazyColumn without keys
Without stable keys in LazyColumn, inserting or removing items causes all items to recompose and loses per-item state (expanded state, animations). Always provide key = { item.id }.
Best Practice — Compose compiler metrics
Enable compiler reports: freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=build/compose_reports"]. The output shows skippable vs restartable composables and identifies unstable parameters. Use this to find performance bottlenecks.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What does it mean for a composable to be "skippable"?
Basic⌄
A skippable composable can be skipped during recomposition if all its parameters are equal to their previous values. Compose checks each parameter using equals(). If all are equal, it assumes the output would be the same and skips executing the function — saving CPU time. For a composable to be skippable, all parameters must be stable types.
Why is List<T> unstable in Compose?
Basic⌄
List<T> is a Kotlin interface. Compose cannot verify that the implementation won't change after the composable receives it — a mutable list could change without notifying Compose. Since Compose can't trust that equals() reliably indicates whether the content changed, it marks List as unstable. Any composable receiving a List parameter is non-skippable and will recompose whenever its parent recomposes.
What is the difference between @Stable and @Immutable?
Basic⌄
@Immutable: all public properties never change after construction — strongest guarantee. Every field is treated as a compile-time constant for stability. Use for value objects (UI models). @Stable: weaker — equals() is reliable AND any changes to public properties are observable (the Compose runtime will be notified). Use for mutable state holders that use mutableStateOf internally. In practice, most UI model classes should use @Immutable.
Why should you always provide keys in LazyColumn?
Intermediate⌄
Without keys, each item's identity is its index. Inserting an item at position 0 shifts all other items' indices — Compose thinks every item changed and recomposes all of them. Remember state per item is also lost. With key = { item.id }, each item has a stable identity. Compose can correctly identify which items moved, which are new, and which are unchanged — only recomposing what actually changed and preserving per-item state.
How do you fix the performance issue caused by passing List<T> to a composable?
Intermediate⌄
Two approaches: (1) Use ImmutableList<T> from the kotlinx.collections.immutable library — it's a stable type by design. Convert in ViewModel: _state.update { it.copy(products = newList.toImmutableList()) }. (2) Wrap in an @Immutable data class: @Immutable data class ProductListState(val items: List<T>) — the annotation makes the wrapper stable, and the inner List is treated as immutable by contract.
When should you use Modifier.graphicsLayer vs setting a modifier property directly?
Intermediate⌄
Modifier.alpha(value) updates a modifier that Compose reads during composition — if the alpha changes, a recomposition is needed to apply the new modifier. Modifier.graphicsLayer { alpha = value } applies the change in the draw phase — no recomposition required. For animated values that change every frame (alpha, scale, translation), graphicsLayer skips the composition phase entirely, giving better performance. For static properties that only change occasionally, direct modifiers are fine.
A product list screen shows 200 items. Typing in a search box causes all 200 items to flicker/recompose. What is the root cause and fix?
Intermediate⌄
Root cause: either (1) ProductCard takes a List parameter (unstable, non-skippable), or (2) the state update changes the list reference even if content is the same, or (3) the search query state is being read by the parent that contains the LazyColumn, causing the LazyColumn's parent to recompose, and without stable/skippable ProductCard, all 200 items recompose. Fix: ensure ProductCard takes @Immutable ProductUiModel (not List). Hoist the search query state to a ViewModel so it doesn't live in the same composable as the list. Add stable keys to LazyColumn.
How do you use Compose compiler metrics to diagnose performance issues?
Senior⌄
Add to app build.gradle: kotlinOptions { freeCompilerArgs += ["-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:reportsDestination=${buildDir}/compose_reports", "-P", "plugin:androidx.compose.compiler.plugins.kotlin:metricsDestination=${buildDir}/compose_metrics"] }. Run an assembleDebug/Release. Open build/compose_reports/*-composables.txt. Each composable is marked: skippable/non-skippable, restartable/non-restartable. Non-skippable composables list their unstable parameters. The metrics JSON provides counts. Focus on non-skippable composables in hot paths (list items).
Explain why a lambda that captures a non-stable type is itself unstable and how to fix it.
Senior⌄
Compose compiler analyzes lambda capture sites. If a lambda captures an unstable value (e.g., List<T>), the compiler cannot guarantee the lambda's output is stable — calling it with the same "arguments" might produce different results because the captured state may have changed. The lambda is therefore marked unstable, preventing composables that receive it from skipping. Fix: (1) ensure the captured value is stable (ImmutableList, @Immutable class); (2) use remember { { } } to create a stable lambda reference; (3) in Compose 1.5+, lambdas with stable captures are automatically stabilized by the compiler.
An automotive dashboard has a speedometer recomposing at 60fps. The needle is animated but the rest of the dashboard should not recompose. How do you architect this?
Senior⌄
Isolate the high-frequency state. The speed value from sensors updates at 60fps — keep it in a separate StateFlow or animatable. The Speedometer composable reads this directly. Use Modifier.graphicsLayer { rotationZ = needleAngle } for the needle rotation — this runs in the draw phase without recomposition. For the rest of the dashboard (current music, temperature, warnings), use derivedStateOf for threshold-crossing booleans. Structure: DashboardScreen (reads all states) → SpeedGauge (reads only speed via derivedStateOf thresholds) + StaticDashboardPanels (@Stable, skippable). The needle rotation via graphicsLayer avoids even SpeedGauge recomposition at 60fps.

Compose UI

Tier 1 Mod 7
Key Concept: Tier 1 Row · Column · Box · LazyColumn · LazyRow · Scaffold · Material 3 · Modifiers · Custom Layouts
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics

8 · Quick Revision Sheet

ComposablePurposeKey parameter
RowHorizontal layouthorizontalArrangement, verticalAlignment
ColumnVertical layoutverticalArrangement, horizontalAlignment
BoxStack / overlaycontentAlignment
LazyColumnVertical scrolling listkey = { item.id }, contentPadding
LazyRowHorizontal scrolling listkey, horizontalArrangement
ScaffoldMaterial 3 screen chrometopBar, bottomBar, fab; use paddingValues

Modifier Order Convention

size → background → padding → border → clip → clickable → semantics

LazyColumn Rules

  • Always provide key = { item.stableId }
  • Never use Column for lists > ~20 items
  • Use Arrangement.spacedBy() for gaps, not item padding
  • Use contentPadding for outer margins
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

  • LazyColumn without keys: Without key, Compose cannot identify item identity — scroll state lost, animations wrong, unnecessary recompositions.
  • Modifier order: .padding(16.dp).background(Color.Red) vs .background(Color.Red).padding(16.dp) produce different results. Background before padding = background under the padding area.
  • Missing padding(paddingValues) in Scaffold: Content overlaps TopAppBar / BottomBar if you don't apply the Scaffold's paddingValues to your content.
  • Column for long lists: Column measures all children eagerly — use LazyColumn for any list that might grow.
  • Modifier.clickable without ripple: Use Modifier.clickable { } (has built-in ripple) not custom pointerInput unless you need fine-grained gesture control.
  • Hard-coded dp in custom layouts: Use LocalDensity to convert px ↔ dp in custom layouts, not hard-coded pixel values.
Best practices: Always pass paddingValues in Scaffold. Always provide key in LazyColumn. Use Arrangement.spacedBy() for consistent gaps. Use fillMaxWidth() on top-level layout composables. Apply Modifier parameters in a consistent order: size → background → padding → border → click.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic Name the three core Compose layout primitives and their XML equivalents.
Row (LinearLayout horizontal), Column (LinearLayout vertical), Box (FrameLayout). LazyColumn and LazyRow are the lazy/scrollable equivalents of RecyclerView.
Q2: Basic Why does Modifier order matter in Compose?
Each Modifier wraps the previous one. Modifiers closer to the composable affect the inner content; modifiers further out affect the outer boundary. Example: Modifier.padding(16dp).background(Red) applies background only to the inner content area. Modifier.background(Red).padding(16dp) applies background to the full area including the padding.
Q3: Basic What is Scaffold and why must you use its paddingValues?
Scaffold is the Material 3 screen scaffold that provides slots for TopAppBar, BottomNavigationBar, FAB, Snackbar, and DrawerLayout. The paddingValues it passes to the content lambda represent the insets consumed by these components (TopAppBar height, BottomBar height). If you don't apply paddingValues to your content, it will be drawn behind the TopAppBar and BottomBar.

Single toplaunchSingleTop = trueNo duplicate destinations
Tab navigationpopUpTo(start) { saveState=true } + restoreState=truePreserves tab state
Typed routes (2.8+)@Serializable data class + toRoute()Compile-time safe
ArgumentsnavArgument("key") { type = NavType.StringType }Pass IDs only, not objects
Deep linksnavDeepLink { uriPattern = "..." }+ intent-filter in manifest
Graph-scoped ViewModelviewModel(navController.getBackStackEntry("graph"))Shared across graph destinations
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas

6 · Pitfalls and Best Practices

  • NavController not at composition top: Create NavController with rememberNavController() at the top of the composition tree and pass it down. Don't create it inside individual screens.
  • Passing complex objects as nav args: Nav args are strings (Bundle-backed). Serialize only IDs; load full data in the destination ViewModel. Navigation 2.8 typed routes support basic types only via kotlinx.serialization.
  • Missing saveState/restoreState in tab navigation: Without saveState = true / restoreState = true, switching tabs recreates the entire tab screen. This loses scroll position and state.
  • Navigating in LaunchedEffect without correct keys: Always use a stable key (e.g., event or state value) in LaunchedEffect to avoid re-triggering navigation on recomposition.
  • Back stack growth from bottom nav: Without popUpTo(startDestination), repeatedly tapping tab icons stacks destinations. Always use the bottom nav pattern with popUpTo + launchSingleTop.
  • ViewModel scope in nested graphs: Use navController.getBackStackEntry("graphRoute") as the ViewModelStoreOwner to scope a ViewModel to a graph, not to individual destinations.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What are the three core components of Navigation Compose?
