NavController (manages back stack state and provides navigate/popBackStack API), NavHost (Composable that renders the current destination from the back stack), NavGraph (the set of composable destinations and their routes, defined within the NavHost builder lambda).
Q2: Basic How do you pass an argument to a composable destination?
Declare the route with a placeholder: composable("product/{productId}", arguments = listOf(navArgument("productId") { type = NavType.StringType })) { backStackEntry -> val id = backStackEntry.arguments?.getString("productId") }. Navigate with: navController.navigate("product/abc123"). With Navigation 2.8+ typed routes: @Serializable data class ProductRoute(val productId: String), then navigate with navController.navigate(ProductRoute("abc123")) and val route: ProductRoute = backStackEntry.toRoute().
Q3: Basic How do you implement a logout flow that prevents the user from pressing Back to the home screen?
navController.navigate(Route.Login) {
    popUpTo(0) { inclusive = true }  // clears entire back stack
}
popUpTo(0) removes all destinations back to the root (id=0). inclusive=true removes the start destination too. The user is left with only the Login screen and pressing Back exits the app.
8A

Architecture Patterns

Tier 1 Mod 8
Key Concept: MVC, MVP, MVVM, MVI — what each solves and its trade-offs. Full layered architecture: UI → ViewModel → UseCase → Repository → Data Sources. When to use each pattern.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Pattern comparison

MVC:  Activity = Controller (fat)
MVP:  Presenter + View interface
MVVM: ViewModel + StateFlow (standard)
MVI:  sealed Intent + single State

Layer diagram

UI: Composable + ViewModel
     ↕ StateFlow
Domain: UseCase (pure Kotlin)
     ↕ interface
Data: RepositoryImpl
     ↕
Remote API + Room DB

UseCase pattern

class GetUserUseCase(
    private val repo: UserRepository // interface
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(id: String) =
        repo.getUser(id)
}

MVI structure

sealed class Intent { ... }
data class State( ... )
// ViewModel:
fun process(intent: Intent) =
  _state.update { reduce(it, intent) }
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1 — Fat ViewModel
Moving all business logic to the ViewModel without UseCases creates a "Fat ViewModel" anti-pattern — the same problem as Fat Controller in MVC, just moved. UseCases should encapsulate discrete business rules; the ViewModel should only orchestrate them.
Pitfall 2 — Repository doing too much
The Repository should be a clean data access abstraction — not the place for business logic. If a Repository method is called "validateAndSaveIfFundsAvailable", the validate part belongs in a UseCase, not the Repository.
Pitfall 3 — Domain layer depending on Android
UseCases should be pure Kotlin with zero Android dependencies — no Context, no ViewModel, no Room entities. This is what makes them unit-testable with JUnit without Robolectric.
Best Practice — Repository interface in domain layer
Define the Repository interface in the domain layer, implementation in the data layer. This inverts the dependency — data layer depends on domain, not the other way. Enables mocking in UseCase tests without a real DB or network.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: What is the main problem with MVC in Android?
Basic⌄
In Android MVC, Activity/Fragment acts as the Controller. This creates a God Class — Activities handle button clicks, network calls, database queries, navigation, lifecycle management, and UI updates all in one place. The Controller is tightly coupled to Android SDK, making it untestable with JUnit. It's also lifecycle-unsafe: the Controller is destroyed on rotation, interrupting ongoing work.
What is the key difference between MVP and MVVM?
Basic⌄
In MVP, the Presenter holds a direct reference to the View interface and calls methods on it — tight coupling that requires careful lifecycle management (detach on destroy). In MVVM, the ViewModel exposes observable state (LiveData/StateFlow) and never holds a View reference. The View subscribes and unsubscribes independently. This makes MVVM lifecycle-safe automatically — ViewModel survives rotation, View re-subscribes on recreation.
Why use UseCases between ViewModel and Repository?
Basic⌄
Three reasons: (1) Single Responsibility — each UseCase encapsulates one business rule; (2) Testability — UseCases are pure Kotlin, no Android dependencies, unit-testable with JUnit using mock Repositories; (3) Reuse — multiple ViewModels can use the same UseCase. Without UseCases, business logic accumulates in ViewModels (Fat ViewModel anti-pattern) or Repositories.
What is MVI and how does it differ from MVVM?
Intermediate⌄
MVI (Model-View-Intent) enforces strict UDF with three components: sealed Intent class (all user actions explicit), immutable State data class (all UI state in one object), and a reducer (Intent + State → new State). Unlike MVVM where ViewModels may have multiple state flows and methods, MVI has one state object and one entry point (processIntent). This makes state transitions auditable and the complete state machine visible. Tradeoff: more boilerplate.
Where should the Repository interface be defined — in the domain layer or data layer?
Intermediate⌄
Domain layer. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle — the domain layer should not depend on the data layer. By defining the interface in domain and the implementation in data, the data layer depends on the domain (not the other way). This means UseCases can reference the interface without knowing about Retrofit or Room. In tests, you inject a fake Repository that implements the domain interface — zero Android SDK needed.
What dependencies should a UseCase have?
Intermediate⌄
Only Repository interfaces (defined in domain) and other UseCases or domain services. A UseCase should have zero Android SDK dependencies — no Context, no ViewModel, no Room entities, no Retrofit annotations. This purity makes it unit-testable with plain JUnit5. If you find yourself adding import android.* in a UseCase, that's a code smell — the logic probably belongs in the data layer or a domain-specific service.
When would you choose MVI over MVVM for a feature?
Intermediate⌄
Use MVI when a screen has many possible states and transitions that are hard to track with boolean flags across multiple StateFlows — checkout flows, complex onboarding, multi-step forms, game UIs. MVI's single state object makes every combination of booleans explicit; you can't have an "impossible state" (loading AND error simultaneously) if the State is a sealed class. Use MVVM for simpler screens — list/detail, settings, profile — where the overhead of sealed Intents and reducers isn't justified.
A junior dev put network retry logic in the ViewModel. Is this correct? Where should it go?
Senior⌄
Not correct for reusable retry logic. Network retry is a data-layer concern — it applies regardless of which screen triggers the request. Retry logic belongs in: (1) Repository (retryWhen on Flow, or manual retry in suspend function), or (2) a generic data source interceptor (OkHttp Interceptor for HTTP retries). The ViewModel should handle UI state for retries (show retry button, update loading state) but not implement the retry policy itself. If it's a business-level retry (e.g., retry payment only if network error, not if card declined), a UseCase can add retry semantics before calling the repository.
How would you test a UseCase that executes a bank transfer?
Senior⌄
class ExecuteTransferUseCaseTest { private val fakeRepo = FakeTransferRepository(); private val sut = ExecuteTransferUseCase(fakeRepo); @Test fun `transfer succeeds when funds available`() = runTest { val result = sut(fromAccount, toAccount, 100.toBigDecimal()); assertTrue(result.isSuccess); assertEquals(1, fakeRepo.recordedTransfers.size) }; @Test fun `transfer fails when API throws`() = runTest { fakeRepo.shouldThrow = IOException(); val result = sut(fromAccount, toAccount, 100.toBigDecimal()); assertTrue(result.isFailure) } }. FakeTransferRepository implements the domain interface — no Retrofit, no Room, no Hilt. Tests run on JVM in milliseconds.
Design the full architecture for a real-time price tracking screen in a banking app.
Senior⌄
UI: Compose screen collecting StateFlow. ViewModel: exposes PriceScreenState via stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5000)); uses SubscribeToPriceUpdatesUseCase. UseCase: SubscribeToPriceUpdatesUseCase(repo): returns Flow<PriceUpdate> — pure kotlin, composable with Flow operators. Repository interface (in domain): PriceRepository.observePrices(symbols): Flow<PriceUpdate>. Repository impl (in data): bridges WebSocket via callbackFlow; shareIn(appScope, WhileSubscribed(5000)) to share one socket among multiple subscribers. Local fallback: Room observeLatestPrices() on network error. Dependencies: ViewModel depends on UseCase; UseCase depends on Repository interface; RepositoryImpl depends on WebSocket client and Room DAO.
8B

Clean Architecture

Tier 1 Mod 8
Key Concept: Three concentric layers, the Dependency Rule, and the art of keeping your domain pure. The architecture standard for production Android apps.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Layer Responsibilities

Presentation: ViewModel, UI State,
  Composables — talks to UseCases

Domain: UseCase, Interfaces,
  Domain Models — PURE KOTLIN

Data: Repository Impls, DTOs,
  Mappers, Room, Retrofit

Dependency Rule

Presentation
  └─depends on─► Domain
Data
  └─implements─► Domain interfaces
Domain
  └─depends on─► NOTHING

UseCase Pattern

class GetUserUseCase @Inject constructor(
    private val repo: UserRepository
) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(id: String) =
        repo.getUser(id)
}

Mapper Pattern

// In :data module
fun UserDto.toDomain() = User(
    id = userId,
    name = fullName,
    email = emailAddress
)
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Violations

Anti-Pattern: Domain importing Android/Retrofit
import retrofit2.Response or import android.content.Context inside a UseCase or domain model instantly breaks the Dependency Rule and makes the domain untestable without Robolectric.
Anti-Pattern: Repository returning DTOs
If UserRepository.getUser() returns UserDto (with JSON annotations), the mapping responsibility leaks into the Presentation layer. Always map to domain models at the Data/Domain boundary.

Best Practices

  • One UseCase per action: GetUserUseCase, UpdateProfileUseCase — not a UserUseCase with ten methods
  • Domain models have no annotations: no @SerializedName, no @ColumnInfo, no @Parcelize (those belong in Data/Presentation)
  • UseCases are operator fun invoke: the idiomatic Kotlin style allows calling them like a function: getUser(userId)
  • Mappers as extension functions: fun UserDto.toDomain() keeps mapping code co-located with the DTO
  • Repository interface in Domain, impl in Data: enforced by separate Gradle modules so you cannot accidentally import the wrong one
  • Test UseCases with pure unit tests: no Mockk Android extensions needed — just mock the repository interface
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What are the three layers of Clean Architecture and what goes in each? ⌄
Presentation: ViewModel, UI State, Composables/Fragments — handles display logic and user events.

Domain: UseCases, Repository interfaces, Domain models, business rules — pure Kotlin, no Android imports.

Data: Repository implementations, DTOs, Mappers, Room DAOs, Retrofit API interfaces — bridges the domain to external systems.
Basic What is the Dependency Rule and why does it matter? ⌄
Source code dependencies must point inward only. Outer layers (Data, Presentation) can depend on inner layers (Domain), but Domain can never import anything from Data or Presentation. This means the business logic is decoupled from framework details, making it independently testable and replaceable.
Basic Why should Domain models be free of JSON/Room annotations? ⌄
Annotations like @SerializedName and @ColumnInfo are data concerns tied to specific frameworks. If you put them on domain models, your business logic becomes coupled to Gson and Room. When you switch serialisation libraries or databases, you'd have to modify domain models — violating OCP and the Dependency Rule. The solution is separate DTOs in the Data layer with mappers at the boundary.
Intermediate Explain the Mapper pattern with a concrete example. ⌄
A mapper converts between layers' models. A UserDto from Retrofit has @SerializedName annotations and potentially nullable fields due to API inconsistency. The domain User has validated, non-null fields. An extension function fun UserDto.toDomain(): User in the Data layer performs this conversion — handling nulls, renaming fields, and transforming types — so the Domain and Presentation layers work with clean, safe models.
Intermediate When would you skip the UseCase layer? ⌄
For screens with no business logic — like a settings toggle that just calls repository.saveTheme(theme) — a passthrough UseCase adds ceremony without benefit. In those cases, having the ViewModel call the repository directly is fine. The UseCase layer pays off when there's real orchestration: validating inputs, combining data from multiple repositories, handling business-specific error cases, or reusing the same logic across ViewModels.
Intermediate How does Dependency Inversion work between Domain and Data? ⌄
The Domain layer defines a interface ProductRepository with methods the UseCase needs. The Data layer provides class ProductRepositoryImpl : ProductRepository. Hilt binds the implementation to the interface via @Binds. The UseCase only knows about the interface — it never imports or instantiates the implementation. This means swapping Room for SQLDelight only requires changing the Data module; Domain and Presentation are untouched.
Intermediate How do you handle errors across the layers? ⌄
The Data layer catches network/database exceptions and converts them into domain errors — either via Kotlin's Result<T> or a custom sealed class. The UseCase propagates or transforms these into business-meaningful sealed results (e.g., InsufficientFunds instead of HttpException(402)). The ViewModel maps these to UI states. The Presentation layer never sees raw IOException — it sees domain-specific failure cases it can display meaningfully.
Senior How do you enforce Clean Architecture boundaries at scale? ⌄
Gradle modules are the primary enforcement mechanism — the :domain module declares no Android or framework dependencies, so any bad import fails the build. For monolithic single-module projects, tools like ArchUnit (via JVM tests) can assert that no class in the domain package imports anything from data or presentation. On large teams, a custom Lint rule or a modularisation guide in the team wiki prevents drift. The key is making violations visible at CI time, not code review time.
Senior Design a Clean Architecture structure for an e-commerce app with offline support. ⌄
Domain: ProductRepository interface with getProducts(): Flow<List<Product>>, GetFeaturedProductsUseCase, domain models Product, Cart, Order.

Data: ProductRepositoryImpl that first emits Room data (instant), then fetches from Retrofit, maps DTOs, saves to Room — so the Flow automatically re-emits the updated list. Room is the single source of truth. TTL-based cache invalidation triggers background refresh.

Presentation: ProductListViewModel collects the Flow, emits UiState.Loading / UiState.Success(products) / UiState.Offline(cachedProducts).

The offline-first pattern works naturally because Room's Flow re-emits whenever the local DB updates, regardless of whether the update came from the network or a local action.
Senior A colleague says UseCases are just "extra classes that call repository methods". How do you respond? ⌄
They're right for trivial cases, and that's fine — not every UseCase needs to justify its existence. The value emerges when:

1. Multiple ViewModels need the same logic — without a UseCase, you'd duplicate it or put it in the repository (wrong layer).
2. Business rules accumulate — a "place order" flow that started as a single repo call now involves inventory check, payment processing, loyalty points, and audit logging. A UseCase is the right seam for that.
3. Testing — a UseCase with mocked repos tests business logic at <1ms, no emulator needed.

The pragmatic approach: start without UseCases, extract them when ViewModels grow beyond display logic. The architecture supports that evolution.
9A

SOLID Principles

Tier 1 Mod 9
Key Concept: Five object-oriented design principles that produce maintainable, scalable Android code. Each principle with definition, Android violation, and correct fix.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

SRP — One Reason to Change

Activity → just inflate & observe
ViewModel → UI state logic
UseCase → business rules
Repository → data access

OCP — Extend, Don't Modify

sealed class Payment {
    class Card(...) : Payment()
    class PayPal(...) : Payment()
    // add Crypto here — no other change
}

LSP — Safe Substitution

// Prefer interfaces over open classes
// Sealed classes = safe exhaustive when
// Avoid: subclass that throws on override

ISP + DIP

// ISP: split fat interfaces
interface ProductReader { getProducts() }
interface ProductWriter { save(); delete() }
// DIP: inject the interface
class VM @Inject constructor(
    val repo: ProductReader  // not Impl!
)
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

SRP in Android — The Activity God Class

Most Common Android SOLID Violation
Activities/Fragments that contain network calls, business logic, database access, date formatting, and navigation. This is the top anti-pattern in legacy Android code. The fix: ViewModel for UI logic, UseCase for business logic, Repository for data, separate formatters and mappers.

DIP in Tests

The most immediate payoff of DIP is testability. When CheckoutViewModel depends on interface PaymentProcessor, you can inject a FakePaymentProcessor in tests. When it depends on class StripeClient, you can't test it without hitting the network.

LSP and Kotlin Sealed Classes

Sealed classes are naturally LSP-compliant: all subtypes are declared in the same file, so you always know the complete set. A when expression on a sealed class is exhaustive — the compiler forces you to handle all cases, preventing substitution surprises.

ISP and Click Listeners

// ❌ Fat listener — every implementer must implement all methods
interface OnItemInteractionListener {
    fun onItemClick(id: String)
    fun onItemLongClick(id: String)
    fun onItemSwipeLeft(id: String)
    fun onItemSwipeRight(id: String)
}

// ✅ Specific lambdas passed only where needed
class OrderAdapter(
    private val onClick: (String) -> Unit,
    private val onSwipeDelete: ((String) -> Unit)? = null
)
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What does SRP mean and give an Android example of a violation? ⌄
SRP: a class should have only one reason to change. Classic Android violation: an Activity that contains Retrofit calls, SharedPreferences access, date formatting, and UI updates. It changes when the API changes, when the database schema changes, when the UI design changes, and when the business logic changes. Fix: extract to ViewModel (UI state), Repository (data), UseCase (business logic), and Formatter (display formatting).
Basic What is DIP and how does Hilt enforce it? ⌄
DIP: high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concretions. In Android, a ViewModel should depend on interface UserRepository, not class UserRepositoryImpl. Hilt enforces this via @Binds in a @Module, which maps the interface to its implementation at compile time. The ViewModel only knows the interface — in tests, you inject a fake; in production, Hilt injects the real impl.
Basic How does OCP apply to handling different payment methods in an app? ⌄
A when(paymentType: String) that keeps growing with new cases violates OCP — every new method modifies existing code. The fix is to define a PaymentProcessor interface with a charge() method, and represent each payment type as a sealed class subtype implementing it. The checkout logic calls processor.charge(amount) and never changes when a new payment type is added — it only extends via a new subclass.
Intermediate Spot the SOLID violations in this code and suggest fixes. ⌄
Scenario: class ProfileViewModel : ViewModel() { val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder().build(); fun loadUser() { retrofit.create(Api::class.java).getUser(); Room.databaseBuilder(...).build().userDao().getAll() } }

SRP violation: ViewModel constructs Retrofit and Room directly — data access is not its responsibility.
DIP violation: Depends on concrete Retrofit and AppDatabase classes, not interfaces.
Fix: Inject a UserRepository interface via Hilt. The ViewModel calls repository.getUser() and knows nothing about HTTP or SQL.
Intermediate Explain ISP with a RecyclerView listener example. ⌄
A fat OnItemInteractionListener with onClick, onLongClick, onSwipeLeft, onSwipeRight forces every implementer to implement all four methods, even if only one is used. ISP says: give clients only what they need. The fix: accept separate lambdas — onClick: (String) -> Unit, onSwipeDelete: ((String) -> Unit)? = null — so the screen only provides what it actually handles.
Intermediate How do sealed classes relate to LSP and OCP? ⌄
LSP: sealed class subtypes are all declared in one file with full visibility — you always know every possible subtype. A when on a sealed type is exhaustive, so the compiler enforces that all cases are handled. No subtype can introduce unexpected behaviour because the set is closed.

OCP: a sealed class with a when expression in a single place isn't OCP (adding a subtype requires modifying the when). But using the subtypes polymorphically — e.g., each subtype implements render() — achieves OCP because calling code never changes.
Intermediate Why can a class that uses Hilt still violate DIP? ⌄
Hilt is a DI framework, not a DIP enforcer. If you write @Inject constructor(val repo: UserRepositoryImpl), you're injecting a concrete class — DIP is still violated. For Hilt to enforce DIP, you must: (1) define an interface UserRepository in the domain layer, (2) implement it as UserRepositoryImpl in the data layer, (3) use @Binds to map the interface to the impl in a Hilt module, (4) inject the interface everywhere. Hilt automates the wiring; you must choose to depend on the interface.
Senior A PR adds a new feature by subclassing a Fragment and overriding onResume() to throw if a condition isn't met. What principle does this violate and what's the correct fix? ⌄
This violates LSP. Any code that uses the base Fragment type and calls resume() now has to defensively check whether it might throw — the subtype is not safely substitutable for the base type. The precondition (the condition that must be met) is stronger in the subtype than in the base, which is precisely what LSP forbids.

Fix: represent the precondition check as part of the Fragment's visible state machine. Use a UiState.RequiresCondition sealed class variant and navigate away or show an error screen. Never throw exceptions from lifecycle methods — the calling framework doesn't expect it and won't recover gracefully.
Senior How would you identify SOLID violations in a codebase of 200,000 lines during a technical interview review? ⌄
I'd look for these signals:

SRP: Classes >300 lines, or classes with methods that import 3+ different subsystems (network + db + UI).
OCP: Files with large when blocks on string/int types, especially in service or handler classes.
LSP: Overridden methods that throw UnsupportedOperationException, or empty overrides.
ISP: Interfaces with 8+ methods; implementers that stub half the methods with empty bodies.
DIP: Classes that construct their own dependencies (val x = ConcreteClass()) inside constructors or init blocks.

Tooling: Detekt rules enforce class/method line counts. ArchUnit assertions verify layer dependencies. These run in CI so violations are caught automatically.
Senior SOLID was defined for OOP. How relevant is it for Kotlin with its functional features? ⌄
Still very relevant, but Kotlin's features change the implementation idioms:

SRP: Even more relevant — Kotlin's extension functions let you decompose behaviour without subclassing.
OCP: Sealed classes are Kotlin's native way to express a closed-for-modification set of types with compile-time exhaustiveness.
LSP: Less of a problem because Kotlin discourages inheritance (open must be explicit) and favours interfaces and composition.
ISP: Functional interfaces (fun interface) and lambdas are naturally segregated — a lambda is a single-method interface.
DIP: Extension functions on interfaces allow default behaviour without breaking DIP. The principle remains; the syntax is more concise.
10A

Creational Patterns

Tier 1 Mod 10
Key Concept: Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, and Builder — the four creational patterns that govern object construction in production Android apps.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Singleton

object Tracker { ... }     // simple
@Singleton @Provides
fun provideDb(): AppDatabase // Hilt managed

Factory Method

companion object {
    fun newInstance(id: String) =
        MyFragment().apply {
            arguments = bundleOf("id" to id)
        }
}

Abstract Factory

interface UiComponentFactory {
    fun createButton(ctx: Context): Button
    fun createInput(ctx: Context): EditText
}
// LightThemeFactory / DarkThemeFactory

Builder

OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(30, SECONDS)
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor())
    .build()
// validate at build(), not at use time
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Singleton Pitfalls

Global Mutable State
A Kotlin object with mutable state (e.g., a mutable list, a mutable property) shared across threads is a race condition waiting to happen. Either make it thread-safe (Mutex, AtomicReference, synchronized) or eliminate the mutability by letting DI manage the instance.
Context Leaks
Never store a reference to an Activity or Fragment Context in a singleton. It will outlive the Activity and cause a memory leak. Use applicationContext only.

Builder Best Practices

  • Validate at build time: throw descriptive exceptions from build() for required fields — not at usage time
  • Return this from setters (or use apply) to enable method chaining
  • Make the built object immutable: the Builder is mutable; the product should be a data class with val properties

Factory Method vs Direct Construction

Use the factory method when construction has conditions or side effects. Fragment.newInstance() exists because Android reconstructs Fragments from the back stack using the empty constructor — passing data via arguments bundle is the required pattern. A factory method hides this implementation detail from callers.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic How does Kotlin's object keyword implement Singleton? ⌄
Kotlin's object declaration creates a class with a private constructor and a INSTANCE static field. The JVM guarantees the initialisation is thread-safe via the class loading mechanism (static initialiser). The instance is lazily created on first access. This is equivalent to the "Initialization-on-demand holder" idiom in Java — thread-safe without synchronized blocks.
Basic Why is Fragment.newInstance() a factory method and why does it exist? ⌄
It's a factory method because it centralises Fragment creation and hides the argument bundle setup from callers. It exists because Android's Fragment system requires a public no-argument constructor — the system recreates Fragments from the back stack using that constructor. Arguments must be passed via setArguments(Bundle), not via a parameterised constructor. newInstance() encapsulates this requirement so callers can't accidentally use a parameterised constructor.
Basic Where does Android use the Builder pattern? ⌄
Builder pattern is pervasive in Android: OkHttpClient.Builder(), Retrofit.Builder(), NotificationCompat.Builder(), AlertDialog.Builder(), Room.databaseBuilder(), WorkRequest.Builder(), NavOptions.Builder(). All share the same characteristics: many optional parameters, method chaining, and a terminal build() that creates the immutable product.
Intermediate What are the problems with the Singleton pattern and how does Hilt address them? ⌄
Problems: (1) Global mutable state — any component can modify it, causing unpredictable behaviour. (2) Hard to test — you can't replace a object with a test fake without reflection. (3) Hidden dependencies — callers don't declare dependencies; they reach globally. (4) Context leaks — storing Activity context in a singleton leaks the Activity.

Hilt's solution: @Singleton scope creates one instance per application component, but the instance is provided via injection. Callers declare the dependency in their constructor; in tests, a test module replaces it with a fake. The singleton is managed by Hilt's component, not by static state.
Intermediate Implement a thread-safe lazy singleton for a Room database. ⌄
@Volatile private var INSTANCE: AppDatabase? = null in a companion object, then double-checked locking: INSTANCE ?: synchronized(this) { INSTANCE ?: Room.databaseBuilder(...).build().also { INSTANCE = it } }. @Volatile ensures the write is immediately visible to other threads. synchronized ensures only one thread creates the instance. In practice, Hilt's @Singleton is preferred over manual double-check locking.
Intermediate When would you choose a Builder over Kotlin named parameters? ⌄
Choose Builder when: (1) Construction requires validation before the object can exist — build() enforces invariants like required fields. (2) The object is being built across multiple method calls or time steps. (3) The API is consumed by Java callers (named parameters aren't available in Java). (4) You need to reuse a partial configuration — hold a Builder reference and call build() multiple times with different last-step variations. For internal Kotlin-only data classes with defaults, named parameters are almost always cleaner.
Intermediate Describe Abstract Factory with a white-label banking app example. ⌄
A white-label banking app serves 10 banks, each with their own brand colours, fonts, button styles, and icon sets. Define interface BrandComponentFactory with methods: createPrimaryButton(), createHeaderView(), createLogoImage(). Each bank gets its implementation: BarclaysFactory, HSBCFactory, etc. The checkout and home screens receive a BrandComponentFactory via injection — they call factory.createPrimaryButton() and get the bank-correct component without knowing which bank it is. Switching banks only requires changing which factory Hilt provides.
Senior How does Hilt's module system map to the Abstract Factory pattern? ⌄
A Hilt @Module is effectively an Abstract Factory for a set of related dependencies. The module interface (@Provides/@Binds methods) defines what the factory creates. Different test/production modules are different factories producing the same interface. For example, a NetworkModule creates OkHttpClient, Retrofit, and API interfaces as a consistent family. A FakeNetworkModule in tests produces fakes for the same interfaces. Hilt selects which module to use at compile time — the client code never changes.
Senior A Singleton holds a reference to a Context. What are the consequences and how do you fix it? ⌄
Consequences: If it's an Activity context, the Activity cannot be garbage collected as long as the singleton exists (application lifetime). This leaks all views, Drawables, and resources attached to that Activity — potentially hundreds of MB. The GC can't reclaim them until the process dies.

Fix: (1) Always use context.applicationContext in singletons — it lives as long as the app process. (2) For UI-related resources that require an Activity context, don't store them in singletons — let the Activity own them and pass them as parameters. (3) Use LeakCanary in debug builds to detect these leaks automatically.
Senior Design an OkHttpClient builder configuration for a production banking app. ⌄
Production banking client builder includes: (1) CertificatePinner — pin the server's certificate to prevent MITM. (2) AuthInterceptor — adds Bearer token from TokenStore, refreshes on 401. (3) HttpLoggingInterceptor — Level.NONE in production, Level.BODY in debug (wrap with BuildConfig check). (4) connectTimeout(15s) / readTimeout(30s) / writeTimeout(30s). (5) ConnectionPool(5, 5, MINUTES) — reuse connections. (6) Authenticator — for automatic token refresh on 401. (7) retryOnConnectionFailure(false) — let the app handle retries with exponential backoff for payment idempotency.
10B

Structural Patterns

Tier 2 Mod 10
Key Concept: Adapter, Decorator, Facade, and Proxy — how Android and its libraries compose objects to build larger structures without tight coupling.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Adapter

RecyclerView.Adapter → adapts
  List<T> to RecyclerView
Moshi @JsonAdapter → adapts
  JSON to custom type

Decorator (OkHttp)

OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor())
    .addInterceptor(RetryInterceptor())
// each wraps the next — chain.proceed()

Facade

// Repository hides Room + Retrofit
class ProductRepo(
    val dao: ProductDao,
    val api: ProductApi
) : ProductRepository

Decorator — Kotlin by

class CachedRepo(
    val d: Repo
) : Repo by d {          // delegates all
    override fun get(id) =
        cache[id] ?: d.get(id)
}
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Decorator / Interceptor Pitfalls

Order Matters in Interceptor Chains
In OkHttp, Application Interceptors run before the network; Network Interceptors run after the connection is established. Placing the AuthInterceptor as a Network Interceptor means it won't run for cached responses. Auth should be an Application Interceptor. Order also matters for retry logic — the retry interceptor must wrap the auth interceptor.

Facade Anti-Pattern: God Repository

God Repository
A UserRepository with 30 methods covering profile, authentication, notifications, preferences, analytics, and billing is a Facade that has become a god object. Split by bounded context: UserProfileRepository, AuthRepository, NotificationRepository.

Adapter Best Practices

  • Use ListAdapter with DiffUtil.ItemCallback over plain RecyclerView.Adapter — diffing on a background thread, smooth animations
  • Adapter should not contain business logic — just binds data to views. Logic belongs in ViewModel or UseCase
  • Use custom Moshi/Gson adapters for non-standard types (BigDecimal, LocalDate, enums) instead of raw String parsing in the ViewModel
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What design pattern does RecyclerView.Adapter implement? ⌄
The Adapter pattern. RecyclerView knows only about ViewHolders — it doesn't know what data you have or how it should be displayed. The Adapter bridges the gap by converting List<Order> (or any data) into the ViewHolder interface RecyclerView expects. The onBindViewHolder() method is the core adaptation — it maps a data item to a view.
Basic How does the Repository pattern relate to the Facade pattern? ⌄
The Repository pattern is the Facade pattern applied to data access. A Repository hides the complexity of multiple data sources (Room database, Retrofit API, DataStore, in-memory cache, third-party SDKs) behind a single, clean interface. Callers — ViewModel, UseCase — call repository.getProducts() without knowing whether data is being fetched from network, served from cache, or loaded from the local database.
Basic What is an OkHttp interceptor and which pattern does it implement? ⌄
An OkHttp interceptor implements the Decorator pattern (also called Chain of Responsibility in GoF terms). Each interceptor receives a Chain object, optionally modifies the request, calls chain.proceed(request) to pass to the next interceptor, and optionally modifies the response. Common interceptors: Auth (adds Bearer token), Logging (logs request/response), Retry (retries on failure), Cache (adds Cache-Control headers).
Intermediate Implement a caching repository decorator in Kotlin using the by keyword. ⌄
class CachedProductRepository(private val delegate: ProductRepository, private val cache: LruCache<String, Product>) : ProductRepository by delegate { override suspend fun getProduct(id: String): Product = cache.get(id) ?: delegate.getProduct(id).also { cache.put(id, it) } }

The by delegate clause auto-generates delegation for every method in ProductRepository. We only override getProduct to add caching behaviour. This is the Decorator pattern — we added behaviour without modifying or subclassing ProductRepositoryImpl.
Intermediate What's the difference between Application Interceptors and Network Interceptors in OkHttp? ⌄
Application Interceptors (added via addInterceptor()): run before OkHttp's core mechanics. They run even for cached responses, see the full original URL (before any redirects), and are called once per call. Best for: auth headers, retry logic, logging business-level requests.

Network Interceptors (added via addNetworkInterceptor()): run after OkHttp decides a real network request is needed. They see the wire-level request, including headers added by OkHttp itself. They are NOT called for cache hits. Best for: modifying gzip compression, low-level traffic analysis.
Intermediate How does ViewModel implement the Proxy pattern? ⌄
ViewModel acts as a Protection Proxy and Virtual Proxy: (1) The UI never directly accesses the UseCase or Repository — it only talks to the ViewModel. (2) The ViewModel controls when data is fetched (lazy init, only when UI subscribes), who can observe it (via StateFlow), and what lifecycle-sensitive cleanup happens. (3) Across configuration changes (screen rotation), the ViewModel survives while the Activity dies and recreates — the UI reconnects to the same proxy and gets the last cached state immediately.
Intermediate How would you use the Adapter pattern to integrate a third-party analytics SDK? ⌄
Define an interface AnalyticsTracker in your domain with methods like track(event: AnalyticsEvent). Create a FirebaseAnalyticsAdapter(val firebase: FirebaseAnalytics) : AnalyticsTracker that translates domain events to Firebase-specific calls. Inject AnalyticsTracker everywhere — never import FirebaseAnalytics in business code. If you switch to Mixpanel, you write a new adapter, not change 50 call sites. This also makes testing trivial — inject a fake adapter that records events.
Senior Design an OkHttp interceptor chain for a banking app with auth, retry, and certificate pinning. ⌄
Application Interceptors (outer to inner): (1) RetryInterceptor — catches network exceptions, retries up to 3 times with exponential backoff, but NOT for payment endpoints (idempotency concern). (2) AuthInterceptor — adds Bearer token; on 401, refreshes token once then retries original request using a Mutex to prevent concurrent refresh. Network Interceptor (none needed for this case). Separately: CertificatePinner — set on the OkHttpClient, not as an interceptor. It validates the server certificate against pinned hashes before any interceptor runs, preventing MITM even if a user installs a rogue CA.
Senior How does Retrofit use the Proxy pattern internally? ⌄
When you call retrofit.create(ApiService::class.java), Retrofit uses Java's Proxy.newProxyInstance() to create a dynamic proxy that implements your API interface. The proxy's InvocationHandler intercepts every method call, reads the Retrofit annotations (@GET, @POST, @Path, etc.) to build an HTTP request, executes it via OkHttp, and passes the response through your converter factory to return the typed result. This is why your API interface has no implementation — Retrofit generates it at runtime via reflection-based proxying.
Senior A Repository has grown to 40 methods. How do you refactor it using structural patterns? ⌄
A 40-method Repository is a "God Facade" — it has violated SRP. Refactor strategy:

1. Identify bounded contexts: group the 40 methods by feature domain (e.g., product listing, cart, orders, user profile). Each group becomes its own facade interface.
2. Apply ISP: split into ProductReader, CartRepository, OrderRepository, UserRepository.
3. Decorator for cross-cutting concerns: caching, logging, and auth are implemented as decorators wrapping the base implementations.
4. Aggregate facade if needed: if some callers legitimately need access to all domains, a thin ShoppingFacade can compose the smaller repositories — without duplicating logic.
10C

Behavioral Patterns

Tier 2 Mod 10
Key Concept: Observer, Strategy, Command, and State — the behavioral patterns that govern communication and responsibility assignment in Android apps.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Observer

StateFlow — for UI state (has value)
SharedFlow — for one-shot events
collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
  — stops in bg, resumes on STARTED

State (Sealed UiState)

sealed class UiState {
    object Loading : UiState()
    data class Success(val d: D) : UiState()
    data class Error(val msg: String) : UiState()
    object Empty : UiState()
}

Strategy

fun interface SortStrategy<T> {
    fun sort(items: List<T>): List<T>
}
// Usage: any lambda is a strategy
val byPrice = SortStrategy { it.sortedBy { p -> p.price } }

Command

interface Command {
    suspend fun execute()
    suspend fun undo()
}
// WorkManager = distributed command queue
WorkManager.enqueue(workRequest)
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Observer Pitfalls

Collecting in the Wrong Lifecycle
lifecycleScope.launch { viewModel.flow.collect { ... } } continues collecting even when the app is in the background, wasting resources and potentially processing stale data. Use repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) or collectAsStateWithLifecycle() in Compose, which automatically pauses and resumes collection with the lifecycle.
Using SharedFlow for UI State
SharedFlow doesn't have a current value — a new subscriber (e.g., after screen rotation) gets nothing. Always use StateFlow for UI state, and SharedFlow only for one-shot events (navigation, Snackbar).

State Pattern Best Practices

  • Use object for stateless states and data class for states carrying data
  • Transitions should be explicit: a canTransitionTo() method on the state prevents invalid transitions in the domain model
  • One ViewModel → one UiState sealed class: don't have separate isLoading, error, data properties — unify into a single state

Command Pattern Best Practices

  • For WorkManager: use unique work names (enqueueUniqueWork) to prevent duplicate background tasks
  • Ensure commands are idempotent when they can be retried (WorkManager retries on failure)
  • Separate the command from its executor — the executor manages history and concurrency, the command encapsulates only the action
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What is the Observer pattern and where does Android use it? ⌄
Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when a subject changes state, all observers are notified. In Android: StateFlow is the subject — ViewModels emit state, Composables and Fragments observe it. Clicking "Collect" registers as an observer; unsubscribing (leaving the screen) removes it. Room's Flow<List<T>> from DAO queries is also Observer — the database is the subject, the ViewModel is the observer, and Room notifies it automatically when the underlying table changes.
Basic Why use a sealed class for UI state instead of multiple boolean flags? ⌄
Multiple booleans (isLoading, hasError, isEmpty) create 8 possible combinations (2³), but most are invalid — e.g., isLoading=true AND hasError=true is nonsensical. A sealed class UiState with subclasses Loading, Success, Error, Empty has exactly 4 valid states. The compiler exhausts all cases in a when expression, ensuring every state is handled. Invalid state combinations are unrepresentable at compile time.
Basic How does WorkManager implement the Command pattern? ⌄
A WorkRequest is a Command object — it encapsulates the work to be done (ListenableWorker subclass), the constraints (network type, charging state), input data, retry policy, and backoff criteria. WorkManager.enqueue(request) is the execute. WorkManager persists commands to a SQLite database and executes them when constraints are met — even across app restarts. This gives you deferred, reliable, persistent command execution.
Intermediate What is the difference between StateFlow and SharedFlow? ⌄
StateFlow: always holds a current value (initial value required); new collectors immediately receive the current value; uses distinctUntilChanged — identical consecutive values are not re-emitted. Best for UI state.

SharedFlow: configurable replay buffer (default 0 — no replay); supports multiple simultaneous emissions; doesn't require an initial value. Best for one-shot events: navigation, Snackbar messages, error popups. A new collector with replay=0 doesn't get past events, which is exactly what you want for "show once" notifications.
Intermediate Implement the Strategy pattern for a text search algorithm in Kotlin. ⌄
fun interface SearchStrategy { fun search(query: String, items: List<Product>): List<Product> }
val exactMatch = SearchStrategy { q, items -> items.filter { it.name == q } }
val fuzzyMatch = SearchStrategy { q, items -> items.filter { it.name.contains(q, ignoreCase = true) } }
val ftsMatch = SearchStrategy { q, items -> ftsEngine.search(q) }

The ViewModel holds a var searchStrategy: SearchStrategy and the UI calls viewModel.setSearchStrategy(fuzzyMatch). The search logic never changes — only the strategy does.
Intermediate How do you implement undo functionality using the Command pattern? ⌄
Define interface Command { suspend fun execute(); suspend fun undo() }. Implement commands like DeleteItemCommand(repo, item) where execute() deletes and undo() re-inserts. A CommandExecutor holds an ArrayDeque<Command> as history. Every executed command is pushed to the deque. undo() pops the last command and calls its undo(). In the UI: show a Snackbar with "Undo" after deletion; the button calls viewModel.undo(). This is exactly how Gmail's "Undo send" or Android's swipe-to-delete work.
Intermediate What lifecycle-aware way should you use to collect a Flow in a Fragment? ⌄
Use viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) inside onViewCreated:

viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) { viewModel.state.collect { render(it) } } }

This automatically stops the collector when the Fragment moves to the STOPPED state (backgrounded) and resumes when it returns to STARTED. Without this, the coroutine runs even when the Fragment is invisible, wasting resources and potentially crashing on updates to destroyed views.
Senior MVI architecture uses multiple behavioral patterns. Identify them and explain how they compose. ⌄
MVI (Model-View-Intent) is three behavioral patterns composed:

1. Command: User interactions produce "Intents" (UserIntent.AddToCart, UserIntent.Search) — each Intent is a Command describing what the user wants to do. They're dispatched to the ViewModel, not executed inline.

2. State: The ViewModel maintains a single sealed UiState that represents all possible screen states. A "reducer" function takes (currentState, intent) and produces the next state — this is a pure State pattern transition function.

3. Observer: The View observes the single StateFlow<UiState> and re-renders entirely when it changes. The View is a passive observer — it never reads state directly, only reacts to emissions.

The composition provides: testable transitions (test the reducer with no Android context), unidirectional data flow (commands → state → view, never backwards), and deterministic replay.
Senior Design a state machine for an automotive app's vehicle connection lifecycle. ⌄ 
sealed class ConnectionState {
    object Disconnected : ConnectionState()
    object Scanning : ConnectionState()
    data class Connecting(val device: BluetoothDevice) : ConnectionState()
    data class Connected(val device: BluetoothDevice, val session: Session) : ConnectionState()
    data class Error(val cause: Throwable) : ConnectionState()
}

fun ConnectionState.canTransitionTo(next: ConnectionState) = when (this) {
    is Disconnected -> next is Scanning
    is Scanning     -> next is Connecting || next is Disconnected
    is Connecting   -> next is Connected || next is Error || next is Disconnected
    is Connected    -> next is Disconnected || next is Error
    is Error        -> next is Disconnected
}
State machine enforces legal transitions, making it impossible to jump from Disconnected to Connected without going through Scanning → Connecting. The ViewModel emits this as a StateFlow; the dashboard UI maps each state to different UI: spinner for Scanning, progress for Connecting, live data for Connected.
Senior How would you test a Strategy pattern implementation in isolation? ⌄
Strategy's key testability benefit: each strategy is an isolated, stateless function — no Android framework needed. Tests:

1. Unit test each strategy: val result = byPriceAsc.sort(sampleList); assertEquals(sortedByPrice, result) — pure Kotlin test, sub-millisecond.
2. Test the context with a fake strategy: inject a SortStrategy { it } (identity — returns items unchanged) when testing the ViewModel. This isolates the ViewModel test from sorting logic.
3. Test strategy switching: verify that calling viewModel.sortBy(byRating) causes the StateFlow to emit a re-sorted list.

This is exactly why Strategy + DIP together produce the highest testability: each algorithm is a function, the context is tested with fakes.
11A

DI &amp; Hilt Basics

Tier 1 Mod 11
Key Concept: Why dependency injection, constructor vs field injection, and Hilt's core annotations: @Inject , @Module , @Provides , @Binds , @InstallIn , scopes, and qualifiers.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Core Annotations

@HiltAndroidApp   → Application class
@AndroidEntryPoint → Activity/Fragment
@HiltViewModel    → ViewModel
@Inject           → constructor or field
@Singleton        → app-wide scope

@Provides vs @Binds

// @Provides — construction needed
@Provides fun provideRetrofit(...) = Retrofit.Builder()...build()

// @Binds — interface mapping
@Binds abstract fun bindRepo(
    impl: RepoImpl
): Repository

Qualifiers

@Qualifier @Retention(BINARY)
annotation class AuthClient

@AuthClient @Provides
fun provideAuthOkHttp() = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor()).build()

Scopes

@Singleton        → App lifetime
@ViewModelScoped  → ViewModel lifetime
@ActivityScoped   → Activity instance
@FragmentScoped   → Fragment instance
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Scope Mismatch

Scope Mismatch — Most Common Hilt Bug
Injecting a @ActivityScoped dependency into a @Singleton component. The Singleton lives longer than the Activity — Dagger catches this at compile time with a "cannot be provided without an @Singleton scope" error. Always match the scope to the shortest-lived component that needs the dependency.

Field Injection and Lateinit

Accessing Field-Injected Property Before Injection
@Inject lateinit var service: MyService — accessing service before super.onCreate() in an Activity (where Hilt performs injection) causes a UninitializedPropertyAccessException. Always access injected fields after super.onCreate().

@Provides vs @Binds

  • Prefer @Binds for interface-to-implementation bindings — it's a compile-time hint, not a function call
  • Never have both @Binds and @Provides for the same type in the same module
  • @Binds requires an abstract class for the module; @Provides can be in an object

@ApplicationContext vs Context

// ✅ Use @ApplicationContext qualifier for Context in Singleton-scoped modules
@Provides
fun provideDatabase(@ApplicationContext ctx: Context): AppDatabase = /* ... */

// ✅ Use @ActivityContext for Activity-scoped components
@Provides
fun provideNavigator(@ActivityContext ctx: Context): Navigator = /* ... */
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What are the three main benefits of Dependency Injection? ⌄
1. Testability: inject a fake or mock implementation instead of the real one — test the class in isolation. 2. Loose coupling: classes depend on interfaces, not concrete types — changing the implementation doesn't require changing the consumer. 3. Single source of truth: dependency creation is centralised in Hilt modules — no scattered new SomeClass() calls, consistent configuration everywhere.
Basic What is the difference between constructor injection and field injection? ⌄
Constructor injection: class Foo @Inject constructor(val dep: Bar) — dependencies are declared in the constructor, immutable, visible, and testable by passing them directly. Preferred everywhere possible.

Field injection: @Inject lateinit var dep: Bar — Hilt sets the field after the object is created. Required for Activities, Fragments, and Views because Android's system creates them using the no-arg constructor and you can't inject via constructor. Fields are mutable and can be accessed before injection.
Basic What is @Binds and when do you use it over @Provides? ⌄
@Binds tells Dagger to use a specific implementation class when a given interface is requested. It's in an abstract module method with no body: @Binds abstract fun bindRepo(impl: RepoImpl): Repository. Use it when the implementation has its own @Inject constructor and you just need to map the interface to it.

Use @Provides when you need to execute code to create the object — calling a builder, configuring a client, or using a constructor with non-injectable parameters. @Binds generates less code and is preferred for pure interface bindings.
Intermediate What does @ViewModelScoped mean and how does it differ from @Singleton? ⌄
@Singleton: one instance per Application component — lives as long as the app process. All ViewModels and classes in the app share the same instance.

@ViewModelScoped: one instance per ViewModel — lives as long as the ViewModel. Different ViewModel instances get different instances. The ViewModel's onCleared() destroys the scoped dependency. Use this for dependencies that logically belong to one ViewModel's operation (e.g., a cart session manager, a paging data source).
Intermediate How do qualifiers solve the "multiple bindings of the same type" problem? ⌄
When you have two OkHttpClient instances — one with auth interceptor, one without — Hilt/Dagger can't distinguish them by type alone. Qualifier annotations act as labels. You define @Qualifier annotation class AuthClient and @Qualifier annotation class PublicClient, annotate each @Provides method with the appropriate qualifier, and annotate the injection site: @AuthClient @Inject val client: OkHttpClient. Dagger matches the qualifier at compile time.
Intermediate How do you inject into a class that Hilt doesn't manage (e.g., a custom View)? ⌄
Use @EntryPoint. Define an interface annotated with @EntryPoint and @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) that exposes the dependencies you need. In the custom View or ContentProvider, retrieve the entry point via EntryPointAccessors.fromApplication(context, MyEntryPoint::class.java) and call the accessor methods. This is the "manual injection" escape hatch — use it sparingly, as it's more fragile than normal injection.
Intermediate Why is Hilt preferred over Koin in large production apps? ⌄
Compile-time validation: Hilt/Dagger validates the entire dependency graph during compilation. Missing bindings, scope mismatches, and circular dependencies are build errors. Koin resolves at runtime — a missing dependency crashes the first time the code path is hit in production. For a banking or e-commerce app with hundreds of dependencies, finding a missing binding in CI (build failure) rather than in production (crash report) is critical.
Senior How do you write a unit test for a ViewModel that has Hilt-injected dependencies? ⌄
For a pure unit test, don't use Hilt at all — just instantiate the ViewModel directly with constructor injection, passing fakes:
val fakeRepo = FakeOrderRepository(); val vm = OrderViewModel(GetOrdersUseCase(fakeRepo))

For integration tests using Hilt (e.g., @HiltAndroidTest): create a test module annotated with @TestInstallIn that replaces the production module with fakes. The test Hilt component uses the test module. Use @UninstallModules(ProductionModule::class) on the test class to exclude the real module.

Prefer the first approach (no Hilt in unit tests) — it's faster and requires no instrumentation.
Senior Explain a scope mismatch error and how to fix it. ⌄
Scenario: @Singleton class UserDashboard @Inject constructor(val activityNav: Navigator) where Navigator is @ActivityScoped. Dagger error: "Navigator cannot be provided without an @ActivityScoped scope".

Why: A Singleton lives forever; an ActivityScoped dependency lives only while the Activity is alive. The Singleton would hold a reference to a dead Navigator after the Activity is destroyed — memory leak and crash.

Fix options: (1) Make Navigator also @Singleton if it doesn't truly require Activity context. (2) Move UserDashboard to @ActivityScoped if it logically belongs to an Activity. (3) Use Provider<Navigator> to defer Navigator creation and always get the current Activity's instance.
Senior How would you migrate a large app from manual DI (AppContainer pattern) to Hilt? ⌄
Incremental migration strategy:

1. Add Hilt to the project; annotate Application with @HiltAndroidApp.
2. Start with leaf nodes of the dependency graph — classes with no dependencies of their own. Add @Inject constructor.
3. Work up the graph: for each class whose dependencies are now injectable, add @Inject constructor. For third-party classes, create Hilt modules.
4. For interfaces, add @Binds modules.
5. Once a subsystem is fully in Hilt, annotate the consuming Activity/Fragment with @AndroidEntryPoint and annotate ViewModels with @HiltViewModel.
6. Remove the corresponding AppContainer code for that subsystem.

Key: don't try to migrate everything at once. The AppContainer and Hilt can coexist during migration — keep the old container for unmigrated parts.
11B

Hilt Components

Tier 1 Mod 11
Key Concept: Component hierarchy and lifetimes, Dagger code generation, @HiltViewModel internals, compile-time graph validation, and SubComponents vs Component dependencies.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Component Lifetimes

Singleton       → App process
ActivityRetained→ Survives rotation
ViewModel       → onCleared()
Activity        → onDestroy() (incl. rotation)
Fragment        → Fragment.onDestroy()

Dagger Code Generation

@Inject constructor
  → generates Foo_Factory

@HiltViewModel
  → generates ViewModel factory
  → registered in ViewModelComponent

Build fails if binding is missing!

Common Build Errors

"cannot be provided without @Provides"
  → add @Inject or @Provides
"depends on scoped components"
  → scope mismatch — fix scope
"found a dependency cycle"
  → use Provider<T> to break it

Provider vs Lazy

Provider<T>
  → new instance per get() call
Lazy<T>
  → one instance, created on first get()
  → cached for subsequent calls
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

ActivityRetainedScoped vs ActivityScoped Confusion

Most Common Scope Confusion
@ActivityRetainedScoped survives rotation — it's the scope backing the ViewModel. @ActivityScoped does NOT survive rotation — it's a new instance every time the Activity is recreated. Never put something that holds a View reference into ActivityRetainedScoped; Views don't survive rotation and you'll leak the old Activity.

Build Errors — Common Dagger Error Messages

Error messageRoot causeFix
"cannot be provided without an @Provides"Type has no binding in the graphAdd @Inject constructor or @Provides method
"is bound multiple times"Two modules provide the same typeAdd qualifiers or remove duplicate binding
"depends on scoped components"Scope mismatchMatch scope to the shortest-lived consumer
"found a dependency cycle"A → B → A circular dependencyUse Provider<T> to break the cycle

@HiltViewModel vs SavedStateHandle

// SavedStateHandle is automatically available in @HiltViewModel constructors
@HiltViewModel
class ProductDetailViewModel @Inject constructor(
    private val savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle,  // injected by Hilt — no @Provides needed
    private val getProduct: GetProductUseCase
) : ViewModel() {
    private val productId = requireNotNull(savedStateHandle.get<String>("product_id"))
}
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic List the Hilt component hierarchy from outermost to innermost. ⌄
SingletonComponent (Application) → ActivityRetainedComponent → ViewModelComponent and ActivityComponent (siblings) → FragmentComponent (child of Activity) → ViewComponent. ServiceComponent runs parallel to the Activity hierarchy, created/destroyed with a Service.
Basic What does Dagger generate when you annotate a class with @Inject constructor? ⌄
Dagger generates a Foo_Factory class that implements Factory<Foo>. The factory has a get() method that creates an instance of Foo by calling its constructor with the required dependencies (obtained from their own Providers). The factory is also used by Dagger to respect scope — if Foo is @Singleton, the component wraps the factory with a DoubleCheck to create only one instance.
Basic What is the difference between @ActivityScoped and @ActivityRetainedScoped? ⌄
@ActivityRetainedScoped: the instance lives inside ActivityRetainedComponent, which is preserved across configuration changes (rotation). One instance per Activity "logical session".

@ActivityScoped: the instance lives inside ActivityComponent, which is destroyed and recreated on rotation. A new instance is created every time the Activity is recreated. Use ActivityScoped for things that depend on the specific Activity instance (e.g., a Navigator using startActivity()).
Intermediate What does Dagger generate for a @HiltViewModel-annotated ViewModel? ⌄
Dagger generates: (1) A ViewModel_Factory that creates the ViewModel with all its injected constructor parameters. (2) A module that provides this factory, installed in the ViewModelComponent. (3) An entry point that Hilt's DefaultViewModelFactories can query to obtain the factory for a specific ViewModel class. When you call viewModels(), Android's ViewModelProvider asks Hilt's factory for the ViewModel type; Hilt looks up the generated factory and creates the ViewModel with injected dependencies.
Intermediate Explain how a child component accesses parent bindings. ⌄
In Hilt, all components are SubComponents. A SubComponent holds a reference to its parent component instance. When a binding is requested in a child component, Dagger first looks in the child's own modules. If not found, it looks in the parent's modules, then the grandparent's, up the hierarchy. This is why a FragmentComponent can inject a @Singleton-scoped OkHttpClient defined in the SingletonComponent — the request propagates up until it's satisfied. This is implicit in Hilt; with raw Dagger Component dependencies, you'd need to explicitly expose each binding.
Intermediate How does Hilt validate the dependency graph at compile time? ⌄
Dagger runs as an annotation processor (kapt or KSP). During the processing phase, it reads all @Module, @Provides, @Binds, @Inject annotations and builds an in-memory graph. Before generating any code, it validates: (1) every requested type has exactly one binding, (2) scope annotations are consistent (no parent-scope type in child component), (3) no cycles, (4) no duplicate bindings. Any violation produces a compiler error with a clear message pointing to the offending class. This happens before .class files are generated, so no runtime overhead.
Intermediate When would you use Provider<T> vs regular injection? ⌄
Use Provider<T> when: (1) You need a fresh instance on each call (not a singleton). (2) The dependency is expensive and may not always be needed — defer creation until first use. (3) You have a circular dependency — Provider<T> breaks the cycle because Dagger doesn't resolve T immediately on component creation. (4) The dependency comes from a child scope and you need to access the current instance at call time (e.g., getting the current Activity's Navigator from a longer-lived class).
Senior How does @Singleton scope work at the Dagger level — what code is generated? ⌄
When you scope a binding with @Singleton, Dagger wraps the generated Factory with a DoubleCheck wrapper in the component implementation. The simplified generated code:

private volatile Object myService = UNINITIALIZED;
On get(): checks if myService == UNINITIALIZED. If so, synchronized(this) check again, then create and store. Otherwise return the cached instance. This is the classic double-checked locking pattern.

Important: @Singleton does NOT make the class thread-safe internally. It only guarantees that Dagger creates one instance. If the class has mutable state accessed from multiple threads, you still need synchronisation inside the class.
Senior A Hilt build fails with "cannot be provided without an @Provides-annotated method" for a class that does have @Inject constructor. What are the possible causes? ⌄
1. One of the constructor's parameters is the missing binding — not the annotated class itself. Read the full error: Dagger traces the chain from the requesting site down to the unresolved leaf.
2. The class is in a Gradle module that isn't visible to the Hilt component module — transitive dependency not configured.
3. The class is abstract or an interface — @Inject constructor doesn't work on interfaces; you need @Binds.
4. Module is not installed — the @Module class exists but @InstallIn is missing or uses the wrong component.
5. Qualifier mismatch — the requesting site has a qualifier annotation but no binding with that qualifier exists.
Senior Design a multi-module Hilt setup for a feature module that needs to register its own bindings. ⌄
In a multi-module app, each feature module can define its own Hilt modules. Hilt aggregates them automatically at compile time via the app module's Hilt component:

:feature:payments module: @Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) abstract class PaymentModule { @Binds abstract fun bindPaymentRepo(impl: PaymentRepositoryImpl): PaymentRepository }

:app module: just needs @HiltAndroidApp on the Application class. Hilt's annotation processing scans all included modules and their transitive dependencies, finds all @InstallIn modules, and includes them in the generated component.

Key rule: the feature module must be on the compile-time classpath of the app module. Dynamic feature modules (DFM) require a separate Hilt component since they're loaded at runtime — use @DefineComponent for custom components in DFMs.
12A

REST &amp; HTTP

Tier 1 Mod 12
Key Concept: HTTP verbs, status codes, headers, authentication, timeouts, retry strategies, HTTP caching, and pagination — the networking fundamentals every Android engineer must know cold.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Status Codes

200 OK         201 Created
204 No Content 304 Not Modified
400 Bad Request 401 → refresh token
403 Forbidden  404 Not Found
409 Conflict   422 Validation
429 Rate limit 500/503 → retry

Verbs — Idempotent?

GET    ✓ safe + idempotent
DELETE ✓ idempotent
PUT    ✓ idempotent
POST   ✗ NOT idempotent → use idempotency key
PATCH  ✗ not usually idempotent

Retry Rules

DO retry:    500, 503, 429 (Retry-After)
             SocketTimeoutException
DO NOT:      400, 401*, 403, 404, 422
CAREFUL:     POST → only with idempotency key

ETag Caching

1. GET /products → 200, ETag: "v5abc"
2. GET /products, If-None-Match: "v5abc"
   → 304 Not Modified (no body, use cache)
   → 200 + new ETag if changed
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Status Code Pitfalls

401 vs 403 Confusion
401 = authentication problem (not logged in or token expired). 403 = authorisation problem (logged in but no permission). Handle them differently: 401 triggers token refresh; 403 shows "permission denied" and does NOT trigger a retry or refresh — the token is valid, the user just doesn't have access.
Retrying non-idempotent requests
Never blindly retry POST requests for financial operations. A retry after a timeout on POST /payments could charge the user twice. Always use idempotency keys for payment POST requests, and only retry with the same key.

Caching Sensitive Data

Never Cache Sensitive Responses
Account balances, transaction details, PII — always return Cache-Control: no-store, private. OkHttp respects this header and will not write the response to disk cache.

Best Practices

  • Version your API: /api/v1/ — never make breaking changes without a version bump
  • Use meaningful 4xx codes — don't return 500 for a validation error
  • Always set appropriate Content-Type on requests and responses
  • Add jitter to retry delays (random 0–500ms added to calculated backoff) to prevent thundering herd
  • Log request/response in debug only; never log Authorization headers or request bodies containing PII
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What is the difference between GET and POST? ⌄
GET is safe (no side effects), idempotent (same result every call), and cacheable. Parameters go in the URL query string. POST is unsafe (may cause side effects like creating a record), not idempotent, and not cached by default. Body carries the payload. GET for reading; POST for creating or triggering non-idempotent actions.
Basic What should an app do when it receives a 401 response? ⌄
401 means the request lacked valid authentication — typically an expired JWT. The app should: (1) Pause the current request. (2) Attempt to refresh the access token using the refresh token. (3) If refresh succeeds, retry the original request with the new token. (4) If refresh fails (e.g., refresh token expired), redirect the user to the login screen. This logic lives in an OkHttp Authenticator or AuthInterceptor to avoid duplicating it everywhere.
Basic What does Cache-Control: no-store mean and when should you use it? ⌄
Cache-Control: no-store means the response must not be stored in any cache — not memory cache, not disk cache, not intermediary proxy cache. The entire response is discarded after use. Use it for sensitive data: account balances, transaction history, authentication tokens, personal information. no-cache is different — it allows caching but requires re-validation with the server before each use.
Intermediate Explain ETag-based conditional GET and its benefit. ⌄
The server includes an ETag: "version_hash" header with its response. The client caches the response and the ETag. On the next request, the client adds If-None-Match: "version_hash". If the resource hasn't changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body — saving bandwidth and processing. If the resource changed, the server returns 200 with the new body and a new ETag. The benefit: freshness check happens every time (no stale data), but bandwidth is only used when the data actually changed.
Intermediate Describe a correct retry strategy for a mobile banking app. ⌄
1. Only retry transient failures: 500, 503, 429, SocketTimeoutException, ConnectException, UnknownHostException.
2. Exponential backoff + jitter: 1s, 2s, 4s ± random(0-500ms) to spread load.
3. Respect Retry-After: for 429/503, wait the specified duration.
4. Max 3 attempts: beyond that, fail and show the user an actionable error.
5. Idempotency keys for payments: generate a UUID before the first attempt; use the same key for all retries of the same payment.
6. Do NOT retry: 400, 401, 403, 404, 422 — retrying won't help.
Intermediate What is the difference between connectTimeout and readTimeout in OkHttp? ⌄
connectTimeout: how long OkHttp waits to establish a TCP connection to the server. A slow DNS lookup or an unresponsive server will trigger this. Typically 10–15 seconds.

readTimeout: how long OkHttp waits between receiving consecutive bytes from the server during data transfer. A server that starts responding but then stalls mid-response will trigger this. Typically 30 seconds for APIs; may need to be longer for large file downloads.

writeTimeout: how long OkHttp waits to finish sending the request body. Important for file uploads on slow connections.
Intermediate Compare cursor-based and offset-based pagination. ⌄
Offset: ?offset=20&limit=10 — skip the first 20 records. Simple to implement. Problem: if a new item is inserted at the top while the user is on page 2, page 3 will show one item they already saw on page 2 (page drift). Also slow for large offsets (database must scan rows to skip them).

Cursor: ?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ&limit=10 — start from after the item with that cursor. The cursor encodes the position (usually last item's ID + sort field). No page drift — you always get items after your last position, regardless of insertions. DB query is efficient (WHERE id > cursor instead of OFFSET). No random access. Best for infinite scroll/feed content.
Senior A payment POST times out. How do you handle it correctly to avoid double charges? ⌄
Network timeout doesn't mean the payment failed — the server may have processed it and the response was lost. Strategy:

1. Before the first POST, generate a UUID as an idempotency key and store it (DataStore/SharedPreferences) alongside the payment state.
2. Add the key to the request: Idempotency-Key: {uuid}.
3. On timeout, retry the same POST with the same idempotency key. The payment API returns the original response (e.g., 200 with the receipt) if already processed.
4. On success: clear the idempotency key.
5. If all retries fail: show a "payment pending" state. Check payment status via a separate GET endpoint using the idempotency key as a reference.
6. On app restart: check for any pending idempotency keys and resolve their status via GET before allowing new payments.
Senior How do you design API error handling that works across the full Android stack? ⌄
Layered error handling:

Data layer (Repository): wraps raw Response<T> in a sealed ApiResult type. Maps status codes: 401 → Unauthorized, 422 → ValidationError with parsed field errors, 5xx → ServerError, IOException → NetworkError.

Domain layer (UseCase): maps ApiResult to domain-specific results: InsufficientFunds, AccountFrozen, etc. The ViewModel never sees HTTP concepts.

Presentation layer (ViewModel): maps domain errors to UI states: UiState.Error("Insufficient balance"). Provides user-visible strings, not error codes.

Benefit: the API's error model can change without touching the ViewModel; the ViewModel's error display can change without touching the repository.
Senior How would you implement HTTP caching for a product catalogue in a Retrofit/OkHttp app? ⌄
1. Add an OkHttp Cache object: Cache(File(cacheDir, "http"), 10 * 1024 * 1024).
2. Set it on the OkHttpClient: .cache(cache).
3. Server must send Cache-Control: max-age=300 (5 min) and ETag: "v5abc".
4. For offline mode, add a network interceptor: if no network, override the request's Cache-Control to only-if-cached, max-stale=86400 — OkHttp will serve stale cache rather than failing.
5. Combine with a Room single source of truth for offline-first: on network response, update Room; UI observes Room's Flow. Even with cache miss, the user sees stale data from Room rather than an error.
12B

Retrofit &amp; OkHttp

Tier 1 Mod 12
Key Concept: Retrofit annotations, suspend vs Call, Moshi/Gson/kotlinx.serialization, OkHttp interceptors, Application vs Network interceptors, and how Retrofit wraps OkHttp.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Retrofit Annotations

@GET("products/{id}")
suspend fun getProduct(
    @Path("id") id: String,
    @Query("include") include: String? = null
): ProductDto

@POST("orders")
suspend fun createOrder(@Body req: OrderRequest,
    @Header("Idempotency-Key") key: String
): OrderDto

Interceptor Types

// Application interceptor
.addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor())
// → runs for EVERY call (incl. cache hits)

// Network interceptor
.addNetworkInterceptor(CacheHeaderFixer())
// → runs only for NETWORK calls

Converter Factory Choice

Gson     → DO NOT USE in Kotlin (no null safety)
Moshi    → preferred; @JsonClass generates adapters
kotlinx  → KMM-compatible, @Serializable annotation

OkHttp Singleton

@Singleton @Provides
fun provideOkHttp(token: TokenStore) =
    OkHttpClient.Builder()
        .connectTimeout(15, SECONDS)
        .readTimeout(30, SECONDS)
        .addInterceptor(AuthInterceptor(token))
        .build()
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Mistakes

Creating Multiple Retrofit Instances
Retrofit and OkHttpClient are expensive to create and should be singletons. Creating a new instance per request or per screen causes multiple connection pools, multiple thread pools, and wasted memory. Always inject via Hilt as @Singleton.
Logging Authorization Headers in Production
HttpLoggingInterceptor.Level.BODY logs the full Authorization header and request bodies. Guard with if (BuildConfig.DEBUG) — never ship BODY logging to production users. Sensitive data in logs is a security violation.

@Path Encoding

// By default, @Path URL-encodes the value
@GET("users/{userId}/orders")
suspend fun getOrders(@Path("userId") userId: String)
// userId = "user/123" → encodes to "user%2F123" (safe)

// To allow slashes (when path segment contains a full path):
@GET("{fullPath}")
suspend fun getResource(@Path("fullPath", encoded = true) path: String)

ConnectionPool

// OkHttp default: 5 connections, 5 min idle timeout — usually fine
// For high-throughput: increase maxIdleConnections
val connectionPool = ConnectionPool(maxIdleConnections = 10, keepAliveDuration = 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectionPool(connectionPool)
    .build()
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What is the role of a Retrofit converter factory? ⌄
A converter factory serialises your Kotlin objects into a request body (e.g., data class → JSON string) and deserialises the response body into Kotlin objects (JSON string → data class). Without a converter factory, you'd have to handle raw ResponseBody and call body.string() manually. Factories are added to Retrofit.Builder; Retrofit tries each in order until one claims it can handle the type.
Basic What is the difference between @Path and @Query in Retrofit? ⌄
@Path("id") replaces a placeholder in the URL path: @GET("products/{id}") with @Path("id") productId: String → GET /products/abc123. The value is URL-encoded by default.

@Query("status") appends a query parameter: @GET("products") with @Query("status") status: String → GET /products?status=ACTIVE. Null values are omitted from the URL.
Basic Why should you not use Gson with Kotlin? ⌄
Gson was designed for Java and doesn't understand Kotlin's type system. If a JSON field is missing, Gson sets the corresponding Kotlin property to null — even if it's declared as non-nullable. This bypasses Kotlin's null safety guarantees and causes NullPointerException at runtime when accessing the property. Moshi and kotlinx.serialization are Kotlin-aware and throw a descriptive exception if a required non-nullable field is missing.
Intermediate Explain the difference between Application Interceptors and Network Interceptors. ⌄
