Application Interceptors (addInterceptor()): added to the application layer, before OkHttp's core. They run for every call — including responses served from cache (no network request is made). They see the final URL after redirects. Best for: adding auth headers (so cached responses also get the header for consistency), retry logic, and request/response logging at the business level.

Network Interceptors (addNetworkInterceptor()): added to the network layer. They only run when an actual network connection is established. They don't run for cache hits. Best for: modifying response headers, adding Cache-Control headers, low-level traffic analysis or compression.
Intermediate Why should OkHttpClient be a singleton, and what happens if it's not? ⌄
Each OkHttpClient instance maintains its own: thread pool (for async calls), connection pool (open TCP connections), DNS cache, and HTTP response cache. Creating a new client per request means: no connection reuse (expensive TCP handshake every call), no shared cache (disk cache opens/closes repeatedly), wasted threads. A Singleton client reuses connections across requests (HTTP keep-alive), shares the thread pool efficiently, and has a single cache. This significantly reduces latency and memory usage.
Intermediate How do you access the HTTP status code and error body when using Retrofit? ⌄
Change the return type from T to Response<T>: suspend fun getUser(): Response<UserDto>. The Response wrapper provides: response.code() (HTTP status), response.isSuccessful() (200–299), response.body() (parsed body if successful), response.errorBody() (raw error body string for 4xx/5xx), response.headers() (all response headers). Parse the error body with your Moshi instance to get structured error objects.
Intermediate How would you build a Moshi instance with a custom adapter for BigDecimal? ⌄
class BigDecimalAdapter { @FromJson fun fromJson(value: String) = BigDecimal(value); @ToJson fun toJson(value: BigDecimal) = value.toPlainString() }

val moshi = Moshi.Builder().add(BigDecimalAdapter()).addLast(KotlinJsonAdapterFactory()).build()

Add adapters before KotlinJsonAdapterFactory so they take priority. Use addLast() for KotlinJsonAdapterFactory as a general fallback. Register the Moshi instance with Retrofit: .addConverterFactory(MoshiConverterFactory.create(moshi)).
Senior Describe in detail how Retrofit creates the implementation of your API interface. ⌄
When you call retrofit.create(OrderApi::class.java):

1. Retrofit uses Proxy.newProxyInstance(classLoader, arrayOf(OrderApi::class.java), handler) to create a Java dynamic proxy.
2. The InvocationHandler intercepts every method call on the proxy.
3. On getOrder("123"): Retrofit reads annotations (@GET("orders/{orderId}"), @Path("orderId")) from the method's reflection metadata.
4. It builds an OkHttp Request with the resolved URL, headers, and body.
5. For suspend fun: Retrofit uses a SuspendCallAdapterFactory that converts Call<T> to a coroutine-compatible execution using suspendCancellableCoroutine.
6. The request passes through OkHttp's interceptor chain and returns a Response.
7. The configured ConverterFactory deserialises response.body() into the return type.
Senior How would you make a synchronous network call inside an OkHttp interceptor to refresh a token? ⌄
Use a separate, unauthenticated OkHttpClient instance and call .execute() (synchronous, not .enqueue()) on a new Call:

val refreshResponse = unauthClient.newCall(refreshRequest).execute()

Key rules: (1) Use the unauthenticated client — never the same client, or you'll infinite loop. (2) Use execute(), not enqueue() — interceptors run synchronously; enqueue() would require a callback and block the interceptor thread awkwardly. (3) Use a Mutex to ensure only one refresh request happens concurrently when multiple API calls fail with 401 simultaneously. (4) After refreshing, update the token store and retry the original request with chain.proceed(newRequest).
Senior A production app is making too many connections. What OkHttp settings would you investigate? ⌄
1. Multiple OkHttpClient instances: each has its own connection pool. Consolidate to a singleton. Check via profiling — unique pool objects.
2. ConnectionPool configuration: default is 5 idle connections, 5 min keep-alive. For high traffic, increase maxIdleConnections so connections aren't closed and reopened.
3. HTTP/2 not being used: HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple requests over one connection. Verify server supports HTTP/2; OkHttp enables it automatically if the server supports ALPN.
4. Aggressive timeouts: very short timeouts cause premature connection closure. Check if keepAliveDuration aligns with server's connection timeout.
5. retryOnConnectionFailure: if true, OkHttp opens new connections on failure — can compound connection issues during server outages.
12C

Advanced Networking

Tier 1 Mod 12
Key Concept: Certificate pinning, token refresh with Mutex, concurrent refresh problem, API error handling with sealed Result, and offline-first networking strategies.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Certificate Pinning

CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.bank.com", "sha256/PROD_HASH=")
    .add("api.bank.com", "sha256/BACKUP=")  // always add backup!
    .build()
// OR: network_security_config.xml

Concurrent Token Refresh

companion object { val mutex = Mutex() }

runBlocking { mutex.withLock {
    if (tokenStore.getAccessToken() != oldToken)
        return@withLock newToken  // already refreshed
    // do actual refresh here
}}

Sealed Network Result

sealed class NetworkResult<out T> {
    data class Success<T>(val data: T)     : NetworkResult<T>()
    data class HttpError(val code: Int)    : NetworkResult<Nothing>()
    data class NetworkError(val e: IOException) : NetworkResult<Nothing>()
}

Offline-First Pattern

// 1. Emit Room immediately
emitAll(dao.getProducts().map { it.toDomain() })
// 2. Fetch network, write to Room
api.getProducts().onSuccess { dao.replaceAll(it) }
// Room Flow re-emits → UI updates automatically
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Certificate Pinning Pitfalls

Forgotten Backup Pin = App Broken on Certificate Rotation
If you pin only the production certificate and the server rotates to a new cert, every installed version of the app breaks until the user updates. Always pin the production certificate AND a backup certificate (can be a pre-generated cert you haven't deployed yet). Include an expiration date in Network Security Config so Trustpilot/Google Play's review catches stale pins.

Token Refresh Pitfalls

Infinite Refresh Loop
If the refresh endpoint itself returns 401 (e.g., refresh token expired), and your interceptor retries on 401, you'll loop infinitely. Always check: if the request is already to the refresh endpoint, don't retry — propagate the 401 up and force re-login.

Offline-First Pitfalls

Not Closing Response Bodies
When you call chain.proceed(), OkHttp returns a Response with an open body stream. If you check the status code and decide to retry without calling response.close(), you leak the connection. Always call response.close() before retrying or returning a different response.

Best Practices

  • Store the Mutex as a companion object property — shared across all interceptor instances
  • Use EncryptedSharedPreferences (or DataStore with encryption) to store refresh tokens — never plain SharedPreferences
  • Seal the NetworkResult type — forces callers to handle all cases at compile time
  • Room as single source of truth: always write network data to Room first; let Room's Flow deliver it to the UI
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What is certificate pinning and why is it needed? ⌄
Certificate pinning hardcodes the expected server certificate (or its public key hash) in the app. Standard TLS trusts any certificate signed by a trusted CA. If an attacker installs a rogue CA certificate on the device (or does a corporate MITM), they can intercept TLS traffic. Certificate pinning rejects any certificate not matching the pinned hash — even if it's signed by a "trusted" CA. This is required for apps handling financial or health data where MITM attacks must be prevented.
Basic What is the concurrent token refresh problem? ⌄
When a JWT expires, multiple in-flight API calls all receive 401 simultaneously. Without coordination, each call would attempt to refresh the token independently — potentially making 5 simultaneous refresh calls, overwhelming the auth server, causing race conditions (which refresh response is "correct"?), and possibly invalidating other refresh tokens in the process. The solution: a Mutex that serialises refresh attempts. The first thread refreshes; subsequent threads wait, then reuse the new token without refreshing again.
Basic What does "offline-first" mean in Android development? ⌄
Offline-first means the app is designed to work without network connectivity. The architecture uses Room as the single source of truth: the UI always reads from Room (never directly from the network), so data is instantly available even without a network. When the network is available, the repository fetches fresh data and writes it to Room — Room's Flow automatically re-emits the update to the UI. The user never sees "no connection" errors for data that was previously loaded; they see slightly stale data, which is preferable to a blank screen.
Intermediate Why must the Mutex be in a companion object in the token refresh interceptor? ⌄
OkHttp creates a new interceptor invocation context per call — but if the Mutex is an instance property, each call could potentially use a different Mutex instance if new interceptor instances are created. The Mutex must be shared across all concurrent calls to the same interceptor. Declaring it in companion object makes it a class-level (static) property, so all instances share the same Mutex. Even if multiple interceptors of the same type exist (which shouldn't happen in production, but might in tests), they share the lock.
Intermediate How does the "check if token changed" optimisation work in the Mutex refresh pattern? ⌄
When Thread 1 acquires the Mutex and refreshes the token, Threads 2–5 are waiting. When they each acquire the Mutex (one at a time), they check: "Is the current token in the token store different from the token that was in my 401 request?" If yes — Thread 1 already refreshed — they skip the refresh and return the new token immediately. Without this check, Threads 2–5 would each perform a sequential refresh, refreshing the token 5 times and invalidating previously issued refresh tokens. The check makes it so only Thread 1 does real work; the rest benefit from it.
Intermediate What should happen when the token refresh request itself returns 401? ⌄
A 401 on the refresh endpoint means the refresh token itself has expired (or been revoked). The session is invalid and cannot be recovered silently. The interceptor should: (1) Call tokenStore.clearTokens() — remove all stored credentials. (2) Return null from the refresh logic. (3) Build a 401 response to propagate up the call chain. (4) The ViewModel observes the 401 state and navigates to the login screen.

Critical: guard against infinite loops — if the request URL is the refresh endpoint, skip the 401 retry logic entirely and propagate the 401 immediately.
Intermediate What is the difference between OkHttp CertificatePinner and Network Security Config? ⌄
CertificatePinner (code-based): configured in OkHttpClient builder. Per-host configuration. Checked by OkHttp on every request to the pinned hostname. More flexible — can be dynamically updated (e.g., via remote config, though that defeats the purpose). Easy to test.

Network Security Config (XML): declared in res/xml/network_security_config.xml, referenced in AndroidManifest. Applied at the OS networking layer — affects all connections from the app including those not using OkHttp. Also controls cleartext traffic (cleartextTrafficPermitted), custom CAs for debug builds, and domain-specific policies. Has an expiration date feature. Verified by Google Play on upload.
Senior Design the full offline-first architecture for a banking transaction history feature. ⌄
Room: TransactionEntity with all fields. TransactionDao returns Flow<List<TransactionEntity>>.

Repository: getTransactions() returns a Flow that: (1) immediately emits Room data (mapped to domain models). Separately, a background refresh: (2) fetches from Retrofit, writes to Room via dao.replaceAll(). Room's Flow auto-re-emits the fresh data.

Stale data handling: each transaction has a server-assigned timestamp. On Room insert, also store a fetchedAt timestamp. Show a "last updated X minutes ago" label in the UI based on this. If fetchedAt is older than 5 minutes and no network is available, show a "data may be outdated" banner.

Balance (accuracy-critical): do NOT use offline-first for balance. Always fetch from network. Show a loading state until fresh data arrives. Cache for display only during temporary connection loss, with a clear "as of [time]" label.
Senior A user's token refresh is failing intermittently in production. How would you debug it? ⌄
Debugging strategy:

1. Add logging (to a secure backend — not Logcat in production): log refresh request timestamps, HTTP status codes, and whether the token-changed check triggered. Never log token values.
2. Check for clock skew: JWT expiry is time-based. If the device's clock is ahead/behind the server's, tokens may appear expired before they are. Check the token's exp claim vs system time at the point of 401.
3. Check for Mutex deadlock: if the Mutex is never released (exception in the refresh block), all calls will hang. Ensure withLock is used (auto-releases on exception).
4. Verify single Mutex instance: check if the Mutex is actually in companion object — a test configuration change could have moved it to an instance property.
5. Server logs: check if multiple refresh requests are hitting the server from the same device — indicating the Mutex isn't working as expected.
Senior How would you handle certificate pinning when using a CDN that rotates certificates frequently? ⌄
CDNs like CloudFront rotate leaf certificates frequently (every 30–90 days), making leaf certificate pinning impractical. Solution: pin the intermediate CA certificate instead. CDN providers control which intermediate CA they use, and these rotate far less frequently (years). This gives you MITM protection without breaking on every leaf cert rotation.

Alternative: use the public key hash (sha256/ of the SubjectPublicKeyInfo) rather than the certificate hash. The public key is stable even when the certificate is renewed — same public key, new certificate = same pin hash.

Also: implement a remote kill-switch — a mechanism to disable pinning for a specific version via a remote config, in case a pin break in production requires an emergency bypass while an app update propagates.
13A

Room

Tier 1 Mod 13
Key Concept: Room's full API — @Entity , @Dao , @Database , relations, @TypeConverter , @Transaction , migrations, Flow integration, FTS, and indexing.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Core Annotations

@Entity(tableName="orders")   → table
@PrimaryKey val id: String    → PK
@ColumnInfo(name="user_id")   → column
@TypeConverters(Converters::class) → custom types
@Dao  → query interface
@Database(entities=[...], version=3)

DAO Methods

@Query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE...")
fun getOrders(): Flow<List<OrderEntity>>

@Insert(onConflict = REPLACE)
suspend fun insert(order: OrderEntity)

@Transaction
suspend fun upsertOrderWithItems(...)

Relations

data class OrderWithProducts(
    @Embedded val order: OrderEntity,
    @Relation(parentColumn = "id",
              entityColumn = "order_id")
    val items: List<OrderItemEntity>
)
// Always add @Transaction to the DAO method!

Migrations

val MIGRATION_2_3 = object : Migration(2,3) {
    override fun migrate(db: SupportSQLiteDatabase) {
        db.execSQL("ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN notes TEXT")
    }
}
// In builder: .addMigrations(MIGRATION_2_3)
// NEVER .fallbackToDestructiveMigration() in prod!
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Mistakes

Querying on Main Thread
Room throws IllegalStateException: Cannot access database on the main thread if you call a non-Flow, non-suspend DAO method on the main thread. Always use suspend fun or Flow. Never call .allowMainThreadQueries() in production — it blocks UI rendering.
@Relation without @Transaction
Loading a parent + its children requires at least two SQL queries. Without @Transaction, another thread could modify a child between the two queries, giving you an inconsistent result. Always add @Transaction to any DAO method that returns a type with @Relation.

Database Migration Best Practices

  • Set exportSchema = true — tracks the schema JSON file in git. This lets you verify migrations haven't missed columns
  • Write migration tests using MigrationTestHelper from Room's test dependency
  • Never use fallbackToDestructiveMigration() in production builds
  • Always run migrations on a background thread (Room handles this, but ensure you're not blocking the main thread during startup)

@Index Best Practices

  • Add indexes on foreign key columns (e.g., account_id on the transactions table)
  • Add indexes on columns used in WHERE clauses in frequent queries
  • Indexes slow down INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE — don't index every column
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What are the three main components of Room and what does each do? ⌄
@Entity: annotates a data class to define a database table. Fields map to columns. @PrimaryKey defines the primary key; @ColumnInfo customises column names.

@Dao: interface that defines methods to interact with the table. Methods are annotated with @Query, @Insert, @Update, or @Delete. Room generates the implementation at compile time.

@Database: abstract class extending RoomDatabase. Declares all entities, the database version, and abstract methods returning DAO instances. Built via Room.databaseBuilder().
Basic How does Room's Flow integration work? ⌄
When a DAO method returns Flow<List<T>>, Room wraps the query in an InvalidationTracker observer. Whenever a row in the queried table is inserted, updated, or deleted, Room marks the table as invalid and re-runs the query. The new result is emitted to all active collectors. This makes Room queries reactive — the UI doesn't need to manually refresh; it just collects the Flow and reacts to emissions.
Basic What is a TypeConverter and when do you need one? ⌄
SQLite natively supports: INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB, and NULL. For any other type — LocalDate, Instant, BigDecimal, enums, List<String> — you need a TypeConverter. A TypeConverter class has two methods: one converting FROM the Kotlin type TO a SQLite-supported type, and one converting back. Register it with @TypeConverters(Converters::class) on the @Database class.
Intermediate Why must @Relation DAO methods be annotated with @Transaction? ⌄
Room's @Relation is NOT a SQL JOIN. It executes multiple SQL queries: one to fetch the parent entities, then one (or more) separate queries to fetch the related children. Between these two queries, another thread could write to the child table — you might get a parent with outdated children or missing children. @Transaction wraps all these queries in a single SQLite transaction, ensuring you get a consistent snapshot of the database at a single point in time.
Intermediate How do you add a column to a Room table in an existing production app? ⌄
1. Add the new column to the @Entity data class. If nullable: val notes: String? = null; if non-nullable, provide a default.
2. Increment the @Database(version = N+1).
3. Write a Migration: val MIGRATION_N_N1 = object : Migration(N, N+1) { override fun migrate(db) { db.execSQL("ALTER TABLE my_table ADD COLUMN notes TEXT") } }.
4. Register: Room.databaseBuilder(...).addMigrations(MIGRATION_N_N1).build().
5. Test with MigrationTestHelper to verify migration works on the old schema.
Never use fallbackToDestructiveMigration in production — it destroys all user data.
Intermediate What is @Fts4 and when would you use it? ⌄
@Fts4 creates an SQLite FTS (Full-Text Search) virtual table. Regular SQL LIKE '%query%' performs a full table scan — O(n) on every search. FTS creates an inverted index, enabling fast token-based searches with the MATCH operator. Use it when: users type search queries against large text content (product descriptions, notes, messages), you need relevance ranking, or you need prefix matching. Trade-off: FTS tables don't support standard SQL operations like JOIN directly — you typically JOIN back to the original table via rowid.
Intermediate Explain the difference between @Embedded and @Relation. ⌄
@Embedded: flattens a nested object's fields directly into the same table row. @Embedded val address: Address means Address's fields (street, city, zip) are columns in the parent table. One row, one query. Good for value objects that belong to one entity.

@Relation: represents a relationship between two different tables. Room runs separate queries for parent and children. Requires @Transaction. Good for one-to-many or many-to-many associations where children are stored in a separate table with a foreign key.
Senior Design the Room schema for a banking app with accounts, transactions, and categories. ⌄
AccountEntity: PK=id, userId, name, type (CHECKING/SAVINGS), balanceCents. Index on userId.

TransactionEntity: PK=id, FK=accountId, FK=categoryId (nullable), amountCents, type (DEBIT/CREDIT), description, date (Instant→TypeConverter), status. Index on accountId, date.

CategoryEntity: PK=id, name, iconName, color.

Relations: AccountWithTransactions(@Embedded account, @Relation transactions). TransactionWithCategory(@Embedded transaction, @Relation category). Both DAOs methods annotated with @Transaction.

Indexes: account_id on transactions (FK queries), date on transactions (sort/filter), userId on accounts.

TypeConverters: Instant, TransactionType enum, TransactionStatus enum.
Senior What happens at compile time when Room processes your DAO annotations? ⌄
Room uses an annotation processor (KSP or kapt). For each DAO interface, Room:

1. Parses SQL strings: validates syntax, resolves column names against the @Entity field names, checks that return types match query result types. A SELECT * FROM orders WHERE uer_id = :id typo is caught here.
2. Generates a concrete implementation class: e.g., OrderDao_Impl. For Flow methods, the generated code wraps the query in RoomTrackingLiveData / CoroutinesRoom.createFlow() with the table invalidation tracker.
3. Generates the Database implementation: AppDatabase_Impl that creates tables, runs migrations, and returns DAO instances.
4. Validates relationships: ensures @Relation column names exist in the referenced entities.
Any error (bad SQL, missing column, type mismatch) is a compile error — not a runtime crash.
Senior A query that was fast in development is slow in production with 100k rows. How do you investigate? ⌄
1. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN: run the SQL with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN prefix on the production database (copy it to dev). Look for "SCAN TABLE" (full scan) vs "SEARCH TABLE USING INDEX" (fast). Full scans on large tables = missing index.

2. Add @Index: on the column(s) in the WHERE clause. Re-run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to verify it uses the index.

3. Check query complexity: multiple JOINs or nested SELECT → consider a denormalised view or restructuring the query.

4. Room profiling: enable SQLite WAL mode and use Android Studio's Database Inspector to trace query execution times.

5. Paging: if the query returns large lists, paginate with Paging 3 — never load 100k rows at once.
13B

Room vs SQLite

Tier 1 Mod 13
Key Concept: Full comparison — compile-time safety, type safety, LiveData/Flow support, migration DSL, @RawQuery , and when raw SQLite still makes sense.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Room Advantages

✓ Compile-time SQL verification
✓ Type safety (data classes, not Cursor)
✓ Flow<List<T>> reactive queries
✓ Migration DSL + schema export
✓ No cursor leak risk

Raw SQLite Advantages

✓ Multi-process access
✓ Zero dependencies
✓ Full SQL control
✓ No annotation processing build time

Use for: SDKs, multi-process, legacy migration-not-worth-it

@RawQuery Pattern

@RawQuery(observedEntities = [ProductEntity::class])
fun searchDynamic(q: SupportSQLiteQuery): Flow<List<ProductEntity>>

// Build query — always use parameterised:
SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ?", arrayOf(input))

Cursor Safety (Raw SQLite)

// Always close cursors!
val cursor = db.rawQuery(sql, args)
try {
    while (cursor.moveToNext()) { ... }
} finally {
    cursor.close()
}
// OR: cursor.use { while (it.moveToNext()) { ... } }
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

SQL Injection in @RawQuery

Never Concatenate User Input into SQL Strings
SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '$userInput'") is vulnerable to SQL injection. Always use parameterised queries: SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ?", arrayOf(userInput)). Room's static @Query methods are automatically safe — Room never concatenates parameters into the SQL string.

Cursor Leaks in Raw SQLite

Always Close Cursors
Unclosed Cursors leak file descriptors. Always close them in a finally block or use Kotlin's use extension: cursor.use { ... }. Room never has this problem — it manages Cursor lifecycle in generated code. This is one of the most common raw SQLite bugs in production apps.

Best Practices for @RawQuery

  • Always specify observedEntities on @RawQuery — Room needs to know which tables to watch for Flow invalidation
  • Validate the sortBy column name against a whitelist before passing to SimpleSQLiteQuery — don't let users inject column names directly
  • Test @RawQuery methods with Room's test database using real data — static analysis can't verify dynamic queries
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What is the main advantage of Room over raw SQLite? ⌄
Compile-time query verification. Room's annotation processor validates your SQL queries against the database schema during compilation. Typos in table/column names, type mismatches between the query result and the return type, and invalid SQL syntax are all build errors — not runtime crashes. Raw SQLite discovers these errors in production via user bug reports or crash logs.
Basic What is a Cursor in raw SQLite and why is it error-prone? ⌄
A Cursor is the result of a raw SQLite query — a pointer into the result set that you iterate manually with cursor.moveToNext(). Pitfalls: (1) you access columns by string name or integer index — typos compile fine but throw IllegalArgumentException at runtime. (2) Cursors are file descriptor resources that must be explicitly closed — forgetting cursor.close() leaks file descriptors and eventually crashes the app. (3) There's no automatic type mapping — you manually call getString(), getLong(), etc., and must cast correctly. Room eliminates all of these.
Basic What is @RawQuery and when would you use it? ⌄
@RawQuery lets you execute a dynamically-constructed SQL query through Room's DAO, while still retaining Room's type mapping and Flow reactive capabilities. Use it when the query can't be expressed as a static @Query annotation — e.g., a search screen where users can select any combination of filters (category, price range, rating, sort order). The observedEntities parameter tells Room which tables to watch for Flow invalidation.
Intermediate Room is built on SQLite, so why doesn't it add performance overhead? ⌄
Room uses annotation processing (KSP or kapt) to generate DAO implementations at compile time — not reflection at runtime. The generated code in OrderDao_Impl is essentially the same boilerplate you'd write manually: open database, build the SQL string, create a Cursor, iterate it, close it. There's no reflection, no dynamic dispatch, no serialisation layer. The only runtime overhead is the InvalidationTracker for Flow queries, which registers a lightweight observer on table writes — this overhead is typically under 1ms.
Intermediate Describe a scenario where you'd choose raw SQLite over Room. ⌄
Multi-process access: If a ContentProvider in one process, the main app in another, and a background service in a third all need database access, Room's locking assumptions may not hold. Raw SQLite with WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode handles multi-reader, single-writer access more predictably across processes.

SDK/library development: A library that embeds SQLite doesn't want to force its consumers to add Room as a dependency — especially if they already use Room for their own data and might get version conflicts.

Legacy working code: Migrating a 5-year-old SQLiteOpenHelper that works correctly provides no user-visible benefit and carries migration risk.
Intermediate How does Room's migration approach differ from SQLiteOpenHelper.onUpgrade()? ⌄
SQLiteOpenHelper.onUpgrade(): called with old and new version numbers; you write nested if (oldVersion < N) checks. No automatic schema validation — if your migration is incorrect, Room won't tell you (unless you test it). Easy to miss a version jump when adding new migrations over time.

Room Migration objects: each Migration(fromVersion, toVersion) is registered separately via .addMigrations(). Room chains them automatically for large version jumps (e.g., 1→3 runs MIGRATION_1_2 then MIGRATION_2_3). With exportSchema = true, Room saves the schema JSON to disk — you can use MigrationTestHelper to verify that your migration produces the exact expected schema.
Intermediate How do you prevent SQL injection with @RawQuery? ⌄
Use SimpleSQLiteQuery with positional parameters (?) instead of string concatenation:

SAFE: SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = ?", arrayOf(userInput))
UNSAFE: SimpleSQLiteQuery("SELECT * FROM products WHERE name = '$userInput'")

The parameterised form escapes the user input before embedding it in the query. Additionally, validate any user-controlled column names (e.g., sort order) against a whitelist of allowed column names before including them in the SQL string — column names cannot be parameterised.
Senior A colleague argues "Room is unnecessary overhead — our app should use raw SQLite for performance." How do you respond? ⌄
The performance argument is incorrect: Room generates identical code to hand-written SQLite at compile time — no reflection, no runtime overhead. Benchmark data from Google confirms this.

The real trade-offs are: (1) Safety: Room catches SQL errors at build time; raw SQLite at runtime in production. In a banking app, a wrong column reference that silently returns null instead of throwing means incorrect data displayed to users — far worse than a build failure. (2) Productivity: 3 lines of Room vs 30 lines of raw SQLite for a basic query. Over a codebase of 500 queries, that's 13,500 fewer lines of boilerplate. (3) Maintainability: when a column is renamed, Room gives a compile error at every affected query. With raw SQLite, you do a global text search and hope you didn't miss anything.

The only legitimate performance concern: Room's InvalidationTracker for Flow queries adds minimal overhead on writes. If you're doing millions of writes per second (atypical), this might matter. Otherwise, it's a non-issue.
Senior How would you migrate a 50,000-line legacy app from raw SQLiteOpenHelper to Room? ⌄
Incremental migration — never big-bang:

1. Assess first: is migration worth it? Identify which tables are most active, have the most bugs, or would benefit most from Flow reactivity.
2. Keep existing SQLiteOpenHelper: create Room entities and DAOs for one table only. Configure Room to use the same database file as the existing helper: Room.databaseBuilder(...).openHelperFactory(...) or use a separate database for new tables.
3. Write migration scripts: Room's schema must be compatible with the existing SQLite schema. Set the database version to the current version; add a Migration that does nothing (schema is already correct).
4. Migrate table by table: replace each SQLiteOpenHelper access with Room DAO calls. Run the full test suite after each table migration.
5. Export schema from the start: version control the JSON — it becomes the audit trail of schema changes.
6. Remove SQLiteOpenHelper once all tables are migrated.
Senior How does Room handle multi-threaded writes and reads? ⌄
Room configures SQLite in WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode by default on Android (API 16+). WAL allows: multiple concurrent readers, one concurrent writer, and readers don't block writers. Room's generated DAO code uses SupportSQLiteDatabase, which handles transaction management. Suspend DAO functions run on Room's Dispatchers.IO dispatcher — they're safe to call from multiple coroutines simultaneously.

Room uses ThreadLocal-based transaction management for @Transaction-annotated functions, ensuring all operations within a transaction block use the same database connection. For Flow queries, Room's InvalidationTracker uses a background thread to coalesce invalidation events and re-run queries. This is safe for single-process apps. For multi-process access, Room's documentation explicitly states it's not designed for that use case — use raw SQLite with explicit locking.
13C

Other Storage

Tier 1 Mod 13
Key Concept: SharedPreferences (legacy), DataStore (Preferences + Proto), Files (internal/external/FileProvider), Android Keystore, and EncryptedSharedPreferences.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

DataStore (New Code)

val DARK_MODE = booleanPreferencesKey("dark_mode")
val Context.dataStore by preferencesDataStore("settings")

// READ
dataStore.data.map { prefs -> prefs[DARK_MODE] ?: false }

// WRITE (atomic)
dataStore.edit { prefs -> prefs[DARK_MODE] = true }

EncryptedSharedPreferences

EncryptedSharedPreferences.create(
    context, "secure_prefs",
    MasterKeys.getOrCreate(MasterKeys.AES256_GCM_SPEC),
    PrefKeyEncryptionScheme.AES256_SIV,
    PrefValueEncryptionScheme.AES256_GCM
)
// Store tokens here — backed by hardware Keystore

Storage Decision

Auth tokens        → EncryptedSharedPreferences
App settings       → Preferences DataStore
Typed settings     → Proto DataStore
Private files      → context.filesDir
Share with other   → FileProvider
Crypto keys        → Android Keystore

Key Warnings

⚠ SharedPreferences — LEGACY, not coroutine-safe
⚠ commit() on main thread — ANR risk
⚠ Keystore keys lost on factory reset
⚠ Never expose file:// URIs — use FileProvider
⚠ Multiple DataStore instances → crash
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

DataStore Pitfalls

Multiple DataStore Instances for the Same File
Creating two DataStore instances pointing to the same file causes IllegalStateException: There are multiple DataStore files with the same name. Use the by preferencesDataStore() property delegate (on Context) which is a Kotlin singleton — only one instance is created per file name. Inject as @Singleton via Hilt.
No Migration from SharedPreferences to DataStore
DataStore doesn't automatically read existing SharedPreferences files. If migrating, use SharedPreferencesMigration to copy values: preferencesDataStore(name, produceMigrations = { SharedPreferencesMigration(it, "old_prefs_name") }). Without this, users lose their settings on first launch after update.

Keystore Pitfalls

Keystore Keys Lost on Factory Reset
Android Keystore keys are bound to the device. Factory reset wipes all Keystore keys. Any data encrypted with a Keystore key (including EncryptedSharedPreferences) becomes unreadable. Always have a recovery path: on KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException, clear the encrypted data and ask the user to log in again.

File Provider Pitfalls

  • Never share a file URI from internal storage directly — use FileProvider. Direct file URIs fail with FileUriExposedException on API 24+
  • Grant read permission to the receiving app via Intent.FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION
  • FileProvider paths must be declared in res/xml/file_paths.xml

Best Practices

  • Store tokens in EncryptedSharedPreferences — never plain SharedPreferences or Room
  • Use DataStore (not SharedPreferences) for new code
  • Handle IOException in DataStore flows — file corruption is possible
  • Set expiry on Keystore keys linked to biometrics to prevent key use after biometric enrollment change
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: Basic What are the main problems with SharedPreferences that DataStore solves? ⌄
1. Main thread blocking: commit() blocks the main thread for disk I/O. DataStore never blocks the main thread — it's fully coroutine-based.
2. Thread safety: SharedPreferences isn't thread-safe — concurrent edit() calls can corrupt the file. DataStore uses Kotlin's serialised execution for writes.
3. No error propagation: SharedPreferences silently ignores I/O errors. DataStore propagates IOException through the Flow.
4. Not atomic: a crash during a SharedPreferences write can leave a partially written file. DataStore writes are atomic.
5. No observability: SharedPreferences requires a change listener that must be managed manually. DataStore returns a Flow.
Basic What is the difference between Preferences DataStore and Proto DataStore? ⌄
Preferences DataStore: stores typed key-value pairs — booleanPreferencesKey("dark_mode"), stringPreferencesKey("locale"). No schema enforcement. Easy to add new keys. Key names are the schema — if you rename a key, you lose the old value. Works without any additional dependencies.

Proto DataStore: stores a single typed Kotlin object generated from a .proto schema file using Protocol Buffers. Fully type-safe — accessing settings.darkMode is a property, not a string key lookup. Schema evolution follows Protobuf rules (field numbers, backward compatibility). Requires the Protobuf Gradle plugin. Better for complex settings with many fields or when you need schema versioning.
Basic What is EncryptedSharedPreferences and how does it work? ⌄
EncryptedSharedPreferences is a drop-in replacement for SharedPreferences that encrypts both key names and values using Android Keystore-backed keys. It uses AES-256-SIV to encrypt key names (deterministic, allows look-up) and AES-256-GCM to encrypt values. The master key is generated and stored in Android Keystore — it never leaves the hardware. The resulting XML file contains encrypted bytes that cannot be read even on a rooted device without the hardware key. Suitable for storing access tokens, refresh tokens, and other secrets that must survive process death but shouldn't be readable from disk.
Intermediate How does Android Keystore protect cryptographic keys? ⌄
Android Keystore stores keys in a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) or a dedicated StrongBox chip — hardware isolated from the main application processor. Cryptographic operations (encrypt, decrypt, sign) happen inside this hardware using the key; the raw key material is never exposed to the application. Even with root access to the device, you cannot extract the key. The only way to use the key is via the Keystore API on the same device. For biometric-protected keys (setUserAuthenticationRequired(true)), the key is additionally locked until biometric authentication succeeds.
Intermediate What happens to EncryptedSharedPreferences data after a factory reset? ⌄
A factory reset wipes all Keystore keys along with all user data. The master key used to encrypt the EncryptedSharedPreferences file is permanently destroyed. The encrypted file (if somehow preserved) becomes unreadable forever — without the key, the data is irretrievably encrypted.

For the app: on next launch after factory reset, accessing EncryptedSharedPreferences may throw KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException or GeneralSecurityException. Handle this by: catching the exception, deleting the old encrypted prefs file, and creating a fresh one. The user will need to log in again to re-populate the tokens.
Intermediate Why can't you share an internal file directly using a file:// URI? ⌄
Since Android 7 (API 24), sharing file:// URIs outside the app's process throws FileUriExposedException. The reason: a file URI gives the receiving app direct path access to your app's internal storage — bypassing Android's permission model. The receiving app would need to have permission to read that path, which ordinary apps don't have.

The solution is FileProvider: it converts an internal file path to a content:// URI that Android routes through a ContentProvider. The receiving app is granted temporary read permission only for that specific URI. No direct file system access is needed.
Intermediate How do you migrate existing SharedPreferences data to DataStore? ⌄
Use SharedPreferencesMigration:

val dataStore by preferencesDataStore(name = "settings", produceMigrations = { context -> listOf(SharedPreferencesMigration(context, "old_prefs_name")) })

On first access to the DataStore, it reads all keys from the named SharedPreferences file and copies them to DataStore. You can filter which keys to migrate. After migration, DataStore deletes the old SharedPreferences file. Without this migration, users lose their settings on first launch after the update.
Senior Design a token storage system for a banking app that survives app updates, handles biometric authentication, and gracefully handles Keystore invalidation. ⌄
Token storage: EncryptedSharedPreferences backed by a Keystore AES-256-GCM master key. Access and refresh tokens stored here. Survives app updates (Keystore keys are per-device, not per-app-version).

Biometric protection: For accessing the token, generate a separate Keystore key with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) and setUserAuthenticationValidityDurationSeconds(30). Biometric prompt must succeed before this key is usable. This prevents token access without the user's consent — even if someone has physical device access.

Invalidation handling: Wrap all EncryptedSharedPreferences operations in try-catch for KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException (biometric enrollment changed) and GeneralSecurityException (factory reset, or key deleted). On exception: (1) delete the encrypted prefs file, (2) emit an "authentication required" event via a StateFlow, (3) navigate to login. The repository layer handles this transparently so ViewModels never see low-level crypto exceptions.
Senior When would you use Proto DataStore over Preferences DataStore and how do you handle schema migrations? ⌄
Choose Proto DataStore when: (1) you have 10+ settings fields and type-safe access matters, (2) the settings have complex structure (nested objects, lists), (3) the project uses KMM (protobuf is multiplatform), or (4) you need strict schema versioning for regulatory compliance (e.g., audit logs).

Schema migrations: Protobuf handles backward compatibility at the format level — adding a new field is safe (older versions read default values). Removing a field requires reserving the field number (reserved 3;) to prevent reuse. For DataStore itself, if you rename the .pb file or change the Serializer, existing data is lost unless you: (1) read the old file as raw bytes, (2) deserialise with the old schema class, (3) write to the new file with the new serialiser. This is manual — no equivalent of Room's addMigrations(). If schema evolution is frequent, consider Preferences DataStore with explicit versioning keys.
Senior A developer reports that DataStore is throwing "There are multiple DataStore files with the same name" in tests. What's the cause and fix? ⌄
The error occurs when two DataStore instances are created pointing to the same file in the same process. Most commonly: (1) the by preferencesDataStore() delegate is defined inside a class (creating one per instance) rather than at the top level as an extension on Context; or (2) in tests, the DataStore from production code and the DataStore from a test module both try to use the same file name.

Production fix: define the DataStore as a top-level property: val Context.settingsDataStore by preferencesDataStore("settings"). Kotlin's property delegation ensures only one instance is created per Context.

Test fix: use TestCoroutineRule + a temporary file per test: PreferenceDataStoreFactory.create(scope = testScope) { context.preferencesDataStoreFile("test_settings") }. Clean up the file in @After. This gives each test an isolated DataStore without file name conflicts.
14A

WorkManager

Tier 2 Mod 14
Key Concept: Guaranteed, battery-efficient, constraint-aware, and SQLite-persisted background task scheduling on Android. Mastering CoroutineWorker, chaining, unique policies, and retry strategies.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

CORE CONCEPTS

CoroutineWorker  -> suspend doWork(): Result
Result types     -> success(), failure(), retry()
Data Limit       -> 10 KB max
Periodic Min     -> 15 minutes minimum interval
Underlying API   -> JobScheduler / Room DB

UNIQUE WORK POLICIES

REPLACE -> Cancel running/pending, start new
KEEP    -> Retain existing, discard incoming
APPEND  -> Chain incoming after existing finishes
APPEND_OR_REPLACE -> Append or start new on error

BACKOFF & RETRY

setBackoffCriteria(
    BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, // or LINEAR
    10, TimeUnit.SECONDS       // min 10s
)

OBSERVING WORK

workManager.getWorkInfoByIdFlow(id)
    .collect { workInfo ->
        when(workInfo.state) {
            State.ENQUEUED, State.RUNNING,
            State.SUCCEEDED, State.FAILED,
            State.BLOCKED, State.CANCELLED -> ...
        }
    }
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Expecting PeriodicWorkRequest to run every minute

Android enforces a hard minimum of 15 minutes for PeriodicWorkRequest (and 5 minute flex interval). Passing 5, TimeUnit.MINUTES will be clamped to 15 minutes automatically. Do not use WorkManager for high-frequency polling.

Pitfall 2: Swallowing CancellationException inside CoroutineWorker

When constraints are lost (e.g., user disables Wi-Fi), WorkManager cancels the worker's coroutine job. If your try-catch catches generic Exception or Throwable without rethrowing CancellationException, WorkManager cannot gracefully acknowledge cancellation and clean up resources.

Pitfall 3: Storing Large Payloads in Data (10 KB Limit)

The Data object (input and output) is stored in the Room DB and passed across processes. It has a strict limit of 10 KB (10,240 bytes). Attempting to pass Bitmaps, large JSON arrays, or byte arrays will throw an IllegalStateException. Store data in Room/disk and pass primary keys (IDs) instead.

Best Practice: Custom WorkerFactory with Hilt

Never construct dependencies directly inside Workers. Use @HiltWorker with @AssistedInject to inject repositories cleanly.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the primary purpose of WorkManager in Android?
WorkManager is designed for guaranteed, deferrable background execution. Unlike standard coroutines or services, tasks are persisted in an internal SQLite database, allowing them to survive process termination and device restarts until execution constraints (like network or charging) are satisfied.
B2 — What are the 3 return options for CoroutineWorker.doWork()?
Easy▼
1. Result.success(): Task completed successfully; triggers dependent tasks in the chain.
2. Result.failure(): Permanent failure; halts execution and marks the task as FAILED.
3. Result.retry(): Transient failure; WorkManager will reschedule the task according to its backoff policy.
B3 — What is the minimum interval for PeriodicWorkRequest?
Easy▼
The minimum periodic interval is 15 minutes (defined by PeriodicWorkRequest.MIN_PERIODIC_INTERVAL_MILLIS). Any shorter interval passed to the builder will be automatically clamped to 15 minutes by the framework to preserve battery.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — Explain the difference between ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP and ExistingWorkPolicy.REPLACE.
Medium▼
When enqueuing unique work with a specific name:
• KEEP: If work with the same name already exists in an ENQUEUED or RUNNING state, the new request is ignored.
• REPLACE: If work with that name exists, it is cancelled and deleted, and the new work request is scheduled immediately.
I2 — How does WorkManager handle task cancellation when constraints are lost?
Medium▼
When a constraint is no longer met (e.g. Wi-Fi drops), WorkManager cancels the worker coroutine's Job by throwing a CancellationException and invokes onStopped(). The worker state is rolled back to ENQUEUED so it can re-run when constraints return. Catching generic Exception without rethrowing CancellationException breaks this flow.
I3 — What is the maximum size allowed for input/output Data in WorkManager and why?
Medium▼
The maximum size is 10 KB (10,240 bytes). This limit exists because Data objects are serialized into Room database tables and passed through IPC Binder transactions. Exceeding this limit throws an IllegalStateException. Large blobs or lists should be stored in local files or Room, passing only IDs or paths in the Data object.
I4 — How do you configure exponential backoff retry criteria in WorkRequest?
Medium▼
You configure it on the WorkRequestBuilder using setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, initialDelay, timeUnit). Minimum initial delay is 10 seconds. On each Result.retry(), delay doubles: 10s, 20s, 40s, 80s, etc., up to a maximum capped delay.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you inject dependencies into a Worker using Hilt?
HardScenario▼
1. Annotate the worker class with @HiltWorker.
2. Use @AssistedInject on constructor passing @Assisted appContext: Context and @Assisted workerParams: WorkerParameters along with regular injected dependencies.
3. Inject HiltWorkerFactory into Application and implement Configuration.Provider returning Configuration.Builder().setWorkerFactory(hiltWorkerFactory).build().
4. Disable default WorkManagerInitializer in AndroidManifest.xml.
S2 — Design a multi-step image sync pipeline: Compress 3 images in parallel, upload them sequentially, and update database.
HardScenario▼
val compressRequests = imageUris.map { uri ->
    OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<CompressWorker>()
        .setInputData(workDataOf("URI" to uri.toString()))
        .build()
}
val uploadWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<BatchUploadWorker>()
    .setConstraints(Constraints.Builder().setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED).build())
    .build()
val updateDbWork = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UpdateLocalDbWorker>().build()

workManager.beginWith(compressRequests) // Runs in parallel
    .then(uploadWork)                   // Runs after all compressions succeed
    .then(updateDbWork)                 // Final DB update
    .enqueue()
S3 — What happens if an app with scheduled WorkManager tasks is force-stopped by the user?
HardScenario▼
When an app is in the "Force Stopped" state on Android, the OS disables all its alarms, JobScheduler registrations, and broadcast receivers. WorkManager will NOT run any scheduled tasks while in this state. The tasks remain persisted in the SQLite database and will automatically reschedule and resume only after the user manually relaunches the application.
14B

Choosing the Right Background Tool

Tier 2 Mod 14
Key Concept: The ultimate background processing decision matrix: WorkManager vs Foreground Services vs AlarmManager vs Coroutines under modern Android battery constraints (Doze, App Standby, API 34+ restrictions).
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

BACKGROUND DECISION

UI only          -> viewModelScope
Deferrable sync  -> WorkManager
Exact alarm      -> AlarmManager
Ongoing & active -> Foreground Service
Immediate BG job -> WorkManager.setExpedited()

ALARM MANAGER APIS

setExact()
setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() // fires in Doze
canScheduleExactAlarms()    // API 31+ check
ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED       // Reschedule alarms

FOREGROUND SERVICE RESTRICTIONS

API 26+: Notification within 5s
API 31+: Cannot start from background
API 34+: foregroundServiceType required
(location, mediaPlayback, health, etc.)

DOZE MODE SUMMARY

Deep Doze   -> Stationary, screen off, on battery
Light Doze  -> Screen off, moving, on battery
Maintenance -> Network enabled, jobs executed
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Failing to handle SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM on Android 12+ (API 31+)

Calling setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() without checking alarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms() will throw a SecurityException if the user revoked permission or the app lacks exemption.

Pitfall 2: Launching a Foreground Service from Background on Android 12+

Android 12+ blocks context.startForegroundService() when the app is in the background, throwing ForegroundServiceStartNotAllowedException. Use WorkManager with expedited jobs (setExpedited()) instead.

Pitfall 3: Not Rescheduling Alarms on Device Reboot

AlarmManager alarms are NOT persisted across device reboots. You must register a BroadcastReceiver for ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED and re-register all alarms from your local Room database.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — When should you choose WorkManager over a Foreground Service?
Choose WorkManager when the task is deferrable and does not require immediate, continuous user awareness via an ongoing notification (e.g. syncing data, compressing logs, uploading analytics). Use Foreground Services only when the user is actively monitoring ongoing work (music, active navigation, active fitness tracking).
B2 — Why doesn't WorkManager fire at an exact minute?
Easy▼
WorkManager is designed for battery efficiency. It batches work and aligns execution with the Android OS's Doze mode maintenance windows and constraint evaluations (e.g., waiting for unmetered Wi-Fi). To preserve device battery, it intentionally trades exact timing for power savings.
B3 — What happens to AlarmManager alarms when a phone reboots?
Easy▼
All alarms scheduled in AlarmManager are cleared from OS memory upon reboot. The application must register a broadcast receiver listening for android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED to query stored reminders from a local database and reschedule each alarm.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — What is the difference between setExact() and setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() in AlarmManager?
Medium▼
setExact() guarantees exact delivery when the device is awake or in light sleep, but delivery is deferred if the device is in Deep Doze mode until the next maintenance window. setExactAndAllowWhileIdle() fires the alarm at the exact specified time even if the device is currently asleep in Doze mode.
I2 — What permission is required for exact alarms on Android 12 (API 31)+?
Medium▼
On API 31+, apps must declare android.permission.SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM (or USE_EXACT_ALARM for calendar/clock apps on API 33+). Before calling exact alarm APIs, the app must call alarmManager.canScheduleExactAlarms(). If false, the app must direct the user to the system Settings page to toggle the permission.
I3 — How does Android's Doze Mode affect background execution?
Medium▼
Doze mode activates when a device is unplugged, stationary, and screen-off. It suspends network access, ignores WakeLocks, defers standard AlarmManager alarms, and defers JobScheduler/WorkManager execution. Execution is only allowed during periodic "maintenance windows", which occur with decreasing frequency over time.
I4 — What is an Expedited Job in WorkManager and when should it be used?
Medium▼
Expedited jobs (setExpedited(OutOfQuotaPolicy.RUN_AS_NON_EXPEDITED_WORK_REQUEST)) allow WorkManager tasks to run immediately, even when the app is in the background. They have higher execution quotas and are designed for critical, urgent background work (e.g. processing an urgent push notification message or payment confirmation).

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — An e-commerce app needs to sync user shopping cart changes across devices immediately. Which tool should you use?
HardScenario▼
For an active user modifying their cart in the app: use viewModelScope with optimistic local Room DB updates for instant UI response, followed by an immediate network call. In addition, enqueue a WorkManager OneTimeWorkRequest with KEEP unique policy to ensure that if the app is killed mid-network-call, the cart sync will still complete reliably.
S2 — An automotive navigation app stops tracking location when the user turns off the screen on Android 14. What is the root cause and solution?
HardScenario▼
Root Cause: On Android 14 (API 34), foreground services must declare a specific foregroundServiceType in the manifest and specify it in startForeground(). If declared as generic or missing android:foregroundServiceType="location" along with FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION and ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION permissions, the OS terminates location updates upon screen-off.
Fix: Declare the location type in manifest, request permissions, and call startForeground(id, notification, FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_LOCATION).
S3 — How would you architect an offline-first fitness tracker that records GPS runs and syncs to a server?
HardScenario▼
1. Live Workout Recording: Foreground Service with foregroundServiceType="location", writing GPS coordinates directly to a local Room database in real-time.
2. UI Observation: Flow from Room DB collected inside ViewModel with lifecycleScope.
3. Post-Run Upload: Upon workout finish, stop the Foreground Service and enqueue a WorkManager OneTimeWorkRequest with NetworkType.CONNECTED constraint to handle the bulk upload and retry logic reliably.
15A

Services

Tier 2 Mod 15
Key Concept: Started Services, Bound Services, Foreground Services (API 34+ types), IntentService deprecation, Background Execution Limits (API 26+), and LifecycleService.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

SERVICE TYPES

Foreground -> startForeground() + Notification
Bound      -> bindService() + IBinder
Started    -> startService() + onStartCommand
Lifecycle  -> LifecycleService + lifecycleScope

ONSTARTCOMMAND FLAGS

START_STICKY           -> Recreate, null intent
START_NOT_STICKY       -> Do not recreate
START_REDELIVER_INTENT -> Recreate with original intent

API 34+ FOREGROUND TYPES

android:foregroundServiceType="
  location | mediaPlayback | health |
  dataSync | connectedDevice | camera
"

CRITICAL RULES

Runs on Main Thread by default!
startForeground within 5 seconds.
IntentService is deprecated -> WorkManager.
Unbind on onDestroy to prevent leaks.
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Blocking the Main Thread in onStartCommand

Services run on the Main Thread. Doing file I/O or network requests directly inside onStartCommand() will trigger an ANR (Application Not Responding) within 5 seconds. Always launch work in a coroutine or background thread.

Pitfall 2: Missing startForeground() within 5 Seconds

Calling startForegroundService() creates a 5-second OS timer. If the service does not call startForeground(id, notification) within that window, the OS throws an ANR / RemoteServiceException: Context.startForegroundService() did not then call Service.startForeground() and crashes the app.

Pitfall 3: Leaking ServiceConnection via Unbind Omission

Every bindService() in an Activity or Fragment MUST have a matching unbindService() in onStop() or onDestroy(). Failure to unbind causes memory leaks and keeps the Service alive indefinitely in memory.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — On which thread does an Android Service run by default?
An Android Service runs on the Main (UI) Thread of the hosting process by default. Performing heavy calculations, database queries, or network requests directly inside a Service will freeze the UI and cause an ANR (Application Not Responding) error. Background work must be offloaded using coroutines or background threads.
B2 — What is the purpose of START_STICKY in onStartCommand()?
Easy▼
START_STICKY tells the Android OS that if the service process is killed due to low memory, the OS should recreate the service when resources become available and call onStartCommand() with a null Intent. It is ideal for continuous background operations like music streaming services.
B3 — Why was IntentService deprecated?
Easy▼
IntentService was deprecated in API 30 because it does not conform to Android 8.0+ (API 26) Background Execution Limits. It cannot be launched from the background without throwing exceptions. Google officially recommends replacing IntentService with WorkManager (via CoroutineWorker) or Jetpack JobIntentService.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — What happens if startForeground() is not called within 5 seconds of startForegroundService()?
Medium▼
If an app calls startForegroundService() and does not invoke startForeground(notificationId, notification) inside the service within 5 seconds, the system throws a RemoteServiceException: Context.startForegroundService() did not then call Service.startForeground(), causing an immediate fatal app crash.
I2 — What is the lifecycle difference between a Started Service and a Bound Service?
Medium▼
A Started Service is started via startService(), runs indefinitely until it calls stopSelf() or another component calls stopService(). A Bound Service is started when a client binds via bindService() and is automatically destroyed by the OS when all clients have called unbindService() (unless it was also started with startService()).
I3 — Explain the difference between START_NOT_STICKY and START_REDELIVER_INTENT.
Medium▼
START_NOT_STICKY tells the OS not to recreate the service if killed under memory pressure, unless new start intents are queued. START_REDELIVER_INTENT tells the OS to recreate the service AND redeliver the exact original Intent (with all extras) that was being processed at the time of the kill.
I4 — What is a LifecycleService and why is it preferred in modern Android?
Medium▼
LifecycleService is an androidx.lifecycle component extending Service that implements LifecycleOwner. It gives the service access to lifecycleScope, allowing coroutines to be launched and automatically cancelled when the service's onDestroy() fires, avoiding coroutine leaks.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you build a multi-process Bound Service using AIDL?
HardScenario▼
1. Define an .aidl file specifying interface methods.
2. Android SDK generates a Java interface with an internal Stub abstract class extending Binder.
3. In the Service, implement the Stub and return it in onBind().
4. In the Client app, implement ServiceConnection; in onServiceConnected(), call IMyAidlInterface.Stub.asInterface(service).
5. Handle RemoteException on all IPC method calls.
S2 — What changes are required to adapt a Foreground Location Service for Android 14 (API 34)?
HardScenario▼
1. Declare <uses-permission android:name="android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_LOCATION" /> and ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION in the manifest.
2. In manifest <service> tag, add android:foregroundServiceType="location".
3. In code, pass ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_LOCATION to startForeground().
4. Request runtime permissions before starting the service; otherwise a SecurityException will be thrown.
S3 — How would you communicate state from a Foreground Service to a Compose UI?
HardScenario▼
Expose a singleton StateFlow repository or shared domain model injected into both the ForegroundService and the ViewModel via Hilt. The Service updates the MutableStateFlow in the repository, and the ViewModel exposes it as a read-only StateFlow collected in Jetpack Compose using collectAsStateWithLifecycle(). This decouples the Service from the UI and eliminates complex Binder connection boilerplate.
16A

BroadcastReceiver

Tier 3 Mod 16
Key Concept: Inter-process and system event messaging: Static vs Dynamic receivers, modern API 26+ broadcast limits, receiver security permissions, ordered broadcasts, and goAsync().
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

RECEIVER BASICS

onReceive(context, intent) -> Main Thread
Timeout                    -> 10 seconds (ANR)
goAsync()                  -> Asynchronous extension
finish()                   -> Completes goAsync

API 33+ REGISTRATION

registerReceiver(
    receiver, filter,
    Context.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED // Or EXPORTED
)

ORDERED BROADCASTS

sendOrderedBroadcast(intent, permission)
abortBroadcast()    // Stop propagation
setResultData()     // Alter downstream data
priority in filter  // Higher integer fires first

MODERN REPLACEMENTS

LocalBroadcastManager -> SharedFlow / Channel
CONNECTIVITY_ACTION   -> NetworkCallback
Static receivers      -> WorkManager / Dynamic
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Leaking Dynamic Receivers

Registering in onStart() without unregistering in onStop() (or onResume() / onPause()) causes an IntentReceiverLeaked error and keeps the surrounding Activity in memory.

Pitfall 2: Launching Async Coroutines without goAsync()

Once onReceive() returns, the Android OS considers the broadcast handled and reduces the process priority. Any background thread launched inside without goAsync() may be abruptly killed by the OS low memory killer.

Pitfall 3: Using LocalBroadcastManager (Deprecated)

LocalBroadcastManager was deprecated in Jetpack. For internal app messaging, use Kotlin Coroutines (SharedFlow, Channel, or EventBus pattern).

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the execution time limit for BroadcastReceiver.onReceive()?
The execution time limit is 10 seconds on the main thread. If onReceive() blocks for more than 10 seconds, the Android OS flags the receiver with an Application Not Responding (ANR) dialog.
B2 — What is the difference between static and dynamic receivers?
Easy▼
Static receivers are declared in AndroidManifest.xml and can wake up a cold process when the broadcast fires. Dynamic receivers are registered at runtime using context.registerReceiver() and are only active during the lifecycle of the registering component.
B3 — What flag is required when dynamically registering a receiver on Android 13 (API 33)+?
Easy▼
You must pass either Context.RECEIVER_EXPORTED (if other apps can send broadcasts to it) or Context.RECEIVER_NOT_EXPORTED (if restricted to your app and the system). Omitting this parameter throws a runtime SecurityException.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — How does goAsync() work and why is it needed?
Medium▼
goAsync() returns a PendingResult object and informs the OS that the receiver intends to complete its work asynchronously on a background thread. This prevents the OS from considering the broadcast completed immediately upon onReceive() return and lowering process priority. Once work finishes, the worker must call pendingResult.finish().
I2 — Why can't you register a static receiver for CONNECTIVITY_ACTION on Android 8.0+?
Medium▼
Android 8.0 (API 26) introduced Background Execution Limits to prevent battery drain. Because network changes occur frequently, waking up hundreds of apps via static broadcast receivers caused severe battery depletion. Apps must use dynamic registration or ConnectivityManager.registerNetworkCallback() instead.
I3 — How do Ordered Broadcasts work?
Medium▼
Sent via sendOrderedBroadcast(), intents are delivered sequentially to receivers based on priority (defined in android:priority). Each receiver can read/modify results via getResultExtras() and setResultData(), or stop further delivery entirely by invoking abortBroadcast().
I4 — How do you restrict a broadcast so that only specific apps can receive it?
Medium▼
1. Define a custom permission in the sender app manifest (e.g. signature protection level).
2. Call sendBroadcast(intent, "com.example.CUSTOM_PERMISSION").
3. Receiver apps must declare <uses-permission android:name="com.example.CUSTOM_PERMISSION" /> signed with the same developer certificate.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you handle ACTION_BOOT_COMPLETED to schedule alarms in an Android 14 app?
HardScenario▼
1. Declare RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED permission in manifest.
2. Register static receiver for android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED.
3. In onReceive(), call goAsync() or enqueue a WorkManager OneTimeWorkRequest to read scheduled alarms from Room DB and register them with AlarmManager. (WorkManager is preferred to avoid ANRs during heavy post-boot device load).
S2 — Why was LocalBroadcastManager deprecated and what is the modern Kotlin replacement?
HardScenario▼
LocalBroadcastManager was deprecated because it relied on global Intent serialization and Context references for what is fundamentally an in-process pub-sub pattern. The modern replacement is Kotlin Coroutines using MutableSharedFlow (or Channel for single-subscriber events), which provides compile-time type safety, zero IPC serialization overhead, and seamless lifecycle awareness.
S3 — An app receives an SMS broadcast via an ordered receiver to parse 2FA OTP. How do you prevent other apps from reading it?
HardScenario▼
Historically, apps used high-priority ordered receivers and called abortBroadcast(), but modern Android restricts SMS broadcast manipulation. The modern, secure Google-recommended solution is the SMS Retriever API (or SMS User Consent API), which delivers the 2FA SMS exclusively to your app without requiring the sensitive RECEIVE_SMS permission.

ContentProvider

Tier 3 Mod 17
Key Concept: Secure inter-app data sharing, ContentResolver clients, URI syntax, MIME conventions, Binder IPC architecture, and FileProvider integration.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

URI ANATOMY

content://com.pkg.provider/table/1
Scheme   : content://
Authority: com.pkg.provider
Path     : table
ID       : 1

MIME PATTERNS

Directory -> vnd.android.cursor.dir/vnd.<auth>.<type>
Single    -> vnd.android.cursor.item/vnd.<auth>.<type>

FILEPROVIDER SETUP

1. file_paths.xml (cache-path, files-path)
2. <provider> in AndroidManifest
3. FileProvider.getUriForFile()
4. FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION

CORE PITFALLS

onCreate() runs before Application.onCreate()!
CursorWindow max 2 MB -> Always paginate!
Never leak Cursor -> use cursor.use { }
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Slow Operations in onCreate() Delaying App Startup

ContentProviders are initialized BEFORE Application.onCreate(). Running heavy database migrations or network calls in ContentProvider.onCreate() will delay entire app launch and freeze cold starts.

Pitfall 2: Exported ContentProvider without Permissions

Setting android:exported="true" without android:readPermission / android:writePermission exposes private user data to every other app on the device (major security vulnerability).

Pitfall 3: CursorWindowAllocationException (1MB / 2MB Limit)

Android's Binder CursorWindow has a strict 2 MB memory buffer limit across IPC. Querying huge blobs or thousands of rows in one query throws a CursorWindowAllocationException. Always paginate with LIMIT and OFFSET.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the primary purpose of a ContentProvider?
A ContentProvider manages access to a structured set of data and encapsulates data security. It is the standard Android mechanism for sharing data securely between different application processes (IPC) and with the Android OS (e.g., Contacts, MediaStore).
B2 — Why is FileProvider required on Android 7.0 (API 24)+?
Easy▼
Sharing raw file:// URIs across apps was prohibited in API 24 to prevent security vulnerabilities and throws a FileUriExposedException. FileProvider generates secure content:// URIs and grants temporary, scoped read/write permissions via Intent flags.
B3 — What does Cursor.use { } accomplish in Kotlin?
Easy▼
Cursor implements Closeable. The use { } inline extension executes the given block and guarantees that cursor.close() is called in a finally block, even if an exception occurs, preventing native cursor window memory leaks.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — On which thread does ContentProvider.onCreate() run vs query()?
Medium▼
onCreate() executes on the Main Thread of the application process when the provider is initialized. In contrast, query(), insert(), update(), and delete() run on Binder worker threads (from the IPC Binder thread pool) and must be implemented in a thread-safe manner.
I2 — What is the purpose of ContentProvider.getType(uri)?
Medium▼
getType(Uri) returns the MIME type of data associated with the given URI. By convention, returning a collection/list uses vnd.android.cursor.dir/..., while returning an individual row/item uses vnd.android.cursor.item/....
I3 — What causes a CursorWindowAllocationException?
Medium▼
When data is returned across process boundaries via Binder, it is copied into a shared memory buffer called CursorWindow, which has a default size limit of 2 MB. If a query attempts to load massive image blobs or unpaginated millions of rows exceeding this limit, the OS throws a CursorWindowAllocationException.
I4 — How does App Startup library utilize ContentProviders?
Medium▼
Because Android initializes ContentProviders before Application.onCreate(), libraries (like WorkManager or Firebase) historically used dummy ContentProviders for automatic zero-code initialization. Jetpack App Startup consolidates all library initializers into a single ContentProvider to eliminate startup overhead.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you notify UI observers when data in a ContentProvider changes?
HardScenario▼
1. In insert(), update(), and delete(), call context?.contentResolver?.notifyChange(uri, null) after mutating data.
2. In query(), call cursor.setNotificationUri(context?.contentResolver, uri).
3. The client can register a ContentObserver or use Room/Flow extensions to receive live updates whenever data matching that URI changes.
S2 — How do you securely export a ContentProvider to only apps with the same signing key?
HardScenario▼
1. Declare a custom permission in the provider app with android:protectionLevel="signature".
2. Apply android:permission="com.example.provider.READ_WRITE" to the <provider> tag in AndroidManifest.xml.
3. Any client app signed with the same developer signing certificate declaring <uses-permission> will automatically be granted access, while third-party apps will be blocked by the OS with a SecurityException.
S3 — Why shouldn't you use ContentProvider for purely internal app databases?
HardScenario▼
ContentProvider introduces significant overhead: Cursor abstraction, IPC marshalling, URI parsing via UriMatcher, and Binder transaction overhead. For in-process data management, Room Database directly returns strongly-typed Kotlin data classes and Flow streams with zero IPC overhead, full compile-time SQL query validation, and simpler testing.
