Navigation &amp; Deep Linking

Tier 2 Mod 18
Key Concept: Jetpack Navigation Component, Compose NavHost, Type-Safe Safe Args, Deep Links vs Verified App Links, and Back Stack manipulation.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

NAV OPTIONS DSL

popUpTo("login") { inclusive = true }
launchSingleTop = true
saveState = true
restoreState = true

APP LINKS VERIFICATION

1. https:// scheme only
2. android:autoVerify="true"
3. Domain hosts /.well-known/assetlinks.json
4. SHA-256 fingerprint matches app signing key

TYPE-SAFE COMPOSE NAV

@Serializable data class Route(val id: String)
composable<Route> { backStack ->
    val route: Route = backStack.toRoute()
}
navController.navigate(Route("123"))

CORE BEST PRACTICES

Pass IDs only (never Parcelables/Bitmaps)
Use single NavHost per feature or root
Share ViewModel via hiltNavGraphViewModel()
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Passing Large Complex Objects as Nav Arguments

Passing Parcelable objects or large lists in Navigation arguments violates Single Source of Truth and risks hitting the 1 MB Binder TransactionTooLargeException. Pass only entity IDs and fetch full state from the repository.

Pitfall 2: Forgetting autoVerify="true" for App Links

Without android:autoVerify="true" and a valid HTTPS /.well-known/assetlinks.json on the server domain, clicking your URL will trigger the Android system app chooser instead of opening your app directly.

Pitfall 3: Not using launchSingleTop on Tab Switches

Tapping bottom navigation tabs multiple times will pile duplicate instances of the same destination onto the back stack if launchSingleTop = true is omitted.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the role of NavController in Jetpack Navigation?
NavController is the central API that manages application navigation within a NavHost. It orchestrates the swapping of destination content, maintains the navigation back stack, and manages transitions and deep link routing.
B2 — What is the difference between popUpTo and inclusive = true?
Easy▼
popUpTo(destinationId) pops the back stack up to the specified destination. If inclusive = false (default), the target destination remains on top of the stack. If inclusive = true, the target destination is also popped off the stack.
B3 — What is the difference between a Deep Link and an Android App Link?
Easy▼
A Deep Link uses custom schemes (myapp://) or unverified HTTP/HTTPS URLs, which trigger a system disambiguation dialog asking the user to choose an app. An Android App Link is an HTTPS URL verified via a digital asset links JSON file on your domain, opening your app directly with zero disambiguation prompts.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — Why should you avoid passing complex objects (e.g. Parcelables) in Navigation arguments?
Medium▼
1. It violates Single Source of Truth (data becomes stale if updated elsewhere in DB).
2. It risks exceeding the Android 1MB Binder transaction buffer limit (TransactionTooLargeException).
3. URLs cannot easily encode large binary blobs for deep linking. Always pass unique IDs and load fresh data from the repository.
I2 — How does launchSingleTop = true protect the navigation back stack?
Medium▼
launchSingleTop = true ensures that if the destination you are navigating to is already at the top of the back stack, a new duplicate instance will not be created. This prevents rapid double-tap bugs and redundant screen stacking.
I3 — How is Type-Safe Navigation implemented in Navigation Compose 2.8+?
Medium▼
Navigation 2.8 uses Kotlinx Serialization. Instead of defining routes as strings ("detail/{id}"), routes are defined as @Serializable data classes or objects. composable<MyRoute>() generates the route schema automatically, and arguments are retrieved with backStackEntry.toRoute<MyRoute>().
I4 — What is the purpose of saveState and restoreState in NavOptions?
Medium▼
When switching between Bottom Navigation tabs, saveState = true saves the back stack and ViewModel state of the tab being left. When the user taps that tab again, restoreState = true restores its exact scroll position, back stack, and screen state.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you structure navigation across multiple feature modules in a modular Android project?
HardScenario▼
Create a shared :core:navigation module containing contract interfaces or @Serializable route definitions. Each feature module exposes a NavGraphBuilder.featureGraph(navController) extension function. The :app module orchestrates all feature graphs into the root NavHost, maintaining clean module decoupling and compilation independence.
S2 — How do you scope a ViewModel to a nested Navigation Graph in Jetpack Compose?
HardScenario▼
Obtain the NavBackStackEntry for the parent navigation graph using remember(backStackEntry) { navController.getBackStackEntry("parent_graph_route") }, and pass that parent entry as the ViewModelStoreOwner to hiltViewModel(parentEntry). All screens within that nested graph will share the exact same ViewModel instance until the parent graph is popped.
S3 — A user opens an App Link leading to a checkout screen when the app is closed. How do you construct the back stack so Back goes to Home?
HardScenario▼
Jetpack Navigation handles this automatically when deep links are defined inside the NavGraph or NavHost. When launched via a verified deep link Intent, Navigation creates a synthetic back stack by tracing the hierarchy from the graph's startDestination (e.g. Home) down to the target destination (Checkout), ensuring pressing Back navigates gracefully through Home before exiting.

Data &amp; Network Security

Tier 2 Mod 19
Key Concept: Android Sandbox, Hardware-Backed Keystore, EncryptedSharedPreferences, SQLCipher, TLS enforcement, Certificate Pinning, Network Security Config, and secrets handling.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

DATA AT REST

Android Keystore -> TEE / StrongBox backed
EncryptedPrefs   -> AES-256 GCM + MasterKey
SQLCipher        -> Encrypted SQLite pages
Never store      -> Plain text tokens / passwords

DATA IN TRANSIT

NetworkSecurityConfig -> Disable cleartext
CertificatePinner    -> OkHttp SHA-256 pin
Backup Pin           -> Mandatory for rotation
TLS 1.3 / 1.2        -> Modern cipher suites

SECRETS & KEYS

BuildConfig / NDK   -> Obfuscation, not encryption
Backend Proxy       -> True secret isolation
Keystore Alias      -> Hardware key reference

LOGGING & PII

Timber.plant(ReleaseTree) -> Strip debug logs
FLAG_SECURE -> Prevent screenshots / recents preview
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Hardcoding API Secrets & Private Keys in Kotlin Code

Strings in Kotlin source code or BuildConfig are trivially extracted in seconds via jadx-gui or strings classes.dex. Sensitive backend secrets must live on a backend proxy server; client-side keys should be obfuscated with NDK C++ JNI and protected via API gateway authentication.

Pitfall 2: Single Certificate Pin Brick Hazard

Pinning a single leaf certificate without configuring a backup pin (intermediate CA or backup public key) means your app will permanently fail to connect to your backend if your production certificate expires or is revoked, requiring an emergency Play Store update.

Pitfall 3: Sensitive Logging in Release Builds (Timber)

Logging user PII, credit card details, or auth tokens via Log.d() exposes them to Android Logcat. In production, use Timber with a release tree that strips debug and sensitive logs.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — How does the Android Application Sandbox isolate app data?
Android assigns each installed application a unique Linux User ID (UID) and runs it in an isolated process. File system permissions ensure that private directories (/data/data/<package_name>) can only be read and written by that specific UID, preventing other apps from accessing private files.
B2 — What is the primary advantage of storing keys in the Android Keystore?
Easy▼
The Android Keystore protects key material from being extracted. Keys are generated and stored inside hardware-backed secure enclaves (TEE or StrongBox). Cryptographic operations (signing, decryption) are performed inside the hardware module; raw key bytes are never exposed in the application's RAM.
B3 — What is Certificate Pinning and why is it used?
Easy▼
Certificate Pinning is a security technique where the client app hardcodes or verifies the exact cryptographic public key hash (SPKI SHA-256) of the server's certificate. This protects against Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks where a compromised or rogue Certificate Authority (CA) issues fraudulent certificates.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — How does EncryptedSharedPreferences work under the hood?
Medium▼
It uses Google's Tink crypto library with a 2-tier key architecture: A hardware-backed MasterKey in the Android Keystore encrypts a local keyset. Key names are deterministically encrypted using AES-256 SIV (so keys can be queried), and key values are encrypted using AES-256 GCM authenticated encryption.
I2 — Why must you always configure a backup pin when using Certificate Pinning?
Medium▼
If you pin only one certificate/key and that certificate expires, is revoked, or the server rotates keys due to a compromise, your mobile app will reject the new server certificate and permanently fail all network calls. A backup pin ensures smooth rotation without breaking existing client apps.
I3 — What is SQLCipher and how does it differ from standard Room DB?
Medium▼
Standard Room DB stores SQLite database files in plaintext on disk. SQLCipher is an open-source extension providing transparent 256-bit AES page-level encryption for the entire SQLite database file, headers, and journal data. It integrates with Room using SupportFactory(passphrase).
I4 — How do you prevent sensitive screens from appearing in Android Recents / App Switcher?
Medium▼
Call window.setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE) in the Activity's onCreate(). This instructs the OS to treat the window surface as secure, blocking screenshots, screen recordings, and masking the window preview in the recent apps task switcher.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you protect a third-party payment gateway API secret in a mobile client?
HardScenario▼
Never store master payment gateway private keys in the client app code or APK. The only secure architecture is a Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) proxy: The Android client authenticates against your own secure backend with a user JWT, your backend communicates with the payment gateway using the secret key, and passes a short-lived, scoped client token/intent back to the Android app.
S2 — How would you implement biometric-bound encryption for high-value banking transactions?
HardScenario▼
1. Generate an AES key in Keystore with setUserAuthenticationRequired(true) and setUserAuthenticationParameters(0, AUTH_BIOMETRIC_STRONG).
2. Initialize a Cipher in ENCRYPT_MODE.
3. Wrap the cipher in BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject(cipher).
4. Present BiometricPrompt.authenticate(promptInfo, cryptoObject).
5. In onAuthenticationSucceeded(), obtain the authenticated cipher from result.cryptoObject.cipher and encrypt transaction payload.
S3 — What happens to Keystore keys when the user changes or removes their device lock screen PIN/biometrics?
HardScenario▼
If a key is generated with setInvalidatedByBiometricEnrollment(true) or bound to user authentication, enrolling a new fingerprint or disabling the lock screen permanently invalidates the key in the TEE. Attempting to use the key throws a KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException. The app must detect this exception, clear local credentials, and force the user to re-authenticate with server credentials.
19B

App Hardening &amp; Auth

Tier 2 Mod 19
Key Concept: BiometricPrompt, Play Integrity API, Root/Hook detection limitations, R8 code shrinking and obfuscation, WebView security, Intent hardening, and OWASP MASVS.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

BIOMETRICS

BIOMETRIC_STRONG -> TEE hardware (<1% SAR)
BIOMETRIC_WEAK   -> 2D Face / Software
DEVICE_CREDENTIAL-> PIN / Pattern / Password
CryptoObject     -> Wraps Cipher / Signature

PLAY INTEGRITY VERDICTS

MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY -> Hardware backed boot
MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY -> Certified Android OS
MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY  -> No known emulators
PLAY_RECOGNIZED        -> Legitimate app binary

R8 / PROGUARD

minifyEnabled true -> Enables R8
shrinkResources true -> Drops unused assets
-keep -> Protects reflection / models

COMPONENT HARDENING

android:exported="false" -> Protect components
FLAG_SECURE -> Mask previews in Recents
WebView -> Disable file access & validate URLs
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Verifying Play Integrity Tokens on the Client Device

Decodes and checks Play Integrity tokens directly inside the Android app can be easily bypassed by attackers hooking the validation method using Frida. The token MUST be sent to your secure backend server and verified using Google's verification API.

Pitfall 2: Exported Components without android:exported="false"

Activities, Services, or Receivers with <intent-filter> are exported by default on older Android versions. Failing to set android:exported="false" allows malicious apps to launch private admin activities or trigger internal services directly.

Pitfall 3: Assuming Client-Side Anti-Tamper is 100% Unbreakable

Any code running on a device owned by an attacker can ultimately be reverse-engineered or hooked. High-value authorization decisions must always be made by the backend server.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the difference between ProGuard and R8?
ProGuard was a separate standalone Java bytecode optimizer that ran before the Android dex compiler (D8). R8 is Google's all-in-one replacement that combines shrinking, optimization, obfuscation, and DEX compilation into a single, faster step while using the same ProGuard keep rules syntax.
B2 — What is the purpose of BiometricPrompt.CryptoObject?
Easy▼
A CryptoObject wraps a cryptographic Cipher, Signature, or Mac initialized with a hardware-backed Keystore key requiring biometric authentication. Successful authentication unlocks the cipher inside the secure hardware to complete sensitive operations (e.g. authorizing a money transfer).
B3 — What does android:exported="false" do?
Easy▼
It ensures that an Android component (Activity, Service, or BroadcastReceiver) can only be launched by components belonging to the same application or the Android system (UID match), preventing external third-party apps from launching private internal screens or services.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — Why are client-side root detection libraries (like RootBeer) insufficient on their own?
Medium▼
Client-side root detection checks for su binaries, specific packages, or build tags. Attackers using tools like Magisk (Zygisk), Shamiko, or Frida can easily hook and override these check functions to always return false. Client checks serve only as a minor deterrent and must be backed by remote attestation (Play Integrity API).
I2 — What are the 3 device integrity levels in Google Play Integrity API?
Medium▼
1. MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY: Device passes basic system checks (not a recognized malicious emulator).
2. MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY: Device is a certified Android device running Google Play services and passes CTS tests.
3. MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY: Device has hardware-backed verified boot with a locked bootloader and uncompromised OS key.
I3 — What security precautions must be taken when using WebViews?
Medium▼
1. Disable file access: setAllowFileAccess(false).
2. Disable universal/file access from file URLs.
3. Enable JavaScript only when required.
4. Validate domains in shouldOverrideUrlLoading().
5. Never expose sensitive Native Java interfaces via addJavascriptInterface to untrusted web content.
I4 — What is OWASP MASVS and why is it important?
Medium▼
The Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS) by OWASP defines industry-standard security requirements across mobile architecture, data storage, cryptography, authentication, network communication, platform interaction, code quality, and resilience. It serves as the official security compliance baseline for banking and enterprise apps.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you design an end-to-end anti-tamper architecture for a banking transaction?
HardScenario▼
1. Client requests a cryptographic nonce from the backend server.
2. Client invokes Play Integrity API passing the nonce to generate a signed integrity token.
3. User authorizes transaction via BiometricPrompt with a TEE Keystore CryptoObject, signing transaction details.
4. Client transmits the signature, transaction payload, and Play Integrity token to backend.
5. Backend decrypts Play Integrity token directly with Google API to verify device and app authenticity, validates the nonce, and verifies the TEE signature before committing funds.
S2 — Why did your app crash with ClassNotFoundException only in the Release build?
HardScenario▼
In Release builds, R8 shrinking and obfuscation is active (minifyEnabled true). If a class (e.g., a Retrofit JSON model or dynamically loaded class via reflection) is not explicitly referenced in static bytecode, R8 strips it or renames its fields. Fix: Add appropriate @Keep annotations or configure -keep class com.example.model.** { *; } in proguard-rules.pro.
S3 — How do you prevent Tapjacking / Overlay attacks on sensitive payment buttons?
HardScenario▼
Set android:filterTouchesWhenObscured="true" on the sensitive Button / View in XML or call view.setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true). In Jetpack Compose, inspect touch event flags or set View.setFilterTouchesWhenObscured(true) on the ComposeView. This discards motion events when another window (e.g. a malicious system overlay) obscures the screen.

Unit Testing

Tier 2 Mod 20
Key Concept: JUnit 4 vs JUnit 5, MockK (Kotlin-first mocking, coEvery, slots, relaxed mocks) vs Mockito, Fake vs Mock vs Stub, Testing Pyramid, and Clean Architecture testability.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

MOCKK ESSENTIALS

mockk<T>()               // Strict mock
mockk<T>(relaxed = true) // Returns defaults
every { obj.fn() } returns value
coEvery { obj.suspendFn() } returns value
verify(exactly = 1) { obj.fn() }
coVerify { obj.suspendFn() }

ARGUMENT CAPTURING

val slot = slot<Param>()
every { repo.save(capture(slot)) } just Runs
assertEquals(expected, slot.captured)

COROUTINE RULE SETUP

@Before: Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
@After : Dispatchers.resetMain()
runTest(testDispatcher) { advanceUntilIdle() }

DESIGN RULES

1. Constructor injection for all deps
2. Inject CoroutineDispatchers
3. Zero Android SDK imports in UseCases
4. Never mock data classes / value types
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Over-Mocking and Fragile Tests

Mocking every single internal collaborator makes tests tightly coupled to implementation details rather than behavior. When refactoring internal code, tests break even if output remains correct. Prefer state verification using Fakes.

Pitfall 2: Forgetting to Reset Main Dispatcher

Calling Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher) without calling Dispatchers.resetMain() in an @After method leaves the static Main dispatcher corrupted, causing flaky downstream test failures.

Pitfall 3: Mocking Data Classes

Never mock Kotlin data class or value objects. Instantiate them directly with actual test data (or create test fixture factory functions).

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — Where do Android unit tests run and why are they fast?
Unit tests live in src/test/java and run on the local host development machine's Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Because they do not require packaging an APK, booting an Android emulator, or interacting with a physical device, they execute in milliseconds.
B2 — What is the difference between a Mock and a Fake?
Easy▼
A Fake is a real, working lightweight implementation of an interface (e.g. an in-memory FakeUserRepository with a MutableList). A Mock is a simulated object created by a mocking library (MockK/Mockito) where return values are programmed (every {}) and interactions are verified (verify {}).
B3 — Why is MockK preferred over Mockito for Kotlin codebases?
Easy▼
MockK is built natively for Kotlin. It mocks final classes and methods by default (which Kotlin classes are), provides first-class support for coroutine suspending functions (coEvery / coVerify), supports Kotlin object / singleton mocking, and offers idiomatic Kotlin DSL syntax.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — What is a relaxed mock in MockK?
Medium▼
Created via mockk<MyClass>(relaxed = true), a relaxed mock provides simple default values (0, empty string, false, empty list) for all methods that haven't been explicitly stubbed with every {}. This avoids throwing MockKException: no answer found for... during test execution.
I2 — Why should you avoid hardcoding Dispatchers.IO in ViewModels?
Medium▼
Hardcoding Dispatchers.IO causes coroutines to run on real background thread pools during unit tests. This makes tests non-deterministic, introduces race conditions, and bypasses virtual time control in runTest. Injecting dispatchers allows tests to inject StandardTestDispatcher for deterministic control.
I3 — What is the purpose of slot<T> in MockK?
Medium▼
A slot<T>() captures the argument passed to a mocked function during execution. Inside every { mock.method(capture(slot)) } or verify { ... }, the slot stores the parameter so you can perform detailed assertions on its internal properties via slot.captured.
I4 — How does spyk differ from mockk in MockK?
Medium▼
mockk() creates a completely fake object where all method calls must be stubbed or return default values. spyk(realObject) wraps an existing real instance, delegating all method calls to the real implementation unless a specific method is explicitly overridden with every {}.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — Why is over-mocking considered an anti-pattern and how do Fakes solve it?
HardScenario▼
Over-mocking ties unit tests to the exact private implementation details (which methods were invoked and in what order) rather than verifying behavioral outcomes. When refactoring code, over-mocked tests break even when the business logic is preserved. Fakes replicate contract behaviors with real state in memory, allowing true behavioral testing and easier refactoring.
S2 — How do you unit test a pure UseCase that validates user input before calling a repository?
HardScenario▼
1. Create a FakeUserRepository or mock with MockK.
2. Instantiate ValidateAndSubmitUseCase(fakeRepository).
3. Test invalid input: assert that it returns Result.failure(InvalidInputException) and verify that repository methods were NEVER invoked.
4. Test valid input: assert that it returns Result.success() and verify the repository received sanitized parameters.
S3 — You inherit legacy code where a ViewModel instantiates Room and Retrofit directly inside its constructor. How do you refactor it for unit testing?
HardScenario▼
1. Extract an interface DataRepository representing the required data contracts.
2. Implement DataRepositoryImpl that takes Room DAO and Retrofit API via constructor injection.
3. Refactor ViewModel to accept DataRepository and CoroutineDispatcher via its primary constructor.
4. Provide Hilt/Koin bindings in the DI module.
5. In the unit test, pass a FakeDataRepository and StandardTestDispatcher to instantiate the ViewModel cleanly on JVM.

Coroutines &amp; Flow Testing

Tier 2 Mod 20
Key Concept: Modern kotlinx-coroutines-test: runTest {}, StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher, advanceUntilIdle(), advanceTimeBy(), and Turbine for testing StateFlow, SharedFlow, and cold Flows.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

RUNTEST APIS

runTest(testDispatcher) {
    advanceUntilIdle()       // Drain queue
    advanceTimeBy(1000)      // Fast-forward delay
    runCurrent()             // Run pending now
}

TURBINE CHEAT SHEET

flow.test {
    awaitItem()              // Get next value
    awaitComplete()          // Confirm finish
    awaitError()             // Assert exception
    cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()
}

DISPATCHER RULES

StandardTestDispatcher   -> Queued (default)
UnconfinedTestDispatcher -> Eager start
Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
Dispatchers.resetMain()

HOT FLOW TESTING

StateFlow / SharedFlow -> Never call .toList()!
Use Turbine or backgroundScope.launch
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Calling toList() on a StateFlow / SharedFlow

StateFlow and SharedFlow are infinite hot streams that never complete. Calling viewModel.uiState.toList() will hang the unit test forever until it hits a JUnit test timeout.

Pitfall 2: Confusing advanceTimeBy() with Thread.sleep()

Thread.sleep() blocks the JVM thread and freezes execution without advancing virtual coroutine time. Always use advanceTimeBy() or advanceUntilIdle() inside runTest.

Pitfall 3: Missing cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() in Turbine

When collecting an infinite hot Flow with Turbine, omitting cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() will cause Turbine to wait for a completion event at the end of the block, throwing an AssertionError: Expected complete, but was uncompleted.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the purpose of runTest {} in kotlinx-coroutines-test?
runTest {} is the standard test builder for coroutines. It executes coroutines using a TestScope and virtual time scheduler, skipping real-world delays (delay(5000) completes in 0 ms) and automatically reporting uncaught coroutine exceptions.
B2 — What is the difference between advanceUntilIdle() and advanceTimeBy()?
Easy▼
advanceUntilIdle() advances virtual time until all scheduled coroutine tasks in the test dispatcher's queue have fully executed. advanceTimeBy(ms) advances virtual time by a specific millisecond duration, triggering any tasks scheduled to execute within that time window.
B3 — What is Turbine and why is it used?
Easy▼
Turbine (by Cash App) is a lightweight testing library for Kotlin Flows. It provides a simple flow.test { ... } DSL with sequential assertion methods like awaitItem() and awaitComplete(), eliminating the risk of hanging tests on hot streams like StateFlow.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — When should you use StandardTestDispatcher vs UnconfinedTestDispatcher?
Medium▼
Use StandardTestDispatcher when you need explicit control over execution order, concurrency, and virtual time advancement (e.g. testing debouncing, delays, or multiple parallel coroutines). Use UnconfinedTestDispatcher for simple tests where coroutines should run eagerly and immediately without having to call advanceUntilIdle().
I2 — Why does collecting a StateFlow with toList() fail in a unit test?
Medium▼
toList() suspends and collects emissions until the Flow emits a completion event. Because StateFlow and SharedFlow are hot streams that remain active indefinitely and never complete, toList() blocks indefinitely and causes the test runner to time out.
I3 — How do you test a ViewModel that uses viewModelScope on the local JVM?
Medium▼
Because viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main (which is Android-specific and uninitialized on the JVM), you must call Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher) in an @Before setup method (or use a JUnit TestWatcher Rule) and call Dispatchers.resetMain() in @After.
I4 — What is backgroundScope in TestScope?
Medium▼
backgroundScope is a coroutine scope provided by TestScope for launching background coroutines that run for the duration of the test (such as collecting infinite Flows). Any coroutine launched in backgroundScope is automatically cancelled when the test body completes, preventing UncompletedCoroutinesError.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you unit test a retryWithExponentialBackoff Flow operator?
HardScenario▼
@Test
fun testExponentialBackoff() = runTest(testDispatcher) {
    val fakeApi: Api = mockk()
    coEvery { fakeApi.fetchData() } throws IOException() andThen "Success"

    val flow = flow { emit(fakeApi.fetchData()) }.retryWithBackoff(initialDelay = 1000)

    flow.test {
        advanceTimeBy(999)
        coVerify(exactly = 1) { fakeApi.fetchData() }

        advanceTimeBy(1) // Hits 1000ms retry delay
        assertEquals("Success", awaitItem())
        awaitComplete()
    }
}
S2 — Why was TestCoroutineDispatcher deprecated and what replaces it?
HardScenario▼
TestCoroutineDispatcher had architectural flaws: it leaked coroutine state across tests, conflated eager and delayed execution modes, and struggled to synchronize virtual time when coroutines launched child jobs across different threads. It was completely replaced in Coroutines 1.6 by StandardTestDispatcher (for queued/deterministic control) and UnconfinedTestDispatcher (for eager execution) coupled with TestScope.
S3 — How do you create a reusable JUnit Rule for Coroutines testing?
HardScenario▼
class MainDispatcherRule(
    val testDispatcher: TestDispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher()
) : TestWatcher() {
    override fun starting(description: Description) {
        Dispatchers.setMain(testDispatcher)
    }
    override fun finished(description: Description) {
        Dispatchers.resetMain()
    }
}

// In Test class:
@get:Rule
val mainDispatcherRule = MainDispatcherRule()

Key Concept: Espresso view assertions, Compose UI testing via SemanticsMatchers, cross-app testing with UI Automator, and OkHttp MockWebServer for reliable network integration tests.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

COMPOSE UI TEST

val rule = createComposeRule()
rule.setContent { Screen() }
rule.onNodeWithText("Submit")
    .assertIsDisplayed()
    .performClick()

ESPRESSO FORMULA

onView(withId(R.id.btn))
    .perform(click())
    .check(matches(isDisplayed()))

MOCKWEBSERVER

server.enqueue(
    MockResponse()
        .setResponseCode(200)
        .setBody("{...}")

UI AUTOMATOR

val device = UiDevice.getInstance(...)
val btn = device.findObject(
    UiSelector().text("Allow")

btn.click()
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Flaky Tests Caused by Thread.sleep()

Using Thread.sleep() in UI tests causes arbitrary delays and flaky CI failures. Espresso automatically syncs with the main thread queue. For custom background tasks, implement an IdlingResource or use Compose mainClock.autoAdvance.

Pitfall 2: Relying on Real Backend APIs in CI

Testing against live staging servers makes UI tests vulnerable to network latency, server downtime, and changing backend test databases. Always use MockWebServer for reproducible network integration tests.

Pitfall 3: Using Hardcoded Coordinates in UI Automator

Clicking by screen coordinates (x, y) breaks across different device screen sizes and densities. Always match by UiSelector().text(), resourceId(), or contentDescription().

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the difference between unit tests and instrumentation tests?
Unit tests (src/test) run on the local development machine's JVM in milliseconds without Android OS dependencies. Instrumentation tests (src/androidTest) are compiled into an APK and run on an Android physical device or emulator, testing real UI rendering, database integration, and OS components.
B2 — How does Jetpack Compose find UI elements during testing?
Easy▼
Compose uses the Semantics Tree. Composable functions attach semantics properties (text, content description, role, test tag, selection state) to nodes. Test matchers like onNodeWithText() or onNodeWithTag() traverse this semantics hierarchy to find elements.
B3 — What is MockWebServer?
Easy▼
MockWebServer (by Square / OkHttp) is a scriptable embedded HTTP server for testing HTTP/HTTPS clients locally. It lets tests enqueue mock HTTP responses (status codes, headers, JSON bodies) and inspect incoming HTTP requests (path, body, authorization headers) with zero external network connectivity.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — When should you use UI Automator instead of Espresso / Compose Rule?
Medium▼
Use UI Automator when your test needs to interact with elements outside your application's process: system runtime permission dialogs ("Allow Notifications / Location"), system settings, launching third-party apps, clicking status bar notification banners, or device hardware keys (Home, Back, Volume).
I2 — What is an IdlingResource in Espresso and how does Compose handle it?
Medium▼
An IdlingResource informs Espresso that background operations (e.g. data loading) are still in progress, telling Espresso to pause UI actions until the resource becomes idle. Jetpack Compose handles synchronization automatically: createComposeRule() automatically synchronizes with Compose's internal clock and waits for recompositions to finish before executing assertions.
I3 — How do you test error responses (e.g., 500 Internal Server Error) with MockWebServer?
Medium▼
server.enqueue(
    MockResponse()
        .setResponseCode(500)
        .setBody("""{"error": "Database unavailable"}""")
)
val result = repository.fetchData()
assertTrue(result.isFailure)
I4 — What is testTag in Jetpack Compose and why should you use it judiciously?
Medium▼
Modifier.testTag("tag_name") assigns a unique identifier to a composable node for onNodeWithTag() lookup. It should be used judiciously because over-tagging introduces test-specific code into production layouts. Prefer testing user-facing semantics (text, content description, accessibility roles) whenever possible.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do you test an end-to-end checkout flow with OkHttp Auth Interceptors using MockWebServer?
HardScenario▼
1. Enqueue a 401 Unauthorized for the initial checkout request.
2. Enqueue a 200 OK for the token refresh request.
3. Enqueue a 200 OK for the retried checkout request.
4. Trigger the checkout action.
5. Inspect server.takeRequest() 3 times: verify that request 1 had the old token, request 2 called /oauth/refresh, and request 3 contained the refreshed Authorization: Bearer <newToken> header.
S2 — How do you isolate and test a single Composable without launching the entire Application / NavHost?
HardScenario▼
Use createComposeRule() (which launches an empty ComponentActivity). Inside composeTestRule.setContent { }, render the isolated Composable passing mock lambda callbacks (e.g. onItemClicked = { }) and dummy UI state. This tests the composable in total isolation from ViewModels, navigation routers, and backend repositories.
S3 — Why do UI tests fail on CI machines with animation timeouts and how do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
Continuous animations (infinite progress spinners, Lottie animations) prevent Espresso and Compose clocks from reaching an idle state, resulting in test timeouts. Fixes:
1. Disable system animations on the test emulator via ADB before running tests: settings put global window_animation_scale 0, transition_animation_scale 0, animator_duration_scale 0.
2. In Compose, use mainClock.autoAdvance = false to manually advance infinite transition clocks.

Android Performance

Tier 2 Mod 21
Key Concept: ANR detection and prevention, StrictMode, Cold vs Warm vs Hot startup optimization, Baseline Profiles, 16ms frame jank budgeting, Macrobenchmark, and Compose stability.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

ANR THRESHOLDS

Input event (touch/key) -> 5 seconds
BroadcastReceiver       -> 10 seconds
Foreground Service      -> 20 seconds
Detection               -> StrictMode / Profiler

FRAME BUDGET

60 FPS  -> 16.6 ms per frame
120 FPS -> 8.3 ms per frame
Choreographer -> Drops frames if missed (Jank)

STARTUP PHASES

Cold Start -> Process create + App + Activity
Warm Start -> Process exists, Activity recreated
Hot Start  -> Activity brought to front

COMPOSE STABILITY

@Immutable / @Stable annotations
ImmutableList<T> instead of List<T>
derivedStateOf for scroll / calculation filters
remember { } for expensive allocations
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Heavy Synchronous Initialization in Application.onCreate()

Initializing analytics SDKs, crash reporters, push notification engines, and local databases synchronously inside Application.onCreate() directly delays the first frame and degrades cold start metrics. Use Jetpack App Startup and offload non-critical SDKs to coroutines.

Pitfall 2: Loading Unscaled Bitmaps into ImageViews

Loading full 4K (4096x2160 ARGB_8888) camera photos directly into memory consumes ~35 MB RAM per image, quickly causing OutOfMemoryError (OOM). Always decode downsampled bitmaps matching the View dimensions using inSampleSize or Coil/Glide.

Pitfall 3: Reading SharedPreferences Synchronously during Startup

Calling sharedPreferences.getString() causes a synchronous disk read on the Main Thread. If SharedPreferences XML is large, it blocks the main thread and can trigger ANRs.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is an ANR and what are the primary thresholds that trigger it?
An ANR (Application Not Responding) occurs when the application's Main (UI) thread is blocked and cannot process system messages. Thresholds:
• 5 seconds: No response to user input (touch, key press).
• 10 seconds: BroadcastReceiver.onReceive() fails to return.
• 20 seconds: Service.onStartCommand() blocks.
B2 — What is the frame rendering time budget on a 60Hz vs 120Hz Android screen?
Easy▼
On a standard 60Hz display, the system must render each frame in under 16.6 milliseconds (1000ms / 60 frames). On high refresh rate 120Hz displays, the budget shrinks to 8.3 milliseconds per frame. Exceeding this budget causes Choreographer to skip a VSYNC pulse, resulting in visible UI jank/stutter.
B3 — What is the difference between a Cold Start and a Hot Start?
Easy▼
A Cold Start creates a new Linux OS process from scratch, initializes the Application class, and inflates the first Activity (slowest). A Hot Start simply brings an already running Activity from the background back to the foreground with zero view inflation or process creation (fastest).

Intermediate Questions

I1 — What is StrictMode and how does it help catch performance bugs?
Medium▼
StrictMode is a developer tool that detects accidental disk I/O, network requests, and SQLite operations executed on the application's Main Thread. It can log warnings, flash the screen, or crash the app in debug builds to catch ANR bottlenecks before releasing to production.
I2 — What are Baseline Profiles and how do they improve app startup time?
Medium▼
Baseline Profiles are rules bundled with an APK that specify classes and methods used during critical user paths (cold start, first screen rendering). Google Play and the Android Runtime (ART) use them to Ahead-of-Time (AOT) pre-compile DEX bytecode into native machine code upon app installation, eliminating JIT compilation stalls and speeding up cold start by ~30-40%.
I3 — Why is List<T> considered unstable by the Jetpack Compose compiler?
Medium▼
In Kotlin, List<T> is an interface that can be backed by a mutable implementation like ArrayList. Because the Compose compiler cannot guarantee that the underlying collection items haven't been mutated, it flags standard List<T> as unstable, forcing the Composable to recompose on every recomposition cycle. Fix: Use kotlinx.collections.immutable.ImmutableList or @Immutable.
I4 — What is derivedStateOf in Jetpack Compose and when should you use it?
Medium▼
derivedStateOf { } creates a state object that calculates its value from other Compose states, emitting a new state ONLY when the calculated result actually changes. It is essential when observing fast-changing states (e.g. lazyListState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0 for a "scroll to top" button) to prevent hundreds of unnecessary recompositions per second during scrolling.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — An e-commerce app experiences dropped frames while scrolling a complex product grid in Compose. How do you diagnose and fix it?
HardScenario▼
1. Diagnose: Run Android Studio Layout Inspector to check Recomposition Count / Skipped Count per item. Use Perfetto / Systrace to check Choreographer VSYNC overruns.
2. Fix Stability: Wrap product list in ImmutableList<Product> to make items skippable.
3. Item Keys: Provide stable key = { it.productId } in items().
4. Image Loading: Ensure Coil uses hardware bitmap configs and downsamples images to exact grid dimensions.
5. Avoid Reallocations: Extract lambdas out of item composition scopes.
S2 — How would you reduce cold start time in an enterprise banking app with 15+ third-party SDKs?
HardScenario▼
1. Profile Startup: Use Android Studio CPU Profiler (Traceview) on Application.onCreate() to identify slowest SDK initializers.
2. App Startup Library: Consolidate initialization into Jetpack App Startup to eliminate ContentProvider startup overhead.
3. Lazy Init: Defer non-critical SDKs (analytics, feedback, in-app messaging) to background coroutines after the first Activity draws its first frame.
4. Baseline Profiles: Generate and bundle a Baseline Profile for the cold start journey.
5. R8 Optimization: Enable full R8 shrinking and dex desugaring.
S3 — How do you use Macrobenchmark to write automated CI performance regression tests?
HardScenario▼
Create a dedicated :macrobenchmark module using MacrobenchmarkRule. Write tests measuring StartupTimingMetric() (measuring timeToInitialDisplayMs) and FrameTimingMetric() during automated UI scrolls. Run the benchmark on physical test devices in CI against release builds with CompilationMode.Partial(BaselineProfileMode.Require), asserting that startup remains below agreed SLA thresholds (e.g. <600ms).

Memory Management &amp; Leaks

Tier 2 Mod 22
Key Concept: JVM/ART Memory Model, Generational Garbage Collection, Reference Types (Strong, Weak, Soft, Phantom), the 7 Classic Android Leaks, and LeakCanary heap analysis.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

REFERENCE TYPES

Strong  -> Never collected if reachable
Weak    -> Collected on next GC
Soft    -> Collected only before OOM
Phantom -> Post-finalization cleanup

TOP 3 LEAK FIXES

Singleton -> Pass context.applicationContext
Fragment  -> _binding = null in onDestroyView
Handler   -> removeCallbacksAndMessages(null)

LEAKCANARY FLOW

1. Activity onDestroy() called
2. Wrapped in KeyedWeakReference
3. Wait 5s + trigger GC
4. Shark parses .hprof leak trace

PROFILER TERMS

Shallow Size  -> Size of object only
Retained Size -> Size freed if object is GC'd
GC Root       -> Active Thread / Static reference
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices
Pitfall 1: Retaining ViewModel in Static / Long-Lived Scope

ViewModels are intended to survive configuration changes, but NOT app process scope. Storing a ViewModel in a static cache will leak the entire ViewModel and any Activity/Context callbacks attached to it.

Pitfall 2: Including LeakCanary in Release Builds

Never include LeakCanary in release production builds (debugImplementation 'com.squareup.leakcanary:leakcanary-android:...'). Heap dumping freezes the UI and leaks user PII stored in memory to disk.

Pitfall 3: Shallow Size vs Retained Size Confusion

Shallow Size is the memory consumed by the object itself (e.g. 32 bytes). Retained Size is the total memory freed if this object is garbage collected (including all dependent objects it holds, which can be 50+ MB for an Activity).

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is a memory leak in Android?
A memory leak occurs when an object that is no longer needed by the application (such as an Activity that has finished and called onDestroy()) cannot be garbage collected because another surviving object with a longer lifecycle holds a strong reference to it. Over time, accumulated leaks exhaust available heap space and cause an OutOfMemoryError (OOM).
B2 — What is the difference between StrongReference and WeakReference?
Easy▼
A StrongReference is the default reference type in Kotlin/Java; as long as an object has a strong reference chain from a GC root, it will never be collected. A WeakReference does not prevent its referent from being collected; on the very next GC cycle, if no strong references remain, the GC immediately reclaims the object.
B3 — Why should you pass applicationContext instead of Activity context to a Singleton?
Easy▼
A Singleton lives for the entire lifetime of the application process. If you pass an Activity Context to a Singleton, that Singleton retains a strong reference to the Activity even after the user closes it, leaking the Activity, its View hierarchy, Bitmaps, and resources permanently. applicationContext is tied to the Application lifecycle and is safe for singletons.

Intermediate Questions

I1 — Why must Fragment ViewBinding be set to null in onDestroyView()?
Medium▼
In Android, a Fragment instance outlives its View hierarchy (e.g., when a Fragment transaction is added to the back stack). When navigating away, onDestroyView() is called and the View is destroyed, but the Fragment instance remains in memory. If _binding is not set to null, the binding property retains strong references to all inflated Views, creating a view hierarchy leak on the back stack.
I2 — How does LeakCanary detect memory leaks automatically?
Medium▼
1. LeakCanary registers ActivityLifecycleCallbacks and FragmentLifecycleCallbacks.
2. When an Activity/Fragment reaches onDestroy(), LeakCanary passes it to an AppWatcher that wraps it in a KeyedWeakReference linked to a ReferenceQueue.
3. After a 5-second delay, it forces a GC check. If the object has not appeared in the ReferenceQueue, it is considered retained.
4. It dumps the heap into a .hprof file and uses Shark parser to find the shortest path from GC roots to the leaking object.
I3 — How can Handler.postDelayed() cause an Activity memory leak?
Medium▼
When you post a runnable via handler.postDelayed(runnable, delay), the Android Looper.MessageQueue holds a Message containing a reference to the Runnable, which has an implicit reference to the outer Activity (if written as an anonymous class or lambda). The Looper is a static GC root, so the Activity cannot be garbage collected until the delay expires and the message is processed.
I4 — What is the difference between Shallow Size and Retained Size in memory profiling?
Medium▼
Shallow Size is the memory allocated to hold the object itself (its fields and header), excluding references to other objects. Retained Size is the total amount of memory that would be freed if this specific object were garbage collected, including all downstream child objects that are exclusively reachable from it.

Senior & Scenario Questions

S1 — How do Kotlin Coroutines prevent memory leaks compared to RxJava or Java Threads?
HardScenario▼
Kotlin Coroutines utilize Structured Concurrency. Scopes like lifecycleScope and viewModelScope are directly bound to the lifecycle of the host component (Activity, Fragment, or ViewModel). When the host is destroyed (e.g. onDestroy() or onCleared()), the scope automatically cancels its parent Job, which recursively cancels all child coroutines and releases object references. In contrast, RxJava requires manual compositeDisposable.clear() and raw Java Threads have no lifecycle integration.
S2 — Android Profiler shows native memory continuously climbing after loading high-res images in a RecyclerView. What is the root cause?
HardScenario▼
Since Android 8.0 (API 26), Bitmap pixel byte buffers are allocated in Native C++ memory (via GraphicBuffer/HardwareBuffer) rather than JVM Java heap. If images are not downsampled (using inSampleSize) and image views retain bitmaps in memory or custom caches without recycling, native memory balloons until ART triggers an OOM. Fix: Use an image loading library like Coil/Glide configured with strict memory cache limits and bitmap pooling.
S3 — How do you diagnose and fix a native cursor window leak reported by StrictMode?
HardScenario▼
StrictMode.VmPolicy.detectLeakedSqlLiteObjects() flags instances where a database Cursor or SQLiteDatabase connection was finalized without calling close(). The root cause is queries opened without try-finally or Kotlin's use {} block. Fix: Wrap all direct Cursor queries in cursor.use { cursor -> ... } or migrate entirely to Room Database, which manages cursor lifecycles automatically.

Gradle Phases

Key Terms

TermMeaning
AGPAndroid Gradle Plugin — adds Android build tasks
D8DEX compiler — converts .class → .dex
R8Shrinker + obfuscator + optimizer (release only)

⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Pitfalls

  • Slow configuration: network/file I/O at top level of build script — wrap in task actions
  • api vs implementation: using api() leaks transitive dependencies to consumers, increasing compilation scope. Use implementation() by default.
  • Not using Version Catalog: version duplication across modules causes drift. Adopt libs.versions.toml.
  • Committed keystore or passwords: security risk. Use environment variables or Gradle secrets plugins.
  • KAPT in new projects: adds ~30–60 sec to large project builds. Migrate to KSP.
  • Missing proguard rules: R8 may strip classes used via reflection (Retrofit, Gson, Moshi). Add keep rules.

Best Practices

PracticeWhy
Use libs.versions.tomlSingle source of truth for all versions
Prefer KSP over KAPT2× faster, incremental, Kotlin-native
Enable build cache + parallelDramatically reduces CI build time
Use implementation not apiReduces recompilation scope across modules
Put signing creds in env varsSecurity — never commit credentials
Profile with --scanIdentify slow tasks before optimizing
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What are the three phases of Gradle's build lifecycle?
Basic⌄
Initialization (reads settings.gradle, discovers projects), Configuration (executes all build scripts, builds the task graph — runs every time), Execution (runs only the requested tasks in dependency order). Key point: configuration always runs, so heavy work there slows every Gradle invocation.
Q2: 2. What is a build variant and how is it formed?
Basic⌄
A build variant is the cross-product of a product flavor and a build type. If you have flavors [dev, prod] and types [debug, release], you get four variants: devDebug, devRelease, prodDebug, prodRelease. Each variant can have its own source set, resources, and BuildConfig values.
Q3: 3. What is the Version Catalog (libs.versions.toml) and why use it?
Basic⌄
A TOML file in the gradle/ directory that centralizes all dependency versions, library coordinates, and plugin IDs. Modules reference them as libs.hilt.android or libs.plugins.ksp. Benefits: single source of truth for versions, no drift across modules, IDE auto-complete, and bundle grouping.

Modularization

Tier 2 Mod 24
Key Concept: Why to modularize, module types and responsibilities, dependency rules, api vs implementation, dynamic feature modules, build performance benefits, and inter-module communication patterns.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Module Structure

:app (entry point)
:feature:home, :cart, :checkout
:core:network, :database
:core:ui, :common, :domain

Dependency Direction

:app → :feature:X → :core:*
Features NEVER depend on each other
:core:common = pure Kotlin (JVM)

api vs implementation

implementation → hidden, faster
api → leaks to consumers
Rule: use implementation by default

Communication Patterns

1. NavBackStackEntry ViewModel
2. SharedFlow event bus
3. Hilt interface binding (best)

Key Terms

TermMeaning
Vertical sliceFeature module containing all layers (UI, domain, data) for one feature
ABI changePublic API change that forces dependent modules to recompile
DFMDynamic Feature Module — downloaded on demand at runtime
api()Exposes dependency transitively to module consumers
implementation()Hides dependency from consumers — preferred default
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Module Communication Patterns

The Problem

Feature modules cannot depend on each other. But they often need to communicate — e.g., :feature:cart needs to know the user logged in (event from :feature:auth). Three patterns solve this:

1. Shared ViewModel via NavBackStackEntry

// Scoped ViewModel shared across feature screens via the nav graph
// Both features define the nav graph in :app — they share a parent entry
@Composable
fun CheckoutScreen(navController: NavController) {
    val parentEntry = remember(navController) {
        navController.getBackStackEntry("checkout_graph")
    }
    val sharedVm: SharedCartViewModel = hiltViewModel(parentEntry)
}

2. SharedFlow Event Bus via :core:common

// :core:common — defines the event contract (no feature dependencies)
sealed class AppEvent {
    data class UserLoggedIn(val userId: String) : AppEvent()
    object CartCleared : AppEvent()
}

// :core:common — EventBus singleton
object AppEventBus {
    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<AppEvent>()
    val events: SharedFlow<AppEvent> = _events.asSharedFlow()
    suspend fun emit(event: AppEvent) = _events.emit(event)
}

3. Service Interface via Hilt (Preferred)

// :core:domain — interface (no feature deps)
interface CartRepository {
    suspend fun addItem(item: CartItem)
    fun getCartFlow(): Flow<List<CartItem>>
}

// :feature:cart — implementation (depends on :core:domain, :core:database)
class CartRepositoryImpl @Inject constructor(
    private val cartDao: CartDao
) : CartRepository { ... }

// :app — Hilt binding wires interface to implementation
@Binds abstract fun bindCartRepo(impl: CartRepositoryImpl): CartRepository
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What are the main reasons to modularize an Android app?
Basic⌄
Build speed (parallel compilation, build cache), feature isolation (each feature owns its code), team scalability (teams work in independent modules), reusability (core modules shared), and dynamic delivery (Dynamic Feature Modules reduce install size).
Q2: 2. What dependency direction rule must modules follow?
Basic⌄
:app → :feature:X → :core:*. Feature modules must NEVER depend on other feature modules. Core modules must never depend on feature modules. This one-way flow ensures isolation and allows parallel compilation.
Q3: 3. What is an ABI change and why does it matter for build speed?
Basic⌄
An ABI (Application Binary Interface) change is a modification to a module's public API — adding, removing, or changing a public function or class. ABI changes force all dependent modules to recompile. Non-ABI changes (private/internal modifications) only recompile the changed module. Maximizing use of internal visibility directly improves build speed.

6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Common Pitfalls

  • Committing keystore/passwords: irreversible security breach. Use GitHub Secrets only.
  • Slow CI due to no caching: always use gradle/actions/setup-gradle for Gradle caching
  • Running UI tests on every PR: expensive. Run unit tests on PR, UI tests only on merge to main or nightly
  • No branch protection: developers can push broken code directly to main. Enforce CI pass + reviews.
  • Uploading APK to Play Store: Play Store requires AAB since August 2021 for new apps
  • Forgetting versionCode increment: Play Store rejects uploads with duplicate versionCode. Automate with CI build number.

Best Practices

PracticeWhy
Fail fast: lint before buildCatch cheap issues early, don't waste build minutes
Cache Gradle dependenciesSaves 3–5 min per CI run
Use GitHub EnvironmentsRequire manual approval before deploying to production

Stage production rolloutStart at 1–10%, monitor crash rate, then expand
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What is the difference between an APK and an AAB?
Basic⌄
An APK (Android Package) contains all resources for all device configurations in one file — large download. An AAB (Android App Bundle) contains split code and resources for all configurations; Google Play generates device-specific APKs from it at download time, reducing install size by 20–30%. Play Store requires AAB for new apps since August 2021. APKs are still used for direct installs and Firebase App Distribution.
Q2: 2. How do you securely handle the release keystore in CI?
Basic⌄
Base64-encode the keystore file and store it as a CI secret (e.g. KEYSTORE_BASE64 in GitHub Secrets). In the CI workflow, decode it: echo "$KEYSTORE_BASE64" | base64 -d > keystore.jks. Pass the path and credentials (STORE_PASSWORD, KEY_ALIAS, KEY_PASSWORD) as environment variables to the Gradle build. Never commit the .jks file or print env vars in logs.
Q3: 3. What Play Store tracks are available for staged deployment?
Basic⌄
Internal testing (up to 100 testers, instant publish), Closed testing / Alpha (specific user groups), Open testing / Beta (any opted-in user), Production (all users, supports gradual rollout percentage). Standard flow: Internal → Alpha → Beta → Production at 10% → 50% → 100%.

6. Technical Debt Management

What is Technical Debt?

Technical debt is the implied cost of future rework caused by choosing a fast/easy solution now instead of the better approach. SonarQube estimates it in hours based on issue count and complexity.

Debt Prioritization

SeverityPriorityExamples
BlockerFix immediately — don't shipNullPointerException risk, data corruption
CriticalFix in current sprintSecurity vulnerability, major performance issue
MajorSchedule in backlogComplex method, code duplication, missing test
Minor/InfoFix opportunisticallyNaming issues, formatting, minor style

Managing Legacy Debt

  • Lint baseline: suppress existing issues, fail only on new ones (ratchet pattern)
  • Detekt baseline: same approach for Detekt issues
  • Boy Scout Rule: leave every file you touch slightly better than you found it
  • Refactor sprints: schedule periodic debt-reduction work alongside features
  • Debt ratio tracking: SonarQube shows debt ratio over time — ensure it trends down
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What is the difference between Android Lint, Detekt, and Ktlint?
Basic⌄
Android Lint: built-in, finds Android-specific issues (wrong API level, missing translations, security). Detekt: Kotlin static analysis for code quality — complexity, naming, style, potential bugs. Ktlint: formatting ONLY — enforces the Kotlin style guide (indentation, spacing, trailing commas). All three complement each other and should run in CI.
Q2: 2. What is a Lint baseline file and why is it useful?
Basic⌄
A baseline file records all existing Lint issues at a point in time. CI is then configured to suppress all baselined issues and fail only when NEW issues are introduced. This is the "ratchet" pattern — it lets you adopt strict Lint enforcement in a legacy codebase without requiring a big-bang cleanup. Over time, fix issues and regenerate the baseline to shrink it.
Q3: 3. What is a SonarQube quality gate?
Basic⌄
A quality gate is a set of conditions that code must meet to be considered releasable. Default conditions: new code coverage ≥ 80%, 0 new blocker or critical issues, reliability rating A, duplication ≤ 3%. If any condition fails, the SonarQube status is "failed" and CI can be configured to block the PR merge.

6. Android Version Evolution
Android VersionAPIPermission Changes
Android 6.0 Marshmallow23Runtime permissions introduced — dangerous perms must be requested at runtime
Android 10 Q29Scoped storage; background location separate permission; ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION added
Android 11 R30One-time permissions (camera, mic, location); background location: system redirects to Settings; MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE added; auto-reset permissions for unused apps
Android 12 S31/32Approximate vs precise location: user can grant coarse instead of fine; Bluetooth permissions split (BLUETOOTH_SCAN, BLUETOOTH_CONNECT)
Android 13 T33POST_NOTIFICATIONS required at runtime; granular media permissions (READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, READ_MEDIA_AUDIO) replace READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE; nearby WiFi permission
Android 14 U34Photo picker: partial media access — user grants specific photos not all; READ_MEDIA_VISUAL_USER_SELECTED for partial access
Senior Mental Model
Android permissions have evolved toward granularity and transparency. Each version restricts more and gives users more control. Always check the target API level and use Build.VERSION.SDK_INT to handle different permission models. Compile against the latest targetSdk so your app gets the new privacy features.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What is the difference between normal and dangerous permissions?
Basic⌄
Normal permissions (like INTERNET, VIBRATE) are automatically granted at install time — no user interaction needed. Dangerous permissions (like CAMERA, LOCATION, READ_CONTACTS) can access sensitive user data or device features, so they must be declared in the manifest AND explicitly requested at runtime on Android 6+ (API 23). The user must grant them; they can be revoked at any time.
Q2: 2. What does shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() return in each state?
Basic⌄
First time asking: false (no rationale needed, show dialog). User denied once: true (show rationale UI explaining why you need it). User checked "Don't ask again": false (same as first time — can't distinguish programmatically). Permission already granted: false. The key gotcha: false doesn't tell you whether it's first-time or permanently denied — you must track "has the user been asked before" separately.
Q3: 3. What changed about notifications in Android 13?
Basic⌄
Android 13 (API 33) made POST_NOTIFICATIONS a dangerous permission requiring a runtime request. On Android 12 and below, apps could post notifications without permission. Apps targeting API 33+ must declare the permission in the manifest and request it at runtime. The user can deny it, in which case all notifications from the app are blocked. Apps upgraded from lower target SDK get a one-time automatic grant prompt.

// ❌ Creating new listeners each bind — set listener in ViewHolder constructor
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. Why is the ViewHolder pattern important?
Basic⌄
ViewHolder caches view references. Without it, onBindViewHolder would call findViewById() on every scroll event — an expensive tree traversal. The ViewHolder stores all view references as properties, created once in onCreateViewHolder. With ViewBinding, references are auto-generated as typed properties — cleaner and null-safe. The key insight: onCreateViewHolder is called rarely (only when no recycled view is available), but onBindViewHolder is called on every visible item during scroll.
Q2: 2. What is the difference between areItemsTheSame and areContentsTheSame?
Basic⌄
areItemsTheSame checks identity — are these two items representing the same entity? Usually compares unique IDs. areContentsTheSame checks equality — do both items have the same data to display? Usually uses data class equals() or field-by-field comparison. If areItemsTheSame is false: item is added/removed (insert/delete animation). If true but areContentsTheSame is false: item is updated (change animation). Both true: no change, skip rebind.
Q3: 3. What is ListAdapter and how does it improve on plain RecyclerView.Adapter?
Basic⌄
ListAdapter wraps AsyncListDiffer which runs DiffUtil.calculateDiff() on a background thread. Plain adapter requires calling notifyDataSetChanged() (expensive — rebinds everything) or manually calling notifyItemInserted/Removed (error-prone). ListAdapter.submitList() automatically diffs old vs new list and dispatches precise updates with animations. It also stores the current list internally — use getItem(position) in onBindViewHolder.

ViewBinding Fragment

val binding get() = _binding!!
onCreateView → inflate → assign

6. Migration to Compose

Why Compose Replaces All of This

Legacy ProblemCompose Solution
Manual state management (setText, setVisibility)State-driven UI — recompose on state change automatically
No type safety in XML attributesPure Kotlin — compile-time type checking everywhere
Complex two-way binding with DataBindingrememberSaveable + ViewModel.uiState — simple and explicit
onMeasure/onDraw boilerplate for custom renderingCanvas in DrawScope, Modifier.drawBehind — Kotlin DSL

ViewStub for conditional inflationif/when expressions — lazy evaluation by default

Incremental Migration Strategy

// Step 1: Add Compose to a Fragment with ComposeView
class ProductFragment : Fragment() {
    override fun onCreateView(...) = ComposeView(requireContext()).apply {
        setViewCompositionStrategy(ViewCompositionStrategy.DisposeOnViewTreeLifecycleDestroyed)
        setContent {
            MyAppTheme { ProductScreen(viewModel = hiltViewModel()) }
        }
    }
}

// Step 2: Embed legacy View in Compose with AndroidView
@Composable
fun LegacyMapView() {
    AndroidView(factory = { context -> MapView(context).apply { ... } })
}

// Step 3: Full migration — replace Fragment with a NavHost entry
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What is ViewBinding and how does it differ from DataBinding?
Basic⌄
ViewBinding generates a typed class for each XML layout file — provides null-safe, type-safe access to views. It replaces findViewByld and Kotlin synthetics. DataBinding also generates typed classes but additionally supports @{} expressions in XML for data binding and @={} for two-way binding. ViewBinding is faster to compile (no annotation processing), simpler to debug (no XML expressions), and preferred for most cases. Use DataBinding only when two-way XML binding is genuinely needed.
Q2: 2. Why must you null the binding reference in Fragment.onDestroyView()?
Basic⌄
Fragments have two lifetimes: the Fragment itself (created to destroyed) and the Fragment's View (onCreateView to onDestroyView). When the Fragment is on the back stack, its View is destroyed but the Fragment instance lives on. The binding holds references to all Views in the destroyed layout. If not nulled, this constitutes a memory leak — the Fragment keeps the entire View hierarchy alive. Always: onDestroyView() { super.onDestroyView(); _binding = null }.
Q3: 3. What are the key advantages of ConstraintLayout over LinearLayout/RelativeLayout?
Basic⌄
Flat hierarchy — all views at one level, no nested containers. This reduces measure/layout passes (nested LinearLayouts require O(n²) measurement). ConstraintLayout can express any layout that would require nested LinearLayouts + RelativeLayouts in a single flat structure. Additional features: chains (spread/pack weight distribution), barriers (dynamic alignment), groups (visibility control), guidelines, and MotionLayout for animations.

Paging Components

prefetchDistance = 5

  .getProductsPaged()
  .cachedIn(viewModelScope)

⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Compose & API Pagination Design

LazyPagingItems in Compose

@Composable
fun ProductListScreen(viewModel: ProductViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val lazyItems = viewModel.products.collectAsLazyPagingItems()

    LazyColumn {
        items(
            count = lazyItems.itemCount,
            key = lazyItems.itemKey { it.id }
        ) { index ->
            val product = lazyItems[index]  // triggers load if null (placeholder)
            if (product != null) {
                ProductItem(product = product)
            }
        }

        // Handle load states
        when (val loadState = lazyItems.loadState.append) {
            is LoadState.Loading -> item { LoadingSpinner() }
            is LoadState.Error  -> item { ErrorRetryItem { lazyItems.retry() } }
            else -> {}
        }
    }
}

API Pagination Design

StyleKeyProsCons
Offset-basedpage=2&size=20Simple, jump to any pageData shift on insert/delete — items skipped or duplicated
Cursor-basedafter=cursor_tokenConsistent — no skips with real-time dataCan't jump to arbitrary page

For real-time feeds (chat, social, catalog updates) cursor-based is strongly preferred — an item inserted at position 5 between page requests won't cause page 2 to duplicate the item that shifted from page 1.

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What are the three main components of Paging 3?
Basic⌄
PagingSource: defines how to load a single page of data — takes LoadParams (key, loadSize) and returns LoadResult.Page or LoadResult.Error. Pager: orchestrates loading, manages the RecycledViewPool, and emits Flow<PagingData<T>>. PagingData: an immutable snapshot of a page — consumed by LazyPagingItems in Compose or PagingDataAdapter in RecyclerView. RemoteMediator is optional — adds network+database (offline-first) support.
Q2: 2. What does prevKey and nextKey represent in LoadResult.Page?
Basic⌄
prevKey: the key to load the page BEFORE this one. null = no more previous pages (start of data). nextKey: the key to load the page AFTER this one. null = no more next pages (end of data). For offset-based: prevKey = page - 1, nextKey = page + 1. When nextKey is null, Pager stops appending and marks endOfPaginationReached = true.
Q3: 3. Why is cachedIn(viewModelScope) necessary?
Basic⌄
Without cachedIn, each new collector of the Flow starts fresh — meaning every screen rotation restarts paging from page 1. cachedIn stores the latest PagingData in the ViewModel's scope. New collectors (after rotation or recomposition) immediately receive the cached PagingData — the user stays on their position in the list. It's the equivalent of calling cachedIn that creates an ActiveFlow that survives config changes.

System Design: Offline-First Product Catalog

Tier 1 Mod 30
Key Concept: Design an Android product catalog with offline browsing, search, pagination, and background sync — a complete senior-level system design answer covering architecture, data flow, trade-offs, and failure handling.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Architecture Stack

Compose → ViewModel
→ UseCase → Repository
→ RemoteMediator + Room
→ Retrofit (API)

Offline Strategy

Single source of truth = Room
Stale-while-revalidate
RemoteMediator writes Room
Room PagingSource reads UI

Sync

WorkManager periodic (6h)
Constraints: connected + battery
NetworkConnectivityObserver
  → triggers refresh on reconnect

Failure Modes

Network fail → serve cache
API 5xx → retry button
Stale → show last_sync_at
Reconnect → auto-refresh
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Scalability & Failure Handling

Scaling to Larger Catalogs

  • Storage pruning: Don't store entire 10K catalog on device. Store last N pages viewed (keep 100 most recent items, prune on sync). Use Room entity with last_accessed timestamp.
  • Partial sync: API supports ?updated_after=timestamp — sync only changed products, not full catalog
  • Category-based prefetch: Pre-sync only the category the user most recently viewed
  • Image caching: Coil's disk cache handles product images; set max disk cache size per available storage

Multi-Module Architecture

:feature:catalog  → CatalogScreen, CatalogViewModel
:feature:search   → SearchScreen, SearchViewModel
:core:product     → ProductRepository, ProductApi, ProductDao, RemoteMediator
:core:database    → Room setup, AppDatabase
:core:network     → Retrofit, OkHttp, interceptors
:core:sync        → CatalogSyncWorker, NetworkConnectivityObserver

Testing Strategy

  • Unit tests: ProductRepository with FakeProductApi + in-memory Room
  • PagingSource tests: TestPagingDataDiffer to collect paginated items
  • RemoteMediator tests: Mock API responses, verify Room state after each LoadType
  • E2E tests: Maestro or Espresso for offline catalog browsing flow
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What does "single source of truth" mean in offline-first architecture?
Basic⌄
Room (local database) is the only source the UI reads from. The network is a supplier of data INTO Room, not a direct source for the UI. This ensures: (a) offline works — Room always has data, (b) UI is consistent — no race between network response and cache, (c) reactivity — Room's LiveData/Flow notifies UI when data changes from any source. Network data → Room → UI (always via Room).
Q2: 2. How does RemoteMediator know which page to load next after app restart?
Basic⌄
RemoteKeys table in Room stores the last fetched page key (cursor or offset). On APPEND, RemoteMediator reads the last key from RemoteKeysDao.getLastKey() to determine which page to fetch next. On REFRESH, it clears the RemoteKeys table along with the product data. Without this table, after app restart APPEND would have no idea where pagination left off and would restart from page 1.
Q3: 3. What is the stale-while-revalidate pattern?
Basic⌄
Show cached (potentially stale) data immediately to the user, then fetch fresh data in the background and update the UI when it arrives. Users see content instantly — no empty screen. The catalog may be hours old on first render, but updates within seconds as the background fetch completes. This is the best pattern for catalogs: it optimizes perceived performance while ensuring data freshness.

6. Scalability

Session Expiry Detection

// Expose session expiry as a Flow from AuthRepository

🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. Where should you store JWT tokens on Android?
Basic⌄
EncryptedSharedPreferences backed by Android Keystore. It uses AES-256-GCM encryption with the key stored in the hardware-backed Keystore — the key cannot be extracted from the device. Never use plain SharedPreferences (plaintext on rooted devices), DataStore (not designed for tokens), or external storage. For extra security: keep access token in memory only (wiped on process kill) and only persist refresh token in EncryptedSharedPreferences.
Q2: 2. How does OkHttp Authenticator differ from an Interceptor for token refresh?
Basic⌄
Interceptor runs before every request — you'd need to check token expiry time and refresh proactively. This can miss edge cases (clock skew, server-side revocation). Authenticator is triggered reactively by the server's 401 response — always accurate. OkHttp calls authenticate() exactly when authentication is needed, passes the failed response, and returns a new Request with updated credentials. Much cleaner and accurate than timestamp-based proactive refresh.
Q3: 3. What is the "concurrent token refresh" problem and how do you solve it?
Basic⌄
Problem: 5 simultaneous API calls all get 401. All 5 call refreshToken() concurrently. Server issues 5 tokens — but each refresh token can only be used once (server rotates them). 4 of the 5 refresh attempts fail → user force-logged-out. Solution: Mutex in the Authenticator. Only one thread refreshes at a time. Threads 2-5 wait for the Mutex. When they get the lock, they check: is the current stored token different from what was in our failed request? If yes, another thread already refreshed — just retry with the new token without calling refresh again.

System Design: Shopping Cart

Key Concept: Design an Android shopping cart: local Room persistence, server sync, optimistic updates, guest-to-auth migration, conflict resolution, promo codes, and order placement flow.

Optimistic Update

1. Write Room (PENDING)
2. UI updates instantly
3. WorkManager syncs
4. SYNCED on success
5. FAILED → retry banner

Guest Migration

guest items in Room (userId=guest)

Save merged cart

→ safe to retry

⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Scalability

Real-time Cart Updates

For cross-device sync (phone + web): use WebSocket or Server-Sent Events to push cart changes. CartViewModel subscribes to websocket flow; when server emits a cart update event, merge with local Room data (server wins for conflicts).

// WebSocket cart update handler
webSocketFlow
    .filterIsInstance<CartUpdatedEvent>()
    .onEach { event ->
        // Server data overrides local for server-authoritative fields
        cartDao.merge(event.items)
    }
    .launchIn(viewModelScope)

Item Quantity Limits

// Validate client-side AND server-side
fun onUpdateQty(productId: String, newQty: Int) {
    if (newQty > MAX_QUANTITY_PER_ITEM) {
        _uiState.update { it.copy(error = "Max $MAX_QUANTITY_PER_ITEM per item") }
        return
    }
    if (newQty <= 0) { onRemoveItem(productId); return }
    quantityUpdateFlow.tryEmit(productId to newQty)
}
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: 1. What are optimistic updates and why use them for a cart?
Basic⌄
Optimistic updates means updating the local UI immediately (as if the server accepted the change) and then syncing in the background. For a cart: user taps "+1" → quantity shows 3 instantly → network sync happens asynchronously. This feels snappy and responsive. If sync fails, show an error and optionally roll back. Contrast with pessimistic updates: wait for server confirmation before updating UI — laggy, especially on poor connections.
Q2: 2. How do you migrate a guest cart to an authenticated cart?
Basic⌄
Store guest cart in Room with userId="guest". On successful login: read all guest items from Room, call POST /cart/guest-merge with items + auth token. Server applies merge strategy: sum quantities for duplicate products (product in both guest + existing auth cart), keep auth-only items, keep guest-only items. Response: merged cart. Client: clear guest items in Room, save merged cart as authenticated user's cart. Show "Your cart has been merged" notification.
Q3: 3. What is an idempotency key and why is it critical for order placement?
Basic⌄
An idempotency key is a unique identifier (UUID) that the client generates before placing an order and includes in the request header (X-Idempotency-Key). If the same key is sent twice, the server returns the existing response instead of creating a duplicate. This handles the "network dropped after server processed but before client received response" scenario — client retries, server detects duplicate key → returns existing order → no double charge. Generate the UUID when the user confirms the order, not on button tap (to survive navigation).

WebSocket Lifecycle

→ onMessageReceived()

Push Notifications for Background Messages

// When app is in background: WebSocket is closed
// Server sends FCM data message (not notification message)
// App's FirebaseMessagingService.onMessageReceived() handles it:
override fun onMessageReceived(message: RemoteMessage) {
    val chatMessage = parseChatMessage(message.data)
    // Save to Room
    CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch {
        messageDao.insert(chatMessage.toEntity())
    }
    // Show notification
