⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Never Put Sensitive Code in AI Context

// ❌ BAD — never prompt AI with real secrets in context
// "Here is my API key: sk-proj-abc123 — generate an auth interceptor"

// ✅ GOOD — use placeholder names, inject real values via BuildConfig/secrets.properties
// "Generate an auth interceptor that reads API_KEY from BuildConfig"

AI chat history may be logged, used for model training (on non-enterprise plans), or exposed via browser history. Treat your AI context like a public Slack channel.

Verify Generated APIs Against Current SDK

// ❌ AI hallucination — this API does not exist in Compose 1.5
// LazyColumn(modifier = Modifier.scrollToTop()) // hallucinated modifier

// ✅ Always check: Compose release notes, Android developer docs, actual import resolution
// If Android Studio can't resolve the import — the API doesn't exist

AI models have a training cutoff. New Compose APIs, updated Hilt versions, and Kotlin 2.x features may be unknown to the model or confused with older API signatures.

Use .cursorrules / Custom Instructions Aggressively

// Without .cursorrules — AI may generate LiveData, Mockito, Java, or mix patterns:
// val userName: LiveData<String> = MutableLiveData()

// With .cursorrules specifying StateFlow — consistent output every time:
// val userName: StateFlow<String> = _userName.asStateFlow()

AI Test Coverage Is Shallow — Add Edge Cases Manually

  • AI generates happy-path tests: success state, one failure case
  • Always add manually: empty results, loading state emission, concurrent calls, null inputs, pagination boundaries, coroutine cancellation behaviour
  • Use AI test output as a scaffold, not a complete test suite

Keep Related Files Open (Copilot Context)

Copilot's context window includes open editor tabs. Keep the UseCase, Repository interface, and domain model open when generating a ViewModel — the AI uses these to produce accurate injection signatures and state types.

Review Multi-File Refactors Change by Change

⚠ Cursor Composer Warning
Multi-file AI edits can silently change behaviour in files you weren't focused on. Always use the diff review UI — accept file by file, not "accept all". Pay special attention to: deleted imports, changed function signatures, replaced error handling blocks.

Privacy: Corporate Code and Cloud AI

  • Check your company's AI usage policy before using Copilot Individual, Cursor Free, or Codeium on corporate repos
  • Enterprise plans (Copilot Enterprise, Cursor Business) guarantee code is not used for training
  • For air-gapped environments: Tabnine Self-Hosted or local LLMs (Ollama + CodeLlama) are the options

Production Best Practices

  1. Commit a .cursorrules / custom instructions file to every project repo
  2. Write precise prompts: name types, interfaces, architecture layers explicitly
  3. Always verify generated imports compile and the APIs exist in your current dependency versions
  4. Never use AI for cryptography, auth token handling, or secret management code
  5. Treat AI test output as a scaffold — complete edge cases manually before merging
  6. Review every file in a Composer multi-file edit individually
  7. Check enterprise data handling agreements before enabling cloud AI tools on corporate code
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is GitHub Copilot and how does it integrate with Android Studio?
GitHub Copilot is an AI pair programmer that provides inline code completions and a chat interface. It integrates with Android Studio via the JetBrains Marketplace plugin. Under the hood, it uses the Language Server Protocol (LSP) to send the current file context (cursor position, open tabs) to the AI model and streams completions back as ghost text. You accept with Tab, reject with Esc. Copilot Chat adds a Q&A panel for explaining code, generating tests, and asking questions grounded in your open files.
B2 — What is a .cursorrules file and why should you commit it to git?
Easy▼
.cursorrules is a plain-text instruction file placed at the project root that Cursor reads before every AI interaction. It lets you define project-specific rules: tech stack (Kotlin only, Hilt for DI, StateFlow not LiveData), architecture constraints (inject UseCases not Repositories), and testing conventions (MockK not Mockito). Committing it to git means every developer on the team benefits from the same AI behavior — generated code is consistent with project conventions without manual correction. Think of it as a prompt prefix that runs on every AI call.
B3 — What is Gemini Code Assist in Android Studio? How do you enable it?
Easy▼
Gemini Code Assist is Google's first-party AI coding assistant integrated into Android Studio. It provides inline Kotlin/Compose completions, context actions ("Explain this code", "Fix this bug"), unit test generation, and commit message generation from staged diffs. Enable it via Settings > Plugins > search "Gemini" (or it may be built-in in AS Ladybug+). Sign in with a Google account. It includes a free tier and is natively aware of Android APIs and Compose semantics.

Intermediate

I1 — What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)? How does it relate to Android development?
Medium▼
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol originally introduced by Anthropic that standardizes how AI models connect to external tools and data sources. Instead of giving an AI model only the text in your editor, MCP lets it interact with: the local filesystem, APIs, databases, build systems, and more — as structured, queryable context.

In Android development: Android Studio's AI agent feature supports MCP servers. You can configure an MCP server to expose your Gradle build files, run test tasks, read Logcat output, or query an internal component library. This enables AI agents to perform real actions — not just generate text — grounded in your actual project state.
I2 — Why is AI-generated test coverage often insufficient? What do you always add manually?
Medium▼
AI models generate tests by pattern-matching common test structures from their training data. This means they reliably produce happy-path tests (success state, one basic failure) but consistently miss:
• Empty/null results — what does the ViewModel do with an empty product list?
• Loading state assertion — does Loading emit before the success?
• Pagination boundaries — what happens on page 0 vs. last page?
• Concurrent calls — what if loadProducts() is called twice rapidly?
• Coroutine cancellation — is the job cancelled cleanly on ViewModel clear?

Always treat AI test output as a scaffold — it saves writing the boilerplate, but the edge cases are your responsibility.
I3 — How does Cursor Composer differ from standard Copilot completions?
Medium▼
Standard Copilot completions are single-location: they complete code at the cursor position in the current file. They're great for boilerplate but can't reason across multiple files simultaneously.

Cursor Composer is a multi-file edit mode: you describe a change in natural language, and Composer applies diffs across as many files as needed — creating new files, modifying existing ones, and updating imports/references. It also has codebase indexing, so it can find the relevant files itself rather than requiring you to have them open. The trade-off: the output requires careful per-file diff review before accepting, as changes in files you weren't focused on can introduce subtle bugs.
I4 — Write a good .cursorrules file for a Jetpack Compose Android project following Clean Architecture.
MediumCoding▼
You are a Senior Android Engineer working on a Jetpack Compose app.

Architecture:
- Clean Architecture: Presentation / Domain / Data layers
- Presentation: ViewModels, Composables, UiState sealed classes
- Domain: UseCases, Repository interfaces, domain Models
- Data: Repository implementations, DTOs, mappers, Room DAOs, Retrofit services

Always use:
- Kotlin only (never Java)
- Hilt for dependency injection
- StateFlow<UiState> in ViewModels (never LiveData)
- viewModelScope for coroutine launches
- Result<T> for error propagation
- Jetpack Compose for all UI (no XML layouts)

Rules:
- ViewModels inject UseCases, never Repositories directly
- Repository implementations are in the Data layer only
- Domain models are separate from DTOs (mappers in Data layer)
- Tests use MockK, never Mockito
- UI tests use Compose testing APIs

When generating tests:
- Happy path + at least one error case
- Note which edge cases I should add manually

Senior / Scenario

S1 — An AI-generated Cursor Composer refactor introduced a memory leak in a Fragment. How do you find and fix it?
HardScenario▼
Common AI-introduced memory leak patterns in Fragments:
1. View binding held beyond onDestroyView — AI often generates private val binding: FragmentXBinding as a field without nulling it in onDestroyView()
2. Listener / callback registered but not removed — AI adds a click listener or observer in onViewCreated without corresponding removal
3. Wrong coroutine scope — using viewModelScope or lifecycleScope incorrectly — e.g., launching in a scope that outlives the Fragment view

How to find it:
• Run the app → navigate away from the Fragment → trigger GC in Android Studio's Memory Profiler
• If the Fragment instance is still in the heap after GC, it's leaked
• Use LeakCanary — it will report the exact reference chain

Fix (binding example): 
// ✅ Correct pattern — null binding in onDestroyView
private var _binding: FragmentProductBinding? = null
private val binding get() = _binding!!

override fun onDestroyView() {
    super.onDestroyView()
    _binding = null  // releases reference before Fragment is destroyed
}
Prevention: Add to .cursorrules: "When generating Fragments with ViewBinding, always null _binding in onDestroyView."
S2 — A colleague says "AI wrote all our tests so we have 90% coverage — we're good to ship." What's wrong with this reasoning?
Hard▼
Three problems with this reasoning:

1. Coverage ≠ correctness: 90% line coverage says every line was executed at least once. It says nothing about whether the assertions are meaningful or whether edge cases were tested. AI-generated tests often call methods without asserting meaningful outcomes — covering lines while testing nothing real.

2. AI systematically misses edge cases: Empty results, null inputs, network timeout paths, concurrent mutations, pagination boundaries, configuration changes — these require domain knowledge of what can go wrong. AI models pattern-match on "normal" test shapes and rarely imagine the failure modes that actually occur in production.

3. False confidence is worse than no confidence: Believing you have solid test coverage when you don't means you skip manual QA and exploratory testing — the very processes that would catch what the AI missed.

The right position: AI test output is a scaffold for boilerplate. Senior engineers own the edge case coverage and are accountable for the test quality — not the AI.
S3 — How do you use AI tools safely in a financial services Android app with strict data handling requirements?
HardScenario▼
Framework for safe AI usage in regulated environments:

1. Choose enterprise-grade tools with data contracts: GitHub Copilot Enterprise, Cursor Business, or Gemini Code Assist Enterprise all provide written guarantees that code is not used for model training and include IP indemnification. Verify the contract applies to your jurisdiction and data classification.

2. Hard exclusions in .cursorrules: Explicitly instruct the AI to never generate code handling API keys, auth tokens, PII, or cryptographic operations — route those prompts to manual implementation.

3. Never include real data in context: Use placeholder types and anonymised schemas in prompts. No production database schemas, no real endpoint URLs, no sample data with PII.

4. For highest-security code paths: Use Tabnine Self-Hosted or a local LLM (Ollama + CodeLlama) — no code leaves the corporate network. Accept the quality trade-off for the security requirement.

5. Mandatory human review of AI output in security-sensitive areas: Auth flows, encryption wrappers, certificate pinning config — require two senior engineers to review, regardless of AI involvement.

Jetpack Compose Animation

Tier 1 Mod 37
Key Concept: Complete guide to Compose animation APIs: animateAsState, updateTransition, AnimatedVisibility, AnimatedContent, rememberInfiniteTransition, and Motion.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

HIGH-LEVEL APIS

AnimatedVisibility(visible) { ... }
AnimatedContent(targetState) { ... }
Modifier.animateContentSize()
Crossfade(targetState) { ... }

LOW-LEVEL VALUE APIS

animateFloatAsState(target, label = "")
animateDpAsState(target, label = "")
animateColorAsState(target, label = "")
val t = updateTransition(targetState)
val anim = remember { Animatable(0f) }

ANIMATION SPECS

spring(dampingRatio, stiffness) // physics
tween(durationMillis, easing)   // time
keyframes { 0f at 0; 1f at 150 }
infiniteRepeatable(animation, RepeatMode)
snap(delayMillis)

INFINITE LOOPS

val inf = rememberInfiniteTransition(label)
val x by inf.animateFloat(
    initialValue = 0f, targetValue = 1f,
    animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable(
        tween(1000), RepeatMode.Reverse
    ), label = "loop"
)

PERFORMANCE RULE

// Prefer draw/graphicsLayer lambda:
Modifier.graphicsLayer {
    alpha = animatedAlpha
    translationX = animatedX.toPx()
} // Skips Recomposition!

ACCESSIBILITY & TOOLING

// 1. Always supply label = "name"
// 2. Fall back to snap() on reduceMotion:
val spec = if (reduceMotion) snap()
           else spring()

API Decision Tree

Is it adding/removing Composable from tree? ├── YES → AnimatedVisibility └── NO → Switching between different Composable screens/views? ├── YES → AnimatedContent / Crossfade └── NO → Container changing size automatically? ├── YES → Modifier.animateContentSize() └── NO → Value animation: ├── Single value? → animate*AsState ├── Multiple synchronized values? → updateTransition ├── Continuous endless loop? → rememberInfiniteTransition └── Gesture / Coroutine Imperative? → Animatable
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

1. Omitting the label Parameter

// ❌ BAD — Anonymous animation; impossible to inspect in Android Studio Animation Preview
val alpha by animateFloatAsState(targetValue = if (visible) 1f else 0f)
// ✅ GOOD — Clearly labeled for tooling, layout inspector, and debugging
val alpha by animateFloatAsState(
    targetValue = if (visible) 1f else 0f,
    label = "header_fade_alpha"
)

2. Unnecessary High-Frequency Tree Recomposition

// ❌ BAD — Animating offset directly causes entire outer container to recompose each frame
val offset by animateDpAsState(targetValue = targetOffset, label = "offset")
HeavyCardContainer(modifier = Modifier.offset(y = offset))
// ✅ GOOD — Lambda-based graphicsLayer / offset bypasses recomposition and goes straight to draw/layout phase
val offset by animateDpAsState(targetValue = targetOffset, label = "offset")
HeavyCardContainer(modifier = Modifier.graphicsLayer { translationY = offset.toPx() })

3. Using rememberInfiniteTransition for One-Shot Animations

// ❌ BAD — rememberInfiniteTransition keeps burning frame ticks indefinitely
val anim = rememberInfiniteTransition() // Used to trigger a single bounce
// ✅ GOOD — Use Animatable or LaunchedEffect for one-shot events
val scale = remember { Animatable(1f) }
LaunchedEffect(trigger) {
    scale.animateTo(1.2f, spring())
    scale.animateTo(1.0f, spring())
}

4. AnimatedVisibility Inside LazyColumn Items Without Keys

// ❌ BAD — Reordering or item removal confuses animation state mapping
LazyColumn {
    items(itemList) { item ->
        AnimatedVisibility(visible = item.isVisible) { ... }
    }
}
// ✅ GOOD — Explicit stable key maintains item animation identity
LazyColumn {
    items(items = itemList, key = { it.id }) { item ->
        AnimatedVisibility(visible = item.isVisible) { ... }
    }
}

5. Ignoring System Accessibility Motion Settings

// ❌ BAD — Forces large disorienting animations on motion-sensitive users
val slideOffset by animateDpAsState(targetValue = 500.dp, label = "slide")
// ✅ GOOD — Check reduceMotion and swap physics springs for instant snaps or gentle fades
val spec = if (isReduceMotionEnabled) snap() else spring()
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — How does Compose animation differ from the traditional View animation system?
Traditional View animations use imperative animators (ObjectAnimator, ValueAnimator) or static XML files that mutate view properties directly, requiring manual lifecycle listener management. Compose animation is declarative and state-driven: UI is a function of state, and animations simply interpolate intermediate values when target state changes. They are coroutine-safe, automatically cancel upon composable disposal, and handle interrupts gracefully.
B2 — What is the purpose of animateFloatAsState and its sister APIs?
Easy▼
animate*AsState functions are low-level fire-and-forget APIs for animating a single value (Float, Dp, Color, Offset, Size, Int). When the provided targetValue changes, Compose automatically starts an animation toward the new target and returns a State<T> that updates continuously throughout the animation.
B3 — What is the difference between AnimatedVisibility and Crossfade?
Easy▼
AnimatedVisibility animates the entry and exit of a single composable (expanding, sliding, fading in/out) as a boolean visibility state changes. Crossfade transitions between two or more distinct pieces of content based on a state key using a smooth opacity fade.

Intermediate

I1 — When would you use updateTransition instead of multiple animate*AsState calls?
Medium▼
Use updateTransition when two or more animated properties (e.g., width, color, elevation, scale) are driven by the same state change and must remain strictly synchronized. Separate animate*AsState calls execute independent animations that can desynchronize or suffer from race conditions when interrupted. updateTransition also enables Android Studio Animation Inspector tooling and allows creating nested child transitions.
I2 — Compare spring() vs tween() AnimationSpec. When should each be chosen?
Medium▼
spring(dampingRatio, stiffness): Physics-based simulation. Has no fixed duration; preserves velocity when interrupted mid-flight, making UI feel natural and responsive. Preferred for touch and user interaction responses.

tween(durationMillis, delay, easing): Time-based animation with a fixed duration and easing curve. Best for pure time-based transitions like opacity crossfades, content reveals, or timed splash transitions.
I3 — Why is it critical to provide the label parameter in Compose animation functions?
Medium▼
The label parameter assigns a human-readable identifier to the animation. This identifier surfaces in Android Studio's Animation Preview and Layout Inspector, allowing developers to inspect curves, pause, scrub, and debug multi-state transitions frame by frame. Without labels, tooling displays generic names that make debugging complex transitions difficult.
I4 — Coding: Implement a pulsing notification badge using rememberInfiniteTransition.
MediumCoding▼
@Composable
fun PulsingBadge(modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    val infiniteTransition = rememberInfiniteTransition(label = "badge_pulse_transition")

    val scale by infiniteTransition.animateFloat(
        initialValue = 1.0f,
        targetValue = 1.4f,
        animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable(
            animation = tween(durationMillis = 800, easing = FastOutSlowInEasing),
            repeatMode = RepeatMode.Reverse
        ),
        label = "badge_scale"
    )

    val alpha by infiniteTransition.animateFloat(
        initialValue = 1.0f,
        targetValue = 0.3f,
        animationSpec = infiniteRepeatable(
            animation = tween(durationMillis = 800, easing = FastOutSlowInEasing),
            repeatMode = RepeatMode.Reverse
        ),
        label = "badge_alpha"
    )

    Box(
        modifier = modifier
            .graphicsLayer {
                scaleX = scale
                scaleY = scale
                this.alpha = alpha
            }
            .size(12.dp)
            .background(Color.Red, shape = CircleShape)
    )
}

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Debug Scenario: A list of animated cards experiences severe frame drops and jank during scrolling. How do you diagnose and fix it?
HardScenario▼
Diagnosis:
1. Recomposition Phase Overload: Animated state values (like animated float or Dp) are being read in the composable's body during the Recomposition phase, triggering full subtree recomposition on every single frame tick (60–120 fps).
2. Missing LazyColumn Keys: List items lack stable keys, forcing Compose to recreate animation state as items recycle.

Fixes:
• Defer state reads to the Draw/Layout phase by using lambda modifiers such as Modifier.graphicsLayer { translationY = animatedY } or Modifier.offset { IntOffset(0, animatedY.toInt()) } instead of Modifier.offset(y = animatedY.dp).
• Provide unique, stable keys in items(list, key = { it.id }).
• Use derivedStateOf to clamp animation thresholds and prevent excessive state notifications.
S2 — How would you build a gesture-driven swipe-to-dismiss card that tracks user finger drags in real time and snaps back or flings away on release?
HardScenario▼
Use Animatable(0f) inside a coroutine scope:
1. On Drag: In pointerInput with detectHorizontalDragGestures, call offsetX.snapTo(offsetX.value + dragAmount) to instantly track touch movement without animation lag.
2. On Drag End / Release: Evaluate swipe velocity and distance against a threshold.
3. If threshold is passed, call offsetX.animateTo(targetValue = screenWidth, initialVelocity = flingVelocity) to fling off-screen and trigger item dismissal.
4. If below threshold, call offsetX.animateTo(targetValue = 0f, animationSpec = spring()) to snap back smoothly with physics damping.
S3 — How do you support the Android OS "Reduce Motion" accessibility setting across an entire Compose app design system?
Hard▼
Create a custom CompositionLocal (e.g. LocalReduceMotion) that observes system accessibility settings (via Settings.Global.TRANSITION_ANIMATION_SCALE or window manager settings). In your design system's motion tokens or animation specs, wrap transitions to check LocalReduceMotion.current: 
@Composable
fun <T> adaptiveSpring(): AnimationSpec<T> {
    val reduceMotion = LocalReduceMotion.current
    return if (reduceMotion) snap() else spring()
}
This cleanly replaces complex bouncing scale/slide transitions with instant snaps or subtle opacity crossfades without modifying individual feature composables.
38A

Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP/KMM)

Tier 2 Mod 38
Key Concept: Sharing Kotlin code across Android, iOS, Web, and Desktop using expect/actual, shared modules, and platform-specific implementations.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

EXPECT / ACTUAL SYNTAX

// commonMain
expect class PlatformDate() {
  fun now(): String
}

// androidMain
actual class PlatformDate actual constructor() {
  actual fun now() =
    SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd")
      .format(Date())
}

// iosMain
actual class PlatformDate actual constructor() {
  actual fun now(): String {
    val formatter = NSDateFormatter()
    formatter.dateFormat = "yyyy-MM-dd"
    return formatter.stringFromDate(NSDate())
  }
}

SOURCE SETS

commonMain   → all platforms
androidMain  → Android specifics
iosMain      → iOS specifics
commonTest   → shared unit tests
androidTest  → Android instrumented
iosTest      → iOS native tests

KEY MULTIPLATFORM LIBRARIES

Networking  → Ktor (not Retrofit)
Database    → SQLDelight (not Room)
DI          → Koin (not Hilt)
Coroutines  → kotlinx.coroutines-core
Serialization → kotlinx.serialization
DateTime    → kotlinx.datetime

BUILD.GRADLE.KTS SNIPPET

kotlin("multiplatform")

kotlin {
  androidTarget()
  iosX64()
  iosArm64()
  iosSimulatorArm64()

  sourceSets {
    val commonMain by getting { ... }
    val androidMain by getting { ... }
    val iosMain by creating {
      dependsOn(commonMain) }
  }
}

Quick Reference Table

ConceptAndroid EquivalentKMP Equivalent
NetworkingRetrofit + OkHttpKtor (multiplatform)
DatabaseRoomSQLDelight
DIHiltKoin or manual
Platform codeAlways Androidexpect/actual per target
iOS outputN/A.xcframework
Swift interopN/AKotlin suspend → Swift async
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

iOS Binary Size Increase

Kotlin/Native includes the Kotlin runtime in the generated .xcframework, increasing binary size by 2–5 MB. Mitigate with:

  • Use isStatic = true (static framework) to allow Xcode linker to dead-strip unused code
  • Enable linkerOpts("-dead_strip") in release builds
  • Measure with xcrun bitcode_strip and monitor size in CI

Coroutine Threading on iOS (Legacy Issue)

⚠ Known Pitfall
In older Kotlin/Native (pre-1.6), objects passed between threads had to be frozen (immutable), which broke standard coroutine patterns. Since Kotlin 1.6+ with the new memory model (kotlin.native.binary.memoryModel=experimental / default since 1.7.20), this is resolved. If you see InvalidMutabilityException or FreezingException, upgrade Kotlin and enable the new memory model. 
// gradle.properties — new memory model (required pre-1.7.20)
kotlin.native.binary.memoryModel=experimental

expect/actual Boilerplate

Every platform-specific class needs an expect declaration plus actual implementations for every target. With many targets (Android, iOS, Web, Desktop), this multiplies quickly. Strategies:

  • Minimise expect/actual surface: push platform code to the edges, share as much as possible
  • Use interfaces in commonMain + factory pattern rather than expect/actual classes
  • Use expect fun for simple utilities rather than whole classes

SQLDelight is More Complex than Room

SQLDelight uses SQL schema files (.sq) and generates typed Kotlin queries — more explicit than Room annotations. Setup gotchas:

  • Driver must be provided per-platform via expect/actual or DI — not automatic
  • Migrations must be written in SQL, not Kotlin DSL like Room
  • Debugging SQL is done via the generated code, not Room's easy @Database inspector

Ktor Requires More Configuration than Retrofit

// commonMain — Ktor client (more verbose than Retrofit)
val client = HttpClient {
    install(ContentNegotiation) {
        json(Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true })
    }
    install(HttpTimeout) {
        requestTimeoutMillis = 30_000
    }
    install(Logging) {
        level = LogLevel.ALL
    }
}

// vs Retrofit — @GET, @POST annotations generate everything
// Ktor: manual request building, explicit endpoint calls

Memory Management — Kotlin/Native GC

Kotlin/Native uses a different garbage collector than JVM. With the new memory model (Kotlin 1.7.20+), it is a tracing GC that runs concurrently. Key differences:

  • No generational GC — full heap traversal; can pause on large heaps
  • Cycle detection is not automatic in all cases with the new MM; avoid reference cycles in long-lived objects
  • Finalizers behave differently — do not rely on finalize() for cleanup; use explicit resource management

Best Practices

  1. Keep commonMain pure — no platform imports, no Android/iOS-specific APIs
  2. Use interfaces in commonMain, expect/actual only for primitives (date, UUID, dispatcher)
  3. Use Dispatchers.Default in shared code — not Dispatchers.Main (platform-specific)
  4. Test commonMain with kotlin.test — runs on both JVM and native
  5. Wrap coroutine scopes for iOS consumption (KMP-NativeCoroutines or SKIE library helps)
  6. Measure iOS binary size in CI — set a size budget and fail builds that exceed it
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is the difference between KMP and KMM?
KMP (Kotlin Multiplatform) is the broad technology for sharing Kotlin code across Android, iOS, Web, and Desktop targets. KMM (Kotlin Multiplatform Mobile) was the name for the mobile-focused subset (Android + iOS only), which JetBrains has since merged back under the KMP umbrella. In 2023, JetBrains officially stabilised KMP and retired the KMM branding — they are now the same thing. When interviewers say KMM they mean KMP targeting Android and iOS.
B2 — What is the purpose of the expect / actual mechanism?
Easy▼
expect declares a contract in commonMain — a class or function that the compiler knows must exist on every platform, but whose implementation differs. Each platform source set (androidMain, iosMain) provides an actual implementation. The compiler enforces that every declared expect has a matching actual on every declared target — if one is missing, it is a compile error. This allows commonMain to call platform-specific APIs (logging, date, UUID) without knowing the platform.
B3 — What is shared in a KMP project? What is NOT shared?
Easy▼
Shared (commonMain): domain models, use cases, repositories, networking (Ktor), database access (SQLDelight), coroutines, Flow, serialization, business logic, validation rules.

NOT shared: UI (Compose is Android-only; iOS uses SwiftUI), dependency injection (Hilt is Android-only), platform-specific APIs (camera, GPS, biometrics), navigation, platform lifecycle management. These stay native and either have an expect/actual abstraction or live entirely in the platform-specific app.

Intermediate

I1 — Why is Ktor used instead of Retrofit in KMP? Why is SQLDelight used instead of Room?
Medium▼
Ktor vs Retrofit: Retrofit is built on OkHttp which is JVM/Android-only. Ktor is multiplatform by design — it uses OkHttp as its engine on Android and NSURLSession (Darwin engine) on iOS. Since commonMain must compile to both JVM and Kotlin/Native, only Ktor works there. Retrofit would fail to compile on iOS targets.

SQLDelight vs Room: Room uses annotation processing and Android-only SQLite APIs. SQLDelight is multiplatform — it generates platform-typed Kotlin code from SQL schema files, and uses platform-appropriate drivers: AndroidSqliteDriver on Android and NativeSqliteDriver on iOS. Room would fail on Kotlin/Native targets.
I2 — How does an iOS app consume a KMP shared module? How do Kotlin coroutines work from Swift?
Medium▼
KMP generates an .xcframework (or .framework) from the shared module during the Gradle build. The iOS team adds this framework to the Xcode project either directly or via CocoaPods/SPM. Kotlin classes and functions are exposed to Swift as Objective-C interop — Kotlin data classes become Swift structs/classes, Kotlin interfaces become Swift protocols.

Kotlin suspend functions are not directly callable from Swift (which has no concept of Kotlin coroutines). The recommended solutions:
• KMP-NativeCoroutines library: generates Swift async/await wrappers automatically
• SKIE (Swift Kotlin Interface Enhancer) by Touchlab: produces idiomatic Swift API
• Manual: wrap suspend functions in a CoroutineScope with a callback/completion handler

With modern libraries, suspend fun getUser(): User becomes async func getUser() async throws -> User in Swift.
I3 — What is the new Kotlin/Native memory model and why does it matter for KMP?
Medium▼
Before Kotlin 1.6, Kotlin/Native used a "frozen" memory model — objects passed between threads had to be explicitly frozen (made immutable), and mutable state was not allowed to be shared across threads. This broke coroutine patterns that rely on shared mutable state between withContext switches and was a major source of InvalidMutabilityException and FreezingException crashes on iOS.

Since Kotlin 1.7.20, the new memory model is the default. It uses a concurrent tracing garbage collector and allows mutable state to be shared across threads (same as JVM semantics). This makes standard coroutine patterns, StateFlow, and mutable ViewModel-like classes work correctly on iOS. Migration: ensure Kotlin 1.7.20+ and remove any .freeze() calls from your shared code.
I4 — [Coding] Write an expect / actual for getting the current platform's date as a formatted string (yyyy-MM-dd). Provide commonMain, androidMain, and iosMain.
MediumCoding▼
// commonMain/PlatformDate.kt
expect fun currentDateString(): String

// androidMain/PlatformDate.kt
import java.text.SimpleDateFormat
import java.util.Date
import java.util.Locale

actual fun currentDateString(): String =
    SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd", Locale.getDefault()).format(Date())

// iosMain/PlatformDate.kt
import platform.Foundation.NSDate
import platform.Foundation.NSDateFormatter

actual fun currentDateString(): String {
    val formatter = NSDateFormatter()
    formatter.dateFormat = "yyyy-MM-dd"
    return formatter.stringFromDate(NSDate())
}
Note: in production you would prefer kotlinx.datetime library which is multiplatform and handles this in commonMain without expect/actual: Clock.System.now().toLocalDateTime(TimeZone.currentSystemDefault()).date.toString()

Senior / Scenario

S1 — [Scenario] An iOS engineer reports: app crashes with FreezingException: freezing of kotlin.coroutines.CancellableContinuation when calling a shared Flow from Swift. What is happening and how do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
What is happening: This is the old Kotlin/Native memory model issue. When code tries to pass a CancellableContinuation (internal coroutine state) across threads — which Kotlin/Native's old model requires to be frozen/immutable before crossing thread boundaries — the freeze operation fails because coroutine internals are mutable.

Root causes:
1. The project is using Kotlin < 1.7.20 (old memory model default)
2. Or: using old coroutines-native-mt version instead of standard coroutines

Fix:
1. Upgrade to Kotlin 1.7.20+ — new memory model is default, this exception class is gone
2. Use standard kotlinx.coroutines-core (not the deprecated -native-mt variant)
3. Use KMP-NativeCoroutines or SKIE to generate safe Swift wrappers
4. If temporarily stuck on older Kotlin: wrap the Flow collection in @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) and use flowOn(Dispatchers.Main) to ensure single-thread execution

Long-term: Standardise on Kotlin 1.9+ and the new memory model — the old model is removed.
S2 — A senior engineer wants to add KMP to an existing 3-year-old Android app that has a large Java legacy codebase. What is your advice? Is it worth it?
Hard▼
Honest assessment — it depends:

Arguments for: If the team needs to deliver an iOS app, KMP avoids rewriting the entire business logic. The shared layer can be extracted incrementally — start with domain models and repository interfaces, then migrate implementations one by one.

Arguments against:
1. Java interop with KMP is imperfect — Java classes can be used from commonMain only if they're pure JVM targets; Kotlin/Native can't use Java directly
2. Legacy Java code must be converted to Kotlin before moving to commonMain
3. Room, Retrofit, Hilt — all Android-only — must be replaced or abstracted
4. Significant iOS infrastructure investment (xcframework builds, iOS CI, Swift team)

Recommended approach if proceeding:
1. Audit what is truly shareable (pure domain + data logic) vs. Android-specific
2. Convert Java domain/data layer to Kotlin first
3. Extract shared module incrementally — start with domain models only
4. Replace Room with SQLDelight and Retrofit with Ktor one module at a time
5. Set a 6-month migration target with clear milestones

If there is no immediate iOS requirement: do not add KMP to a legacy Java app for its own sake — the migration cost exceeds the benefit.
S3 — How do you test shared KMP code? What test frameworks are available in commonMain?
Hard▼
kotlin.test is the multiplatform test framework — it provides @Test, assertEquals, assertTrue, assertFails. Tests in commonTest run on all platforms:
• ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest — runs on JVM (Android unit tests)
• ./gradlew iosX64Test — runs on Kotlin/Native (iOS simulator)

For coroutines testing: kotlinx.coroutines.test (TestScope, runTest) is multiplatform since coroutines 1.6.

For mocking: Mockito and MockK do not work on Kotlin/Native. Use either:
• Manual fakes/stubs (recommended for shared code)
• Mockative — a KMP-compatible mocking library using KSP

Best practice: Test use cases and repositories with fake data sources in commonTest. Platform-specific tests (database driver, HTTP engine) go in androidTest / iosTest. This keeps the most important business logic tested cross-platform.
39A

Android Accessibility

Tier 2 Mod 39
Key Concept: Building accessible Android apps: TalkBack, semantics in Compose, content descriptions, focus management, and WCAG compliance.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

SEMANTICS API CHEATSHEET

Modifier.semantics {
  contentDescription = "..."
  stateDescription = "Selected"
  role = Role.Button
  heading()
  liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite
  onClick("label") { ... }
}

Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants=true){}
Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics { ... }

CONTENT DESCRIPTION RULES

null         = decorative, skip
""           = avoid (ambiguous)
"Back"       = minimal (bad)
"Go back to account list" = good

Icon inside Button with Text:
  → Icon contentDesc = null ✅
  → Text provides the label

Icon-only Button:
  → MUST have contentDesc ✅

TOUCH TARGET RULES

Minimum: 48dp × 48dp

IconButton(
  modifier = Modifier
    .minimumInteractiveComponentSize()
) { Icon(...) }

// or explicit:
Modifier.size(48.dp)

Spacing between targets: ≥ 8dp

LIVE REGION MODES

LiveRegionMode.Polite
  → Announces after TalkBack
    finishes current speech
  → Use for: loading states,
    search results, success msg

LiveRegionMode.Assertive
  → Interrupts immediately
  → Use for: errors, warnings,
    critical status changes

TALKBACK GESTURES (TEST WITH)

Swipe right    → next element
Swipe left     → previous element
Double tap     → activate
2-finger swipe → scroll
2-finger tap   → pause reading
Volume up+down → accessibility menu
Swipe up+right → headings / links
              (custom navigation)

COLOUR CONTRAST MINIMUMS

Normal text:  4.5:1 ratio (AA)
Large text:   3.0:1 ratio (AA)
  (18px+ or 14px+ bold)
UI components: 3.0:1 ratio
Focus indicator: 3.0:1

Tools: Accessibility Scanner,
Android Studio colour picker,
contrast checker (Web)

Quick Reference: Compose vs View System

FeatureComposeView System
LabelModifier.semantics { contentDescription }android:contentDescription
Rolesemantics { role = Role.Button }Inferred from View type
Live regionsemantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite }ViewCompat.setAccessibilityLiveRegion()
Merge childrensemantics(mergeDescendants = true)importantForAccessibility="no" on children
Headingsemantics { heading() }ViewCompat.setAccessibilityHeading()
DecorativecontentDescription = nullimportantForAccessibility="no"
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Icon Buttons with Null contentDescription

// ❌ BAD — TalkBack reads "Button" — useless, cannot differentiate
IconButton(onClick = { navigateBack() }) {
    Icon(Icons.Default.ArrowBack, contentDescription = null)
}

// ✅ GOOD — TalkBack reads "Navigate back, Button"
IconButton(onClick = { navigateBack() }) {
    Icon(Icons.Default.ArrowBack, contentDescription = "Navigate back")
}

contentDescription = "" vs contentDescription = null

⚠ Critical Distinction
  • contentDescription = null on an Image → TalkBack announces nothing (correct for decorative images)
  • contentDescription = "" (empty string) → TalkBack may say "Image" or announce an empty label — ambiguous; avoid
  • contentDescription = null on an IconButton → TalkBack announces "Button" without a label — NOT accessible
  • Rule: null = decorative, skip entirely. Non-null = meaningful, read aloud.
// Decorative icon inside a button that already has text
Button(onClick = { submit() }) {
    Icon(Icons.Default.Send, contentDescription = null)  // ✅ decorative — button text provides label
    Text("Send")
}

// Icon-only button — MUST have contentDescription
IconButton(onClick = { deleteItem() }) {
    Icon(Icons.Default.Delete, contentDescription = "Delete item")  // ✅ required
}

Duplicate Announcements from mergeDescendants + explicit contentDescription

// ❌ BAD — TalkBack reads "John Smith" then also "John Smith profile, Button" = double reading
Card(
    modifier = Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {
        contentDescription = "John Smith profile, Button"
    }
) {
    Text("John Smith")   // this text will ALSO be merged in
}

// ✅ GOOD — use clearAndSetSemantics to fully control the announcement
Card(
    modifier = Modifier.clearAndSetSemantics {
        contentDescription = "John Smith profile"
        role = Role.Button
    }
) {
    Text("John Smith")   // invisible to TalkBack — clearAndSetSemantics takes over
}

Custom Touch Targets Below 48dp

// ❌ BAD — 24dp icon with no touch target expansion
Icon(
    imageVector = Icons.Default.MoreVert,
    contentDescription = "More options",
    modifier = Modifier.size(24.dp).clickable { showMenu() }
)

// ✅ GOOD — minimumInteractiveComponentSize() or size(48.dp)
IconButton(
    onClick = { showMenu() },
    modifier = Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize()
) {
    Icon(Icons.Default.MoreVert, contentDescription = "More options")
}

Do Not Override Focus Order Unless Necessary

Focus order should match visual reading order (top-left to bottom-right). Overriding it creates disorientation for TalkBack and Switch Access users. Only override focus order when the visual layout genuinely differs from the logical reading order (e.g., RTL layouts, custom dialogs).

Color Contrast & "Color Alone" Anti-pattern

// ❌ BAD — uses only color to distinguish transaction types
Text(
    text = transaction.description,
    color = if (transaction.type == TransactionType.CREDIT) Color.Green else Color.Red
)

// ✅ GOOD — color + explicit semantics + icon
Row(modifier = Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {}) {
    Icon(
        imageVector = if (isCredit) Icons.Default.Add else Icons.Default.Remove,
        contentDescription = if (isCredit) "Credit" else "Debit"
    )
    Text(
        text = transaction.description,
        color = if (isCredit) creditGreen else debitRed  // must be 4.5:1 contrast ratio
    )
}

Always Test with TalkBack On

Rule
Accessibility Scanner finds structural issues. TalkBack finds UX issues. You need both. Every new screen or component must be tested by a developer with TalkBack enabled using only swipe gestures — no looking at the screen while navigating. If you can't navigate to every interactive element and understand what it does, it is not accessible.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What is TalkBack and how does it access the UI content of an Android app?
TalkBack is Android's built-in screen reader — an AccessibilityService that reads UI elements aloud using text-to-speech for visually impaired users. It does not directly read pixels; instead, the Android framework exposes the UI as an AccessibilityNodeInfo tree — a hierarchical structure where each node represents an interactive or meaningful UI element with properties like contentDescription, role, state, and bounds. TalkBack subscribes to accessibility events, queries this tree, and reads the relevant node properties aloud. In Compose, the Modifier.semantics { } API populates these node properties.
B2 — What is the difference between contentDescription = null and contentDescription = "" on an Image composable?
Easy▼
contentDescription = null marks the image as decorative. TalkBack completely ignores it and does not announce it. This is the correct choice for purely decorative images that add no informational value (background illustrations, decorative borders).

contentDescription = "" (empty string) has ambiguous behaviour — on some Android versions TalkBack may still say "Image" or announce something empty, creating a confusing pause. It should be avoided.

Rule: Use null for decorative; use a descriptive string for meaningful images. Never use an empty string.
B3 — What is the minimum touch target size per WCAG and how do you enforce it in Compose?
Easy▼
The minimum interactive target size is 48dp × 48dp, per WCAG 2.5.5 and Google Material Design guidelines. This ensures that users with motor impairments can reliably tap the target.

In Compose, enforce it with:
1. Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize() — automatically ensures the touch target is at least 48dp without changing the visual size of the element
2. Modifier.size(48.dp) — explicitly sets the composable size
3. Wrapping in IconButton — its default size is 48dp × 48dp

Note: the visual size of the icon can remain 24dp while the touch target is 48dp — the extra space is transparent but tappable.

Intermediate

I1 — Explain mergeDescendants vs clearAndSetSemantics. When would you use each?
Medium▼
mergeDescendants = true: Combines all child semantic nodes into a single TalkBack announcement. The parent node becomes the focus point and TalkBack reads all children's text and descriptions as one unit. Use this for cards, list items, and compound components where children individually would produce too many separate TalkBack stops. The child semantics are still present — they're just merged up into the parent.

clearAndSetSemantics { }: Completely replaces the semantics of the node AND all its descendants with the semantics you define in the block. Children's text and descriptions are invisible to TalkBack. Use this when you need full control over what TalkBack says and the default merged output would still be wrong or incomplete — for example, a product card with a price like "$12.99" that TalkBack would read as "Dollar 12 period 99" — you want to set contentDescription = "12 pounds 99" explicitly.

Key difference: mergeDescendants preserves child semantics but consolidates focus; clearAndSetSemantics discards child semantics entirely and replaces with custom content.
I2 — What is a LiveRegion? When should you use Polite vs Assertive?
Medium▼
A LiveRegion tells accessibility services to automatically announce when the content of that node changes — without the user navigating to it. This is essential for dynamic UI states that appear after user actions (loading completion, error messages, search results count).

LiveRegionMode.Polite: The announcement is queued and delivered after TalkBack finishes whatever it is currently saying. Use for non-critical updates — loading states, result counts, success confirmations. The user's current focus is not interrupted.

LiveRegionMode.Assertive: The announcement interrupts TalkBack immediately, even if it is mid-sentence. Use only for urgent, time-sensitive information — form validation errors, security alerts, session expiry warnings. Overusing Assertive is disruptive and will frustrate users.

Rule of thumb: Polite for informational updates, Assertive for errors and warnings.
I3 — How do you test accessibility in Compose UI tests (automated)?
Medium▼
Compose UI testing exposes the semantic tree via ComposeTestRule. You can query nodes by semantic properties and assert their values:

@Test
fun submitButton_hasCorrectContentDescription() {
    composeTestRule.setContent {
        TransferButton(amount = "50", recipient = "John")
    }
    composeTestRule
        .onNodeWithContentDescription("Transfer 50 pounds to John")
        .assertIsDisplayed()
        .assertHasClickAction()
}

@Test
fun errorMessage_isAnnounced() {
    composeTestRule.setContent { AmountField(error = "Amount required") }
    composeTestRule
        .onNodeWithText("Amount required")
        .assertIsDisplayed()
    // Verify LiveRegion property via semantics:
    composeTestRule
        .onNodeWithText("Amount required")
        .assert(hasScrollAction().not()) // sanity check
}
Key test methods: onNodeWithContentDescription(), onNodeWithText(), assertHasClickAction(), onNode(hasSemantics { ... }). Use printToLog() to dump the semantic tree for debugging.
I4 — [Coding] Add proper semantics to a row of icon buttons: Delete, Edit, and Share. Each has only an icon and no text.
MediumCoding▼
@Composable
fun ActionButtons(
    itemName: String,
    onDelete: () -> Unit,
    onEdit: () -> Unit,
    onShare: () -> Unit
) {
    Row(
        modifier = Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = false) {},
        horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp)
    ) {
        IconButton(
            onClick = onDelete,
            modifier = Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize()
        ) {
            // Context-aware: includes item name so user knows what they're deleting
            Icon(
                imageVector = Icons.Default.Delete,
                contentDescription = "Delete $itemName"
            )
        }
        IconButton(
            onClick = onEdit,
            modifier = Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize()
        ) {
            Icon(
                imageVector = Icons.Default.Edit,
                contentDescription = "Edit $itemName"
            )
        }
        IconButton(
            onClick = onShare,
            modifier = Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize()
        ) {
            Icon(
                imageVector = Icons.Default.Share,
                contentDescription = "Share $itemName"
            )
        }
    }
}
Key points: each button's contentDescription includes the item name for context — TalkBack reads "Delete Invoice #1234" not just "Delete". minimumInteractiveComponentSize() ensures 48dp targets. Each button is a separate TalkBack focus point (not merged) so users can individually navigate to each action.

Senior / Scenario

S1 — [Scenario] A user reports: "TalkBack reads the product price as 'Button 12 99' on the product card. It should say 'Product: Wireless Headphones, Price: 12 pounds 99'." The card is a Card composable with Image, two Texts (name and price), and an IconButton. How do you fix it?
HardScenario▼
Root causes:
1. The price Text "£12.99" is being read character-by-character because TalkBack doesn't know it's a monetary amount
2. The IconButton inside is probably not merged correctly — creating a "Button" announcement
3. mergeDescendants = true on the card merges ALL children including the button, producing "Button 12 99"

Fix — use clearAndSetSemantics on the card, and handle the button separately: 
Card(
    modifier = Modifier
        .clickable { onCardClick() }
        .clearAndSetSemantics {
            // Full control — format price for correct TalkBack reading
            contentDescription = "Product: ${product.name}, " +
                "Price: ${product.priceLabel}"  // priceLabel = "12 pounds 99"
            role = Role.Button
        }
) {
    Image(
        painter = rememberAsyncImagePainter(product.imageUrl),
        contentDescription = null  // card description covers it
    )
    Text(product.name)
    Text(product.priceLabel)
    // Add to cart button — OUTSIDE the clearAndSetSemantics scope or wrapped separately
    IconButton(onClick = onAddToCart) {
        Icon(
            Icons.Default.Add,
            contentDescription = "Add ${product.name} to cart"
        )
    }
}
Alternative: Keep mergeDescendants = true on the outer card but exclude the IconButton by wrapping it in a non-merged container. The best production pattern is clearAndSetSemantics for the card content + a separate IconButton outside that block with its own contentDescription. Also: priceLabel should be a formatted string like "12 pounds 99" not "£12.99" — the screen reader cannot reliably parse currency symbols.
S2 — A banking app fails an EU accessibility audit. The auditor's report says: "Form validation errors are not announced when they appear; users must manually navigate to discover them." How do you fix this architecturally?
Hard▼
The problem: Validation errors appear on screen but TalkBack does not announce them because the error message node does not have a LiveRegion set. TalkBack only reads nodes when the user navigates to them — it doesn't spontaneously read new content unless it's a LiveRegion.

Architectural fix — add at the component library level so all forms are covered automatically: 
@Composable
fun AppTextField(
    value: String,
    onValueChange: (String) -> Unit,
    label: String,
    error: String? = null,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
) {
    Column(modifier = modifier) {
        OutlinedTextField(
            value = value,
            onValueChange = onValueChange,
            label = { Text(label) },
            isError = error != null
        )
        if (error != null) {
            Text(
                text = error,
                color = MaterialTheme.colorScheme.error,
                style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodySmall,
                modifier = Modifier.semantics {
                    // Assertive: interrupts TalkBack to announce error immediately
                    liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Assertive
                    contentDescription = "Error: $error"
                }
            )
        }
    }
}
Additional steps:
1. After form submission fails, move TalkBack focus to the first error field using FocusRequester.requestFocus()
2. Add a summary live region at the top: "3 errors found. Please correct the highlighted fields."
3. Ensure the error parameter is not a static string — it must change when the error appears (empty/null → error text) for LiveRegion to trigger
4. Write Compose UI tests that verify onNodeWithText(errorMessage).assertIsDisplayed() after submission
5. Test manually with TalkBack: submit invalid form, verify error is announced without touching the screen
S3 — How do you handle accessibility for a completely custom composable drawn with Canvas (a custom chart, a signature pad, a progress ring)?
Hard▼
The problem: Canvas drawing produces no AccessibilityNodeInfo entries — TalkBack sees nothing. Custom Canvas composables are completely invisible to accessibility services by default.

Solution: add explicit semantics to the Canvas composable: 
@Composable
fun AccountBalanceChart(
    dataPoints: List<Float>,
    currency: String,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier
) {
    val latestValue = dataPoints.lastOrNull() ?: 0f
    val trend = if (dataPoints.last() > dataPoints.first()) "upward" else "downward"

    Canvas(
        modifier = modifier.semantics {
            // Describe the chart content meaningfully
            contentDescription = "Balance trend chart. " +
                "Current balance: $latestValue $currency. " +
                "Trend over last 30 days: $trend."
            // Mark as an image role so TalkBack announces it correctly
            role = Role.Image
        }
    ) {
        // canvas drawing code
    }
}

// For interactive Canvas (e.g., signature pad):
Canvas(
    modifier = Modifier
        .semantics {
            contentDescription = "Signature pad. Draw your signature here."
            role = Role.Image
            onClick("Clear signature") { clearSignature(); true }
        }
        .pointerInput(Unit) { /* gesture handling */ }
) { /* canvas drawing */ }
Key rules for Canvas accessibility:
1. Always add Modifier.semantics { contentDescription = "..." } — describe what the canvas shows, not how it's drawn
2. For decorative charts/illustrations: contentDescription = null if the data is described elsewhere on screen
3. For interactive canvas elements: add onClick action in semantics
4. For complex data visualisation: consider providing a text alternative (toggle button to switch to data table view) — much more useful than a long description

Key Concept: Key new APIs and behavioral changes in Android 12/13/14/15/16: Predictive Back, Photo Picker, Health Connect, per-app language, Credential Manager, edge-to-edge.
⚡ Quick Revision & Mechanics
8. Quick Revision Sheet

Per-Release Change Table

FOREGROUND SERVICE (API 34+)

<service
  android:foregroundServiceType=
    "dataSync"/>

startForeground(ID, notif,

enableEdgeToEdge()
setContent {
  Scaffold { innerPadding ->

  }
}

POST_NOTIFICATIONS (API 33+)

if (SDK_INT >= TIRAMISU) {
  launcher.launch(

  )
}

PHOTO PICKER

val picker = rememberLauncher(
  PickVisualMedia()
) { uri -> handle(uri) }

picker.launch(PickVisualMediaRequest(
  PickVisualMedia.ImageOnly
))

PREDICTIVE BACK

onBackPressedDispatcher
  .addCallback(viewLifecycleOwner) {
    if (dirty) showDialog()
    else {
      isEnabled = false
      dispatcher.onBackPressed()
    }
  }

android:exported

<!-- Every component with
     an intent-filter MUST
     have exported declared -->
android:exported="true"  // launcher
android:exported="false" // internal
⚠️ Traps & Production Gotchas
6. Pitfalls & Best Practices

Pitfall 1 — Forgetting android:exported

// ❌ BAD — crashes on Android 12+ if component has intent-filter
<activity android:name=".DeepLinkActivity">
    <intent-filter>...</intent-filter>
</activity>
// ✅ GOOD — always explicit
<activity android:name=".DeepLinkActivity" android:exported="true">
    <intent-filter>...</intent-filter>
</activity>

Why it matters: Apps targeting API 31+ that have components with intent-filters but no exported attribute fail at build time or crash on install. Many third-party libraries also add receivers — check merged manifest after adding deps.

Pitfall 2 — Missing foregroundServiceType

// ❌ BAD — throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException on API 34+
<service android:name=".UploadService"/>

class UploadService : Service() {
    override fun onStartCommand(...): Int {
        startForeground(ID, notification)  // crashes on API 34+
        ...
    }
}
// ✅ GOOD — type in manifest + type in startForeground()
<service android:name=".UploadService"
         android:foregroundServiceType="dataSync"/>

if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.UPSIDE_DOWN_CAKE) {
    startForeground(ID, notification, ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_DATA_SYNC)
} else {
    startForeground(ID, notification)
}

Pitfall 3 — Not Handling Edge-to-Edge on Android 15+

// ❌ BAD — content hidden behind navigation bar on API 35+
// No inset handling → bottom content clipped

// ✅ GOOD — Scaffold handles insets in Compose
Scaffold(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize()) { innerPadding ->
    LazyColumn(contentPadding = innerPadding) { ... }
}

// ✅ GOOD — View-based: apply insets explicitly
ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener(recyclerView) { v, insets ->
    val nav = insets.getInsets(WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars())
    v.setPadding(0, 0, 0, nav.bottom)
    insets
}

Pitfall 4 — Not Requesting POST_NOTIFICATIONS

On Android 13+, all notifications are silently dropped without the runtime permission, even if the channel is created. There is no crash, no error — push messages just don't appear. Test on API 33+ emulator.

Pitfall 5 — Using READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE on API 33+

// ❌ BAD — READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE denied on API 33+
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) {
    // you're fine on 32-
} else {
    // must use READ_MEDIA_IMAGES / READ_MEDIA_VIDEO, or Photo Picker
}

Pitfall 6 — Bumping targetSdk Without Testing

Never Do This
Bumping targetSdk to comply with Play Store requirements without running a behavioral-change test pass. Google requires targetSdk 34 from August 2024, but each release has its own breaking behaviors. Always test on a physical device or emulator running that exact API level.

Best Practices

  1. Check merged manifest after adding any dependency — third-party libs add components.
  2. Use ActivityResultContracts for all permission requests — lifecycle-safe.
  3. Always call enableEdgeToEdge() at the top of onCreate(), before setContent().
  4. Test every targetSdk bump on an emulator running that exact API level.
  5. Maintain a migration checklist document per major Android release version.
  6. Add Lint checks to CI: many of these issues are caught by AndroidLint with proper targetSdk set.
🎯 High-Yield Interview Q&As
Q1: B1 — What change in Android 12 most commonly crashes apps that bump to targetSdk 31?
The missing android:exported attribute. Android 12 requires all Activities, Services, and BroadcastReceivers that have intent-filters to explicitly declare android:exported="true" or android:exported="false". If omitted, the app fails at build time (or install time) with a manifest validation error. Many apps were broken because third-party libraries also added receivers without this attribute — check the merged manifest.
B2 — What happens if you don't request POST_NOTIFICATIONS on Android 13+?
Easy▼
All notifications from your app are silently dropped. There is no crash, no exception, no error in logcat — they simply don't appear. This includes push notifications from FCM. The user also won't see any prompt asking for permission; you must explicitly request Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS at runtime, just like location or camera. Apps that don't do this will have silent push failures on Android 13+ devices.
B3 — What is the advantage of using the Photo Picker over requesting READ_MEDIA_IMAGES?
Easy▼
The Photo Picker requires no storage permission at all. It's a system-managed picker where the user selects media in a sandboxed UI — your app only receives the URI(s) for the specifically selected items, not broad access to the device gallery. It's better for privacy, better UX, and is backported to Android 4.4 (API 19) via Google Play Services. READ_MEDIA_IMAGES grants access to the entire images directory which is broader than needed for a single media selection.

Intermediate

I1 — What is a foreground service type and why is it required on Android 14+?
Medium▼
A foreground service type declares what job the service is doing: location, camera, microphone, dataSync, mediaPlayback, phoneCall, connectedDevice, health. Android uses this to enforce appropriate policies — for example, a service claiming location type must hold the location permission.

On Android 14+, failing to declare the type in the manifest AND pass it to startForeground() throws MissingForegroundServiceTypeException. You must also declare the corresponding permission (e.g., FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC) in the manifest. The goal is to prevent apps from abusing foreground services as a background execution workaround.
I2 — How does edge-to-edge enforcement in Android 15 differ from just calling enableEdgeToEdge() on earlier versions?
Medium▼
On Android 14 and below, enableEdgeToEdge() is opt-in — the window still fits system windows by default, so content doesn't go behind bars unless you call WindowCompat.setDecorFitsSystemWindows(window, false) or enableEdgeToEdge().

On Android 15 targeting API 35, edge-to-edge is enforced by default — setDecorFitsSystemWindows(true) no longer works. Content always extends behind system bars regardless of window flags. Apps that don't handle WindowInsets will have UI elements hidden behind the navigation bar or status bar. This is a silent visual bug, not a crash — making it dangerous in production.
I3 — What replaced READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE on Android 13+ and how do you handle backward compatibility?
Medium▼
On Android 13+, READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE was replaced by granular media permissions:
• READ_MEDIA_IMAGES for image access
• READ_MEDIA_VIDEO for video access
• READ_MEDIA_AUDIO for audio access

For backward compatibility:
if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) {
    requestPermissions(READ_MEDIA_IMAGES, READ_MEDIA_VIDEO)
} else {
    requestPermissions(READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE)
}
However, for media selection, prefer the Photo Picker entirely — it requires no permission on any API level and is the recommended approach.
I4 — Coding Fix this service so it works on Android 14+ without crashing:
Medium▼
Problem code: 
// AndroidManifest:
<service android:name=".FileUploadService"/>

// Service:
override fun onStartCommand(...): Int {
    startForeground(NOTIF_ID, notification)
    return START_STICKY
}
Fixed code: 
// AndroidManifest: add type + permission
<uses-permission android:name=
  "android.permission.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_DATA_SYNC"/>
<service
    android:name=".FileUploadService"
    android:foregroundServiceType="dataSync"
    android:exported="false"/>

// Service: pass type on API 34+
override fun onStartCommand(...): Int {
    val notification = buildNotification()
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= Build.VERSION_CODES.UPSIDE_DOWN_CAKE) {
        startForeground(NOTIF_ID, notification,
            ServiceInfo.FOREGROUND_SERVICE_TYPE_DATA_SYNC)
    } else {
        startForeground(NOTIF_ID, notification)
    }
    return START_STICKY
}

Senior / Scenario

S1 — Scenario Your app has a 1-star review surge after a Play Store update: "Notifications stopped working." App targets SDK 33. What happened and how do you debug?
Hard▼
Root Cause: The app bumped targetSdk from 32 to 33 without requesting POST_NOTIFICATIONS. When targeting API 33+, existing users who installed prior to the update do not automatically get the permission — their permission state is DENIED (not granted). The app never shows a permission dialog because no code requests it.

Debug Steps:
1. Confirm on a test device running API 33+: adb shell dumpsys package <app_id> | grep POST_NOTIFICATIONS — will show DENIED
2. Check FCM delivery report in Firebase Console — messages delivered but not displayed
3. Check notification channel creation logs — channels exist but permission is denied

Fix: Add POST_NOTIFICATIONS request in the main Activity or onboarding flow. For existing users, show an in-app banner explaining why notifications were silently disabled and directing them to grant permission. Handle the case where shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() returns false (user previously denied permanently) by linking to app Settings.
S2 — Scenario After bumping targetSdk to 35, QA reports all screen bottoms are clipped on Android 15 devices. The same build works fine on Android 14. What is the cause and fix?
Hard▼
Cause: Android 15 enforces edge-to-edge by default for apps targeting API 35. Content now renders behind the navigation bar. Previously, setDecorFitsSystemWindows(true) (the default) prevented this. On API 35, this flag is ignored — content always goes edge-to-edge regardless.

Fix Strategy:
1. Call enableEdgeToEdge() in every Activity's onCreate() before setContent()
2. In Compose: use Scaffold's innerPadding to pad all scrollable content and bottom bars
3. In View-based layouts: use ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener to apply WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars() padding
4. Watch for custom bottom sheets, FABs, and floating elements — they need explicit bottom inset padding
5. Run screenshot tests across all major screens against an API 35 emulator in CI

Key insight: This is a silent visual bug — it doesn't crash, won't show up in ANR/crash reports, and only appears on Android 15 devices. Screenshot regression tests are the only way to catch it systematically.
S3 — How would you design a permission request flow that handles all the POST_NOTIFICATIONS edge cases on Android 13+?
Hard▼
States to handle:
1. Already granted — do nothing, proceed
2. Not yet asked — request permission directly
3. Denied once — shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() returns true — show rationale dialog explaining why notifications are important, then request again
4. Permanently denied — shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale() returns false AND permission denied — can't re-request; direct user to Settings > App > Notifications
5. API < 33 — permission auto-granted, skip entire flow

fun handleNotificationPermission(activity: ComponentActivity) {
    if (Build.VERSION.SDK_INT < Build.VERSION_CODES.TIRAMISU) return
    val perm = Manifest.permission.POST_NOTIFICATIONS
    when {
        checkSelfPermission(perm) == PERMISSION_GRANTED -> { /* ok */ }
        shouldShowRequestPermissionRationale(perm) ->
            showRationaleDialog(onConfirm = { launcher.launch(perm) })
        else -> launcher.launch(perm)
    }
}
Track whether the user has been asked before in SharedPreferences to distinguish "never asked" from "permanently denied."
41A

Key Gotchas at a Glance

GotchaRule
Profile debug buildsAlways profile release variant — debug is 2-3x slower
LeakCanary in releasedebugImplementation only — never production
StrictMode penaltyDeath in releaseGate on BuildConfig.DEBUG always
Trace.beginSection without finallyAlways end in finally — leaking section corrupts trace
Heap dump triggers GCShows post-GC state; use allocation tracking for live view
